skb_pull's kernel semantics (returns NULL and performs no pull when len > skb->len, and skb->len is 0 for a fresh skb) are external to the given code; consequently the alignment adjustment at line 14 is a silent no-op — a functional/logic defect with no memory-safety effect.
rsi_prepare_beacon's internals are not shown; the analysis treats its nonzero return as a runtime state this code can produce and branch on, since this code is the owner of the skb at that point.

The 'common' pointer is internal driver state from in-driver callers (rsi_send_beacon is static, not an exported API); it is not attacker-influenced, and its dereference inside rsi_prepare_beacon is outside the given code.
limitations: Ignored NULL return of skb_pull at line 14 (and the use of skb_pull where skb_reserve semantics were intended): the dword-alignment logic is dead code because a fresh skb has len 0, so skb_pull returns NULL and data is never advanced. Dismissed as non-security: no bad pointer is dereferenced, no memory is corrupted, and no attacker influence exists over the allocator alignment bits; the only effect is a functionally misaligned TX buffer.

If rsi_prepare_beacon can only fail under allocation failure that an attacker cannot induce, the leak's exploitability is reduced; however, the missing free on the error path is unconditionally present and beacon attempts are periodic, so the exhaustion path is treated as reachable.
No attacker-controlled data is parsed within this function itself (no beacon body bytes are handled here), so no injection, overflow, or uninitialized-read candidates were generated for its inputs.

verdict.summary: rsi_init_usb_interface performs driver probe-path initialization with all allocations guarded and all error paths freeing allocated memory exactly once; sizes are compile-time constants, so no attacker-reachable memory-safety, bounds, injection, or fail-open defect exists in this code.

assumptions: adapter and pfunction are supplied by the kernel USB probe glue; this code treats their validity as a caller-owned precondition, and no dereference here depends on attacker-controlled fields of them.
MAX_DEBUGFS_ENTRIES is a compile-time constant greater than 0; its debugfs-array consumers are outside the given code, so the '- 1' adjustment cannot be edge-tested here.

usb_set_intfdata/usb_get_intfdata consumers (disconnect, URB completion) are outside the given code; based on the given code alone, no consumer of the interface drvdata is reachable after a failed probe.
rsi_usb_init_rx and rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints internal behavior is not visible; only their boolean returns are consumed here.
limitations: Stale drvdata: usb_set_intfdata(pfunction, adapter) is set before the fail_rx path; if rsi_usb_init_rx fails, rsi_dev is freed while the interface drvdata still references adapter->rsi_dev. Dismissed as a vulnerability because a failed probe prevents driver binding, so no disconnect/completion callback of this driver runs against this interface; a defensive usb_set_intfdata(pfunction, NULL) on the failure path is nonetheless absent from this code.
Error mislabel: rsi_usb_init_rx failure is reported as -ENOMEM regardless of the actual cause; cosmetic/misleading return code with no fail-open or security consequence.
kfree(rsi_dev->tx_buffer) at fail_rx does not NULL the pointer; harmless here because the container is immediately freed, but it would matter if the cleanup paths were extended.
tx_buffer allocated with kmalloc (uninitialized); no use of its prior contents occurs within this code, so no uninitialized-read finding can be substantiated here.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor validates only that input_indices_in is 2-D (IsMatrix) and never checks that its column count (input_indices_in.shape().dim_size(1)) equals input_shape.dims(). An attacker can supply, e.g., indices of shape [5,1] with input_shape [2,3] and target shape [6]; every guard in the function passes, and the ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor call then indexes the indices matrix by the input rank, reading past the end of each row (heap OOB read / crash).

evidence.reason: Sink: the functor is invoked with input_shape (rank taken from attacker-supplied input_shape_in) and input_indices_in.matrix<int64>(), but no check anywhere in this code enforces input_indices_in.shape().dim_size(1) == input_shape.dims(). With indices shaped [5,1] and input_shape [2,3] (target [6]), every guard passes and the functor reads input_indices(i, d) for d up to the input rank, past the 1-column rows — OOB read (CWE-129 leading to CWE-125).

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context, TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix(input_indices_in.shape()),
              errors::InvalidArgument(
                  "Input indices should be a matrix but received shape ",
                  input_indices_in.shape().DebugString()));
  OP_REQUIRES(context, TensorShapeUtils::IsVector(input_shape_in.shape()),
              errors::InvalidArgument(
                  "Input shape should be a vector but received shape ",
                  input_shape_in.shape().DebugString()));
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: these are the only checks applied to input_indices_in and input_shape_in. IsMatrix/IsVector validate container rank only; neither constrains the indices matrix's column count relative to the rank of the shape built from input_shape_in at line 20, leaving the arity-consistency precondition of the functor call unvalidated.

assumptions: The implementation of functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor is not shown; the OOB read is inferred from its contract (it reshapes indices from input_shape's rank to output_shape's rank) and the standard TensorFlow implementation, which reads input_indices(i, d) for d < input_shape.dims().

Tensor dtype (DT_INT64) is assumed to be enforced by op registration/framework outside this code; a mismatch would make vec<int64>()/matrix<int64>() CHECK-fail, which is external enforcement, not quotable here.

TensorShape semantics for negative dims and num_elements overflow (e.g. whether AddDim CHECKs, whether num_elements wraps) are external to the given code and were not relied upon for any confirmed finding.
limitations: Signed integer overflow in 'product *= size' (line 44) and 'product * missing == dense_size' (line 56) is present (size may be up to INT64_MAX; the size >= 0 guard accepts it, and the product > 0 guard runs only on the unknown_index branch), but no memory-safety consequence is provable inside this function without assuming TensorShape overflow behavior; the num_elements equality check at line 66 usually rejects the resulting shapes. Recorded, not confirmed.

Resource consumption via a very large output_rank (target_shape_in length) requires the attacker to supply an equivalently large tensor, and allocation failures are handled by OP_REQUIRES_OK; not treated as a distinct amplification.

input_indices values themselves are not range-checked against input_shape dims; flat-position computation in the functor may wrap or go negative, but writes stay inside the [nnz, output_rank] allocation within this op; downstream misuse is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: pj_scan_get_char increments scanner->curptr and then dereferences it without any comparison against scanner->end or a post-increment terminator check. The only guard, `if (!chr)`, validates the byte at the pre-increment position, so when the consumed character is the final byte of the scanned buffer the pointer advances one-past-limit and the read at that point is out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unguarded post-increment dereference. After `++scanner->curptr` there is no check that curptr is still within the scanned buffer (no reference to scanner->end and no NUL re-check exists anywhere in the function); the `if (!chr)` guard at line 5 only validates the byte at the pre-increment position. Trigger: a caller of this exported API supplies a scanner whose curptr holds the last byte of the buffer (exactly-at-limit, non-zero); the guard passes, curptr moves one-past-limit, and line 12 reads out of bounds (CWE-125).

assumptions: pj_scan_syntax_err, pj_scan_skip_whitespace, and PJ_SCAN_IS_PROBABLY_SPACE are not part of the given code; their end-of-buffer/NUL handling could not be verified or quoted.

The pj_scanner NUL-terminated-buffer invariant (that a terminator byte always follows the consumed character) is established by scanner initialization code outside this snippet; since it cannot be quoted here, the post-increment dereference is treated as unbounded for this analysis.
pj_scan_syntax_err is assumed to either throw via the scanner's error handler or return; its behavior is outside the given code.
limitations: Line 3 dereferences scanner->curptr with no NULL check; this crashes only if a caller directly passes a NULL/wild curptr (degenerate pointer-contract misuse with no data-driven path), so it is not reported as a confirmed finding.
Signed-char widening to int can make the returned chr negative for high-bit bytes; within this function the value is only returned, with no security effect.
If pj_scan_syntax_err's handler is non-throwing, the function returns 0 without advancing curptr; any resulting infinite loop depends on unshown caller behavior and was not confirmed.

verdict.summary: selinux_ptrace_traceme passes the correct SIDs to avc_has_perm: task_sid_subj(parent) is the source (the would-be tracer) and task_sid_obj(current) is the target (the tracee), which is exactly the authorization PTRACE_TRACEME requires. No memory, arithmetic, parsing, or injection sink exists in this code, and no attacker-reachable value can violate the function's preconditions.

assumptions: No NULL check on the parent parameter exists in the given code; the analysis assumes the ptrace framework never passes a NULL task_struct to this LSM hook. This guarantee is not quotable in the given code and is recorded here rather than relied upon.

Capability/uid-based ptrace-mode checks (PTRACE_MODE_*) are assumed to be performed by the surrounding ptrace framework before this LSM hook is invoked; they are not present or quotable in the given code.

The semantics of avc_has_perm(state, ssid, tsid, class, perm, audit) are taken as: grant permission from source context ssid to target context tsid, matching the usage in the sibling SELinux ptrace hook.
limitations: Candidate 'swapped source/target SIDs causing wrong-direction ptrace authorization' was tested: a hypothetical fix would swap the arguments to task_sid_subj(current), task_sid_obj(parent), but the code already has the correct tracer-as-source/tracee-as-target order, so the candidate is not real.

Candidate 'NULL parent dereference' was dismissed because triggering requires the in-kernel caller of the hook to pass NULL, an environment/caller failure no attacker input to this code can induce; no attacker-controlled value crosses this function's boundary as a pointer.

Candidate 'missing capability prerequisite check inside the hook' is not a defect of this code taken alone; the SELinux-specific authorization this hook is responsible for is correctly enforced, and generic ptrace credential checks belong to the framework layer outside this snippet.

verdict.summary: This SELinux ptrace_traceme hook is a single, fail-closed authorization check: it evaluates avc_has_perm with the parent (tracer) as source SID and the current task (tracee) as target SID, and returns the decision verbatim. The only attacker-influenced value (the parent's security ID, chosen by arranging process parentage) is precisely the input the permission check authorizes. No memory-access, arithmetic, length, format-string, injection, or lifetime sinks exist; there are no branches or loops that could bypass the check, and no fail-open error path.

assumptions: parent is a valid, non-NULL task_struct pointer supplied by the LSM hook dispatch (the kernel PTRACE_TRACEME path passes current->real_parent); this code contains no NULL check for it, so that invariant is an external assumption, not a guard in this code.

task_sid_obj() returns an initialized u32 SID for any live task (SIDs are established at task creation/exec), and avc_has_perm(ssid, tsid, ...) semantics are 'subject ssid is granted the permission over object tsid'; both facts are needed to confirm the argument order means 'may the parent ptrace the current task'.
avc_has_perm and task_sid_obj are treated as correctly implementing their documented contracts (permission lookup / SID extraction); their internals are outside the given code.
limitations: Candidate CWE-476 (parent dereferenced without a NULL check in this code) was dismissed: triggering requires the in-kernel hook caller to pass NULL, a kernel state that no attacker input can produce (every live task has a real parent); it is not attacker-reachable at this entry point.

Candidate CWE-863 (swapped ssid/tsid authorization direction) was refuted: the quoted order 'task_sid_obj(parent), task_sid_obj(current)' places the tracer as subject and the tracee as object, which is exactly the permission the hook must enforce.

Fail-open, TOCTOU, and uninitialized-SID candidates were refuted: the sole return statement 'return avc_has_perm(&selinux_state, ...)' propagates the decision on the only path, and the SID reads and check occur in one expression with no intervening window.
No loops, arithmetic, index/length, copy, format-string, or free() sinks exist in this code, so boundary-value (0, -1, at-limit, overflow) edge testing has no sink to which it can apply.

verdict.summary: In pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi, the guard 'if (hdr->rtcp_common.length < 3)' compares the raw network-byte-order RTCP length field without pj_ntohs. On little-endian hosts a wire length of 1 (raw 0x0100) bypasses it, so 'rpsi_len = (pj_ntohs(...)-2) * 4' underflows to SIZE_MAX-3; the subsequent 'length < rpsi_len + 12' check wraps to 8 and passes, the bit-length check '(rpsi_len * 8) < (unsigned)(16 + padlen)' also passes due to wraparound, and pj_strset registers an ~8KB read ('(rpsi->rpsi_bit_len + 7)/8') starting at offset 14 of a >= 12-byte attacker-supplied buffer — a heap out-of-bounds read exposed to the caller via rpsi->rpsi.

evidence.snippet: if (hdr->rtcp_common.length < 3) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the taint: the guard tests the un-converted network-order length field, while line 24 proves the field needs pj_ntohs. On little-endian hosts a wire length of 1 reads as 0x0100=256 and passes, defeating the intended '>= 3 words' minimum.

Unsigned wrap: with converted length 1, (1-2)*4 = -4 wraps to SIZE_MAX-3 in pj_size_t; rpsi_len + 12 wraps to 8, so any length >= 12 passes the bounds check and the underflowed value propagates to every later computation.

Sink: the wrapped rpsi_len yields a bogus rpsi_bit_len (~65488 after truncation) and pj_strset records an ~8186-byte slen at offset 14 of a buffer only guaranteed to be >= 12 bytes — heap out-of-bounds read handed to the caller; additionally 'padlen = *p++' at line 29 reads offset 12 before any check guarantees length > 12.

assumptions: Host is little-endian (pj_ntohs byte-swaps); on big-endian hosts wire lengths 1 and 2 are rejected by the line-18 check and the function is safe.
pjmedia_rtcp_common.length is a pj_uint16_t stored in network byte order, as evidenced by the code's own pj_ntohs conversion at line 24.
sizeof(pjmedia_rtcp_fb_common) == 12 (4-byte rtcp_common + two 4-byte SSRCs), consistent with the literal 12 used at line 25.
pjmedia_rtcp_fb_rpsi.rpsi_bit_len is a 16-bit field (pjproject definition); any width still yields a huge/OOB slen.
pj_strset stores (ptr, slen) without copying, so the out-of-bounds range is read when the caller uses rpsi->rpsi.
limitations: In the stock in-tree RTCP receive path, sub-packet lengths are derived from the same length field ((len+1)*4 = 8 bytes), so the line-12 assert would reject the trigger there; the trigger is reachable via direct calls to this exported public parser (e.g., applications parsing RTCP FB packets from SIP/other sources), which per trust-boundary rules is an untrusted entry point.
A wire length of 2 with buffer length exactly 12 causes only a single-byte over-read at offset 12 before the bit-length check rejects; subsumed by the primary finding's root cause.
A wire length of 0 is rejected on both endiannesses.

verdict.summary: QuantizeV2's Compute never validates the attacker-controlled `axis` attribute against the input's rank (only `if (axis_ > -1)` is checked), so `input.dim_size(axis_)` and the pre_dim loop index the shape out of bounds. It also never validates `num_slices` (derived from the input's shape) against the sizes of the attacker-supplied min/max range tensors or the `minmax_shape`-sized output tensors, so the slice loop performs out-of-bounds reads (`min_ranges(i)`/`max_ranges(i)`) and computes out-of-bounds write pointers (`&output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)`) passed to QuantizeSlice — a heap out-of-bounds write. The scalar branch reads `flat<float>()(0)` without checking the range tensors are non-empty.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled `axis_` attribute (graph/node attribute) is only lower-bounded (`axis_ > -1`); no statement compares axis_ with input.dims(). Trigger: axis_ = 5 with input shape [2,2] (or axis_ = 0 with a scalar input) reaches `input.dim_size(axis_)` out of bounds, and lines 39-41 later call `output->dim_size(i)` for i up to axis_-1, past the rank. Out-of-bounds shape access / CHECK-fail DoS; root cause is missing index validation (CWE-129).

The output min/max tensors are sized with `minmax_shape = ctx->input(1).shape()` (line 11), an attacker-chosen shape that is never checked against `num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_)`. With input shape [2,3,4], axis_=1, and min/max range tensors of shape {1}, these outputs have 1 element while the loop at line 49 iterates 3 times, making `&output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)` for i>=1 an out-of-bounds address.

The loop bound `num_slices` comes from the input tensor's shape while the indexed objects come from different attacker-controlled tensors; no statement validates `num_slices` against `min_ranges.size()`, `max_ranges.size()`, or the output min/max tensor sizes. Trigger: input shape [2,3,4], axis_=1 (num_slices=3), input_min_range/input_max_range of shape {1}: `min_ranges(1..2)` reads out of bounds and `&output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(1..2)` is a heap out-of-bounds write pointer passed to QuantizeSlice — attacker-controlled OOB read and heap OOB write (CWE-129 / CWE-787).

evidence.snippet:
const float min_range = input_min_range.template flat<float>()(0);
      const float max_range = input_max_range.template flat<float>()(0);
evidence.reason: Element 0 is read from the attacker-supplied min/max range tensors without any check that they contain at least one element. Trigger: default axis=-1 with input_min_range of shape {0} (0 elements): `flat<float>()(0)` reads past a zero-element (empty/null buffer) tensor, an attacker-reachable out-of-bounds read / null dereference causing a crash (DoS).

assumptions: Input dtypes (float) and the op's registered shape-function constraints are enforced by the TensorFlow runtime outside this code; they are not relied on and, if absent, only widen the attack surface.

Eigen TensorMap bounds checks are `eigen_assert` (debug-only); in release builds `min_ranges(i)` and `flat()(0)` perform unchecked indexing. Regardless, the loop bound and the computed write pointers originate in this code.
`QuantizeTensor`/`QuantizeSlice` (helpers not shown) are assumed to write only through the pointers passed to them; the pointers themselves are computed out of bounds here.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK fail closed by canceling the kernel execution.
limitations: A negative axis other than -1 (e.g. -5) is treated as whole-tensor mode (`axis_ > -1` false, num_slices=1); this is questionable semantics but not memory-unsafe since flat()(0) still requires a non-empty range tensor (covered by the line 21-22 finding).
Truncation of int64 dim_size into `int num_slices` only matters through the already-reported missing size validation; a negative truncated value yields zero loop iterations with no write.
The pre-allocations and `mode_` guard (`OP_REQUIRES(ctx, mode_ != QUANTIZE_MODE_MIN_FIRST, ...)`) were examined and found fail-closed; no defect attributed to them.

verdict.summary: elo_probe acquires a reference to the USB device with usb_get_dev(udev) but the err_free path — reached whenever hid_parse(hdev) or hid_hw_start(hdev, HID_CONNECT_DEFAULT) fails — executes kfree(priv) and returns without any usb_put_dev(). Because the last pointer to the reference (priv->usbdev) is destroyed, the reference is leaked permanently and struct usb_device is never released. hid_parse failure is fully attacker-influenceable: a malicious USB device presenting ELO vendor/product IDs and a malformed report descriptor takes this path, and such a device can autonomously disconnect/re-enumerate, leaking one usb_device per cycle and accumulating kernel memory without bound (denial of service).

evidence.reason: The error path frees priv (destroying the only pointer to the acquired USB device reference) without releasing it; there is no usb_put_dev on any path in this code. Trigger: a malicious USB device whose report descriptor makes hid_parse() return nonzero (line 23 'goto err_free'), or a failing hid_hw_start (line 29), leaks one struct usb_device reference per probe attempt; repeated re-enumeration gives unbounded memory consumption.

evidence.snippet:
udev = interface_to_usbdev(to_usb_interface(hdev->dev.parent));
	priv->usbdev = usb_get_dev(udev);
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked value: usb_get_dev() increments the USB device refcount and stores it in priv->usbdev; the reference is acquired unconditionally before any error branch, yet no matching usb_put_dev() exists anywhere in this function, so every failed probe leaks it.

assumptions: hid_is_usb(hdev) returning true is taken to imply hdev->dev.parent is a valid usb_interface and its parent a usb_device; this is a HID/usbhid bus-driver invariant enforced outside this code and cannot be quoted here, so the unchecked to_usb_interface()/interface_to_usbdev() casts are treated as non-exploitable (only bus BUS_USB, set solely by usbhid, reaches line 15).
The companion elo_remove() (not shown) is assumed to release priv->usbdev on the success path; the confirmed finding concerns only the error paths visible in this code.
hid_parse()/hid_hw_start() failures are assumed attacker-influenceable because they operate on USB device-supplied descriptors (data crossing the USB trust boundary).
limitations: hid_set_drvdata(hdev, priv) runs before the error branches, so a failed probe leaves the hid_device's driver-data pointer dangling after kfree(priv); no consumer of hid_get_drvdata on a failed probe exists within this code, so a use-after-free trigger could not be constructed from this code alone — robustness concern, not scored.
The return value of queue_delayed_work() is unchecked; failure only skips the broken-firmware workaround with no security effect.
The leak accrues one struct usb_device per failed probe cycle, so exhausting memory requires sustained attacker-driven re-enumeration (feasible for a self-reconnecting malicious device, but slow).

verdict.summary: mrb_vm_exec trusts jump offsets decoded from the irep instruction stream: OP_JMP/OP_JMPIF/OP_JMPNOT/OP_JMPNIL do 'pc += (int16_t)a/b' and OP_JMPUW does 'pc = irep->iseq + a' with no comparison of the resulting index against irep->ilen on any ordinary path (the only range statement is an mrb_assert on the exception-restore branch, compiled out in release). With irep loaded from untrusted serialized bytecode, an attacker-chosen signed 16-bit offset (or the uint32-wrapped combination in OP_JMPUW, where a negative sum becomes ~0xFFFF8000) moves pc outside the iseq buffer; the dispatch loop then reads and executes out-of-bounds memory as opcodes whose decoded operands index the register stack.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: `a` is an attacker-influenced jump target computed from the bytecode operand and used to index irep->iseq with no `a < irep->ilen` check on this path; with an untrusted .mrb containing OP_JMPUW with operand 0x7FFF in a 4-byte irep, pc is set ~32KB past the instruction buffer and executed.

Origin and missing guard: the offset is wrapped into a uint32_t (a negative sum, e.g. -0x8000, sign-flips to 0xFFFF8000), and the only range check in the whole case is `mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen);` — an assert, on the restore branch only, absent on the ordinary path and a no-op in release builds.

Same root cause on the sibling unconditional jump: the signed 16-bit operand `a` decoded from attacker-supplied bytecode is added to pc and executed with no bounds comparison against irep->ilen anywhere in the case (OP_JMPIF/OP_JMPNOT/OP_JMPNIL share this pattern via `pc += (int16_t)b;`).

assumptions: irep contents can originate from untrusted serialized bytecode (e.g. mrb_load_irep on an attacker-supplied .mrb); the loader's validation, if any, is outside the given code and cannot be quoted, so per the guard-anchoring rule it does not count as a guard here.
mrb_assert is disabled in release builds (MRB_NDEBUG); the commented-out entry precondition `/* mrb_assert(MRB_PROC_CFUNC_P(proc)) */` confirms asserts are not enforcement.
Line numbers are counted from the first line of the provided snippet as line 1.
limitations: Operand indices into pool/syms/regs (e.g. pool[b] in OP_LOADL, syms[b] in OP_LOADSYM, regs[a..a+b] in OP_ARRAY) share the same missing-bounds-validation root cause as the confirmed finding; they are not separately evidenced to avoid duplicate findings for one root cause.

Reviewed and not triggered: OP_MATH integer paths are guarded by mrb_int_*_overflow checks with an L_INT_OVERFLOW raise; OP_APOST index arithmetic is in-range at post=0/post=1 boundaries; OP_GETUPVAR/OP_SETUPVAR explicitly bounds-check `b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e)`; OP_ARGARY/OP_BLKPUSH check env length on the outer-variable path.

If the deployment only ever executes ireps produced by the local mruby compiler and never loads serialized bytecode, the trigger requires that compiler to emit an out-of-range jump, which it does not — the vulnerability is specific to executing untrusted compiled bytecode.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect in the given code. All attacker-influenced indices derived from the einsum equation string are guarded by quotable, edge-tested statements: count vectors are resized to num_labels before indexing, the ellipsis sentinel is excluded by 'if (label != kEllipsisLabel)', and the two-operand access '(*input_label_counts)[1]' is short-circuit protected by 'num_inputs == 1 ||' when only one input exists. The single unguarded boundary (num_inputs == 0 reaching '(*input_label_counts)[0]') is not reachable: the external ParseEinsumEquation splits the equation on separators and always yields at least one input piece, so no concrete attacker equation triggers it — recorded as an assumption, not a quotable guard.

assumptions: ParseEinsumEquation and MapToLabels are external to the given code. Their semantics are assumed, not quoted: the equation is split into at least one input string and one output string (splitting any string yields >=1 piece, so input_str.size() == 0, the only value that would make '(*input_label_counts)[0]' at the 'unique' computation an OOB read, is unreachable); MapToLabels assigns consecutive labels 0..n-1 and maps '.' to kEllipsisLabel; kEllipsisLabel is defined externally as -1, making 'if (label == kEllipsisLabel) continue;' dead but harmless (if it were non-negative and < num_labels, one label_types entry would be left uninitialized, CWE-457).

The 'einsum supports at most 2 inputs' limit is enforced outside the given code; within this code, num_inputs > 2 causes no out-of-bounds access (indices 0 and 1 of input_label_counts are resized to num_inputs >= 3).
limitations: int num_inputs = input_str.size(); narrows size_t to int; wrapping to a non-positive value would require an equation producing ~2^31 inputs (a multi-gigabyte string), which is a resource-exhaustion precondition rather than a demonstrated, attacker-practical trigger, and the truncated value is used consistently for all resizes.
The code mixes checked at() (output_label_counts->at(label)) and unchecked operator[] (input counts); both are currently in bounds, so the asymmetry is hardening-relevant only.

verdict.summary: rsi_init_usb_interface kzallocs rsi_dev (line 7) and assigns adapter->rsi_dev, but neither error path frees it: the fail_rx block only does kfree(rsi_dev->tx_buffer) and the fail_eps block does nothing before `return status`. A malicious or malformed USB device that makes rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints fail (line 15) drives the goto fail_eps path (status = -EINVAL), leaking the rsi_91x_usbdev allocation on every failed probe, and the leak is repeatable via device re-plugging. No kfree(rsi_dev) exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Both error labels unwind only tx_buffer (and only on the fail_rx path); neither frees the rsi_dev object allocated at line 7 with kzalloc. The missing free site: a `kfree(rsi_dev);` (and adapter->rsi_dev = NULL) belongs here on every error path. Trigger: a USB device whose descriptors cause rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints to return nonzero (goto fail_eps, line 17), so each failed probe leaks the allocation.

Origin of the leaked allocation: rsi_dev is kzalloc'd and stored into adapter->rsi_dev, but the success path's only pairing frees in the error block are for tx_buffer; no kfree(rsi_dev) exists in the function, so every error exit (fail_eps via lines 17/27, fail_rx via line 32) leaks it.

assumptions: rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints returns nonzero when the device exposes no valid bulk-in/bulk-out endpoints (function body not given, cannot be quoted); this is what makes the -EINVAL path attacker-triggerable via a malformed USB device.
rsi_usb_init_rx is assumed to free its own internal allocations on failure (body not given).

pfunction and adapter are assumed to be valid kernel-core-constructed objects passed by the driver's own probe path (static function, single internal caller); a NULL pfunction is therefore not attacker-reachable within this code.
The stale usb_set_intfdata(pfunction, adapter) on the RX-init failure path could only become a defect via the caller's disconnect logic, which is not part of the given code.

assumptions: call_callback() fills rettv with a well-formed typval on success and leaves it untouched on FAIL; the FAIL path never reads rettv, so this contract only affects reachability of line 32, not the defect.

dict_alloc_lock() returns a dict whose dv_refcount starts at 0, so `++d->dv_refcount;` and `dict_unref(d);` form a balanced create/destroy pair; the initial refcount is not quotable from the given code.
clear_tv() tolerates NULL list pointers; irrelevant to the finding since the dereference at line 35 executes first.
limitations: Line 1 declares no return type while the function returns list_T* via `return NULL;` and `return qftf_list;`; taken literally this is an implicit-int return causing pointer truncation (undefined behavior) on 64-bit builds, but it appears to be an artifact of the excerpt (the original signature is `static list_T *`), and no CWE in the allowed palette names it precisely.
start_idx and end_idx are only stored as dict numbers; they are never used as bounds, so no integer/overflow sink exists for them.
The NULL-deref worst case is a crash (denial of service) of the editor process; no memory-corruption primitive was identified from this defect.

verdict.summary: ex_copy() consumes the ex-command address parameters line1, line2, and n (unsigned linenr_T) without any validation at this command handler's intake. count = line2 - line1 + 1 underflows when line2 < line1 (e.g., 2-5+1 wraps to 2^64-2), and the wrapped count flows into b_op_end.lnum = n + count and appended_lines_mark(n, count). Independently, line1/line2/n are used directly as buffer-line indices in ml_get(line1) and ml_append(curwin->w_cursor.lnum = n) with no range check; if n is out of range the ignored ml_append return lets the loop's ++line1 walk ml_get past the end of the buffer. No guard on any path rejects out-of-range or reversed addresses in the given code.

evidence.reason: count = line2 - line1 + 1 is computed on unsigned linenr_T with no check that line1 <= line2; for a reversed command range (line1=5, line2=2) it wraps to 2^64-2 (CWE-190), and n + count at line 10 wraps again, storing garbage marks and later passing the huge count to appended_lines_mark(n, count).

line1 (from the command range) and curwin->w_cursor.lnum (= n, set at line 28) are used as buffer-line indices with no range validation anywhere in this function; the ml_append return is ignored, so with an out-of-range destination n the buffer never grows while ++line1 keeps advancing and ml_get is called past the end of the buffer (CWE-129).

assumptions: In the real Vim source tree, get_address()/do_one_cmd clamp addresses to the buffer line count and reject or swap backwards ranges (E493) before ex_copy is invoked; that enforcement is outside the given code and could not be quoted, so per the analysis rules it is treated as an assumption, not a guard. This is the main reason confidence is not higher.

Whether ml_get()/ml_append()/u_save() internally reject out-of-range line numbers (e.g., E315 abort in ml_get) is not quotable from the given code; their behavior is unknown here, so the in-code analysis treats the indices as unguarded.
cmdmod.cmod_flags is treated as trusted internal configuration; it only gates the mark-update branch and never reaches a sink as tainted length or index.
linenr_T is assumed to be an unsigned integral type (unsigned long in Vim), which is what makes line2 - line1 + 1 wrap rather than go negative.
limitations: ml_append's return value is ignored (line 36): under allocation failure a source line is silently skipped and subsequent ml_get calls may run past the buffer end. Triggering requires OOM/environment failure an attacker cannot induce, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.
b_op_start/b_op_end are updated (lines 9-11) before the u_save(n, n+1) == FAIL early return (lines 25-26), leaving stale marks on abort; consistency/cosmetic issue only.
msgmore((long)count) sign-flips for wrapped counts, producing a bogus 'more lines' message; cosmetic only.

The concrete heap-corruption impact depends on ml_get/ml_append internals that are not part of the given code; the provable in-code impact is out-of-range index use and wrapped counts reaching mark/undo bookkeeping (denial of service at minimum).

verdict.summary: yank_copy_line() allocates exactly startspaces+endspaces+textlen+1 bytes and every memset/memmove/NUL write is exactly sized against that allocation; the trailing-whitespace backscan is provably in-bounds because the loop guard admits only ASCII whitespace bytes (for which mb_head_off returns 0, so s and pnew decrement in lockstep) and 's > 0' is re-tested each iteration, and endspaces is pre-zeroed on the only path that adds it to s. The function does not validate y_idx or the sign/range of the bd fields, but it is an internal helper whose runtime callers (block_prep/op_yank) are the only reachable producers of those values, and no attacker-reachable path delivers out-of-range values; these caller invariants are recorded as assumptions.

assumptions: bd->startspaces, bd->endspaces, bd->textlen are assumed >= 0 and bd->textstart is assumed to reference at least bd->textlen readable bytes; these are produced by block_prep() in the caller and are NOT checked in the given code (a negative textlen would sign-flip in '(size_t)bd->textlen' at the mch_memmove sink).
0 <= y_idx < y_current->y_size and y_current->y_array != NULL are assumed, maintained by op_yank(); the store 'y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew;' has no bounds check in the given code.

VIM_ISWHITE(x) is assumed to be the ASCII predicate ((x) == ' ' || (x) == '\t'), and mb_head_off is assumed to return 0 for bytes < 0x80; this is what makes the pnew/s decrement lockstep safe in the while loop.
alloc() is assumed to take a size_t and return NULL on failure, which the code handles by 'return FAIL'.
limitations: Unchecked array write 'y_current->y_array[y_idx] = pnew;' (CWE-129/787 candidate): no check exists in this snippet, but no runtime caller path passes an out-of-range index; dismissed on runtime-reachability, not on a quotable guard.

Negative bd->textlen/startspaces/endspaces would cause huge (size_t)-cast memmove/memset lengths; no such values are producible at runtime by the enclosing code's callers; dismissed on runtime-reachability, not on a quotable guard in this snippet.

Integer overflow of 'startspaces + endspaces + textlen + 1' (CWE-190) requires a single line near 2 GB; a wrapped negative sum converts to a huge size_t and fails allocation safely, so this is theoretical only.
Multibyte trailing whitespace (e.g., U+3000) is not excluded by the loop because VIM_ISWHITE matches only ASCII bytes; this is a functional/cosmetic gap with no memory-safety effect.
Allocation-failure paths return FAIL without any NULL dereference or leak; not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans validates its span-array inputs only with `if (num_spans == 0)`; the do-while loop then reads spans[1].x unconditionally, so a call with num_spans == 1 reads past the end of the array, and the resulting (or any caller-supplied) span length flows unbounded into `*m++` / `memset(m, coverage, --len)` writes through the running pointer m into the externally-sized mask buffer r->_buf. m is only reset by the long-opaque and fully-transparent flush branches, and no statement in this function bounds m against the end of _buf, so any span data whose accumulated partial-coverage length (or a single long partial span) exceeds the buffer capacity causes a heap out-of-bounds write; the num_spans==1 off-by-one additionally makes len itself garbage-derived.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787). Every partially-covered span (coverage not 0xff/0x0) writes len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x coverage bytes at the running pointer m into r->_buf. m is only reset by `m = r->_buf;` in the two flush branches (lines 51 and 80, taken only for long fully-opaque or fully-transparent runs); no statement in this function checks m or m+len against the end of _buf, so caller-supplied spans whose accumulated partial-coverage length (or one span longer than the buffer) exceeds the allocation write past it. `*m++` even writes and advances 1 byte when len <= 0, and the num_spans==1 out-of-bounds read of spans[1].x makes len itself garbage-derived.

evidence.snippet:
do {
	int len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x;
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The do-while body reads spans[1].x before the loop condition `} while (--num_spans > 1);` (line 90) is ever evaluated, so the structure requires num_spans >= 2. With num_spans == 1 (the exactly-at-limit value the entry guard does not reject) spans[1] is read past the end of a one-element array; after `spans++` the tail `if (spans[0].x != x0)` (line 92) reads element 1 again, and the garbage len feeds the memset at line 85.

evidence.snippet:
if (num_spans == 0)
	return CAIRO_STATUS_SUCCESS;
evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the only entry validation of num_spans rejects 0 but not the boundary value 1 that the do-while loop structure (unconditional first read of spans[1] before `--num_spans > 1` is tested) requires to be rejected (num_spans < 2). This off-by-one enables the out-of-bounds read of spans[1]; no `num_spans < 2` or equivalent check exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: r->_buf is allocated and sized by the renderer setup outside this function; its capacity is not stated or checkable in the given code, so no bound tying span coverage accumulation to that capacity can be assumed.

The span rasterizer is expected (by cairo's design) to emit monotonic, non-overlapping spans clipped to the destination width and at least two spans per row; none of these invariants is enforced or quotable in the given code, so spans/num_spans are treated as untrusted at this entry point.

pixman_image_composite32 is assumed to clip its own source/destination coordinates and widths; the unvalidated values passed to it (spans[0].x - x0, spans[1].x - spans[0].x, h) are pixman's intake, not a direct memory sink in this code.
abstract_renderer is assumed non-NULL and to point to a correctly initialized cairo_image_span_renderer_t; r->u.composite.run_length is assumed configured to a sane positive value by the caller.
limitations: A NULL r->_buf (m = r->_buf then *m++) is only possible if the external allocation failed; not attacker-induced, so not counted as a vulnerability.
r->u.composite.run_length is configured elsewhere; a zero or negative run_length only changes how often m is reset, not the missing-bound root cause.
Unvalidated widths/coordinates handed to pixman_image_composite32 could trigger defects inside pixman, but that behavior is outside the given code and was not counted.
The `#if PIXMAN_HAS_OP_LERP` and `#else` halves are equivalent for this analysis; the vulnerability paths run through both variants identically.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO shared-memory update, when the client-supplied STOR filename length is exactly sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, the else-branch index 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' wraps to SIZE_MAX, so memcpy reads one byte before the start of 'name' (out-of-bounds read / undefined pointer arithmetic) and copies a non-NUL-terminated filename into shared memory. The guard 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)' does not reject the exactly-at-limit value; the client controls the filename length, and no in-code statement bounds it.

evidence.reason: Unsigned wraparound in the memcpy source index: for sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (exactly at the field limit), 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' evaluates to SIZE_MAX, so &name[SIZE_MAX] is name-1 and memcpy reads name[-1], one byte out of bounds before the attacker-controlled filename; the branch also never NUL-terminates the shared filename. The only guard, 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)', routes this boundary value into the underflow instead of rejecting it.

evidence.snippet:
if (shm_data_cur != NULL) {
        const size_t sl = strlen(name);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: sl is the length of 'name', the client-supplied filename crossing the network trust boundary; the attacker chooses sl by choosing the filename, and no statement in this code bounds strlen(name) before it reaches the boundary-sensitive index arithmetic at lines 154-156.

assumptions: checknamesanity(), get_atomic_file(), ul_init(), quota_update(), tryautorename(), and the shm_data_cur->filename field width are external; their enforcement cannot be quoted from this code. In particular, whether checknamesanity bounds strlen(name) is unknown, so no length bound is treated as existing.

The finding requires a build with FTPWHO enabled (the faulty code is inside '#ifdef FTPWHO'); sizeof shm_data_cur->filename is a fixed width unknown from this code, and the trigger needs a filename of exactly that length.
'name' is assumed to point into the FTP command buffer; name[-1] may therefore often lie within that buffer, reducing practical impact to one leaked byte or a fault at a buffer start.
limitations: ulhandler.total_uploaded is read (uploaded += ..., ul_quota_update(...), displayrate(...)) even when ul_init(...) != 0 leaves it uninitialized (CWE-457/CWE-908); the trigger requires ul_init failure, which cannot be shown attacker-inducible from this code.
Under SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE, FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) is executed after '(void) close(f);' — normally returns EBADF; at worst a wrong 'disk space' reply line (cosmetic).

QUOTAS: max_filesize is initialized to (off_t)-1 and its only assignment is guarded by 'max_filesize >= (off_t) 0' (always false), so the per-file quota ceiling is likely never computed (potential CWE-400 disk exhaustion); this depends on the QUOTAS build flag and on ul_init's interpretation of -1, both external.
The string returned by get_atomic_file(name) is never freed on success paths (resource leak bounded by the per-session process lifetime of a forked FTP server; no exhaustion path).
'no_truncate = 1' is set for autorename but never restored in this function; cross-command state effects are not analyzed here.

A TOCTOU between checknamesanity(name) and open()/rename(name, ...) requires a local attacker able to modify path components; O_NOFOLLOW only protects the final component. Not confirmed from this code.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses the caller-supplied 'facet' parameter and the parsed 'neighbors_start[].neighbor[]' / 'which_vertex_not[]' values as array indices with no range validation. The only guards are a != -1 sentinel check and an stl->error early return; values such as facet = -1, neighbor = -2, or vnot = -2 (making (vnot+1)%3 == -1) flow directly into stl->facet_start[...] / stl->neighbors_start[...] reads and writes, causing attacker-influenced out-of-bounds reads and writes (arbitrary-index write of an attacker-influenced value at line 61/65/73).

evidence.reason: The caller-supplied int 'facet' is used directly to index stl->facet_start (and later stl->neighbors_start at lines 45-58) with no bounds check anywhere in the function; the only guard is 'if (stl->error) return;'. facet = -1 or any value >= the facet count yields an out-of-bounds read, and it is passed unchecked to stl_remove_facet (CWE-129).

neighbor1/neighbor2 (attacker-influenced values read from stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[]) are used as array indices guarded only by '!= -1', so any value like -2 or an out-of-range index passes and produces an OOB write of the attacker-influenced value neighbor2. Additionally (vnot1 + 1) % 3 is negative for vnot1 = -2 (and vnot1 + 1 overflows for vnot1 = INT_MAX), giving a negative OOB write index. Symmetric defects exist at lines 64-66 and 71-73 (CWE-129 -> CWE-787).

evidence.snippet: stl_remove_degenerate(stl_file *stl, int facet) {
evidence.reason: Trust-boundary origin of the unchecked index: 'facet' is a parameter of this exported function (untrusted caller) and is never range-checked before its uses at lines 14-16, 26, 31, 36, 45-58, 69.

assumptions: The stl_file contents (facet_start, neighbors_start, which_vertex_not, error) are parsed/derived from an external STL file and cross a trust boundary; in the upstream admesh codebase neighbors are computed internally, but no enforcing statement bounding them is present or quotable in the given code.
Arrays behind stl->facet_start and stl->neighbors_start are non-NULL and sized to the model's facet count; the size/count itself is not visible in this snippet.
limitations: A NULL stl->facet_start/neighbors_start on an empty or failed-to-load model would cause a NULL dereference, but constructing that state from the shown code alone requires allocation/empty-file conditions not demonstrated here; it is not counted as a finding.
The degenerate memcmp cascade itself (vertex comparisons) operates only on bytes and is not a memory-safety issue beyond the unchecked 'facet' index.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke walks the caller-supplied QVectorPath stream with only `while (points < lastPoint)` as a bound. The CurveToElement case consumes 6 qreals (points[0..5]) and 3 type entries where the loop guard guarantees just 2 qreals remain, so a path whose types array contains a CurveToElement with fewer than 3 elements (e.g. elementCount()==1 or 2) reads up to 32 bytes past the points array and walks past the types array (CWE-125). Any other element value, including the legal CurveToDataElement, hits `default: break;` which advances neither `points` nor `types`, so the loop condition never changes and the loop never terminates (CWE-400). Both defects are duplicated in the cosmetic-pen branch. No statement in this code validates element types or the remaining element count on any path to these sinks.

evidence.snippet:
case QPainterPath::CurveToElement:
                    d->activeStroker->cubicTo(points[0], points[1],
                                              points[2], points[3],
                                              points[4], points[5]);
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The only bound is `while (points < lastPoint)` (l.111), i.e. at least 2 qreals remain, but this case reads points[2]..points[5] and then does `points += 6; types += 3;`. Trigger: stroke(path with points={x,y}, elementCount()==1, elements={CurveToElement}, solid non-cosmetic pen) — l.111 is true, l.123 matches, l.124-126 read 32 bytes from a 16-byte buffer; with elementCount()==2 after a MoveTo, points[4]/points[5] lie 16 bytes past the end; `types += 3` also overruns the 1-entry types array. No `lastPoint - points >= 6` check exists on any path.

                    break;
evidence.reason: Non-terminating loop (CWE-400). The default case advances neither `points` nor `types`, so the loop's only exit condition `while (points < lastPoint)` (l.111) is permanently true. Trigger: stroke(path with points={x,y}, elementCount()==1, elements={CurveToDataElement} or any value other than MoveTo/LineTo/CurveTo) — the switch breaks without state change and the loop spins forever, hanging the paint engine thread. No element-type validation statement exists on any path to l.112.

evidence.snippet:
while (points < lastPoint) {
                switch (*types) {
evidence.reason: The sole loop bound and dispatch. `lastPoint` is computed at l.88 as `points + (pointCount<<1)` from the caller-controlled elementCount(), and `types` (l.84) carries no length; this guard therefore guarantees only 2 remaining qreals and one readable type entry per iteration, which is the invariant both the CurveToElement sink (6 qreals / 3 entries) and the default case (0 progress) violate. The minimal fixes — a `lastPoint - points >= 6` check before cubicTo and a progress/validity requirement in the default case — are absent from every path.

Duplicate CWE-125 sink on the cosmetic-pen branch (pen.isCosmetic() and state()->matrix.type() < QTransform::TxProject). Same guard absence: `while (points < lastPoint)` (l.167) guarantees 2 qreals, but ((const QPointF *)points)[0..2] reads 6 qreals (48 bytes) from a possibly 16-byte buffer; the same trigger values reach this branch via a cosmetic pen.

assumptions: d->activeStroker is assumed initialized by the QPaintEngineExPrivate constructor on the first call; that constructor is outside the given code and not quotable, so no finding is based on it.

path.elements(), path.points() and path.elementCount() are treated as caller-controlled and mutually consistent only by convention: QVectorPath's raw-pointer constructor permits a types array, a points array and a count that disagree, and nothing in this code enforces their consistency.
Behavior of the stroker hooks (qpaintengineex_moveTo/lineTo/cubicTo) and of StrokeHandler is external to this code; only the bounds visible at this function's own loop were relied upon.

Recorded as performance degradation only.

First-use of d->activeStroker at l.74 when `!qpen_fast_equals(pen, d->strokerPen)` is false on the very first call depends on initialization performed outside the given code; no in-code trigger or guard is quotable either way.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse validates only 3 bytes of the remaining capability buffer ("if (pnt + 3 > end)") but then copies sizeof(struct capability) bytes via memcpy, reading past the end of the received BGP message (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125). Additionally, when a peer is configured with override-capability, the MP-capability path executes "continue;" without advancing pnt, producing an infinite loop and denial of service (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: The only pre-copy bound check guarantees 3 readable bytes; the memcpy then copies sizeof(struct capability) (> 3) bytes from pnt + 1. With exactly 3 bytes remaining (pnt + 3 == end, the boundary value that passes the check), the copy reads past the end of the attacker-supplied BGP capability message. The later check "if (pnt + (cap.length + 3) > end)" occurs after the use and validates the declared cap.length, not the copy size, so no guard on any path enforces the memcpy's precondition.

On the MP-capability path with override-capability configured, "continue;" returns to "while (pnt < end)" without executing the loop-bottom "pnt += cap.length + 3;" — the only pnt-advancing statement in the function. An attacker peer sending an MP capability triggers an infinite loop (denial of service); no advancement exists on this path.

assumptions: The caller is assumed to validate that length matches the actual BGP message buffer size and that pnt+length does not wrap; this is not enforceable or quotable within the given code, so no defect is attributed to end = pnt + length.
sizeof(struct capability) is assumed to be strictly greater than 3 (the struct holds at least code, length, afi, reserved, and safi fields); this depends on a header not shown.
peer->flags/PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is operator configuration state, not attacker-controlled; the infinite loop requires the operator to have enabled override-capability for the attacking peer.
limitations: The out-of-bounds read is bounded by sizeof(struct capability) - 3 bytes past the message end; its impact is a potential crash (DoS) or minor information exposure rather than memory corruption, since afi/safi derived from the over-read are whitelisted before array indexing.
The afi/safi array indexing at peer->afc_recv[afi][safi] is guarded by a quoted on-path whitelist check and was dismissed as not vulnerable.
Length-driven pointer overflow in "end = pnt + length" was dismissed only because no in-code constraint is quotable; it is recorded as an assumption, not verified safe.

verdict.summary: Integer wraparound in this EXR decoder's own validation arithmetic lets file-controlled values bypass the checks. (1) The chunk-offset bounds checks `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int) * 2 > size` and `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int) * 5 > size` are performed in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, so offset-table entries within 8 (resp. 20) of 2^64 wrap the sum to a tiny value, pass the check, and make `head + offsets[...]` point up to 8/20 bytes BEFORE the buffer, where memcpy reads out of bounds. (2) In the scanline path, `line_no + num_scanline_blocks` overflows signed int for line_no = INT_MAX, wrapping num_lines to a small positive value that bypasses the `num_lines <= 0` guard; the unvalidated line_no (up to INT_MAX) and num_lines are then passed to tinyexr::DecodePixelData for an image with only data_height rows — an out-of-range row index reaching a memory-writing decoder with no upper-bound check anywhere in this code.

evidence.reason: Signed integer overflow at the boundary value line_no = 0x7FFFFFFF (a plain 4-byte file field): `line_no + num_scanline_blocks` wraps negative, `num_lines = end_line_no - line_no` wraps back to a small positive value (e.g. 16), so the `num_lines <= 0` guard is bypassed exactly at the int boundary. No subsequent check compares line_no against data_window[3] or data_height.

evidence.snippet:
if (!tinyexr::DecodePixelData(
                      exr_image->images, exr_header->requested_pixel_types,
                      data_ptr, static_cast<size_t>(data_len),
                      exr_header->compression_type, exr_header->line_order,
                      data_width, data_height, data_width, y, line_no,
                      num_lines, static_cast<size_t>(pixel_data_size),
evidence.reason: Sink: with data_window[1]=0, data_window[3]=8388607 (data_height=8388608) and a chunk line_no of 0x7FFFFFFF, the overflow above delivers line_no=2147483647 and num_lines=16 to the pixel-writing decoder for an 8388608-row image; the only guards on this path (`num_lines <= 0`, the int64 lno range check, `line_no < 0`) reject no part of this input, so an attacker-chosen out-of-range row index crosses into memory-writing code unvalidated.

The bounds check is done in wrappable unsigned 64-bit arithmetic: for an offset-table entry of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC, `offsets[y_idx] + 8` wraps to 4, the check `4 > size` passes, and `head + offsets[y_idx]` becomes `head - 4`; the subsequent `memcpy(&line_no, data_ptr, sizeof(int))` and `memcpy(&data_len, data_ptr + 4, sizeof(int))` read out of bounds before the buffer.

Same wrap defect in the tiled path: an offset entry of 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0 makes `offsets[tile_idx] + 20` wrap to 4, the guard passes, `data_ptr = head - 16`, and `memcpy(tile_coordinates, data_ptr, sizeof(int) * 4)` reads 16 bytes out of bounds before the buffer.

assumptions: `offsets`, `head`/`size`, and all `exr_header` fields originate from an untrusted EXR file and reach this decoder without upstream validation that can be quoted here; this function is treated as the last line of defense.
`tinyexr_uint64` is a 64-bit unsigned type and the platform is LP64, so `offsets[i] + sizeof(int)*N` and `head + offsets[i]` wrap modulo 2^64.

Internals of tinyexr::DecodePixelData, DecodeTiledPixelData, AllocateImage and ComputeChannelLayout are not given; their bounds handling cannot be verified, so the line_no candidate is judged on this code's missing validation at the intake point.
limitations: `exr_header->data_window[3] + 1` can overflow signed int (data_window[3]=INT_MAX, data_window[1]=INT_MAX-8388607 passes the threshold check), but the modular arithmetic keeps line_no + num_lines == data_height, so under two's-complement wrap it is benign UB rather than an exploitable OOB.
`exr_image->num_tiles = static_cast<int>(num_tiles)` truncates only when num_tiles > INT_MAX (offset table > ~16 GiB) and is shadowed by the earlier attacker-scaled `calloc` at line 82.

The `calloc` result for `exr_image->tiles` is not NULL-checked, but reaching a NULL deref requires allocation failure from an attacker-sized tile count (resource-exhaustion path, not confirmed as memory corruption here).
`tile_size_x/y == 0` passes the `< 0` checks (lines 62, 71); whether that causes harm depends on unseen AllocateImage/DecodeTiledPixelData behavior.

On 32-bit builds the `total_data_len` overflow check is hard-coded false (`sizeof(void*) == 8 ? ... : false`, line 162), so the #104 workaround does not apply there; platform-conditional, not confirmed in this analysis.
Benign OpenMP data race on `invalid_data` (only ever set to true), acknowledged by the in-code TODO.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced values (tool number, drill size, peeked characters) reaching memory-access, allocation, and index sinks in this function are guarded by checks present in the given code: tool_num is bounded by 'if (tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX) { ... return -1; }' before all three image->aperture[tool_num] uses; the peek reads are guarded by '((fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen)'; apert NULL derefs are prevented by 'if (apert != NULL) {' and the post-loop 'if (apert == NULL) {' re-initialization; the while loop terminates at EOF via the default: case setting 'done = TRUE'; and all message formatting uses fixed literal format strings with attacker data passed only as arguments. Residual risks depend on constants and helpers (TOOL_MAX vs aperture[] dimension, gerb_fgetint/read_double/get_line internals, image->drill_stats NULLability) not shown in this code.

assumptions: TOOL_MAX is <= the declared dimension of image->aperture[]; both the constants and the gerbv_image_t struct are defined outside the given code, so the relation between the checked bound 'tool_num >= TOOL_MAX' and the array being indexed cannot be verified here. If TOOL_MAX exceeded the array dimension, 'image->aperture[tool_num]' would be an out-of-bounds access — an in-code check would then be missing.

The 'T' character preceding this call was already consumed by the caller, so fd->ptr >= 1 at entry and 'fd->ptr -= 4;' cannot underflow; this contract is implied by the function's own comments ('Sneak a peek at what's hiding after the T') but not enforced in the given code.

Helper functions gerb_fgetc, gerb_ungetc, gerb_fgetint, read_double, get_line, drill_stats_add_to_drill_list, and gerbv_get_tool_diameter are assumed to be memory-safe and to bound their own reads; their bodies are outside the given code.

g_new0 never returns NULL (glib semantics); the subsequent 'if (apert == NULL) GERB_FATAL_ERROR(...)' checks are dead code under that assumption.
limitations: Candidate dismissed as dead code: inside 'if (EOF == temp) {' the block 'if ('\n' == temp || '\r' == temp) gerb_ungetc(fd);' is unreachable because temp equals EOF there — cosmetic indentation artifact, no security effect.

Candidate dismissed: 'get_line(fd++)' post-increments the fd parameter pointer; subsequent 'fd->filename' uses in the same return statement operate on the incremented local pointer value. This is fragile but causes no memory-safety violation within the function's scope.

Candidate dismissed: at EOF the while loop performs one extra iteration (the '(char)temp' switch falls to default:) before exiting; bounded, attacker-controlled only in the sense that any file can cause one extra iteration — not a resource-exhaustion vector.

verdict.summary: No security-relevant defect is reachable within this function. The allocation NULL return is checked (if (!skb) return -ENOMEM;), memset writes exactly MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE bytes into the identically sized dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) buffer (at-limit, not past), the rsi_prepare_beacon return is checked with a single free on the error path and a queue on the success path (no double-free/UAF), and no injection, authz, or format sink exists. The only anomaly is the unchecked skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) return value: with a freshly allocated skb (len 0), the pull amount (1..63) always exceeds skb->len, the call fails as a no-op returning NULL that is discarded and never dereferenced, and skb->data is left unchanged — a robustness/alignment nit with no memory-safety, integrity, or availability consequence demonstrable from this code; the return check that would harden it is genuinely absent.
