verdict.summary: In load_image, brush header dimensions (32-bit fields) are multiplied in 32-bit arithmetic: size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes (line 121) and g_malloc (4 * bh.width * bh.height) (line 164) wrap modulo 2^32, while the only guard (G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1, line 51) is evaluated in 64-bit gsize and therefore cannot catch the wrap. The resulting undersized heap allocation is then indexed by loops bounded by the same (unwrapped at these values) products, producing heap out-of-bounds reads and writes. A ~9 KB crafted .gbr with width=height=46341, bytes=2, version=2 and a valid magic yields a 9,266-byte allocation but a 2,147,488,281-iteration loop (line 189) that reads *buf past the buffer and writes brush_buf[i] (line 205) far out of bounds; a wrapping-to-zero size also yields a NULL buffer deref. The pattern-compatibility path (lines 164-176) has the same defect via 4 * bh.width * bh.height.

evidence.snippet:
size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: bh.width/bh.height/bh.bytes are 32-bit header fields (values assigned from g_ntohl, which returns guint32), so the product is computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic and wraps mod 2^32 before being assigned to gsize. The only sanity check, '(G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1)' (line 51), is evaluated in 64-bit gsize units and passes for e.g. width=46341, height=46341, bytes=2, for which the true product 4,294,976,562 wraps to size=9,266. The allocation is therefore far smaller than every downstream consumer (case-2 loop, pattern loop, gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect) assumes.

Heap out-of-bounds read/write sink (CWE-787 consequence of the CWE-190 wrap at line 121). Trigger: width=height=46341, bytes=2, version=2 with GBRUSH_MAGIC; sanitize at lines 47-51 passes, size wraps to 9,266, g_malloc(9266), the read at line 124 succeeds with a ~9 KB file, then this loop runs i < 2,147,488,281 iterations: *buf (line 199) reads past the buffer from i=4,633 and brush_buf[i] = (guchar)(short_float.f * 255.0 + 0.5) (line 205) writes past it from i=9,266. Width=32768, height=65536, bytes=2 makes size wrap to 0 so g_malloc(0) returns NULL, and the same loop NULL-derefs *buf. No check anywhere between line 122 and line 189 compares the buffer size to the loop bound.

Second instance of the same 32-bit allocation-size overflow (CWE-190): '4 * bh.width * bh.height' wraps mod 2^32 when width*height >= 2^30, while the loop bound 'ph.width * ph.height' equals the true product because lines 155-156 enforce ph.width == bh.width and ph.height == bh.height. Trigger: bytes=1, version=2, width=33025, height=32513 (product = 2^30+1, both <= GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE, sanitize passes), a ~1 GB brush body so the read at line 124 succeeds, then a valid pattern header with matching dimensions: the allocation is 4 bytes but the loop runs 2^30+1 times, with read(fd, brush_buf + i*4, 3) at line 168 and brush_buf[i*4+3] = plain_brush[i] at line 176 writing far past the 4-byte heap buffer starting at i=1. No guard on the 4*width*height product exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: BrushHeader and PatternHeader field declarations are not shown in the given code; they are assumed to be 32-bit guint32 members (consistent with assignment from g_ntohl, which returns guint32, and with GIMP's actual definitions), so bh.width*bh.height*bh.bytes, bh.width*bh.height, 4*bh.width*bh.height and ph.width*ph.height are 32-bit unsigned arithmetic that wraps mod 2^32 on mainstream platforms.
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is assumed to be at least 46341 (it is 262144 in GIMP 2.x), so the crafted dimensions pass the 'bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE' checks at lines 47-48.
gsize/G_MAXSIZE are assumed 64-bit (typical 64-bit build). Even on a 32-bit build the trigger at line 51 passes: (2^32-1)/46341/46341/2 = 1.
GLib semantics assumed: g_malloc(0) returns NULL and g_malloc/g_new abort the process on allocation failure.
GBRUSH_MAGIC and GPATTERN_MAGIC are fixed constants the attacker can embed in a crafted file; nothing in this code secretizes them.
limitations: bn_size (line 95) is unbounded above (header_size up to ~2^31 passes 'bh.header_size > sizeof (BrushHeader)' at line 86 for version 2), so a tiny file can request a ~2 GB g_new at line 97; impact is limited to transient memory use or a g_malloc abort that occurs only under allocation failure an attacker cannot force, so this is not counted as a vulnerability.

lseek (fd, -8, SEEK_CUR) at line 67 (version 1) has an unchecked return value; worst case the brush name and data are read from a shifted file offset, but every subsequent read is length-checked, so there is no memory-safety or injection effect.

The brush name string is converted with gimp_any_to_utf8 (NUL-terminated result) and used only with constant format strings ('Unsupported brush depth: %d\n...') and as parasite/layer names; no format-string, SQL, command, or markup sink was found.
read() may return short on signals/regular files larger than SSIZE_MAX paths are irrelevant here because size has already wrapped to small values; no additional defect attributed to read semantics.

gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect receives a buffer sized by the wrapped 'size' with a full bh.width x bh.height rect; this is a further consequence of the confirmed line 121 wrap, not counted as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: The 4-byte fast-path guard 'if (needle + 4 < to)' uses wrapping ut64 addition: when 'to' is near UT64_MAX the guard passes an out-of-range needle, causing a heap over-read at 'r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from)' (up to 3 bytes past buf), and if the wrapped bytes are zero, 'needle += 4' wraps needle below 'from' so 'buf + needle - from' underflows and the loop scans/decodes heap memory outside the allocation, potentially leaking heap bytes into dumped strings (CWE-190 wrap in a bounds check). Separately, 'RBin *bin = bf->rbin;' dereferences 'bf' before the NULL guard 'r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1);' (CWE-476), and 'int outlen = len * 4;' truncates for len up to ST32_MAX, passing a negative/zero bound to r_charset_encode_str (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: The guard 'needle + 4 < to' wraps modulo 2^64 when needle > UT64_MAX-4 (e.g. to = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, from = to-15, len = 15 passes every earlier check), so it accepts needle = to-3..to-1 and 'r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from)' reads up to 3 bytes past the 'len'-byte heap buffer; if those bytes are zero, 'needle += 4' wraps needle below 'from' and subsequent 'buf + needle - from' offsets underflow, scanning heap memory outside the allocation into decoded strings. Root cause: unsigned integer wrap inside the bounds check (CWE-190); the author's comment at line 71 ('// may oobread') marks the site.

'RBin *bin = bf->rbin;' dereferences the 'bf' parameter at line 3, but the NULL guard 'r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1);' appears only at line 10 — a check placed after the use. A NULL 'bf' (an input the guard itself anticipates) crashes before the guard runs: NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476).

len is admitted up to ST32_MAX by 'if (len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX)', so 'len * 4' (up to ~2^33) is truncated into the int 'outlen' — e.g. len = 2^29 yields outlen = INT_MIN (sign flip), len = 2^30 yields 0 — and this corrupted bound is passed as the output-buffer limit to r_charset_encode_str. No overflow check precedes the computation: integer overflow/truncation producing an invalid bound (CWE-190).

assumptions: r_utf8_decode / r_utf16le_decode / r_utf32le_decode are assumed to respect their length argument (to - needle); their implementations are not shown, so this bound cannot be quoted.
The security consequence of the truncated 'outlen' depends on how r_charset_encode_str handles a negative/zero bound; that callee is not shown — the truncation itself is proven in this code.
Callers of this static function are not shown; per the last-line-of-defense rule, from/to are judged as unconstrained ut64 entry values (no in-code bound keeps them away from UT64_MAX).
r_utf_block_list is assumed to return parallel, -1-terminated block_list/freq_list arrays; the 'block_list[j]' access inside the freq_list loop relies on that parity and cannot be verified here.
limitations: Stack writes into tmp are safe: 'i < sizeof (tmp) - 4' guards r_utf8_encode (max 4 bytes), '(i + 32) < sizeof (tmp) && r < 93' guards the 2-byte escape write and the 93-entry table index, and post-loop 'tmp[i++] = '\0'' lands at most at sizeof(tmp)-1.
'needle -= 2' cannot underflow below 'from': runes >= 2 guarantees needle >= str_start + 2 because each counted rune advanced needle by rc >= 1.
Division 'num_chars / num_blocks' is guarded by 'num_blocks ? ... : 0'.

The ascii_only rescan ('needle = str_start; ... continue;') cannot loop forever: rescanned content is ASCII-only (break on r > 0x7f), so num_blocks == 1 and actual_ascii == expected_ascii, which never re-triggers the heuristic.

The charset path's replacement buffer is always calloc(len, 4) with the original len, so subsequent reads bounded by the original to-from stay inside the allocation; only the truncated outlen bound is defective.
A short/failed r_buf_read_at is benign: buf is calloc-zeroed before the read.

verdict.summary: All attacker-reachable sinks in get_visual_text have verifiable in-function guards: the same-line precondition is enforced by 'if (VIsual.lnum != curwin->w_cursor.lnum)', the NULL cap by 'if (cap != NULL)', the zero-length case by 'if (**pp == NUL) *lenp = 0;', and the 'pp + (*lenp - 1)' pointer arithmetic by 'if (has_mbyte && *lenp > 0)', which rejects the lenp==0 boundary that would underflow to pp-1. The remaining theoretical hazard — a position column exceeding the current line length reaching ml_get_pos — has no in-function bound, but is not reachable from the values this function receives: byte columns top out at the line's terminating NUL (col == strlen, in-buffer), and a larger column requires a defect in the position-adjustment machinery outside this code. No candidate survives the trigger proof and the counterfactual patch test.

assumptions: VIsual and curwin->w_cursor are maintained within their line (col <= line length) by Vim's position machinery outside the given code; no in-function check enforces this, so a stale position from a buffer change during active Visual mode (e.g., timer or <Cmd> callback) could in principle reach ml_get_pos out of bounds — unprovable from this code and classified as an external-machinery defect, not a defect of this function.

unadjust_for_sel()'s behavior when 'selection' is exclusive, including any col>0 guard before its decrement, is external to the given code; a col==0 decrement to -1 on the same line would not be caught by the quoted lnum check, but producing it requires unadjust_for_sel itself to lack its own guard.
Callers (e.g., the '*'/'#' Visual-mode handling in normal.c) invoke this function only while Visual mode is active and always pass non-NULL pp/lenp output addresses.
(*mb_ptr2len) returns 1 for a NUL or invalid lead byte and does not read past the line's terminating NUL, bounding the last-character length correction inside the buffer.
limitations: C2 (pp-1 underflow read if lenp==0 reaches the mbyte correction): dismissed — guard 'if (has_mbyte && *lenp > 0)' is quoted, on the only path, and rejects the boundary value.

C3 (selection length can include the terminating NUL byte when a column equals the line length with virtualedit=onemore): all bytes read remain in-buffer; worst case is an embedded NUL in the returned text, a functional/robustness issue with no memory-safety effect.
C4 (integer overflow in VIsual.col - curwin->w_cursor.col + 1): requires a multi-gigabyte single line and a column near INT_MAX; not reachable with positions this code can actually receive.

C5 (unadjust_for_sel producing an out-of-range column that survives the lnum check): the producing statement is outside the given code and its col>0 guard cannot be quoted here; trigger not constructible from this code alone.

Analysis is confined to the given function; ml_get_pos, ml_get_curline, unadjust_for_sel, reset_VIsual_and_resel, and the position-adjustment machinery are treated as external and their invariants recorded as assumptions rather than facts.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke consumes the caller-supplied QVectorPath's raw points pointer, elements pointer, and int elementCount with no validation. The stroking loops' only guard is 'while (points < lastPoint)', which guarantees just one point (2 qreals) remains, but 'case QPainterPath::CurveToElement' reads six qreals (points[0..5]) — a path ending in a CurveToElement with fewer than 3 remaining points reads up to 4 qreals past the end of the points buffer (both the non-cosmetic and cosmetic branches). Additionally, the 'default:' case advances neither points nor types, so any unhandled ElementType value (e.g. CurveToDataElement) in the caller-supplied types array causes an infinite loop ( denial of service).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The enclosing loop guard 'while (points < lastPoint)' guarantees only 2 qreals remain, but cubicTo dereferences points[0]..points[5] (6 qreals). Trigger: a caller-supplied QVectorPath with points = {MoveToElement, CurveToElement} and only 2 points (4 qreals): the second iteration enters the curve case with exactly one point left and reads points[4], points[5] past the buffer. No 'points + 6 <= lastPoint' check exists anywhere in the code.

Same out-of-bounds read in the cosmetic-pen branch: the loop condition 'while (points < lastPoint)' admits an iteration with only 1-2 points remaining, but ((const QPointF *) points)[2] reads the third point pair beyond the buffer. Trigger is identical to the non-cosmetic case with a cosmetic pen and a non-projective transform.

evidence.snippet:
default:
                    break;
evidence.reason: Infinite loop / uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400). The default case of the switch inside 'while (points < lastPoint)' advances neither 'points' nor 'types', so any ElementType value not handled by the switch (e.g. QPainterPath::CurveToDataElement or an out-of-range byte in the caller-supplied path.elements() array) makes the loop condition permanently true: the function spins forever. The same unguarded default exists at lines 193-194.

assumptions: Semantics of path.isEmpty(), path.hasImplicitClose(), and the invariant len(path.elements()) == path.elementCount() are not visible in the given code; analysis assumes elementCount>0 implies at least one point exists when isEmpty() is false, so the hasImplicitClose first-point reads (lines 135-136, 145-146, 197-199, 211-212) were not confirmed as independent defects.
StrokeHandler internals (pts.reset()/types.reset(), allocation growth) are not shown; sink capacity of the output buffer is assumed handled by that class and is outside the given code.

QVectorPath is treated as trust-boundary input because stroke is a public/protected virtual of the paint engine; in-process Qt callers usually build well-formed paths, but this code is judged as the last line of defense.
limitations: Secondary/theoretical instance of the same missing input validation: 'pointCount<<1' (line 88) and 'path.elementCount()+4' (line 13) can overflow signed int for elementCount >= 2^30 (~2GB point arrays) or near INT_MAX, producing UB in pointer arithmetic; triggering requires a caller passing such an extreme count, so it is not counted as a separate confirmed finding.
The out-of-bounds reads are reads (not writes); worst direct impact is disclosure of adjacent heap data into stroked geometry plus potential crash, hence medium severity.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate uses the unvalidated 32-bit parameter `facet` and unvalidated neighbor/which_vertex_not integers read from parsed mesh state as array subscripts. The only guard before the first indexing sink is `if (stl->error) return;`, which checks an error flag, not bounds. `facet` out of range (e.g., equal to the facet count or negative) causes out-of-bounds reads of stl->facet_start/stl->neighbors_start and forwards the bad index to stl_remove_facet. Additionally, `neighbor1/2/3` are only tested with `!= -1` (values like -2 or any index >= the facet count pass) and `(vnot + 1) % 3` yields a negative subscript for vnot <= -2, producing heap out-of-bounds writes such as `stl->neighbors_start[neighbor1].neighbor[(vnot1 + 1) % 3] = neighbor2;`. Root cause: improper validation of array indices (CWE-129) with OOB read/write consequences (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: The parameter `facet` (int, 32-bit) is used directly to index stl->facet_start (and later stl->neighbors_start at lines 45-46, 56-59, and is forwarded to stl_remove_facet at lines 22 and 70) with no bounds validation. The only guard on the path is `if (stl->error) return;`, which checks an error flag, not the index range; there is no `facet >= stl->stats.number_of_facets` or `facet < 0` check anywhere in the function. Trigger: any caller of this public entry point passing facet == number_of_facets, a negative value, or any out-of-range int performs out-of-bounds reads at the memcmp sinks. Root cause CWE-129 (improper validation of array index).

Heap out-of-bounds write sink: `neighbor1` (read from parsed mesh state at line 45) is used as an outer array subscript guarded only by `!= -1`, which admits -2, INT_MAX, and any index >= the facet count (or a stale index left after previous stl_remove_facet calls by this function). The inner subscript `(vnot1 + 1) % 3` is computed from the unvalidated `vnot1`; for vnot1 = -2 it evaluates to -1 (C modulo of a negative dividend is negative), and for vnot1 = -3 it evaluates to -2, yielding a negative element index. Additionally the unvalidated value `neighbor2` is written into the table, propagating bad indices. No range check exists on any path to this sink; root cause CWE-129 manifesting as an OOB write (CWE-787). The same defect pattern repeats at lines 66-67 and 72-74.

evidence.snippet:
neighbor1 = stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge1];
  neighbor2 = stl->neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge2];
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index values: `neighbor1/2` (and `neighbor3`, `vnot1/2/3` read at lines 56-59) are loaded from the neighbor table, which is model/parsed data derived from an untrusted STL file. This code performs no range validation on them before using them as subscripts or passing them to stl_update_connects_remove_1 (lines 49, 52, 73), so any value outside [-1, facet_count) reaches the out-of-bounds write sinks at lines 62-67 and 74.

Second write sink: after `stl_remove_facet(stl, facet)` has already mutated the facet table, `neighbor3` is used as a subscript guarded only by `!= -1` (admits any out-of-range or stale index), and `(vnot3 + 1) % 3` is negative for unvalidated vnot3 <= -2. `stl->neighbors_start[neighbor3].neighbor[(vnot3 + 1) % 3] = -1;` is therefore an unguarded out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced indices (CWE-129/CWE-787); line 73 also forwards `neighbor3` to stl_update_connects_remove_1 unvalidated.

assumptions: Any guarantee that neighbors_start entries are always -1 or valid facet indices is produced outside this snippet (e.g., by the loader/repair routines) and cannot be quoted here; per the guard-anchoring discipline this code is judged as the last line of defense, so such a bound does not exist for this analysis.

The body of stl_remove_facet is not shown; if it moves the last facet and decrements the count (typical for this library), neighbor3 equal to the last index becomes out-of-range after line 70 and any stored neighbors referencing removed facets become stale. This aggravates candidate 2 but is not the basis of the verdict.

The body of stl_update_connects_remove_1 is not shown; passing -1 (possible at line 49 when both neighbor1 and neighbor2 are -1, and line 52 symmetrically) is flagged as unvalidated index marshalling rather than a proven OOB access.

The stl_file struct definition and stl->stats.number_of_facets are assumed to exist as in the parent library; line numbers in evidence are relative to the snippet as given (line 1 = function signature).
limitations: printf at line 20 uses a constant format string; no format-string vulnerability.
The all-vertices-equal early path (lines 14-24) and the no-degenerate early return (lines 41-44) introduce no additional sinks beyond the already-reported unvalidated `facet` indexing.
Integer wrap of `vnot1 + 1` at INT_MAX yielding a negative modulo result shares the same root cause (missing vnot range validation) as candidate 3 and is not reported separately.

Exploitability (controlled vs. uncontrolled corruption) depends on heap layout and the neighbor-table contents; the confirmed defect is attacker-reachable memory corruption at minimum (crash/DoS), potentially worse.

verdict.summary: This QuantizeV2 axis-handling code validates every attacker-influenced value it consumes: axis_ is bounds-checked against input.dims() (input.dims() > axis_), min/max range tensors are checked for rank 1 and size equal to num_slices (or exactly one element when axis is absent), the per-slice loop iterates strictly below the validated slice count, and the reshaped 3-D views ({pre_dim, num_slices, post_dim}) are consistent with the output tensor allocated with input.shape(). The only boundary defect found is a theoretical int64-to-int truncation of num_slices, which requires a >=2^32-element axis dimension (multi-gigabyte attacker tensor) and then aborts safely at the bit_casted_shaped size CHECK before any out-of-bounds access; it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES aborts the op with an error when its condition is false; this macro behavior is outside the given code.

The dtype of input/min_range/max_range (float) and the output dtypes are enforced by the op registration (QuantizeV2 op def), not by the statements shown; the flat<float>()/vec<float>() calls rely on that.

flat_inner_outer_dims<float,3>(axis_ - 1) is assumed to produce {prod dims[0..axis_), dim_size(axis_), prod dims(axis_+1..dims)}; for axis_ = 0 the start index is -1, assumed to denote an empty inner product of 1, matching the pre_dim loop which also yields 1 for axis_ = 0. This helper is outside the given code.
QuantizeTensor and QuantizeSlice (not shown) are assumed to honor their contracts; the values passed to them here are bounded by the quoted checks.
bit_casted_shaped/shaped perform release-mode CHECK validation of element counts; this is Tensor API behavior outside the given code.
limitations: Dismissed candidate (int truncation, CWE-190-like): int num_slices = input.dim_size(axis_) truncates when dim_size(axis_) >= 2^32; the guard input_min_range.dim_size(0) == num_slices compares against the truncated value, so a min_range whose length equals the wrapped value would pass. Trigger requires actually allocating an input with >= 2^32 slices along axis_ (>= 16 GB of floats) plus a multi-gigabyte range tensor, and the first use, output->bit_casted_shaped<T,3>({pre_dim, num_slices, post_dim}), fails its release-mode size CHECK (p*n*q != NumElements) before any chip access, so no out-of-bounds read/write is reachable — only a CHECK abort under impractical allocation sizes.
int64 overflow of pre_dim/post_dim products would require a tensor with near-2^63 total elements, which cannot be allocated; not attacker-reachable.
When axis_ > -1 and dim_size(axis_) == 1, outputs 1 and 2 are allocated as scalars {} rather than shape [1]; this is an API-shape nuance with no memory-safety effect.
QuantizeTensor/QuantizeSlice bodies were not provided and were not audited; the analysis covers only the shown Compute function.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse trusts a remote peer's dynamic-capability message. The only pre-memcpy bounds check, (pnt + hdr->length + 3) > end, bounds the read by the attacker-controlled one-byte hdr->length instead of the fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data), so a trailing capability declaring length < 4 with fewer than 7 bytes remaining makes the unconditional memcpy read up to 4 bytes past the buffer (heap out-of-bounds read, CWE-125). Additionally, both 'continue' statements (invalid afi/safi at line 66, override-capability at line 59) bypass the loop's sole advancement 'pnt += hdr->length + 3;' at line 102, so a peer sending an MP capability with an invalid AFI/SAFI (e.g., afi=0, safi=1) causes an infinite loop that pegs the CPU and hangs the BGP daemon (uncontrolled resource consumption, CWE-400).

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The sink memcpy(&mpc, pnt + 3, sizeof(struct capability_mp_data)) requires pnt + 3 + 4 <= end, but the only guard bounds the region by the attacker-controlled hdr->length (u_char). Edge case: exactly 3 bytes remaining with hdr->length = 0 makes both 'pnt + 3 > end' and 'pnt + hdr->length + 3 > end' evaluate false at the boundary (==, strict '>'), so the memcpy reads 4 bytes starting at end, past the heap buffer. No check anywhere ties hdr->length to sizeof(struct capability_mp_data). Trigger: a message ending with the bytes [action=SET, code=MP, length=0].

BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ is assumed to be 8 and round_up(x,8) to round upward; both are external definitions.

The ringbuf data area is assumed to be allocated with the kernel ringbuf's double-mapping layout (data pages mapped twice) so that a record/header starting near the end of the area and logically wrapping stays within mapped memory; this allocation layout is not shown in the given code.

rb->consumer_pos is assumed writable by unprivileged userspace via the mmap'd consumer page, which is why it was treated as attacker-influenced; the analysis showed both manipulation directions are fail-closed under the quoted checks.
limitations: Candidate: u32 truncation of len if RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ >= 2^32-8 — dismissed only under the assumed (standard) macro value; not provable from the given code.

Candidate: header write of 8 bytes at prod_pos & mask == mask spilling past rb->data + (mask+1) — depends on the external allocation layout (double-mapped pages); the in-code masking bounds the offset to [0, mask] and cannot be shown out-of-bounds from this snippet alone.

Candidate: userspace-controlled consumer_pos — verified fail-closed: a huge cons_pos underflows the unsigned subtraction to a value > rb->mask, causing a NULL return; a smaller/older cons_pos only tightens the check. No fail-open direction exists.
Candidate: cons_pos loaded before the spinlock — a racing consumer only increases the true consumer_pos, so the checked (stale) value is always the conservative bound; no fail-open ordering exists.
Candidate: off-by-one in 'new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask' — boundary test shows allowing span == mask leaves one byte free of the mask+1 window; the strict '>' is correct and conservative.
The u64 flags parameter present in the upstream prototype is absent here, so no flags-validation finding applies.

verdict.summary: This is the patched form of SQClass::NewSlot: the member-count gate 'if (_members->CountUsed() >= MEMBER_MAX_COUNT) { return false; }' lies before every insertion path and keeps _defaultvalues/_methods indices strictly within the 24-bit _member_idx tag width, preventing the known index-overflow/OOB defect. All index sinks are guarded: _defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)] is guarded by '_members->Get(key,temp) && _isfield(temp)', _methods[_member_idx(temp)] is only reached when temp is a previously stored method index, and _metamethods[mmidx] is guarded by '(mmidx = ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key)) != -1' with the upper bound fixed by internal VM state. No reachable vulnerability was found.

assumptions: MEMBER_MAX_COUNT is 0x00FFFFFF, matching the 24-bit _member_idx mask used by _make_field_idx/_make_method_idx/_member_idx (macro and masks are defined outside the given code); with any larger value the count gate would not cover the tag width.

SQSharedState::GetMetaMethodIdxByName returns only -1 or an index in [0, MT_LAST) taken from the VM-internal metamethod-name map; the attacker-influenced key can only select among those entries, so the unquoted upper bound of _metamethods[mmidx] holds by internal construction.

SQVM::IsEqual sets its bool out-param on all type combinations (including incomparable types), so the uninitialized-looking 'bool isconstructor' is always assigned before 'if(isconstructor)'; if the callee could return without assigning, this would be CWE-457.
SQObjectPtr's default constructor yields OT_NULL and SQTable::Get leaves the out value untouched on a miss, so 'sq_type(temp) == OT_NULL' reliably detects a brand-new key.
The VM is single-threaded with respect to this function, so no race on _members/_locked.

SQTable::NewSlot updates an existing node's value in place even when returning false, so ignoring its return value does not desynchronize the member table from the _methods/_defaultvalues vectors except under allocation failure.
limitations: Candidate: unbounded member growth causing 24-bit member-index truncation (CWE-190/CWE-129) — NOT real; the fix is present verbatim: 'if (_members->CountUsed() >= MEMBER_MAX_COUNT) { return false; }' precedes both insertion paths, and the method-to-field overwrite path cannot repeat for the same key because 'if(_members->Get(key,temp) && _isfield(temp))' intercepts it thereafter.

Candidate: out-of-range _metamethods[mmidx] write (CWE-129) — dismissed; only the -1 sentinel is rejected in the given code ('(mmidx = ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key)) != -1'), but no runtime-reachable key can produce an index outside [0, MT_LAST) because the index map is fixed VM-internal state.
Candidate: uninitialized 'isconstructor' (CWE-457) — dismissed; depends on SQVM::IsEqual's out-param contract outside the given code; no input to this function can change the callee's behavior.
Candidate: memory exhaustion via unbounded push_back (CWE-400) — not reachable; the MEMBER_MAX_COUNT gate caps total members at 0xFFFFFF.

Candidate: ignored return value of _members->NewSlot — only manifests under allocation failure (environment failure, not attacker-inducible input), and the in-place update still occurs for existing keys.

The _locked bypass for static/closure members ('_locked && !belongs_to_static_table') is by design per the in-code comment and has no memory-safety effect; treated as language semantics, not an authz vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The PCX RLE encoder is memory-safe and functionally correct for all attacker-influenced raster byte values. Every dereference is guarded on every path by quotable checks ('while (from < end)', the short-circuit 'from >= end || data != *from', 'while ((from < end) && (*from == data))'), the emitted run-count byte is provably capped at 0xcf by 'while (from - start >= max_run)' with max_run = step*15 (edge-verified at remainder 0, 14*step, and exactly 15*step), and literals >= 0xc0 are escaped by 'if (data >= 0xc0) gp_fputc(0xc1, file);' and '|| data >= 0xc0'. The only defects require the trusted same-module caller to pass step <= 0 (infinite loop or out-of-bounds read below the buffer) or step > INT_MAX/15 (signed overflow in step*MAX_RUN_COUNT); no guard for step exists in this code, but step is internal pixel geometry, not trust-boundary data, so no attacker-reachable trigger exists in this code.

assumptions: The snippet omits the storage-class/return-type line; in the upstream module this is a file-local helper whose 'step' is a pixel/plane stride computed from the device's fixed color format (e.g., 1 or 3), not document-controlled. This constraint is NOT quotable from the given code, so the step-related triggers cannot be excluded by the snippet alone; if pcx_write_rle were treated as an exported API taking arbitrary caller values, step <= 0 would be a valid CWE-400/CWE-125 finding.
from <= end and both point into one allocated raster buffer (caller invariant, not quotable here).
byte is unsigned char and gp_fputc accepts an int, so no truncation occurs at the emit sites.
limitations: Dismissed candidate: missing validation of 'step'. step == 0 gives an infinite loop in 'while ((from < end) && (*from == data)) from += step;' and step < 0 makes 'from += step' walk below the buffer so 'data != *from' / '*from == data' read out of bounds (CWE-400/CWE-125). STEP 5 confirmed no 'step <= 0' guard exists anywhere in the code; dismissed solely because step is internal geometry that trust-boundary data (raster bytes) cannot influence, not because a caller/framework bound was assumed to exist.

Dismissed candidate: 'int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT;' can overflow signed int for step > 143165576 (CWE-190), making max_run negative, skipping run capping, and allowing '(from - start) / step + 0xc1' to exceed 0xff; triggering additionally requires a >62-step uniform run, i.e., a multi-gigabyte raster at that stride — unreachable geometry.

Dismissed candidate: 'from += step' can advance the pointer more than one element past 'end' (formally undefined behavior in C); the subsequent 'from >= end' comparison catches it and there is no dereference or security effect.

Encoding correctness was explicitly verified, not assumed: run lengths 1, 2, 3, 15, 16, 17, 30, 31, 40, and 46 and byte values 0x00, 0xbf, 0xc0, 0xff all reconstruct exactly, so the tricky run-length arithmetic (count byte subsumes the bottom 'gp_fputc(data, file)') contains no off-by-one.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId detects a missing key (find() == end()) but only logs via STFATAL without returning or throwing, so execution falls through to 'return it->second;' which dereferences the end() iterator. Any caller-supplied id not present in idInfoMap (a public-API parameter, hence attacker-influenced) triggers an out-of-bounds read past the map's sentinel node whose contents are copied into the returned TerminalUserInfo; if STFATAL aborts instead, the same input causes attacker-induced process termination. No guard in the given code prevents the use.

evidence.reason: The not-found branch tests the exact failing condition (it == idInfoMap.end(), including the empty-map/absent-id boundary) but contains no return, throw, or abort, so control falls through and line 7 dereferences the end() iterator — an out-of-bounds read at the sink. The minimal fix (early return/throw after the log) does not exist anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet: TerminalUserInfo UserTerminalRouter::getInfoForId(const string &id) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: 'id' is an unconstrained public-method parameter crossing the caller trust boundary; any id absent from idInfoMap (e.g., an arbitrary or empty string) reaches the unguarded iterator dereference at line 7.

assumptions: The semantics of the STFATAL macro are external to the given code and cannot be quoted. If STFATAL aborts the process, the defect becomes an attacker-induced fatal termination (denial of service) rather than an out-of-bounds read; either way the trigger is the same attacker-supplied unknown id and no statement in this code handles it.

idInfoMap is assumed to be mutated only under routerMutex by other code paths; within this function, the quoted 'lock_guard<recursive_mutex> guard(routerMutex);' protects the find/dereference pair from concurrent map mutation.
TerminalUserInfo is assumed to be a plain value type; its copy construction from out-of-bounds memory is what exposes the read contents to the caller.
limitations: Log injection (CWE-117) was considered and rejected: the STFATAL operand is a static literal and does not include the attacker-controlled id.
A race condition on idInfoMap was considered and rejected for this function: synchronization is quoted at line 2 and covers the entire map access.
Exact runtime effect of the end() dereference (OOB heap read vs. crash) depends on the standard library implementation and on STFATAL, neither of which is visible in the given code.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO branch, when strlen(name) exactly equals sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename), the source index 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' wraps to (size_t)-1, so memcpy reads one byte before the name buffer; for any sl >= sizeof(filename), sizeof(filename) bytes are copied with no NUL terminator, leaving the fixed-size shm filename array non-terminated. Additionally, if ul_init() fails, the else branch leaves 'ULHandler ulhandler' uninitialized, yet 'ulhandler.total_uploaded' is read unconditionally into the global 'uploaded' and passed to displayrate().

evidence.reason: Root cause: off-by-one/unsigned-underflow source index and missing NUL termination. At the boundary value sl == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' evaluates to (size_t)-1, so memcpy reads sizeof(filename) bytes starting one byte before the attacker-controlled 'name' buffer (out-of-bounds read of name[-1]); for any sl >= sizeof(filename), the else branch fills the entire fixed-size filename array with non-NUL bytes and never stores a terminator on any path, causing downstream over-reads of the shared-memory field. Trigger: FTP client sends STOR with a filename whose length equals or exceeds sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename); only the guard 'if (sl < sizeof shm_data_cur->filename)' exists and it routes exactly these boundary values into the unguarded else branch.

evidence.snippet: const size_t sl = strlen(name);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted length: sl is computed from the attacker-controlled command argument 'name' (dostor's parameter, line 1) with no length bound anywhere in this function; this unbounded sl feeds the faulty else-branch memcpy at lines 153-155.

Root cause: use of uninitialized value (CWE-457). 'ULHandler ulhandler;' is declared uninitialized (line 3); when ul_init() fails, the else branch only sets ret = -1 and leaves ulhandler's members uninitialized, yet control then falls through to the unconditional read 'uploaded += (unsigned long long) ulhandler.total_uploaded;' (line 192) and to displayrate(MSG_UPLOADED, ulhandler.total_uploaded, ...) (line 250) when overflow == 0, leaking uninitialized stack content into global state and reply output. Trigger: any STOR session in which ul_init() returns nonzero (e.g., data/TLS session setup failure under client control).

assumptions: sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (N) is not visible in this code; the sl == N trigger assumes the attacker can supply a command argument of that length. No quotable bound on strlen(name) exists in this function, so the code is treated as the last line of defense.

checknamesanity(name, dot_write_ok) is called (line 33) but its semantics (length limits, rejection of CR/LF or traversal) cannot be verified from this code, so bounds or reply-injection guarantees it might provide are assumptions, not facts.

The conditions under which ul_init() fails are external to this code; the CWE-457 finding assumes at least one failure path is reachable or influenceable by the remote client (e.g., data/TLS session setup).
FTPWHO (and QUOTAS) blocks are assumed compiled in for the respective findings; the ftpwho guard 'if (shm_data_cur != NULL) {' is treated as satisfiable at runtime.
limitations: TOCTOU window on 'name' between checknamesanity (line 33) and open/rename (lines 46, 58, 60, 224): a local attacker could swap the path; open uses O_NOFOLLOW and fstat enforces S_ISREG, so no memory-safety impact is provable from this code alone.
FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 179 executes after close(f) at line 173; it fails with EBADF and has no security effect.
The string returned by get_atomic_file(name) is never freed (memory leak on every atomic upload); no exhaustion path is shown, so not counted as a vulnerability.

Quota delta arithmetic (atomic_file_size - original_file_size with the clamp original_file_size = restartat) may undercount quota usage, a logic/accounting quirk without memory-safety impact in this code.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf never validates the signed request length: when `remain >= len` it sets rlen = len without any `len >= 0` check, so a negative len passed through the IO-context getbuf callback reaches `memcpy(buf, dp->data + dp->pos, rlen)` where the negative int widens to a huge size_t, causing a massive out-of-bounds read of dp->data and out-of-bounds write to buf. The inner `remain <= 0` check is in the else-branch and tests remain, not len, so it cannot block this path.

evidence.reason: The guard `if (remain >= len) { rlen = len; }` accepts any negative len (e.g., len=-1 with remain=10 makes 10 >= -1 true), and no statement in the function checks len's sign; rlen then reaches memcpy (line 20) where it is converted to size_t as SIZE_MAX, producing an out-of-bounds read of dp->data and out-of-bounds write to buf. Trigger: invoke this getbuf callback with any negative int len while dp->logicalSize - dp->pos >= len.

assumptions: The invariant that the allocated size of dp->data is at least dp->logicalSize is enforced only in sibling dynamic-context code (allocation/grow logic) that is not part of the given snippet; it is assumed, not verified here.
dp->pos is assumed to be within [0, logicalSize] on entry; its initialization and any seek behavior live outside the given code.
The size of the caller-provided buf is assumed sufficient for the requested len in the positive-length case; no statement in this code can verify it.
For the positive-length path, remain = logicalSize - pos is assumed not to overflow because pos is assumed within [0, logicalSize] externally.
limitations: A candidate heap over-read via dp->logicalSize exceeding the allocated dp->data buffer could not be confirmed: producing that state requires allocation/writer code that is not present in the given snippet, so no trigger reachable from this code alone exists.
NULL-deref candidates for dctx/dp/dp->data depend on construction or pointer-failure conditions outside this code and were not confirmed.

verdict.summary: getInfoForId looks up an attacker-supplied id in idInfoMap and detects the not-found case (it == idInfoMap.end()), but the error branch only logs via STFATAL and does not return or throw; control falls through to 'return it->second;', dereferencing the end iterator. Any caller-supplied id absent from the map produces undefined behavior / an out-of-bounds read returning garbage TerminalUserInfo or a crash (attacker-reachable DoS).

evidence.reason: The not-found guard (line 3) detects an attacker-supplied id that is absent from idInfoMap, but the branch body contains no return/throw/abort, so execution falls through and line 6 dereferences the end iterator 'it->second' — undefined behavior / out-of-bounds read triggered by any external id not present in the map. The required early-exit check is absent from the code (verified in STEP 5).

assumptions: id is treated as attacker-influenced because it is the parameter of an exported/public method (a terminal ID router lookup); no constraint on its value exists in this code.

If the STFATAL macro happens to abort or throw, the dereference at line 6 would be unreachable; that behavior is external to the given code and cannot be quoted, so per guard-anchoring it is recorded here rather than relied upon.
Contents/lifetime of idInfoMap (whether entries are concurrently erased) are outside the given code; no assumption about them is used in the verdict.
limitations: If STFATAL is proven to terminate the process in the actual build, the defect degrades to a harmless fatal-log path; the analysis of the given code alone cannot establish that.

The concrete impact of dereferencing the end iterator (crash vs. disclosure of out-of-bounds memory copied into the returned TerminalUserInfo) is implementation-defined UB; either way it is attacker-triggerable via an unknown id.

verdict.summary: call_qftf_func consumes the return value of a user-controlled 'quickfixtextfunc' callback and dereferences the list pointer after checking only the typval's type tag. The guard `if (rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST)` does not reject a VAR_LIST typval whose v_list pointer is NULL (e.g., Vim9 null_list), so `qftf_list->lv_refcount++` writes through a NULL pointer, crashing the editor. The missing NULL check is absent from every path, making this an attacker-reachable NULL dereference (denial of service).

evidence.reason: The sink `qftf_list->lv_refcount++` requires a non-NULL list pointer, but the only guard is a type check (`rettv.v_type == VAR_LIST`) which passes for a VAR_LIST typval with a NULL pointer (Vim9 null_list returned by the user-set callback). The increment then writes through NULL and crashes; no `v_list != NULL` check exists on any path to this sink.

evidence.snippet: if (call_callback(cb, 0, &rettv, 1, args) != FAIL)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: `call_callback` invokes the user-supplied 'quickfixtextfunc' and stores its arbitrary, attacker-influenced return typval in rettv, which is then consumed at lines 40-43 with only a type check.

assumptions: call_callback initializes rettv on the non-FAIL path (framework contract, not quotable in the given code); clear_tv is therefore not reached with an uninitialized rettv.
dict_alloc_lock returns a fresh dict with refcount 0, so `++d->dv_refcount;` (line 33) and `dict_unref(d);` (line 47) balance on the single path.
Vim is single-threaded, so the static `recursive` flag has no race; user-script re-entry is blocked by the lines 7-9 guard.
call_callback/call_func holds the callback's partial reference during user code execution, so `cb` (possibly pointing into qfl) is not used after the callback returns.
The returned list reference is correctly kept alive across `clear_tv(&rettv)` because the increment at line 43 precedes the clear at line 45.
limitations: If call_callback returns FAIL after partially populating rettv, the value would leak (not freed); this depends on framework behavior and has no security effect beyond a minor leak.
start_idx/end_idx/qf_winid are placed into a dict handed to user script by design; the script can inspect them but they are internal values with no further sinks here.

The NULL-list trigger requires the Vim runtime to materialize a VAR_LIST typval with a NULL pointer (Vim9 null_list); in runtimes that strictly guarantee non-NULL list pointers for VAR_LIST, the crash would not be reachable — this invariant is not enforced anywhere in the given code.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot writes the attacker-supplied slot value into _metamethods[mmidx] where mmidx comes from ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key) driven by the script-controlled key. The only validation performed is `(mmidx = ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName(key)) != -1`, which rejects only the value -1; no upper bound against _metamethods.size() exists anywhere in the function, so any index at or past the vector size passes the check and produces an out-of-bounds write of an attacker-chosen SQObjectPtr (CWE-129).

evidence.reason: The index mmidx is derived from the attacker-influenced key via ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName and used directly as a vector subscript. The sole quoted guard, `!= -1`, rejects only -1; edge values such as mmidx == _metamethods.size(), one-past-size, or a sign-wrapped positive value all pass and reach the out-of-bounds write of the attacker-chosen val. No `mmidx < _metamethods.size()` check exists on any path in the given code (STEP 5 search confirmed absence), so the sink is unguarded at this code's trust boundary.

assumptions: The bound on mmidx in the real Squirrel runtime comes from outside this snippet: ss->_metamethodsmap is assumed to contain only indices 0..MT_LAST-1 and the SQClass constructor is assumed to size _metamethods to match. Neither statement is quotable in the given code, so under guard anchoring the write is treated as unguarded here; if both hold at runtime, the OOB trigger is not reachable via script keys alone.

SQObjectPtr's default constructor initializes temp to OT_NULL, and SQTable::Get leaves temp unchanged on lookup failure; this makes `if(sq_type(temp) == OT_NULL)` a reliable new-slot discriminator. The initialization is external to the snippet.

_members is assumed to contain only the encoded integer indices written by _make_field_idx/_make_method_idx in this code (and consistent base-class clones thereof), which keeps _defaultvalues[_member_idx(temp)] and _methods[_member_idx(temp)] in bounds by construction.
SQVM::IsEqual is assumed to assign its by-reference out-parameter on every path, so the uninitialized `bool isconstructor` is always written before its use in `if(isconstructor)`.
limitations: `bool isconstructor;` (line 26) is uninitialized (CWE-457 style) and assigned only by SQVM::IsEqual, whose body is outside the snippet; no trigger without that call failing to write could be constructed here.

Member indices use a 24-bit payload mask (_member_idx), so a class with >= 0x1000000 (16M+) members would alias indices (CWE-190), but the masked result stays in-bounds, producing a wrong-slot write rather than memory corruption, and requires hundreds of MB of attacker allocations.

A closure-valued slot overriding an existing field of a locked class (line 9 reached with belongs_to_static_table true) mutates _defaultvalues despite the _locked check; this is upstream Squirrel semantics with no memory-safety, injection, or authorization-boundary effect.
Only the source snippet was analyzed; SQTable::Get/NewSlot internals, SQSharedState::GetMetaMethodIdxByName, SQVM::IsEqual, and the SQClass constructor were not available for guard quoting.

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck fails to verify that a closing double quote was found before subtracting the scanned length from the remaining length. When the quoted issuer or thisUpdate value has no closing quote, the scan loop leaves is->bv_len (or tu->bv_len) equal to x.bv_len, and the unsigned ber_len_t subtraction 'x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1' wraps to (ber_len_t)-1 while x.bv_val advances one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied input buffer. Subsequent reads (the eat-spaces loop and the ',' check) dereference x.bv_val[0] out of bounds, and if the past-end byte is a space or comma the wrapped huge x.bv_len drives further out-of-bounds reads. A crafted 37-byte attribute value such as '{issuer rdnSequence:"AAAAAAAAAAAAAAA}' triggers it, enabling remote denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
x.bv_val += is->bv_len + 1;
			x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1;
evidence.reason: The issuer scan loop 'for ( ; is->bv_len < x.bv_len; )' (line 65) can terminate with is->bv_len == x.bv_len when no unescaped closing quote exists; there is no check between the loop and these lines. 'x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1' then wraps the unsigned ber_len_t to (ber_len_t)-1 and x.bv_val is advanced one byte past the end of in's buffer. Trigger: '{issuer rdnSequence:"AAAAAAAAAAAAAAA}' (37 bytes, passes the line-19 minimum-length and line-21 brace checks) causes out-of-bounds reads at the eat-spaces loop (line 122) and the ',' check (line 130).

evidence.snippet:
x.bv_val += tu->bv_len + 1;
			x.bv_len -= tu->bv_len + 1;
evidence.reason: Identical unguarded wrap in the thisUpdate branch: the scan 'for ( ; tu->bv_len < x.bv_len; tu->bv_len++ )' (line 107) exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len when no closing quote is present, and the unsigned subtraction wraps x.bv_len while advancing x.bv_val past the end of the buffer. Trigger: '{thisUpdate "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA}' (37 bytes); the line-100 check 'if ( !x.bv_len || x.bv_val[0] != '"' )' validates only the opening quote, not the closing one, so the out-of-bounds reads at lines 122 and 130 are reached.

assumptions: ber_len_t (the type of berval.bv_len) is unsigned, as in OpenLDAP (ber_uint_t); the wraparound analysis depends on this.
The 'in' berval is non-NULL and its bv_len reflects the actual allocated buffer; this function is the trust-boundary intake point for the attribute value, so no caller-side validation is credited.
The value buffer may or may not be NUL-terminated at its end; the OOB read at the wrapped x.bv_val occurs one byte past the last in-bounds byte either way.
limitations: strncasecmp calls (lines 35, 52, 83) can read up to one byte past the shrinking x window when x is a keyword prefix, but that byte is always the in-bounds final '}' pinned by line 21, which mismatches every keyword character — not an out-of-bounds access.
The pair check 'is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1]' (line 70) reads at most index x.bv_len, which is the in-bounds '}' position; it can never spuriously match '"' and cannot push is->bv_len past x.bv_len.

The unescape loop (lines 147-155) writes at most ni.bv_len-1 bytes plus a NUL inside a ni.bv_len+1 allocation, and is unreachable with a wrapped x.bv_len because line 139 returns first; no write overflow found.
If slap_sl_malloc (line 148) fails, ni.bv_val is NULL and line 153 dereferences it; this requires allocation failure an attacker cannot directly induce, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.
tu is never validated as a well-formed UTC time string; the function only locates the quoted slice. This is a validation gap with no memory-safety sink inside this code and is not counted.

Impact is limited to denial of service / out-of-bounds reads: the OOB bytes are only compared against ' ' and ',' and never returned to the attacker. However, if the byte past the buffer is ' ' or ',', the wrapped huge x.bv_len can drive substantially longer out-of-bounds scans.

verdict.summary: This function is a thin, lock-balanced dispatcher over an attacker-supplied packet batch. All in-code guards are total: the dl_type validator branch covers every 16-bit value with an explicit else-refill (no fail-open), the only local bound is the pre-mutation batch-size snapshot 'const size_t pb_cnt = dp_packet_batch_size(pb);' taken before any refill can alter the count, and the mutex pair 'ovs_mutex_lock(&ipf->ipf_lock);' / 'ovs_mutex_unlock(&ipf->ipf_lock);' is balanced with no intervening return/break/goto. Every security-critical sink reachable from packet bytes (fragment parsing, reassembly bounds, ownership, eviction/expiry accounting) lives inside ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag and the batch iteration macro, none of which are quotable in the given code, so no defect can be confirmed here. Latent items — the missing return statement/declared return type, unchecked ipf/pb pointers, int-vs-size_t index width, lock-free validation, and attacker-driven fragment retention — are recorded as limitations because their enforcing or triggering statements are not present in this code and none is reachable from data this function itself receives.

assumptions: DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH iterates exactly pb_cnt times, keeps pb_idx within [0, original batch size) even as successful extracts shrink the batch, and performs the macro-level index comparison; its source is not given.

dp_packet_batch_size returns the element count of a well-formed, consistent batch; batch consistency (e.g., NETDEV_MAX_BURST-style cap enforced at insertion) is enforced by code outside this function.
ipf_is_valid_v4_frag and ipf_is_valid_v6_frag perform complete L3 header and length bounds checks on pkt and return ownership-neutral booleans; their source is not given.

ipf_handle_frag returns false without consuming pkt, and on true takes ownership of pkt for later reassembly or expiry via ipf_expire/ipf_release; both the ownership contract and any outstanding-fragment cap live outside this code.
ovs_mutex_lock/ovs_mutex_unlock are the standard OVS non-recursive lock primitives with no failure path that skips the unlock.

verdict.summary: PipeSocketHandler::listen copies an unvalidated, arbitrarily long endpoint name from a public API parameter into the fixed 108-byte sockaddr_un::sun_path stack buffer via strcpy with no length check, causing an attacker-controlled stack buffer overflow (one-past-limit at exactly 108 characters, unbounded beyond that).

evidence.reason: strcpy writes pipePath (unbounded std::string from endpoint.name(), a public API parameter) plus a NUL terminator into the fixed-size sun_path member of the stack-local sockaddr_un 'local'. No length check exists anywhere in the function; a name of exactly 108 chars overflows by one (NUL), and longer names overwrite the rest of the stack frame, enabling memory corruption. The subsequent unlink also reads a possibly unterminated sun_path.

evidence.snippet: string pipePath = endpoint.name();
evidence.reason: Taint origin: attacker-influenced endpoint.name() crosses a trust boundary into an unconstrained std::string that flows unvalidated to the strcpy sink at line 15; the only prior branch (line 5) checks map membership, not length.

assumptions: sizeof(sockaddr_un::sun_path) is assumed to be 108 bytes as on Linux (POSIX requires at least 92); regardless of the exact width, no check against any width is present in the code.
FATAL_FAIL is assumed to throw/abort on negative return values; it does not bound pipePath.
initServerSocket(fd) is assumed to only configure socket options; nothing in the given code shows it constrains pipePath.
Callers of this public method are untrusted per the analysis rules, so no external validation of endpoint.name() is credited.
limitations: Secondary candidate: unlink(local.sun_path) deletes an attacker-named filesystem path before bind (the standard stale-socket pattern, but with an unvalidated name it gives arbitrary file deletion, CWE-22-adjacent); kept as secondary since the memory-safety defect is decisive.
Trailing uninitialized bytes of 'local' are passed to bind via sizeof(sockaddr_un); the kernel treats the path as NUL-terminated, so exposure of stack garbage is minimal (CWE-908-class, low impact).

fd is leaked (never closed) on the FATAL_FAIL throw paths after socket() succeeds, and the return of ::listen(fd, 5) is unchecked; no attacker-driven exhaustion path is demonstrated, so treated as a robustness issue.
TOCTOU window between unlink and bind could be raced by another local process to pre-place a file at the path; this requires a hostile local actor and is superseded by the direct overflow.

verdict.summary: listen() copies the caller-supplied endpoint name into the fixed 108-byte sockaddr_un.sun_path with strncpy and no length check; a path of length >= sizeof(sun_path) is silently truncated and left without a NUL terminator, so the subsequent unlink(local.sun_path) and chmod(local.sun_path, ...) perform out-of-bounds stack reads past the end of 'local' and act on an uncontrolled, non-terminated path.

evidence.snippet:

  unlink(local.sun_path);
evidence.reason: strncpy with n == sizeof(sun_path) writes no NUL terminator when pipePath.size() >= sizeof(sun_path) (boundary: exactly 108 chars; one-past: 109). No check of pipePath.size() exists anywhere in the function, so unlink() (and the chmod() on line 21) call strlen on an unterminated stack buffer, reading past the end of 'local' and passing an uncontrolled stack fragment as a filesystem path — the OOB read sink for the unchecked copy.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL is a macro defined outside this code and is assumed to abort/throw on -1 or error returns; its exact semantics are unverifiable here.
sizeof(sockaddr_un::sun_path) assumed 108 per the Linux/POSIX definition; the defect holds for any fixed member size.
The SocketEndpoint parameter is the trust-boundary entry point; its caller's validation, if any, is outside this code and cannot be relied on.
limitations: fd leak if FATAL_FAIL aborts between socket() and return — resource leak with no demonstrated exhaustion path.

The unsigned subtraction wraps to SIZE_MAX, so the loop executes unboundedly and `memset(&die->attr_values[i], ...)` plus `parse_attr_value`'s output slot `&die->attr_values[i]` and the read of `&abbrev->defs[i]` index far past the end of their heap allocations, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write / memory corruption reachable from a malicious input file.

		memset(&die->attr_values[i], 0, sizeof(die->attr_values[i]));
evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned underflow in the loop bound. `abbrev->count` is attacker-influenced data parsed from the file's .debug_abbrev section; when count == 0, `abbrev->count - 1` wraps to SIZE_MAX, the condition `i < SIZE_MAX` holds, and the loop performs unbounded writes via memset (and via `&die->attr_values[i]` / `&abbrev->defs[i]` at lines 9-10) past the allocated arrays. No statement in the given code checks `abbrev->count > 0` or rewrites the comparison as `i + 1 < abbrev->count`; the guard is absent on the only path to the sinks.

evidence.snippet:

			&die->attr_values[i], hdr, debug_str, debug_str_len, big_endian);
evidence.reason: Same underflowed index `i` reaches two more array-access sinks: `&abbrev->defs[i]` is read and `&die->attr_values[i]` is passed as parse_attr_value's output slot. With count == 0 the loop never terminates within the arrays' bounds, so these become out-of-bounds heap accesses driven entirely by attacker-supplied DWARF data.

assumptions: `abbrev->count` is unsigned (size_t-like); if it were signed, count == 0 would still make `count - 1` == -1 and, compared against unsigned i, the loop would still run essentially forever, so the defect holds under either signedness.
The allocation size of `die->attr_values[]` and `abbrev->defs[]` is not shown; regardless of their allocated size, an unbounded sequential index walk corrupts memory or crashes.

Whether `parse_attr_value` clamps `buf` to `buf_end` or can return NULL is not visible in the given code; `buf_end - buf` on line 9 is therefore an unverified length computation (potential wrap if buf > buf_end), recorded as assumption rather than a confirmed finding.

The reachability of `abbrev->count == 0` in the upstream abbrev decoder cannot be quoted from the given code; per guard-anchoring rules this code is judged as the last line of defense for the value it consumes, and the check is absent here.
`die->count` is assumed to be pre-initialized before parse_die; its initialization is outside the given snippet.
limitations: Candidate C2/C4 (`buf_end - buf` wrapping, parse_attr_value returning NULL/beyond buf_end) could not be confirmed or refuted from the given code alone since parse_attr_value's body is not shown.
The `count - 1` off-by-one at count == 1 (zero iterations, last attribute slot never filled) is a benign boundary case with no security effect observed in this snippet.

verdict.summary: ReadTGAImage reads the TGA image-ID/comment without validating the ReadBlob return count, so a truncated file leaves the heap-allocated comment buffer partially uninitialized; the uninitialized bytes are then NUL-terminated and stored via SetImageProperty as the image 'comment' property, disclosing process heap memory in output metadata.

evidence.reason: The return value of ReadBlob (number of bytes actually read) is assigned to count but never checked, unlike the header read ('if ((count != 1) || ... ThrowReaderException') and the pixel reads ('if (ReadBlob(image,2,pixels) != 2) ThrowReaderException'). With an attacker-supplied truncated file (e.g., 18-byte header with id_length=255 and no trailing bytes), ReadBlob returns fewer bytes than id_length, leaving comment[count..id_length-1] as uninitialized heap memory, which is then NUL-terminated and published as the image comment property (CWE-908 heap info disclosure; root cause is the unchecked short read, CWE-20).

assumptions: AcquireImageColormap rejects colors==0 or colors exceeding MaxColormapSize and returns MagickFalse; the given code only checks that return ('if (AcquireImageColormap(image,image->colors,exception) == MagickFalse) ThrowReaderException(...)'). QueueAuthenticPixels validates the row/column arguments and returns NULL out of range (external); the in-code offset/base logic was independently verified to keep 'real' within [0,rows-1].
ReadBlobByte returns EOF (-1) on failure (external); this makes the unchecked 8-bit index a robustness issue rather than an out-of-bounds access in this code.
AcquireQuantumMemory does not zero the allocation (malloc-like); this is required for the uninitialized-comment finding to hold.

For PseudoClass images with bits_per_pixel 24/32, SetPixelIndex(image,index,q) writes a stale index (0 or a leftover 15/16-bit value); cosmetic only.

In ping mode ('if (image_info->ping != MagickFalse) { (void) CloseBlob(image); return(image); }') a PseudoClass image with colormap_type!=0 is returned with image->colors set but colormap not yet allocated; any consequence depends on external consumers of the pinged image.

verdict.summary: parallels_open is the trust-boundary intake point for Parallels disk images and sizes both a heap allocation and a file read directly from the attacker-controlled header field catalog_entries. The only bound present is `if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4)`, which still permits 536,870,911 catalog entries, i.e. a ~2 GiB g_malloc and a ~2 GiB bdrv_pread, even when the image file itself is only ~40 bytes, because no check relates the claimed catalog size to the actual file size before the allocation and read. A hostile image with catalog_entries = 0x1FFFFFFF (exactly INT_MAX/4, which passes the `>` check) forces a ~2 GiB allocation — g_malloc aborts the process on failure — plus a ~2 GiB read attempt before any failure path, yielding an attacker-reachable memory/IO exhaustion denial of service (CWE-400). All arithmetic and loop/indexing on catalog_size are otherwise correctly bounded (no overflow: 536870911*4 = 2147483644 fits in int/32-bit), so the defect is purely the unvalidated resource-amplification relative to the file, not memory corruption.

The only bound is `if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4)` above, which passes for catalog_entries = 0x1FFFFFFF. Trigger: a ~40-byte hostile image with valid magic/version and catalog_entries = 0x1FFFFFFF reaches these lines and forces a ~2 GiB allocation (g_malloc aborts on failure) and a ~2 GiB read attempt — uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400).

The only guard on it is the INT_MAX/4 comparison quoted here, which prevents integer overflow in `catalog_size * 4` but still admits up to 536,870,911 entries (~2 GiB of allocation/read) regardless of the real file size; no statement checks the catalog size against the image file's actual length.

Whether a non-negative short read (partially uninitialized `ph` or `catalog_bitmap`, CWE-457) is possible cannot be determined from this code and is therefore not relied upon for any finding.

If bdrv_pread can return a non-negative short count, `ph` and the catalog bitmap would be partially uninitialized; this depends on block-layer behavior outside the given code and is recorded as an assumption rather than a finding.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses the caller-supplied column 'col' in pointer arithmetic 'p + col' on the current line fetched by ml_get_curline(), without ever validating col against the line length. When col exceeds the line length (e.g., a column past end-of-line), mb_head_off(p, p + col) dereferences memory beyond the line's NUL terminator, causing an attacker-influenced out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS, possible info exposure).

p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: The current line 'p' (attacker-controlled file text of arbitrary length, possibly empty) and the unbounded parameter 'col' are combined at line 17: 'mb_head_off(p, p + col)' reads bytes at p + col. No statement in the function compares col to the line length (the only guards are 'if (!redrawing())' and 'if (has_mbyte)'), so col == strlen(p)+1 or greater makes p + col point past the terminating NUL, producing an out-of-bounds read whenever a past-end-of-line column value reaches this function.

assumptions: colnr_T is an unsigned integer type (as in the original codebase); negative col values are therefore impossible, so the defect triggers via col > line length, not sign confusion.

mb_head_off(base, p) dereferences the byte at p and neighboring bytes to locate a multi-byte character head; this is its documented contract in this codebase and is not verifiable from the given snippet.

The concrete runtime path that delivers col > strlen(p) (e.g., cursor/virtual-column state beyond end-of-line when display_dollar is invoked for the '$' replacement indicator) lies in the callers, which are outside the given code; per this code's role as the last line of defense at the sink, the missing length check is attributed here.
limitations: curs_columns(FALSE) is called with a possibly out-of-range cursor column; any OOB behavior inside curs_columns itself cannot be audited from the given snippet and is not counted as a finding.

A potential unsigned underflow at 'w_cursor.col -= mb_head_off(...)' is only reachable if mb_head_off returns a value greater than col, which presupposes the already-reported out-of-bounds condition; it is subsumed by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder clamps only the upper bounds of the seed coordinates (x >= im->sx, y >= im->sy) and never checks y < 0, so a caller-supplied negative y flows directly into the row-index arguments of gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel as an out-of-range index, and into the self-recursion in the 'Below' branch, which advances y by only 1 per frame; choosing y as low as INT_MIN yields a recursion chain roughly 2^31 frames deep that exhausts the stack, and (if the pixel accessors are unchecked) out-of-bounds row reads/writes.

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: y is used as the row index in gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel although only its upper bound is normalized (lines 16-18); no statement in the function rejects y < 0, so boundary inputs y = -1 through INT_MIN reach these memory-access calls with an out-of-range negative row index.

The only y normalization present clamps just the upper boundary (y == im->sy); there is no counterpart for y < 0. The missing lower-bound check belongs here, and this same statement produces a negative y whenever a caller passes y >= sy with im->sy <= 0.

Unbounded recursion (CWE-400): the guard `if (y < ((im->sy) - 1))` is true for every negative y, and line 63 recurses with y incremented by only 1 and no depth limit, so a seed y = INT_MIN drives a chain ~2^31 frames deep, exhausting the stack before y reaches 0 (denial of service); each level also passes the still-negative y into the pixel accessors.

assumptions: The bodies of gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel are not part of the given code, so whether they internally reject out-of-range y cannot be quoted; if they do not, the negative-y trigger additionally causes out-of-bounds row reads/writes (CWE-125/787) at lines 21/24/33/36, while if they do (returning -1 / no-op) the unbounded-recursion stack exhaustion still follows from this code alone.
im->sx and im->sy are treated as attacker-supplied (decoded image dimensions); nothing in the given code constrains them to be positive.
Any wrapper (e.g., a language binding) that pre-validates x/y is outside this code and is not treated as a guard; this function is the intake point for its own parameters.
limitations: x < 0 is not exploitable: `for (i = x; i >= 0; i--)` never executes and `if (leftLimit == -1) { return; }` exits before any pixel access.
`i = (x + 1)` cannot overflow because `if (x >= im->sx) { x = im->sx - 1; }` caps x at sx-1 and the loop terminates at `i < im->sx`.
For in-bounds y the recursion depth is bounded by the image height; the unbounded-depth case requires the missing y < 0 validation identified above.

verdict.summary: ex_copy implements the :copy/:t Ex-command handler and consumes the command's line addresses (line1, line2, n) with no validation against the buffer: no check that 1 <= line1 <= line2 <= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count and none that n is within [0, line count]. The only bound in the code, 'while (line1 <= line2)', compares the two tainted values to each other, not to the buffer. Consequently line1 (possibly 0, negative, or past the last line) reaches ml_get(line1) (out-of-bounds read) and curwin->w_cursor.lnum = n reaches ml_append() with an out-of-range destination, and count = line2 - line1 + 1 can be non-positive or wrong, flowing into b_op_end.lnum and appended_lines_mark(). Trigger: an Ex command such as ':1,2t<large>' past the end of the buffer, or ':0t0' (line1 = line2 = 0).

evidence.reason: The sinks: the cursor line number is set directly from the unvalidated destination parameter 'n' (line 28) and the loop is bounded only by 'while (line1 <= line2)' (line 29), which compares two tainted addresses to each other rather than to curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count; 'ml_get(line1)' (line 33) then reads at line1, which can be 0 (e.g. ':0t0' passes 0 <= 0) or past the last line when line2 is out of range, and 'ml_append(curwin->w_cursor.lnum, ...)' (line 36) inserts at the unvalidated destination. No statement on any path bounds these values against the buffer.

Origin of the taint: line1, line2 and n are the Ex-command line addresses entering the handler across the user/script-to-command trust boundary, and 'count = line2 - line1 + 1' is computed with no check that line1 >= 1 or line1 <= line2, so count can be non-positive (line2 < line1) or over-counted (line1 == 0); this value and n then flow unguarded into b_op_end.lnum (line 10), appended_lines_mark (line 50) and the ml_get/ml_append sinks.

assumptions: linenr_T is Vim's signed long line-number type; this typedef and any MAXLNUM cap are not present in the given code.

In the full Vim program, do_one_cmd/get_address parse the Ex addresses and may clamp or reject out-of-range values (E16/E493), and memline.c's ml_get/ml_append may internally handle out-of-range line numbers; none of that is present or quotable in the given code, so it is not relied on and this code is judged as the last line of defense.
u_save(n, n + 1)'s internal range validation of n is not quotable here; only its FAIL return is checked at line 25.
limitations: The concrete memory-safety outcome at ml_get/ml_append depends on memline.c internals not shown; if modern Vim's ml_get returns an empty string for invalid lnum, the effect degrades to logic/state corruption (spurious lines, wrong marks) plus attacker-scaled loop cost rather than a raw OOB read.

The allocation-failure path 'if (p != NULL)' (line 34) silently skips a copied line while count stays fixed, desynchronizing appended_lines_mark; this requires allocation failure the attacker cannot induce and was not counted as a vulnerability.
msgmore((long)count) truncation is cosmetic.

If the surrounding Vim dispatcher does enforce range clamping upstream (likely in the shipped program), the practical exploitability is lower than the high severity assigned from this code's own view.

verdict.summary: copy_page_to_iter_pipe() repurposes a recycled pipe ring slot for a page-cache page but never initializes buf->flags: it sets buf->ops, buf->page, buf->offset and buf->len, yet no statement in the function writes buf->flags. A slot previously used by an anonymous pipe write can still carry PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE, so after an unprivileged splice(2) of one byte of a read-only file's page into the pipe, a subsequent write(2) to that pipe merges attacker bytes directly into the page cache of the read-only file. This is the Dirty Pipe vulnerability (CVE-2022-0847), enabling overwrite of cached pages of root-owned files (e.g., /etc/passwd) and local privilege escalation; the one-line fix (buf->flags = 0;) is verified absent from every path in the given code.

verdict.summary: update_topline() contains no unguarded memory, injection, or loop-bound sink. All loops are bounded by quoted in-loop guards ('if (lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count || n >= halfheight) break;', 'if (lnum <= 0 || line_count > curwin->w_height + 1) break;', 'if (n >= *so_ptr) break;') that fire before every hasFolding/botline_forw call and reject the boundary values (0, 1, one-past-limit). assumptions: w_cursor.lnum is maintained >= 1 and <= ml_line_count by cursor-check machinery (check_cursor_lnum/check_cursor_moved) outside this code; this function contains no validation of it at its own entry beyond the fold-loop break conditions.

'scrolloff' (w_p_so/p_so) values are produced by Vim's option machinery (user :set, scripts); this code performs no range validation on them, and no modeline/file-content intake for them exists in this code.
botline_forw(&loff) advances loff.lnum or loff.fill on each call, and hasFolding() returns its arguments to valid values; these contracts are external to the given code.
screen_valid, check_top_offset, diff_check_fill, scrolljump_value, validate_botline, scroll_cursor_top/halfway/bot behave per their external contracts.
