C3: 'n += loff.height' (int) could overflow only with more than 2^31 accumulated screen rows below the cursor plus a huge 'scrolloff'; not attacker-reachable here and consequences are only a wrong branch decision.
C4: the botline_forw while loop has no in-code progress guard; non-termination would require botline_forw to stall, which no input value shown in this code can cause.

C5: hasFolding is called with lnum values taken from the cursor; both fold loops' quoted break conditions reject lnum <= 0 and lnum >= ml_line_count before every call, so an invalid cursor cannot drive an out-of-range call from within this code.

verdict.summary: gdImageFillToBorder performs unbounded recursion (lines 50-51 and 73-74) and an unbounded left-seek loop (line 13) driven by unvalidated public-API coordinates (x, y) and attacker-controlled image dimensions (im->sx, im->sy). No recursion depth cap and no x/y bounds validation exist anywhere in the function. A crafted tall image (or simply a large or one-past-limit x/y argument) causes stack exhaustion or CPU exhaustion — an attacker-reachable denial of service.

evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursion: gdImageFillToBorder recurses into itself at (i, y - 1) with no depth counter or limit anywhere in the function. With a crafted image of height 200000 (im->sy attacker-controlled) and a uniform non-border background, the recursion chain descends one row per frame to a depth of ~200000 nested calls, overflowing the stack. No guard in this code caps the depth.

Second unguarded recursion sink (y + 1 direction). Combined with the y - 1 sink, when pixels are never actually painted (out-of-range x), rows y and y+1 recurse into each other indefinitely; even fully in-range, depth is bounded only by im->sy, which is attacker-controlled image geometry. No depth bound or y-range validation is present on any path.

evidence.snippet: gdImageFillToBorder (gdImagePtr im, int x, int y, int border, int color)
evidence.reason: Origin of unvalidated attacker-influenced inputs: x and y are 32-bit signed parameters of this exported public API, and im->sx/im->sy come from attacker-controlled decoded images. The only entry validation in the entire function is 'if (border < 0)' (line 8); there is no check of x or y against the image bounds, which is the root cause enabling the unbounded loop and recursion.

Unbounded loop: the left-seek loop is bounded only by 'i >= 0', not by im->sx (the function's only width bound, 'i < im->sx' at line 28, applies to a different loop). A caller-supplied x of 10^9 makes this loop execute ~10^9 GetPixel/SetPixel iterations (CPU exhaustion), and out-of-range i means pixels are never painted, so the (c != color) termination condition for the recursion never becomes true.

assumptions: gdImageGetPixel returns a default value (0) and gdImageSetPixel no-ops for out-of-range coordinates; this is enforced inside libgd, not quotable in the given code. The infinite mutual-recursion trigger (out-of-range x ping-pong between rows) depends on this assumption; the tall-image stack-exhaustion and large-x CPU-exhaustion triggers do not.
Callers of this exported function may pass arbitrary int x/y; the function is the public API intake point, so its parameters are attacker-influenced per the trust-boundary rule.
im->sx and im->sy are set from attacker-controlled image-file dimensions when this operates on a decoded image.
limitations: No memory-corruption defect is provable from the given code alone: the actual pixel-array indexing happens inside gdImageGetPixel/gdImageSetPixel, whose bounds safety cannot be quoted here.
The signed overflow 'x + 1' at line 28 with x = INT_MAX is undefined behavior but is subsumed by the same missing-validation root cause (CWE-400) and was not reported separately.
The missing 'color < 0' check (asymmetric with the guarded 'border < 0') was folded into the recursion-termination analysis rather than reported as a standalone finding.

verdict.summary: uECC_sign_with_k consumes the caller-controlled length hash_size (unsigned, unbounded at entry) and passes it, together with the fixed stack buffer tmp[uECC_MAX_WORDS] and the attacker-derived message_hash, directly to bits2int() with no size validation anywhere in the function. No statement between the parameter declaration and the call bounds hash_size against the curve size or tmp's capacity, so an oversized hash_size reaches the copy sink and can overflow the fixed stack array / read past message_hash (stack corruption). The counterfactual clamp (reject/limit hash_size to BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) before the call) is absent from the code on every path, confirming the missing-check defect.

evidence.snippet:
bits2int(tmp, message_hash, hash_size, curve);
    uECC_vli_modAdd(s, tmp, s, curve->n, num_n_words); /* s = e + r*d */
evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-influenced length hash_size (declared unsigned at entry) is handed to bits2int() which converts message_hash into the fixed-size stack array tmp (uECC_word_t tmp[uECC_MAX_WORDS], line 8). No guard anywhere in the function bounds hash_size against curve->num_bytes, BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits), or uECC_MAX_WORDS before this call; a caller-supplied hash_size exceeding the curve octet length reaches this copy unchecked, enabling a stack buffer overflow of tmp / out-of-bounds read of message_hash. Root cause: missing validation of an externally supplied size (CWE-129 / CWE-120).

Origin of the tainted value: hash_size enters as an unsigned 32-bit parameter of the signing API with no constraint at the trust boundary; this unbounded length is the value that reaches the bits2int sink at line 70 without any intervening check.

assumptions: The helper bits2int() may internally clamp num_bytes to the curve's octet count; that clamp is not present in the given code, so per guard-anchoring it is not relied upon. If it exists in the unshown callee, the overflow is prevented and this finding degrades to a hardening issue.

curve (num_words, num_n_words, num_n_bits, num_bytes) is assumed to come from trusted internal curve constants; this code performs no validation of curve fields, so all curve-derived bounds are assumptions.
Contracts of the unshown helpers regularize_k(), EccPoint_mult(), uECC_generate_random_int(), and the uECC_vli_* primitives are assumed memory-safe; their internals cannot be quoted here.
The signature output buffer is assumed by callers to be 2*curve->num_bytes bytes; this code cannot verify that contract.
limitations: For curves whose num_n_bits is not a multiple of 8, lines 61/63 (bcopy/uECC_vli_bytesToNative of private_key with BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) bytes) may read one byte past a num_bytes-sized key; the required relation between num_n_bits and num_bytes is not derivable from the given code, so this candidate is not confirmed.
Line 66 's[num_n_words - 1] = 0;' would write out of bounds if num_n_words were 0; only a curve with num_n_bits == 0 triggers it and no such curve is producible by this code.
Line 23 validates k with mixed word counts (isZero over num_words, cmp over num_n_words); no memory-safety sink for the mismatched high words was found on any path in this function.
If g_rng_function is NULL, blinding is replaced by the constant 1 (lines 43-45), reducing side-channel resistance; this is documented degradation, not a memory-safety or authorization defect.

verdict.summary: This util-linux mount main() consumes only CLI arguments. Every security-relevant path is guarded: the non-root restricted-mode allowlist (`mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) && !strchr("hlLUVvpris", c) && c != MOUNT_OPT_TARGET && c != MOUNT_OPT_SOURCE` -> exit_non_root) runs before the switch on every getopt iteration, blocking non-root use of -T (custom fstab), -o (arbitrary options), -t (helper selection), -a (mount all), and all propagation/bind flags; the argc==1/argc==2/else-usage chain prevents any argv out-of-bounds indexing; xasprintf uses only a constant `%s` format (no format-string injection); and the source/target combination checks for restricted users (exit_non_root(NULL)) are fail-closed. The strchr-terminator edge case (c==0) is unreachable because every longopt entry has a NULL flag field. No guard tested failed at its boundary values.

assumptions: mnt_context_is_restricted() correctly distinguishes root/non-root callers; this code relies on it for the restricted-mode guard but the guard itself is present and quoted.
exit_non_root(), usage(), print_version(), and err() terminate the process; if usage() returned, case 'h'/'V' would continue with default state (cosmetic only).
getopt_long behaves per POSIX: optind <= argc, and returns 0 only when an option's flag field is non-NULL (all are NULL here).

libmount setters (mnt_context_set_source/target/append_options) copy their string arguments before the frees of srcbuf; the free(srcbuf) after mnt_context_set_source(cxt, srcbuf) assumes a deep copy in libmount.
The MS_* mount flag constants fit in unsigned long oper; no overflow possible from fixed-constant ORs.
limitations: Case 'p' (--pass-fd) prints 'warnx(_("--pass-fd is no longer supported"))' and continues; deprecation notice with no security effect.

-L/-U xasprintf does not escape embedded double quotes in optarg, producing a malformed LABEL=/UUID= source string; within this code the value only flows into mnt_context_set_source (libmount parsing) and non-root mounts remain subject to libmount fstab user-entry authorization, so no vulnerability is demonstrable in this code alone.
This analysis covers only main(); sinks inside libmount (helper exec, fstab parsing) are outside the given code and treated as assumptions.

verdict.summary: Ghostscript search_impl: all memory-access sinks are guarded by quoted, on-path checks. The size-vs-subject guard `if (size > r_size(op1))` plus the `if (size == 0) goto found;` diversion keep the scan loop and memcmp strictly inside the subject string (exactly count+1 iterations, offsets 0..r_size(op1)-size); the found-path rsize arithmetic (including the backward `op[-3].tas.rsize -= count + size;`) provably cannot underflow or leave the original buffer, and every pushed result slot is initialized. This bound cannot be quoted from the given code.

The macro body is not present in the given code, so this bound cannot be quoted here.

carve_deps_at_address, va2pa, resolve_symbols_off, get_lib_name, create_path_to_index are external and not analyzed.

verdict.summary: In issuerAndThisThisUpdateCheck (GSER parser for LDAP certificate syntax values), the issuer-string and thisUpdate-string scan loops can terminate without finding a closing double quote, leaving the scan length equal to the entire remaining length. The subsequent pointer/length update (x.bv_val += len + 1; x.bv_len -= len + 1) then subtracts one more than x.bv_len from an unsigned ber_len_t, wrapping it to a huge value while advancing x.bv_val one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied input buffer. The do-while loop then performs out-of-bounds heap reads (space-eating, ',' checks, strncasecmp) driven entirely by client-supplied data, causing denial of service and potential out-of-bounds disclosure. No check exists on any path that the closing quote was found before the subtraction.

evidence.reason: The scan loop can exit via its condition with is->bv_len == x.bv_len (no closing quote in the remainder, e.g. input "{issuer rdnSequence:\"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa}"); there is no check for termination before the update. Then x.bv_len -= is->bv_len + 1 underflows the unsigned ber_len_t to a huge value and x.bv_val advances one past the end of the input buffer, so all subsequent x.bv_val[0]/strncasecmp reads in the do-while loop are out-of-bounds heap reads controlled by attacker data (CWE-191 leading to CWE-125).

If no closing quote exists in the remainder (e.g. "{issuer rdnSequence:\"x\",thisUpdate \"01234567890123Z}"), the loop exits with tu->bv_len == x.bv_len. The only guard checks a minimum length (tu->bv_len < 15), which passes, so x.bv_len -= tu->bv_len + 1 underflows the unsigned length to a huge value and x.bv_val moves one past the buffer end; subsequent parsing reads out of bounds (same CWE-191 root cause, second sink).

assumptions: ber_len_t is an unsigned integer type (consistent with the code's use of plain subtraction and loop conditions that would be unsafe if signed), so x.bv_len -= len + 1 wraps to a huge value rather than going negative.
in->bv_val points to exactly in->bv_len readable bytes; STRLENOF is a compile-time strlen; the literal at the length check is 38 characters, so in->bv_len >= 38 past that check.
This function is an LDAP syntax validator invoked on client-supplied attribute values, i.e., it is the trust-boundary intake point; nothing outside this code pre-validates the GSER string.
limitations: ber_dupbv_x() and slap_sl_malloc() return values are not checked, but failure requires allocation failure an attacker cannot directly induce; not counted as a vulnerability.

The read is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1] at line 70 was edge-tested: at is->bv_len == x.bv_len-1 it reads x.bv_val[x.bv_len], which is the final '}' guaranteed in-bounds by the line-21 check, so that specific read is not out of bounds.

The dquote-collapse copy loop's potential one-past read (src++ when a quote is the last char) is unreachable because a valid parse cannot end in an unmatched quote; strings ending in a double-dquote pair without a terminator instead take the confirmed underflow path.
Exploit impact beyond denial of service (crash or prolonged OOB scanning) depends on heap layout, not on this code; no write past the buffer was found.

verdict.summary: eval7() is an expression-atom parser; every direct use of attacker-influenced parsed bytes inside this function is guarded by quotable checks (`if (len <= 0) ret = FAIL;` before eval_func/eval_variable, `len == 4`/`len == 5` bounds before STRNCMP, the leading-'.' invalid-expression check). All remaining sinks (get_reg_contents, get_lambda_tv/pt_func deref, get_name_len's alias, eval7_leader, eval1 recursion) have their preconditions enforced in callee functions outside the given code; no guard omission within this function yields a provable attacker-reachable memory-safety or injection defect.

get_name_len() initializes *alias on every path, including failure; otherwise the `if (alias != NULL) s = alias;` and `vim_free(alias);` uses would read/free an uninitialized pointer.
get_lambda_tv() returning OK implies rettv->v_type == VAR_PARTIAL with non-NULL v_partial->pt_func; the deref `ufunc_T *ufunc = rettv->vval.v_partial->pt_func;` is unguarded in this code.

After the Vim9 '@' error branches (`emsg_invreg(**arg);` / `semsg(_(e_syntax_error_at_str), *arg);`), `ret` remains OK while rettv->v_type stays VAR_UNKNOWN; the value flows into handle_subscript/eval7_leader. verdict.summary: input_bmp_reader is the intake point for untrusted BMP files. It reads the attacker-controlled header field biSize ('Bitmap_File_Head.biSize = ToL(&buffer[0x00]);') and, in the BMP v4/v5 branch, calls ReadOK(fd, buffer, Bitmap_File_Head.biSize - 4) with biSize constrained to 108 or 124, i.e. a 104- or 120-byte copy into the fixed 64-byte stack buffer 'unsigned char buffer[64];'. No check anywhere bounds the copy length to sizeof(buffer), so a BMP with biSize=108 or 124 overflows the stack buffer by 40-56 bytes with fully attacker-controlled file content.

evidence.reason: Sink and missing-check site: biSize is attacker-controlled file data; this branch admits exactly biSize=108 and biSize=124, then copies biSize-4 = 104 or 120 bytes into the 64-byte stack buffer. The branch condition itself selects the overflowing lengths and no statement in the function compares the read length to sizeof(buffer)/64, so the overflow is unguarded on the only path to this sink.

evidence.snippet: unsigned char buffer[64];
evidence.reason: Origin of the violated bound: the destination of the line-193 ReadOK copy is a fixed 64-byte stack array, while the copy length reaches 104/120 bytes for biSize=108/124, producing a 40-56 byte attacker-controlled stack overwrite.

assumptions: ReadOK(fd, dst, len) performs a read of len bytes into dst (its body is not in the given code); this is the standard autotrace helper and the only reading primitive used.
ToL/ToS decode little-endian 32/16-bit values from the byte buffer; Bitmap_Head and Bitmap_File_Head are file-scope structures.
ReadColorMap, ReadImage, ReadChannelMasks, setMasksDefault and at_bitmap_init are not part of the given code, so sinks located inside them cannot be verified here.

biClrUsed is only validated when biBitCnt <= 8 ('if (Bitmap_Head.biClrUsed > 256 && Bitmap_Head.biBitCnt <= 8)'); for 16/24/32 bpp it is passed unvalidated to ReadImage, but ReadImage's use of it is not in the given code.

The '(unsigned short)' casts of biWidth/biHeight at the final at_bitmap_init call can truncate large dimensions (e.g. 65537 -> 1); the security effect depends on at_bitmap_init/ReadImage, which are not shown, and truncation under-reports relative to the storage ReadImage allocated.
fseek(fd, bfOffs, SEEK_SET) ignores its return value; a failed seek only changes which bytes ReadImage subsequently reads and has no memory-safety effect in this code.

verdict.summary: jsP_dumpsyntax only reads prog->type, dispatches to internal AST printers, and conditionally emits a constant newline. The AST node contents printed by pstmlist/pstm originate from parsed source text and could in principle cause issues inside those functions (e.g., string handling), but those functions are outside the given code and cannot be analyzed.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found in this code. All restricted-user (non-root) authorization gates are present, precede their sinks, and edge-test cleanly: the option gate 'if (mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) && !strchr("hlLUVvpris", c) && c != MOUNT_OPT_TARGET && c != MOUNT_OPT_SOURCE) exit_non_root(...)' runs before the switch on the only path, rejecting every privileged option including invalid options (fail-closed) and the enum-valued --make-* flags; positional-arg gates (exit_non_root when restricted users combine source and target, or supply two operands) all precede the argv[0]/argv[1] uses. The remaining risk surface (LABEL/UUID spec quoting, final mount(2) authorization, fstab parsing) lives in libmount and helper functions not shown, and is recorded in assumptions/limitations rather than asserted as guarded.

assumptions: xasprintf terminates the process on allocation failure (util-linux convention); not verifiable from the given code.

mnt_context_set_source/set_target/append_options duplicate their string arguments, so free(srcbuf) after set_source (lines 151, 157) causes no dangling pointer inside libmount; not verifiable from the given code.

usage(), exit_non_root(), and err() terminate the process; if usage() returned, the 'h' and default cases would fall through with attacker-controlled context, but no exit statement is quotable in the given code.

mnt_context_is_restricted(cxt) correctly reports non-root invocation; the actual mount(2) privilege decision and fstab user-option enforcement are performed inside mnt_context_mount(), which is external to this code.
append_fstab, print_all, mount_all, sanitize_paths, table_parser_errcb, and close_stdout behave as their util-linux contracts specify; none are inspectable here.

--pass-fd (-p) is accepted but only prints a warning and performs no action; no security effect.
An invalid option (c == '?') from a restricted user triggers exit_non_root(option_to_longopt('?',...)); this is a rejection, not a bypass.

The definitive mount authorization is delegated to mnt_context_mount() and libmount; if that library has a flaw, this file would not contain the defect, and such a flaw cannot be audited from the given code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The apparent integer-underflow trap `i < abbrev->count - 1` is fully guarded by the quoted `if (abbrev->count)` on the only path to the subtraction, which rejects the boundary value count==0 (and count==1 yields zero iterations with no wrap). The remaining concerns — the loop skipping the last attribute spec, missing re-validation of buf against buf_end after parse_attr_value, attr_values capacity, and the signedness of abbrev->count — cannot be triggered by any value this code itself produces, and their enabling preconditions lie in code not given (callee return contract, caller-side allocation and struct definitions), so they are recorded as assumptions/limitations rather than confirmed defects.

assumptions: The declared type of abbrev->count is unsigned (its declaration is not in the given code); if it were a signed type, `if (abbrev->count)` would not exclude negative values and the loop bound could wrap, but no statement in this code can produce a negative count.

die->attr_values and abbrev->defs have capacity >= abbrev->count, established by the caller; this code performs no capacity check of its own, but no trigger demonstrating insufficient capacity is constructible from the given code.

parse_attr_value honors the length argument it receives (this code always passes the exact remaining length buf_end - buf) and therefore never returns a pointer beyond buf_end nor dereferences a NULL buf; its contract is not quotable here.
debug_str strings referenced by attribute->string.content are NUL-terminated within debug_str_len by the callee; strdup(comp_dir) relies on that contract.
The internal caller of this static function resets/initializes die (including die->count) and passes buf <= buf_end on entry.
limitations: Off-by-one (non-security): the loop condition `i < abbrev->count - 1` parses only count-1 of count attribute specs, silently dropping the last attribute of every DIE (e.g., a missed DW_AT_comp_dir or DW_AT_stmt_list). All array accesses stay in bounds; the effect is missing analysis data only.

No check that buf is non-NULL or <= buf_end after parse_attr_value before the next `buf_end - buf`; would become a defect only if the callee (outside the given code) can return NULL or an out-of-range pointer on malformed DWARF.

A very large abbrev->count (near the width maximum) would produce a multi-billion-iteration loop (potential CWE-400), but reaching it requires a multi-gigabyte abbrev section and a successful matching allocation by the caller first; not attacker-producible through this code's own values.
A DW_AT_stmt_list constant legitimately equal to UT64_MAX is conflated with the 'unset' sentinel, causing a fail-closed dropped cache entry (informational only).

verdict.summary: The ring-buffer space check `if (new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask)` subtracts the userspace-writable, never-validated `rb->consumer_pos` from `prod_pos + len` in unsigned arithmetic. No statement in this code enforces cons_pos <= prod_pos, so a consumer page value set ahead of the producer (cons_pos = prod_pos + len - mask, or any value in (prod_pos, new_prod_pos]) makes the wrapped difference fall at or below the mask boundary and the guard passes while len exceeds the entire ring. The function then hands out a region of up to RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ bytes inside a ring that can be as small as PAGE_SIZE, and the caller's payload write goes out of bounds past the ring data area — an attacker-controlled kernel out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: The guard's own arithmetic wraps: with attacker-controlled consumer_pos in (prod_pos, prod_pos+len], new_prod_pos - cons_pos = len - m can be <= mask even when len > ring size (boundary case: mask=0xFFF, prod_pos=0, len=0x100008, cons_pos=0xFF009 gives diff=0xFFF which is not > 0xFFF, so the check passes). The reservation of len bytes from rb->data + (prod_pos & rb->mask) then exceeds the ring's data area and the caller writes size bytes out of bounds. No validation of cons_pos against prod_pos exists on any path.

evidence.snippet: cons_pos = smp_load_acquire(&rb->consumer_pos);
evidence.reason: Taint origin: rb->consumer_pos is the mmap'd, userspace-writable consumer page of the BPF ring buffer; it is loaded here with no bounds or sanity check anywhere in this function and flows directly into the wrapping subtraction on line 26 that gates memory reservation.

assumptions: rb->consumer_pos is mapped read-write into userspace (external mmap code, not in this snippet) — this is the basis for treating it as attacker-influenced; nothing in the given code constrains it either way.

The value of RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is external to the given code; it is assumed small enough that `len = round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8)` (u64 -> u32) and `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT` do not truncate and do not collide with the BUSY/DISCARD flag bits. If the macro were >= 2^32 (or >= 2^30 for flag bits), additional truncation/flag-collision defects would exist but cannot be proven from this code.

rb->data is assumed externally mapped with twice the ring size so records wrapping within the ring are contiguous; the OOB claim assumes payload writes past prod_pos&mask + available space exceed that mapping.
The BPF verifier is assumed to permit the caller to write exactly `size` bytes into the returned pointer, which is the sink that realizes the out-of-bounds write.

Security impact assumes an attacker can create a BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF map, mmap it, and load a BPF program calling bpf_ringbuf_reserve — historically reachable by unprivileged users when unprivileged BPF is enabled, otherwise by any local privileged user.
limitations: Candidate rejected as fail-safe: reading consumer_pos before acquiring the spinlock (line 11) can only observe a stale, smaller value, which makes the space check stricter, not weaker.
Candidate rejected as fail-closed: the in_nmi() trylock failure path and the huge/negative-wrapped consumer_pos values (e.g. cons_pos = 2^63) cause the guard to reject, which is safe.

Candidate unprovable: u64->u32 truncation of `len` and busy-bit collision in `hdr->len = size | BPF_RINGBUF_BUSY_BIT` depend on the RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ macro value, which is not defined in the given code.

verdict.summary: The guard `if((unsigned)strlen(dnscenv->provider_name) >= (unsigned)0xffff0000)` is intended to prevent integer overflow in the rrlen calculation, but rrlen is a uint16_t and the true wrap threshold is around 65536 - (16 + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2) (~65KB), four orders of magnitude below the guard's bound. A config-supplied provider_name of that length passes the guard, the size_t sum truncates on assignment to uint16_t (e.g. to 0), malloc(rrlen) yields a minimal buffer, and `snprintf(rr, rrlen - 1, ...)` converts 0-1 to SIZE_MAX and copies the full provider_name into it, causing a heap buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: The only guard on provider_name length rejects values >= 0xffff0000, but rrlen is uint16_t (line 19): any attacker-influenced config provider_name of length >= 65518 - 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) (~65KB, e.g. 65038 if the struct is 120 bytes) passes the guard, the size_t sum truncates on assignment (e.g. to 0), and malloc(rrlen) undersizes the buffer. The needed check (sum >= 65536, or a size_t rrlen) is absent from the code.

evidence.snippet: snprintf(rr, rrlen - 1, "%s 86400 IN TXT \"", dnscenv->provider_name);
evidence.reason: Overflow sink: when rrlen wraps to 0, `rrlen - 1` is promoted to int -1 and converted to size_t SIZE_MAX, so snprintf copies the unbounded provider_name (plus the 16-byte fixed prefix) into the malloc(0) buffer from line 50 — a heap buffer overflow. The same underflow affects lines 59, 61, and 70 via `rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)`.

assumptions: sizeof(struct SignedCert) is a fixed compile-time constant not defined in this code; for any plausible struct size the wrap threshold for rrlen (~65518 - 4*S bytes of provider_name) lies far below the 0xffff0000 guard bound, so the truncation defect holds regardless of the exact value.
dnscenv->provider_name is configuration-file-derived data crossing a trust boundary; no length or non-NULL constraint on it is present or quotable in this code.
signed_certs_count is assumed to correctly bound the dnscenv->signed_certs array (pairing established outside this code).

malloc(0) is assumed to return a non-NULL minimal allocation (typical glibc behavior), making the line 55 overflow reachable; if it returned NULL the function returns -2 but the adjacent sizes rrlen=1..N produce the uninitialized-read/size-underflow variant at lines 59-61 via strlen on an unwritten buffer.
limitations: Line 43 contains `continue` without a terminating semicolon, a syntax error that prevents the code from compiling as given; the analysis assumes the intended statement (skip the cert) and shows the guard is still insufficient even then.
provider_name == NULL causing strlen(NULL) was considered but cannot be triggered by any data visible in this code (config parsing occurs elsewhere); not counted as a vulnerability here.

Secondary effect of the same trigger: when rrlen truncates to 1, snprintf at line 55 writes nothing, strlen(rr) at line 59 reads an uninitialized malloc'd buffer and the size argument `rrlen - 1 - strlen(rr)` underflows — a CWE-908 consequence of the same root-cause truncation.

verdict.summary: The DNS record length computed as a size_t sum (strlen(provider_name) + strlen(ttl_class_type) + 4*sizeof(struct SignedCert) + 2) is truncated into the 16-bit variable rrlen. When the config-supplied provider name makes the sum exactly 65536 (mod 65536), rrlen becomes 0, malloc(0) returns a minimal chunk, and 'rrlen - 1' promotes to int -1 and converts to size_t SIZE_MAX, so snprintf copies the entire attacker-controlled provider name (about 64 KB) into the tiny allocation — a heap buffer overflow with fully attacker-chosen bytes. No statement in this code bounds the provider name length or the computed size.

evidence.reason: Sink: with rrlen truncated to 0, malloc(0) returns a minimal non-NULL chunk that passes 'if(!rr)', and the size argument 'rrlen - 1' evaluates to int -1 converted to size_t SIZE_MAX, so the snprintf writes the entire config-supplied provider_name plus the 15-byte prefix past the allocation. evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: a size_t expression (strlen of an unbounded config-supplied string plus a struct-scaled term) is assigned to uint16_t rrlen declared at line 19, truncating modulo 65536. No bound on strlen(dnscenv->provider_name) exists anywhere in this function, so the truncation to 0 (and to 1, which additionally makes strlen(rr) read an uninitialized malloc byte) is reachable from the config trust boundary.

assumptions: dnscenv->provider_name is a config-file-parsed C string; its length is not bounded by any statement in this code, so per guard-anchoring rules it is treated as unbounded attacker-influenced input.

dnscenv->signed_certs / signed_certs_count and rotated_certs / rotated_certs_count are assumed internally consistent, being set up by the same module outside this function; no divergence is producible from within this code.

verdict.summary: This static Lua parser helper (singlevar) consumes only a lexer-produced name string, fixed parser state, and the fixed '_ENV' name; it performs no raw length/index arithmetic, copying, or sink operations with attacker-controlled values in the given code. The only weak spot — the debug-only 'lua_assert(var->k != VVOID)' guarding the env lookup before luaK_indexed — has no attacker-reachable trigger: the '_ENV' lookup cannot be made to fail by any value (token, name, or script text) this function receives at runtime, since env resolution depends on parser-internal state the parsed source cannot alter. verdict.summary: display_dollar() clamps its column argument only against negative values ('colnr_T col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg;') and never bounds it against the length of the line returned by ml_get_curline(). When has_mbyte is set and col exceeds the line length, '(*mb_head_off)(p, p + col)' forms a pointer past the line's NUL terminator and dereferences out-of-bounds heap bytes, an attacker-reachable out-of-bounds read (crash / heap over-read).

p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Sink: 'p + col' is formed and passed to mb_head_off with no check that col is within the current line's length. col comes from the untrusted public-function parameter and may exceed the line's allocated buffer (line length + 1 byte); with col >= line_len + 2 the pointer lies past the NUL terminator and mb_head_off dereferences out-of-bounds heap memory. No upper-bound guard exists anywhere on the path to this sink.

evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the only validation applied to col_arg is a lower-bound clamp for negative values; positive values up to INT_MAX, including values far beyond the current line length, pass through unchanged and reach the unguarded pointer arithmetic at line 18.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed int (32-bit) as in the Vim codebase; the non-static display_dollar is a public/exported entry point whose parameter is treated as untrusted caller input.
ml_get_curline() returns a buffer holding exactly the current line's bytes plus a NUL terminator (line contents are attacker-supplied file data); no extra slack is assumed.

mb_head_off(base, p2) dereferences the byte at or immediately before p2 to locate a multibyte head; therefore p2 must not point beyond the line's NUL terminator. Its exact implementation is external to the given code and cannot be quoted here.
Behavior of curs_columns() and edit_putchar() is external and unverified; the quoted guard 'if (curwin->w_wcol < curwin->w_width)' is a screen-coordinate check, not a line-length bound.

The subtraction at line 18 cannot drive w_cursor.col negative for in-bounds col because mb_head_off returns a non-negative offset not exceeding p2 - base; dismissed as a candidate.
Severity limited to a read primitive (crash / limited heap exposure); no attacker-controlled write was identified.

verdict.summary: ReadCINImage computes the quantum pixel-buffer row size in `extent` and then explicitly discards it with `(void) extent;`, instead using `length=GetBytesPerRow(image->columns,3,image->depth,MagickTrue)` — derived from unvalidated file header fields (bits_per_pixel up to 255, arbitrary 32-bit columns) plus row padding — as the copy size in `stream=ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count)`. No statement in this code bounds `length` by the size of the `pixels` buffer, and the `count != length` check occurs only after the out-of-bounds write. A crafted CIN file with small dimensions (e.g., columns=1, rows=1, depth=8) passes all quoted guards (`image_offset < 712`, `columns*rows/8 > GetBlobSize`, `SetImageExtent`) and causes a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled file data.

evidence.reason: Missing-check site: the buffer row extent is computed and immediately discarded via `(void) extent;`, while `length` is derived from attacker-controlled image->depth (0-255 from the file's bits_per_pixel) and image->columns with row padding (MagickTrue). `length` is never compared to `extent` or to the allocated size of `pixels` on any path — the minimal one-line guard `if (length > extent) ThrowReaderException(...)` is absent from the entire function.

Sink: ReadBlobStream copies up to `length` attacker-derived bytes from the file into the heap buffer `pixels`, which was sized for the quantum extent (discarded above). The only size check, `if (count != (ssize_t) length) break;`, is performed after the write and compares against `length` itself, not the destination buffer size, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds write. Trigger: a CIN file with columns=1, rows=1, bits_per_pixel=8, image_offset=712 passes every prior guard and overflows `pixels` with file-controlled data.

Taint origin: depth, columns, and rows are taken verbatim from the file header (unsigned char and 32-bit unsigned values) with no range validation. The only quoted sanity check divides by 8 (1 bit per pixel), so at the boundary case columns=1, rows=1 it evaluates to 0 and passes for any file size; it does not bound the per-row copy length `length`, which scales with depth (up to 255) and 3 samples.

assumptions: ReadBlobStream (blob.c) copies up to `length` bytes into the caller-supplied `pixels` buffer when the image is a file-backed (non in-memory) blob; its implementation is outside the given code.

GetBytesPerRow (helper outside the given code) computes the row byte count from columns*samples*bits/8 rounded up, applying CIN row padding when the final argument is MagickTrue; the padding is what makes `length` exceed the quantum buffer extent for small dimensions.
GetQuantumPixels returns the quantum pixel buffer allocated by AcquireQuantumInfo/SetQuantumPad, sized approximately to `extent` for the current quantum settings and image->columns/depth.
External ImageMagick resource limits (policy.xml) may cap some allocation sizes; not visible in this code.
limitations: Unvalidated image->depth (0-255) and 32-bit columns/rows allow allocation amplification of roughly 8x-1500x the input file size (SetImageExtent and the quantum buffer); this is a resource-consumption concern but is typically bounded by external ImageMagick resource limits, so it is not counted as a confirmed finding.
The header string fields are copied with CopyMagickString from fixed-size ReadBlob reads into the same-size property buffer; no overflow found there.
The user-data profile path is guarded by `if (cin.file.user_length > GetBlobSize(image))` and reads into an exactly user_length-sized StringInfo; no overflow found there.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability found. The only external/hardware-derived value consumed (trans->hw_rev read from MMIO) is checked for the failure sentinel 0xffffffff before use and is only ever used as an identifier, not as an index, length, or pointer. Every failure path propagates an error via ERR_PTR (no fail-open), and each manually allocated resource (workqueue, percpu page, ICT) is freed exactly once, on paths that only reach the corresponding label after successful allocation: the workqueue allocation failure jumps to out_free_trans (skipping destroy_workqueue), and the ICT free label is only reachable from the non-MSI-X branch that allocated it. Remaining candidates (potential uninitialized read of trans_pcie->msix_enabled, free_percpu(NULL) on the alloc_percpu failure path) depend solely on allocation behavior outside this code (iwl_trans_alloc zeroing, allocation failure) that attacker input cannot influence, and at worst degrade into a detectable init failure.

assumptions: iwl_trans_alloc is assumed (but not shown in the given code) to return zeroed memory; if it did not, the read of trans_pcie->msix_enabled at 'if (trans_pcie->msix_enabled)' would be an uninitialized read (CWE-457), since no statement in this code initializes that field before the read.

free_percpu is assumed NULL-tolerant for the path where alloc_percpu failed and out_no_pci frees a NULL tso_hdr_page; this path is reachable only on allocation failure.
pcim_* / devm_* APIs are assumed to auto-release device, iomap regions, and IRQ vectors on error, so the error labels intentionally do not undo them.

cfg_trans, ent, and pdev are driver-internal/kernel-core objects, treated as trusted provenance, not raw attacker data; only the MMIO-derived hw_rev is treated as crossing a trust boundary, and it is checked in this code.
limitations: Candidate: uninitialized read of trans_pcie->msix_enabled (CWE-457) — dismissed because the triggering precondition (non-zeroing allocation) lies outside this code and cannot be induced by attacker input; worst case is wrong IRQ-mode selection that fails audibly during subsequent init, not memory corruption.
Candidate: free_percpu(NULL) on the out_no_pci path when alloc_percpu failed — dismissed because it requires an allocation failure no attacker can induce, and free_percpu tolerates NULL.

Candidate: trans->hw_rev bit manipulation 'trans->hw_rev = (trans->hw_rev & 0xfff0) | (CSR_HW_REV_STEP(trans->hw_rev << 2) << 2)' — dismissed: no memory-safety sink consumes the result; the value is only used as an identifier and in a debug print, and the 0xffffffff sentinel is rejected beforehand.
Candidate: pdev->device << 16 potential overflow — dismissed: 16-bit value promoted to int fits within 31 bits; no truncation with security effect.

Candidate: resource leak on error paths — dismissed after walking every goto chain: out_free_ict -> out_no_pci -> out_free_trans frees ICT, percpu page, workqueue, and trans in order, each only on paths where it was successfully allocated.

verdict.summary: In the GIMP brush (.gbr) decoder load_image, the allocation size is computed as 'size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;' in the 32-bit width of the attacker-controlled header fields, so dimensions that pass the 64-bit-oriented sanitize check '(G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1)' (e.g. width=262144, height=16385, bytes=1 gives a true product of 2^32+2^18) wrap to a small value. g_malloc then returns a 256 KiB (or NULL for width*height=2^32) buffer that gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect and the bytes==2 conversion loop consume for width*height*bytes (~4 GiB) elements, yielding a heap out-of-bounds read / NULL dereference from a crafted brush file. Additionally, bn_size = bh.header_size - sizeof(BrushHeader) has only a lower bound ('bh.header_size > sizeof (BrushHeader)'), allowing a ~2 GB g_new allocation to be attempted from a ~40-byte file.

size = bh.width * bh.height * bh.bytes;
  brush_buf = g_malloc (size);
evidence.reason: Root cause (CWE-190): the allocation size is the product of the 32-bit header fields evaluated in 32-bit arithmetic. The only size guard, '(G_MAXSIZE / bh.width / bh.height / bh.bytes < 1)' (line 51), promotes to 64-bit and bounds only the mathematical product; it does not reject width=262144, height=16385, bytes=1 (all pass '== 0' and '> GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE' tests on lines 47-50), whose product 4295163904 wraps to 262144. Trigger: a crafted version-2 .gbr with these dimensions and 256 KiB of data passes the read check at line 125 and reaches the sinks with an undersized buffer.

evidence.snippet:
gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect (&pixel_rgn, brush_buf,
                           0, 0, bh.width, bh.height);
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: with width=262144, height=16385, bytes=1, brush_buf holds only the wrapped size of 262144 bytes but this call consumes width*height*bytes ~ 4 GiB bytes, causing a heap out-of-bounds read (crash/DoS and potential disclosure of heap contents into the image). With width=height=65536 the wrapped size is 0, g_malloc(0) returns NULL, and this dereference crashes on NULL. No check between lines 122-263 re-validates size against bh.width*bh.height*bh.bytes.

CWE-400: bn_size is derived solely from the attacker-controlled bh.header_size with only a lower bound ('bh.header_size > sizeof (BrushHeader)', line 86) and no upper bound before g_new. A ~40-byte file with header_size = 0x7FFFFF00 makes bn_size ~2^31, attempting a ~2 GB allocation before the read-length check on line 99 can reject the file (memory exhaustion / GLib abort).

assumptions: BrushHeader/PatternHeader fields are 32-bit unsigned; the struct definitions are not in the given code, but 'bh.header_size = g_ntohl (bh.header_size);' (guint32->guint32) and the '(unsigned long int)bh.width' casts imply 32-bit fields, which is what makes the line-122 product wrap.
G_MAXSIZE and gsize are 64-bit on the target platform (LP64), so the line-51 division promotes to 64-bit and cannot bound a 32-bit-evaluated product.
g_malloc(0) returns NULL and g_malloc aborts the process on failure (GLib semantics); gimp_pixel_rgn_set_rect reads width*height*bytes bytes from the supplied buffer (PDB/plugin library behavior).
GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE is 262144 (external constant), so width=262144 passes 'bh.width > GIMP_MAX_IMAGE_SIZE'.
limitations: fd and buffer leaks on the early-return error paths (the sanitize-failure return at lines 52-59 omits close(fd); the 'Unsupported brush depth' return at lines 234-239 omits close(fd) and g_free(brush_buf)) are resource leaks with no exhaustion path in a single plug-in invocation; not counted as vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: In the source_from_buf branch, `buf[ga.ga_len++] = NUL;` advances ga_len past the terminator, so `len = ga.ga_len + (int)STRLEN(buf + ga.ga_len);` computes the line length by scanning uninitialized heap memory one byte past the written NUL. verdict.summary: nft_verdict_init accepts NFT_JUMP/NFT_GOTO verdicts targeting a bound chain on the ordinary (non-set-element) path. evidence.reason: The use-counter increment and pointer store at 'chain->use++; data->verdict.chain = chain;' are reached for a bound chain because the sole binding guard is gated on 'desc->flags & NFT_DATA_DESC_SETELEM': for a rule verdict the left operand is false, the && short-circuits, and no check of the chain's bound state exists anywhere on the path. An NFT_GOTO verdict referencing a chain created with NFT_CHAIN_BINDING via NFTA_VERDICT_CHAIN_ID therefore stores a pointer whose lifetime is governed by the binding, not by chain->use; when the binding is destroyed the stored verdict->chain dangles and is dereferenced at evaluation time (use-after-free). No check of d_name length, len, or STRLEN(path_end) exists on any path; the fix (bounds check or realloc before these copies) is absent from the code.

Its budget for the appended entry name is complen + BASENAMELEN + 1 bytes, which is smaller than legal filesystem filename lengths (NAME_MAX 255 vs BASENAMELEN 250), so the boundary-value d_name (254/255 bytes) overflows it.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is an external constant not defined in the given code; vim.h defines it as 250. The overflow trigger (d_name_len > complen + BASENAMELEN + 1) requires BASENAMELEN < NAME_MAX - 2; with BASENAMELEN = 250 and Linux NAME_MAX = 255 the trigger values are 254- and 255-byte filenames.
readdir() is assumed to return NUL-terminated names of at most NAME_MAX bytes; this bound is an OS guarantee, not enforced by any statement in this code.

Top-level external callers of unix_expandpath are assumed to pass wildoff within [0, STRLEN(path)]; all wildoff values produced inside the given code ((int)(s - buf), len + 1) are in-bounds by construction.
has_mbyte helpers (mb_ptr2len) are assumed not to advance past the NUL terminator in the copy loop; no in-code guard enforces this.
mac_precompose_path (MACOS_CONVERT block) is assumed to never grow the string beyond precomp_len; unverifiable in the given code.
limitations: The '**' recursion depth is bounded in code by quoted checks ('stardepth < 100' at lines 120 and 153) and is interruptible via ui_breakcheck()/got_int (lines 24-28), so uncontrolled recursion depth is dismissed; the inherent exponential cost of '**' expansion bounded to depth 100 is glob semantics, not a defect in this code.

STRCPY(s, dp->d_name) (line 150) and STRCPY(buf + len, path_end) (line 164) fit at the boundary values (d_name = NAME_MAX = 255) only under the BASENAMELEN = 250 assumption; no explicit length check protects them, so any filesystem allowing names longer than BASENAMELEN + 7 would make these additional overflow sites.
vim_regfree is assumed to tolerate a NULL regprog (regmatch.regprog can be NULL when EW_NOTWILD is set).

verdict.summary: In the per-channel gradient path (axis_ != -1), the kernel calls input_min_tensor.dim_size(0) and input_max_tensor.dim_size(0) after only checking that their rank is 0 or 1 ('input_min_tensor.dims() == 0 || input_min_tensor.dims() == 1'), which explicitly permits rank-0 (scalar) tensors. There is no 'dims() == 1' guard on this branch, so dim_size(0) performs an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read of the scalar tensor's shape, and the garbage value is then used as a validation decision; if it happens to equal depth, the scalar min/max tensors are passed to the per-channel gradient functor, which indexes them as depth-element vectors, producing a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: The sink: dim_size(0) is called on input_min_tensor/input_max_tensor without any check that their rank is at least 1 on this branch. A scalar min/max (dims()==0) passes the earlier rank check, so dim_size(0) indexes a nonexistent dimension, reading uninitialized/out-of-bounds shape data that then gates whether the scalar tensor is passed to the per-channel functor (heap OOB read of depth min/max values). Trigger: axis != -1 with scalar input_min and input_max.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(ctx,
                input_min_tensor.dims() == 0 || input_min_tensor.dims() == 1,
                errors::InvalidArgument(
                    "Input min tensor must have dimension 0 or 1. Received ",
                    input_min_tensor.dims(), "."));
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty state: this guard explicitly accepts rank-0 (scalar) min tensors, and the axis_ != -1 branch contains no additional 'dims() == 1' requirement before dim_size(0) is used, so the OOB/uninitialized shape read and the conditional downstream heap OOB read are reachable.

assumptions: axis_ is assumed to be an int member initialized from the op's 'axis' attribute in the (unshown) constructor; for graphs/saved models it is attacker-influenced. The guards 'axis_ >= -1' and 'axis_ == -1 || axis_ < input.shape().dims()' in the given code were verified and block negative-below-(-1) and out-of-range axes on every path.

The behavior of Tensor::dim_size / TensorShape::dim_size on rank-0 shapes is internal to TensorFlow (DCHECK-guarded only, disabled in release builds, yielding an uninitialized/OOB read of the inline dim storage); this enforcement site is outside the given code and is treated as an assumption, which is why the missing rank-1 validation in this code is the defect.
flat_inner_outer_dims<T,3>(axis_ - 1) reaches offset -1 when axis_ == 0; whether Eigen's ComputeFlatInnerOuterDims handles offset -1 is enforced outside this snippet and could not be quoted.
Input dtype consistency across gradient/input/min/max is assumed enforced by op registration type constraints outside this code.
limitations: The downstream heap OOB read in QuantizeAndDequantizePerChannelGradientFunctor additionally requires the uninitialized dim_size(0) value to coincidentally equal depth (potentially groomable), so the primary defect is the unguarded dim_size(0) call itself; worst-case unconditioned outcomes are a crash or nondeterministic validation failure.

Truncation of the int64 dim_size into 'const int depth' requires tensors with a dimension >= 2^31 elements and results in the size check rejecting (negative depth never equals a non-negative dim size), so it produces no memory corruption.

verdict.summary: thread_call pushes the target thread's roottable plus (nparams-1) attacker-supplied arguments onto the target thread's stack (lines 7 and 9), but on the failure path of sq_call it returns SQ_ERROR without removing any of them; the only cleanup (sq_pop(_thread(o),1), line 12) exists solely on the success path. A script that repeatedly invokes thread.call on a thread whose main function errors grows the target thread's stack without bound (one or more slots per call), causing unbounded memory allocation and exhaustion (CWE-400), and leaves the thread's stack top elevated so subsequent calls stage operands over stale attacker-supplied values.

evidence.reason: The only reclamation of the values pushed onto _thread(o)'s stack is sq_pop(_thread(o),1) on the success branch (line 12). The failure branch falls through to v->_lasterror = _thread(o)->_lasterror; return SQ_ERROR; with no pop, settop, or restore of the thread's stack, so every failing thread.call permanently leaks the pushed roottable and argument slots; repeated attacker-driven failing calls grow the thread stack without bound (memory exhaustion, CWE-400) and leave the thread's _top elevated for subsequent calls.

Origin of the accumulating values: this function unconditionally pushes the roottable and copies nparams-1 attacker-controlled arguments (i = 2..nparams) onto the target thread's stack; when sq_call fails, none of these are removed on any path in this code.

assumptions: stack_get(v,1) is assumed safe because native delegate closures are always invoked with at least the 'this' slot at index 1; this bound is not quotable inside the given code.

The success-path accounting relies on the external sq_call contract that it consumes exactly 'nparams' staged operands and pushes the return value; nothing in the given code enforces this, which is why the author's own sq_pop(_thread(o),1) balances only on success and nothing balances on failure.
The calling VM is assumed to reserve space for the native closure's return slot so sq_move(v,_thread(o),-1) (line 11) cannot overflow v's stack; this reservation is not present in the given code.
sq_gettop(v) is assumed to return exactly this + explicit arguments with no hidden temporaries; not verifiable from the given code.
The concrete behavior of sq_call/Execute when the target thread is suspended or mid-frame (no VM-state check exists here) depends on VM internals outside the snippet and was not counted as a finding.
limitations: Integer overflow of nparams + 3 (line 6) is infeasible: nparams is bounded by the calling VM's stack size, far below the SQInteger wrap point.

No immediate stack overflow of the reservation is possible: the function pushes exactly nparams items (1 roottable + nparams-1 args) against a reservation of nparams+3, verified at the nparams=1, nparams=0-style, and large-nparams boundaries.
The type-confusion sink on the stack slot 1 object is fully guarded by the quoted check sq_type(o) == OT_THREAD.

CWE-400 was selected as the root cause (missing reclamation on the error path causing unbounded accumulation); no memory-corruption consequence is provable from the given snippet alone, so no consequence CWE is listed.

verdict.summary: No provably reachable vulnerability exists in this code. get_recurse_data_length() walks PCRE2 compiled bytecode that is machine-generated by pcre2_compile in the same process (there is no bytecode serialization/deserialization path), and every candidate defect (unchecked OP_COND forward dereference '*alternative', cc[1]-driven advances, the unchecked optimized_cbracket[GET2(...)] index, the release-build NULL path past SLJIT_ASSERT, and theoretical int overflow of 'length') requires malformed or multi-gigabyte bytecode that this code cannot actually receive at runtime. Notably, the function contains NO in-function bounds guards on any of these sinks — the only runtime check is 'while (cc < ccend)' guarding the opcode fetch, and all SLJIT_ASSERTs are debug-only — so the safety of this function rests entirely on bytecode well-formedness invariants enforced upstream in pcre2_compile, which are not quotable here and are therefore recorded as assumptions.

assumptions: The bytecode range cc..ccend is well-formed, self-consistent, and contained within one compiled pattern: this is assumed to be guaranteed by pcre2_compile (not shown in the given code) — no opcode ever straddles the ccend boundary, OP_MARK/SKIP_ARG argument lengths never cross group ends, and OP_COND's GET(cc,1) offset always points to a valid KET within the pattern. No statement in the given code enforces this.
common->optimized_cbracket is assumed sized so that every GET2(cc,1+LINK_SIZE) capture number emitted by the compiler is a valid index; no bounds check exists in this function.

PRIVATE_DATA, GET, GET2, HAS_EXTRALEN, GET_EXTRALEN and next_opcode are assumed to read only within the compiled pattern buffer for compiler-generated bytecode; their definitions are external to the given code.

SLJIT_ASSERT is a no-op in release builds (NDEBUG/no SLJIT_DEBUG); all in-function consistency checks ('SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend)', 'SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL)', 'SLJIT_ASSERT(PRIVATE_DATA(cc) != 0)') are therefore debug-only.
common fields (mark_ptr, capture_last_ptr, control_head_ptr, has_set_som, utf) are assumed to truthfully reflect the compiled pattern's features, as set by earlier JIT compile phases.
limitations: Candidate C1 (OOB read): 'alternative = cc + GET(cc, 1); if (*alternative == OP_KETRMAX ...' dereferences a bytecode-derived offset with no ccend check in this function — unguarded in the given code, but only triggerable if pcre2_compile emits an OP_COND whose matching KET lies outside the pattern, for which no trigger could be constructed from the given code.

Candidate C2 (OOB advance): 'cc += 1 + 2 + cc[1];' and the iterator cases ('cc += 2;', 'cc += GET_EXTRALEN(cc[-1]);') can overshoot ccend with no in-function check; requires a compiler-phase defect that splits an opcode across the scan boundary.

Candidate C3 (unchecked index): 'common->optimized_cbracket[GET2(cc, 1 + LINK_SIZE)]' has no index validation in this function; requires a capture number exceeding the array, which only a pcre2_compile defect could emit.

Candidate C4 (NULL deref): 'cc = next_opcode(common, cc); SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL);' — in release builds a NULL return leads to 'switch(*cc)' on NULL; next_opcode only returns NULL for opcodes the compiler never emits.

Candidate C5 (CWE-190 shape): 'int length' accumulates unchecked; overflow to negative would yield wrong JIT frame sizing, but requires multi-gigabyte single recursion-group bytecode (and non-default LINK_SIZE to even be representable), which is not demonstrably receivable.
Candidate C6 (CWE-400): dismissed — the scan is linear in group bytecode size with no amplification.

Hardening note: this function would be more defensive with an in-loop 'if (cc >= ccend) abort' check and length-overflow detection, but absence of such checks is not a reachable vulnerability in this code as given.

verdict.summary: ReadTGAImage fails to validate the short-read return of ReadBlob for the attacker-sized image comment: on a truncated file, bytes between the actual count and tga_info.id_length remain uninitialized heap, are NUL-terminated only at id_length, and are stored as the image comment property, disclosing heap memory. Separately, in the 8-bit/default pixel path the raw colormap index from ReadBlobByte (0..255) is stored via SetPixelIndex into PseudoClass images without any range constraint (ConstrainColormapIndex is applied only to the local pixel lookup for colormap_type!=0, and only the 15/16-bit case constrains the stored index), so image->colors can be as small as 4 while index 255 is stored, violating the index<colors invariant and enabling out-of-bounds colormap reads downstream.

evidence.reason: The return value of ReadBlob is never compared to tga_info.id_length. A file truncated after the 18-byte header (e.g. id_length=255 with only 3 bytes remaining) makes ReadBlob fill 3 bytes, leaving bytes [3..254] of the non-zeroed AcquireQuantumMemory buffer uninitialized; comment[255]='\0' terminates past them and SetImageProperty copies the uninitialized heap contents into the retrievable comment property — information disclosure (CWE-908). No short-read guard exists anywhere on this path.

evidence.snippet:
if (image->storage_class == PseudoClass)
        SetPixelIndex(image,index,q);
evidence.reason: For PseudoClass images the raw per-pixel index (0..255 from ReadBlobByte) is stored without any range check against image->colors. No ConstrainColormapIndex is applied to the value reaching this sink on the 8-bit/default path (unlike the 15/16-bit case which constrains index), so an attacker stores e.g. index 255 into an image whose colormap has 4 entries — improper validation of array index (CWE-129) enabling out-of-bounds colormap reads by later consumers.

Origin of the tainted index: ReadBlobByte yields an attacker-controlled 0..255 value; the ConstrainColormapIndex call constrains only the local colormap lookup expression, never the variable index that is later stored via SetPixelIndex; with colormap_type==0 (colors = 1<<bits_per_pixel, e.g. 4 for bpp=2) no constraint is applied at all.

assumptions: AcquireQuantumMemory returns non-zeroed (malloc-based) memory; the given code contains no memset/calloc of comment.
ConstrainColormapIndex records an exception and returns 0 for out-of-range indices but does not modify the caller's variable, and does not abort the read.
SetPixelIndex stores the given index into the pixel cache without validation.
AcquireImageColormap clamps the allocated colormap to at least one entry, so the colormap loops stay in bounds.
limitations: PseudoClass with colormap_type==0 and bits_per_pixel 24/32 makes image->colors up to 1<<32; the allocation is explicitly checked (AcquireImageColormap failure -> ThrowReaderException) so it degrades to a clean error; 1<<24 colors (~1GB) is a memory-amplification concern but bounded and matches the checked-allocation design.
ReadBlobByte at EOF returns -1, cast to unsigned char 255, producing wrong colors but no memory-safety effect; the trailing EOFBlob check records UnexpectedEndOfFile.
The 'if (status == MagickFalse)' check inside the pixel loop is dead code (status is always MagickTrue after SetImageExtent success); harmless.

verdict.summary: No reachable security defect found. All attacker-influenced inputs (command argument, command range, edited buffer-line content) flow to sinks (line indexing, allocation sizing, memmove lengths, loop bounds, ml_replace lifetime) that are guarded by quotable in-code checks: the tabstop range check 'if (new_ts < 0 || new_ts > TABSTOP_MAX)', the NUL-check loop discipline, exact-fit allocation arithmetic 'alloc(old_len - col + start_col + len + 1)' matching every write extent, the virtual-column bound 'if (vcol >= MAXCOL) ... break', and immediate re-anchoring of ptr after ml_replace. Boundary tests (empty line, whitespace-only line, col == old_len, vcol at MAXCOL, repeated retab on one line) do not produce an out-of-bounds access.

assumptions: 'ts' (curbuf->b_p_ts) is validated to [1, TABSTOP_MAX] by the option layer outside this code; this function's 'if (new_ts == 0) new_ts = curbuf->b_p_ts;' would divide by zero only if that external validation failed.
tabstop_set() FAILs on malformed/empty 'vartabstop' arguments and returns a non-empty allocated array on success; its internals are outside the given code.
ml_get(lnum) returns a valid NUL-terminated line for lnum in [eap->line1, eap->line2]; the ex-command range validation against curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count happens in ex_docmd, outside this code.

set_string_option_direct("vts", ...) does not itself free or replace curbuf->b_p_vts_array (the code manually assigns it and frees old_vts_ary captured before the call); if that call did free the old array this would be a double free, but that behavior is not visible in the given code.
(*mb_ptr2len) returns a safe length for truncated multi-byte sequences at end of line.
eap->arg is NUL-terminated within the command-line buffer, so the digit/comma skip loop terminates.
limitations: On a 32-bit build, 'old_len - col + start_col + len + 1' could overflow signed long for a line whose virtual width approaches MAXCOL (requiring ~215KB of tabs with ts=9999); the wrapped value converts to a huge size parameter that fails allocation, which is handled gracefully by 'if (new_line == NULL) break;'. No controlled out-of-bounds write could be demonstrated; recorded as theoretical UB, not a confirmed vulnerability.

Memory amplification: ':retab' converting tabs to spaces can attempt an allocation of up to ~2GB from a ~215KB tab-heavy line, but this is explicitly bounded by the quoted 'if (vcol >= MAXCOL)' guard and degrades gracefully on allocation failure; considered designed behavior.
'retab -5' is not reported as an error (getdigits returns 0 and the 'if (new_ts < 0 && *eap->arg == '-')' check misses it), silently keeping the existing tabstop; cosmetic only.
If ml_replace() fails, the allocated new_line leaks (bounded, only on internal failure); no exhaustion path demonstrated.

verdict.summary: esp_output_head (IPsec ESP output, kernel code) handles attacker-influenced skb geometry and trailer lengths, but every sink in the given code is guarded by a check that is present on the only path reaching it: the skip_cow trailer write requires 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)', the frag-slot write '__skb_fill_page_desc(skb, nfrags, ...)' requires 'nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS', the page-frag trailer write requires successful 'skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC)' (with allocsize = ALIGN(tailen) >= tailen), the cow path checks 'if (nfrags < 0) goto out;' before using the trailer, and esp->esph is recomputed from a pre-cow offset after skb_cow_data, eliminating the stale-pointer window. Candidate defects (allocsz overflow, >= vs > at ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE, frag-slot OOB, trailer OOB, uninitialized nfrags) were each either blocked by a quotable guard, unreachable at runtime (no ~4GB skb), or demonstrably without memory-safety effect (the pfrag allocation depends only on tailen, not on skb->data_len).

assumptions: ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE is not defined in the given code; its exact value and the semantics of '>' versus '>=' at equality cannot be verified. No sink's safety depends on it: the page-frag allocation is 'allocsize = ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES)', independent of skb->data_len.

Kernel helper contracts are assumed per their standard semantics: skb_page_frag_refill() success guarantees at least allocsize bytes available at pfrag->offset in pfrag->page; skb_cow_data() success guarantees tailen bytes of tailroom in the returned trailer; esp_output_fill_trailer() writes within the tailen-sized region whose start is passed to it; skb_tailroom() returns writable bytes. These are API guarantees, not statements in the given code.

esp->tailen, esp->tfclen, esp->plen and esp->esph are produced by the caller (esp_output_tail/esp_output_encap) from xfrm/crypto state; tailen is assumed a small positive value (padding + 2 + auth tag) with tailen >= tfclen + 2, and esp->esph a valid pointer into the skb. A negative or inconsistent tailen cannot be constructed from packet data within these bounds.
skb->data_len and skb->len are physically bounded far below 2^32 (MAX_SKB_FRAGS pages, GSO/MTU limits), so the unsigned addition 'skb->data_len + tailen' and ALIGN() cannot wrap at runtime.
limitations: Candidate: integer overflow in allocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) — dismissed as unreachable: no constructible skb has data_len near 2^32, and even on hypothetical wrap the only effect is choosing the pfrag path, whose allocation is sized from tailen alone and independently guarded.

Candidate: boundary condition at 'if (allocsz > ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE)' (equality passes through) — no defect demonstrable without the macro definition, and the pfrag path's safety does not depend on skb->data_len.
Candidate: frag-slot out-of-bounds write via __skb_fill_page_desc — rejected; '(skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS)' is on the only path and rejects nr_frags == MAX_SKB_FRAGS.
Candidate: stale esp->esph after skb_cow_data (use-after-free class) — rejected; esph_offset is captured before cow and esp->esph is recomputed after it.
Candidate: trailer OOB write — rejected at both paths via 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' and the skb_page_frag_refill failure branch.

The 'nfrags++;' double increment in the pfrag path returns orig_nr_frags+2; within the given code the return value is only consumed via 'if (nfrags < 0)', and the increment can only over-count, never under-count, so no defect is provable here.

verdict.summary: In gen_hash, the NODE_KW_REST_ARGS flush path (`if (len > 0) { pop_n(len*2); ... pop(); pop(); ... genop_1(s, OP_HASHCAT, cursp());`) is executed without the `val` context guard that the other two flush sites enforce (`if (val && cursp() >= slimit)` and `if (val && len > 0)`). When called with val==0 (NOVAL), `len` counts pairs whose key/value codegen pushed no stack slots (the `val &&` guards at lines 36 and 51 prove the author's own invariant), yet pop_n(len*2) and pop();pop() subtract those never-pushed slots from s->sp. An attacker-supplied hash literal containing one or more pairs followed by a `**` element in void context drives s->sp negative/out-of-frame; the resulting negative cursp() is encoded as a register operand (OP_HASH/OP_HASHCAT/OP_HASHADD) and returned as 'variable length' (-1), producing bytecode with invalid register indices (out-of-bounds stack access at run time) and/or a compiler crash.

evidence.reason: Sink of the defect: this flush has no `val` guard, so with val==0 (NOVAL) pop_n(len*2) removes 2*len stack slots that were never pushed (pairs were counted at line 33 without val and generated via codegen(...,val) which pushes nothing in NOVAL context per the code's own val-guards), underflowing s->sp and passing the resulting negative cursp() as a register operand to genop_2. Trigger: val=0, tree = one plain pair followed by a NODE_KW_REST_ARGS element, small entry sp (e.g. 1): sp becomes -1.

Second unguarded sink on the same path: `if (len > 0 || update)` also lacks a `val` guard, so in NOVAL context pop();pop() subtracts two more never-pushed slots and genop_1 receives the further-negated cursp() as a register operand (OP_HASHCAT), deepening the compiler stack-pointer underflow.

evidence.snippet: if (val && cursp() >= slimit) {
evidence.reason: Proof of the missing-guard asymmetry (counterfactual patch test): the loop-end flush is guarded by `val &&`, and the final flush by `if (val && len > 0)` — the exact check whose absence at lines 10 and 22 constitutes the defect. Searching the whole function for a `val` guard on any path to the NODE_KW_REST_ARGS pop_n/pop finds none, confirming the vulnerability.

assumptions: codegen(s, ..., val==0) (NOVAL context) generates side-effect code without pushing value-stack slots; this is not quotable from the given code but is the only reading consistent with the author's own `if (val && cursp() >= slimit)` and `if (val && len > 0)` guards, which would be meaningless if len always tracked pushed slots.
pop_n(n) / pop() / push() are unchecked s->sp arithmetic (s->sp -= n; s->sp++) and cursp() is s->sp; no bounds check exists in the given code.
genop_1/genop_2 encode their register operands without validating them against the frame's stack bounds (mruby codegen behavior; not quotable here).

Values of GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX are not visible in the given code; the branch `if (cursp() >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX) slimit = INT16_MAX;` raises the flush threshold when the stack is already deep, and whether ~INT16_MAX live registers fit the compiler/VM stack cannot be verified from this code alone.
limitations: The `limit` parameter (line 1) is never used; dead parameter / latent code smell, not a security defect by itself.
Integer overflow of len*2 (CWE-190) would require roughly 2^30 hash pairs in one literal with val==0; dominated by the stack-underflow defect that triggers at len==1, so not reported separately.
nint(tree->car->car->car) dereferences three pointers without NULL checks; reachable only via a malformed AST produced by an internal parser bug, not by data crossing this code's trust boundary.

Real-world reachability of a val==0 call with a KW_REST element depends on callers outside the given code; under this code's entry-point contract (val and tree are caller-supplied), the trigger is in-scope.

verdict.summary: update_topline consumes the 'scrolloff' option (curwin->w_p_so / p_so, settable via :set, vimscript, or sourced config) with no range validation against the window height. A huge 'scrolloff' is used unclamped in arithmetic: it is truncated long-to-int at `n = curwin->w_topline + *so_ptr - curwin->w_cursor.lnum;` (CWE-190), and it flows into the scroll decisions that invoke scroll_cursor_bot/scroll_cursor_halfway/scroll_cursor_top with the out-of-range value still active, driving line arithmetic outside the buffer and causing out-of-bounds heap access (cf. CVE-2022-2124, fixed upstream by clamping so_ptr in this function). No statement in the code bounds *so_ptr.

evidence.snippet:
long        *so_ptr = curwin->w_p_so >= 0 ? &curwin->w_p_so : &p_so;
    int		save_so = *so_ptr;
evidence.reason: Attacker-influenced 'scrolloff' enters here with no range check; the only statements that touch it are this local-vs-global selection, this save, and `*so_ptr = mouse_dragging - 1;`. The missing clamp (e.g., limit *so_ptr to the window height) belongs here; it is absent on every path.

Long-width arithmetic including the unvalidated 'scrolloff' is stored into int n (CWE-190). Trigger: scrolloff=3000000000, topline=1, cursor=1 gives 3000000000 > INT_MAX; no guard bounds *so_ptr, so the truncation flips the `if (n >= halfheight)` branch.

The unclamped 'scrolloff' is added to line_count and drives the scroll_cursor_bot/scroll_cursor_halfway dispatch while the out-of-range value is still in effect (it is only restored by `*so_ptr = save_so;` at function end). With scrolloff far exceeding the window height, the callee's line arithmetic runs outside [1, ml_line_count], producing out-of-bounds heap access (CWE-787); the fold path at lines 195-203 even caps line_count at w_height+2, guaranteeing scroll_cursor_bot is called with a huge 'so' active.

assumptions: linenr_T and long are signed machine-word types; w_height, n, halfheight are int; 'scrolloff' can be set to arbitrary large values via :set/vimscript/sourced configuration, which is the trust boundary for this function.

The actual out-of-bounds access occurs inside scroll_cursor_bot/scroll_cursor_halfway/scroll_cursor_top and hasFolding/botline_forw, which are not part of the given code; this code is the intake point where the value should be validated (the upstream fix for this function's heap-overflow issue clamps so_ptr to the window height).
Invariants such as cursor.lnum within [1, ml_line_count] and topline validity are established by the editor's command processing outside this code; they are assumed, not quoted.
botline_forw(&loff) is assumed to advance loff.lnum so the while loop terminates; this is not verifiable in the given code.
limitations: The internal loops were verified guarded: `if (lnum >= curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count || n >= halfheight) break;`, `if (lnum <= 0 || line_count > curwin->w_height + 1) break;`, and `if (halfheight < 2) halfheight = 2;` are present, checked before use, and edge-tested at 0, 1, and the exact limits; no OOB was found inside the loops themselves.
The truncation at line 103 alone only flips the halfway-vs-top scroll branch; its security weight comes from sharing the same missing scrolloff clamp as the downstream out-of-bounds scroll.
`*so_ptr = mouse_dragging - 1;` only alters display behavior and was not counted as a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: input_bmp_reader has two attacker-reachable defects: (1) on the fopen-failure path it jumps to cleanup and calls fclose(fd) with fd == NULL, a NULL-pointer dereference triggered by any unopenable filename; (2) after carefully validating biWidth up to 0x1fffffff and deliberately allowing negative biHeight (only -2147483648 and 0 are rejected), it truncates both dimensions to unsigned short in at_bitmap_init — (unsigned short)65536 == 0 and (unsigned short)(-1) == 65535 — so the returned bitmap's declared dimensions mismatch the image_storage allocated from the full 32-bit values, enabling out-of-bounds access by consumers of the bitmap.

evidence.reason: CWE-190 (with CWE-476 on the cleanup path). The width/height guards permit biWidth as large as 0x1fffffff and any negative biHeight except -2147483648 ("if (Bitmap_Head.biWidth < 0 || Bitmap_Head.biHeight == -2147483648)"), and image_storage is allocated by ReadImage from those full 32-bit values; this line then truncates both to 16 bits, so width 65536 becomes 0 and height -1 becomes 65535, making the bitmap's declared dimensions inconsistent with the allocated storage (out-of-bounds access by any consumer using the reported dims). Additionally, the cleanup label immediately below calls fclose(fd) unconditionally, and the fopen-failure path ("if (!fd) { ... goto cleanup; }") reaches it with fd == NULL, a NULL-pointer dereference triggered by any nonexistent filename.

CWE-476 origin: on the fopen-failure boundary case (fd == NULL), control jumps to the cleanup label, whose only statement is fclose(fd) with no NULL guard anywhere in the function, so fclose(NULL) executes — undefined behavior / crash reachable by an attacker-supplied filename (public API parameter).

evidence.snippet:
if (((unsigned long)Bitmap_Head.biWidth) > (unsigned int)0x7fffffff / Bitmap_Head.biBitCnt ||
	  ((unsigned long)Bitmap_Head.biWidth) > ((unsigned int)0x7fffffff /abs(Bitmap_Head.biHeight)) / 4)
evidence.reason: Origin of the truncated values: these are the only width/height magnitude guards, and they permit biWidth far above 65535 (up to 0x1fffffff with height 1) and (together with "Bitmap_Head.biHeight == -2147483648" being the only negative-height rejection) permit biHeight = -1; no statement bounds the values to the 16-bit range later imposed by the (unsigned short) casts in at_bitmap_init.

assumptions: Implementations of ReadOK, ToL, ToS, ReadColorMap, ReadImage, ReadChannelMasks, setMasksDefault, at_bitmap_init, at_exception_fatal, and the types of the global Bitmap_File_Head/Bitmap_Head fields are not given; ToL/ToS are assumed to decode little-endian 32/16-bit values into unsigned/signed widths, at_exception_fatal is assumed to record the error and return (not exit/longjmp, so cleanup executes), and at_bitmap_init is assumed to store the passed width/height as the bitmap's dimensions.

If ToL returned a signed value and bfOffs/biSize were signed, ColormapSize could go negative; the clamp "if (ColormapSize > 256) ColormapSize = 256;" does not handle that case, but the declared unsigned decoding makes this unreachable in the assumed types.
limitations: Potential mismatch between ColormapSize (computed from bfOffs/biSize/Maps, range 0..256 after clamp) and biClrUsed (up to 256) could leave parts of the uninitialized stack array ColorMap[256][3] consumed by ReadImage; ReadImage's code is not given, so this candidate could not be proven and is not reported.
The BA-record while loop iterates once per 14 file bytes, so it is bounded by attacker-supplied file size — not an unbounded loop.

The width/height overflow guards bound ReadImage's allocation to roughly 256MB; large-but-bounded allocation is noted as potential resource pressure (CWE-400-like) but is capped by the quoted checks and not reported as a finding.
fseek's return value is unchecked, which at worst re-reads from the wrong offset — no security effect established in the given code.

verdict.summary: This kernel PCI-probe function validates every value it consumes at the boundaries it owns: the hardware-supplied hw_rev is rejected when 0xffffffff ('if (trans->hw_rev == 0xffffffff)'), hw_base and tso_hdr_page allocations are NULL-checked, DMA-mask failures (primary and 32-bit fallback) abort via 'goto out_no_pci', and the hw_id string is written with a constant format string and a sizeof() bound ('snprintf(trans->hw_id_str, sizeof(trans->hw_id_str), ...'), so the u16 PCI IDs cannot overflow or inject. Error paths free tso_hdr_page exactly once (no double-free/UAF/leak). No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, integer, crypto, or authz defect exists in this code.

assumptions: cfg_trans and cfg_trans->base_params are compiled-in static driver config tables on the probe path; treating them as trusted because no attacker-controlled data can flow into them via this code.
