verdict.summary: In octet-counting framing, each octet-counter digit is appended to the fixed-size message buffer via `*(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c;` with no bounds check on pThis->iMsg. iMsg can legally equal iMaxLine at the end of a frame (the truncation logic caps it at exactly iMaxLine, and the end-of-frame paths reset inputState but never iMsg). A remote attacker who first sends a frame that fills/truncates the buffer and then starts a new frame with octet-counting digits causes writes at pMsg[iMaxLine], pMsg[iMaxLine+1], ... — a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled digit bytes. The sibling write in octet-stuffing mode is guarded by `if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine)`, proving iMaxLine is the buffer capacity and that the same check is missing on the digit path.

evidence.snippet: *(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c;
evidence.reason: Unguarded write sink: while parsing octet-counting frame headers, every digit is copied into the message buffer at index pThis->iMsg with no comparison of iMsg against iMaxLine (the buffer capacity, enforced elsewhere by `if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) {` before the stuffing-mode copy). iMsg persists across frames — no reset exists on any end-of-frame path in this code — and can equal iMaxLine after a truncated frame, so the next frame's counter digits are written past the end of pMsg. Trigger: TCP client sends a frame that fills the buffer to iMaxLine (e.g. an oversized octet-counted frame truncated by the `octatesToCopy = iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg` logic, or a stuffed frame ending in '\n'), then begins the next frame with digits ('9','9','9',...); each digit performs an out-of-bounds heap write.

Origin of the faulty index value: the truncation logic (`octatesToCopy = iMaxLine - pThis->iMsg`) saturates pThis->iMsg at exactly iMaxLine, and the end-of-frame branch resets only inputState (never iMsg) before the next frame begins at eAtStrtFram, so iMsg carries its at-the-limit value into the unguarded digit append.

assumptions: pThis->pMsg is a fixed buffer of capacity iMaxLine; the allocation is not shown, but the code's own guard `if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) {` before the stuffing-mode write establishes iMaxLine as the capacity within this code.

The body of doSubmitMsg() is not shown; if it resets pThis->iMsg to 0, one leg of the trigger (iMsg persisting at iMaxLine across doSubmitMsg) would be blocked externally — but no such reset exists in the given code, and the missing bounds check at the digit append is a defect regardless relative to the code's own invariant.
iMaxLine is a global configuration value assumed positive; its validation is not present in this code.
buff/*buff are assumed to contain buffLen valid readable bytes; that contract is enforced by the (not shown) network receive path.
limitations: Negative-octatesToCopy memcpy scenario (iMaxLine - iMsg < 0 producing a huge size_t length at line 118) is NOT reachable: the only entry into the bulk-copy branch passes `pThis->iMsg = 0;` (line 64), and lines 113–116 keep iMsg <= iMaxLine thereafter.
Signed overflow of the octet counter is prevented by the quoted guard `if(pThis->iOctetsRemain <= 200000000) {` (max accumulated value 2000000009 < INT_MAX).
The emergency-flush path can call doSubmitMsg twice for one delimiter (lines 81–82 then 94–95), a message-duplication/logic issue with no memory-safety impact.
isdigit() called with a possibly negative char is technically undefined behavior but has no security effect here.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot is not vulnerable. The only array index is bounded by the strict loop guard 'for(i = 0; i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS; i++)' on the sole path to 'object = &s_objects[i]', the optional caller pointer is guarded by 'if(handle)' before the write '*handle = i + TRANSIENT_FIRST', and the MemorySet size is the compile-time constant sizeof(OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES) matching the member. No attacker-influenced data crosses into this function, and no boundary value (i = 0, i = MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS-1, i = MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, handle = NULL) produces an out-of-range access.

assumptions: The global array s_objects is declared elsewhere with exactly MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements; the declaration is not in the given code, so the loop bound's correspondence to the array size cannot be quoted and is assumed.

TRANSIENT_FIRST and MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS are compile-time constants such that TRANSIENT_FIRST + MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS - 1 does not overflow the 32-bit TPMI_DH_OBJECT handle type; their numeric values are not shown.

The TPM core executes single-threaded with respect to this routine; the given code contains no locking, and concurrent invocation causing two callers to receive the same unoccupied slot is not triggerable within the shown control flow.
By module design, the caller is responsible for setting attributes.occupied on the returned slot; this function intentionally returns a slot still marked CLEAR.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: TOCTOU/double-claim of the same slot if the function is invoked twice before the caller sets occupied (no locking; occupied is not set inside this function). Not attacker-reachable within this code's single-threaded contract; robustness/design note for the caller.
Candidate dismissed: return NULL when all slots are occupied; safe in this function, callers must handle it.

Candidate dismissed: MemorySet only clears OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES, not the whole OBJECT struct; stale non-attribute fields persist in a reused slot — a hygiene issue for callers, not a memory-safety defect in this function.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot indexes the s_objects global under an explicit loop bound (i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS), guards the optional OUT handle with 'if(handle)', and zeroes the returned object with MemorySet before returning it. No attacker-influenced input crosses a trust boundary into this function; all sinks (array indexing, handle write, handle arithmetic, memset) are guarded by quotable statements on every path, and edge cases (i=0, last index, i=MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, handle=NULL) are correctly handled.

assumptions: The global array s_objects is declared with MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS elements; its declaration is not in the given code, so index safety is proven only by the loop guard using the same named constant.
TRANSIENT_FIRST is the TPM 2.0 constant 0x80000000; with UINT32 i bounded by the small MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS, i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot wrap.
This function executes in the single-threaded libtpms/TPM emulator context, so no TOCTOU race on the occupancy check is considered.
limitations: Returning an object whose occupied flag remains CLEAR until the caller fills it is a lifecycle convention relying on the caller; if a caller never marks or frees the slot, behavior degrades but no memory-safety defect exists in this code.

If MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS and the actual dimension of s_objects ever diverged (in the unshown declaration), the loop guard would not protect the index; that defect would live in the declaration, not here.
The commented-out partial MemorySet line is dead code with no security effect.

verdict.summary: The octet-counting frame decoder accumulates the attacker-supplied octet count without any bound: pThis->iOctetsRemain = pThis->iOctetsRemain * 10 + c - '0'. A 10+ digit count overflows the signed int; the subsequent 'invalid octet count' branch only logs an error and does not reset iOctetsRemain or the framing mode before switching inputState to eInMsg. The negative value then flows into octatesToCopy, bypassing both clamps (buffLen < octatesToCopy and octatesToCopy + iMsg > iMaxLine are both false for negative values), and reaches memcpy(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg, *buff, octatesToCopy), which widens the negative int to a huge size_t, causing a remote pre-auth heap buffer overflow.

evidence.snippet: pThis->iOctetsRemain = pThis->iOctetsRemain * 10 + c - '0';
evidence.reason: Origin: attacker-controlled framing digits accumulate into the signed int iOctetsRemain with no bound check on any iteration. Sending a frame header such as "2147483648 " (10 digits) overflows the int and wraps the count negative. There is no per-digit clamp, and the only post-hoc checks (iOctetsRemain < 1 / > iMaxLine at lines 40 and 45) merely log errors and never reset iOctetsRemain, so the negative value survives into the message-copy path.

Sink: memcpy length is the unvalidated iOctetsRemain. Both clamps are ineffective for sign-flipped values: 'buffLen < octatesToCopy' is false when octatesToCopy is negative, and 'octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg > iMaxLine' is false for negative octatesToCopy. After the invalid-count error path only logs (lines 40-44) and unconditionally sets inputState = eInMsg (line 54), the next received byte reaches this memcpy with the negative count, which widens to a huge size_t and writes far past pThis->pMsg — an attacker-triggerable heap buffer overflow via a single crafted TCP syslog frame header.

assumptions: pThis->iOctetsRemain and iMaxLine are signed ints (consistent with the %d format usage and the int locals); the overflow analysis assumes 32-bit int width, the platform norm.
pThis->pMsg is allocated with at least iMaxLine bytes by code outside this function; the clamps at lines 103-105 are correct only under that assumption.

buffLen is the number of valid bytes remaining from *buff, and the caller advances *buff by one after each invocation (consistent with the '- 1' at line 111); if buffLen were in a different unit, the scan loop at line 64 would need re-evaluation.
doSubmitMsg resets pThis->iMsg after submitting the buffered message; without that, the stuffing-mode single-byte guard at line 92 would be insufficient.
limitations: Zero octet count ("0 ") is explicitly unhandled per the TODO at line 41: the count-check branch only logs, leaves iOctetsRemain == 0 with OCTET_COUNTING framing, and line 111 then executes *buff += (0 + 0 - 1), decrementing the buffer cursor one byte — potential pointer reprocessing/one-byte underflow relative to the buffer start, contingent on caller cursor semantics; secondary to the confirmed overflow finding.

Signed overflow is formally undefined behavior in C; the negative-to-memcpy path was verified against typical wraparound semantics of mainstream compilers. Under aggressive optimization the UB could manifest differently, but the unbounded attacker-controlled arithmetic defect itself is present regardless.

The oversize-count branch (line 45) only logs and does not truncate or reset, but the per-chunk clamps at lines 103-105 do bound the memcpy for positive counts, so no separate positive-value overflow of the copy was confirmed.

Behavior of qf_buf_add_line, ml_delete, ml_append bounds checking, and check_lnums is not shown; no defect was claimed that depends on their internals.
'quickfixtextfunc' is assumed settable by config/plugin (not via modeline); the attacker is a malicious VimL plugin or crafted configuration, consistent with Vim's published CVE threat model.
limitations: NULL-deref of qfp was dismissed: guarded by 'if (qfl != NULL && qfl->qf_start != NULL)' (line 23), non-NULL assignment in the else branch (lines 39-42), and 'if (qfp == NULL) break;' (lines 72-73) before each next use.

If one judges user-configured VimL callbacks as fully trusted code, the UAF reduces to an internal robustness issue; under the standard Vim/plugin threat model it is a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual consumes only editor-internal state (regex engine state, cursor/Visual positions, 'selection' option) and performs no memory writes; its guards (rex.reg_buf != curbuf, VIsual.lnum == 0, and the quotable lnum range check 'if (lnum < top.lnum || lnum > bot.lnum) return FALSE;') cover every path to the getvvcol/win_linetabsize sinks. Edge-testing the arithmetic at boundary values (end == 0 with exclusive selection yields -1 and correctly matches nothing; end == MAXCOL yields MAXCOL-1) shows correct or fail-closed behavior. The only unguarded expression, 'col >= bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')' in 'v' mode, could overflow only if bot.col == MAXCOL, a state not producible in charwise mode by this code, and its sole effect would be over-restrictive (excluded) matching — no memory safety, injection, or availability impact. assumptions: Cursor and Visual positions (wp->w_cursor, VIsual, b_visual.vi_start/vi_end) are maintained in-buffer by the editor; this code cannot quote an in-code bound for them and relies on those engine invariants.

colnr_T is a signed int in Vim; 'end - (*p_sel == 'e')' at end == 0 therefore evaluates to -1 (signed), not an unsigned wrap.

verdict.summary: In spell_suggest(), a Visual-mode selection length (badlen, computed as the absolute column difference plus one with no cap) flows into sug.su_badlen and is then copied into the fixed-size stack buffer char_u wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2] at offset stp->st_wordlen via vim_strncpy(wcopy + stp->st_wordlen, sug.su_badptr + stp->st_orglen, sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen). No check anywhere in the function bounds badlen or the destination offset against MAXWLEN + 2, so a single-line Visual selection longer than the buffer (influenced by attacker-supplied file text) causes an out-of-bounds stack write of attacker-controlled bytes.

evidence.reason: Sink: writes sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen bytes of the bad word (attacker-influenced buffer text) into char_u wcopy[MAXWLEN + 2] at offset stp->st_wordlen. The only guard, `if (sug.su_badlen > stp->st_orglen)`, merely makes the length positive; nothing bounds st_wordlen + (su_badlen - st_orglen) + 1 to MAXWLEN + 2. Trigger: Visual-select more than ~130 columns on one line and run z=; badlen becomes the selection size and overflows the stack buffer.

Origin of the tainted length: badlen is the absolute difference of two cursor columns plus one; for a long line the selection can exceed MAXWLEN + 2, and no statement in this function caps badlen before it is passed as the bad-word length to spell_find_suggest and later copied into wcopy.

assumptions: spell_find_suggest() is not included in the given code; any clamping it might apply to badlen/su_badlen or to suggestion word lengths cannot be quoted, so per guard anchoring it does not exist for this analysis.
MAXWLEN is a compile-time constant (128 in Vim); wcopy is char_u[MAXWLEN + 2] = 130 bytes on the stack.
st_wordlen is assumed to be the byte length of st_word; its exact relation is established inside spell_find_suggest(), not visible here.
prompt_for_number() is assumed to initialize mouse_used; its definition is outside this code.
limitations: If st_orglen > su_badlen (a case the code itself anticipates at the comment 'The word may replace more than "su_badlen".'), reads such as STRCAT(p, sug.su_badptr + stp->st_orglen) and the %.*s at line 151 could over-read past the bad word; whether st_orglen can exceed the distance to the line's NUL is decided in spell_find_suggest(), which is not given, so this is not confirmable here.

AppendToRedobuffLit(p + c, stp->st_wordlen + sug.su_badlen - stp->st_orglen) can receive a negative or undercounted length when st_orglen > st_wordlen + su_badlen; the callee's handling of negative lengths is outside the given code.
limit = (int)Rows - 2 can be zero or negative when Rows <= 2 and is passed as maxcount to spell_find_suggest(); its effect is not analyzable from this code.

The alloc at line 215 trusts STRLEN(st_word) <= st_wordlen and c + st_orglen <= STRLEN(line); these invariants, if they exist, are enforced in the (unseen) suggestion machinery, so no finding is based on them.

verdict.summary: tipc_crypto_key_rcv copies a peer-supplied TIPC key message without validating it first: skey->keylen is a raw 32-bit value read from the received message and is used directly as the memcpy length into a kmalloc buffer sized only by msg_data_sz(hdr). The sole sanity check (size != tipc_aead_key_size(skey)) executes only after both memcpys, so any keylen greater than size - 68 causes a heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled length and content before the check can reject it; additionally, when size < 68 (including size == 0, where kmalloc(0) returns the non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR) the reads of data + 64 and the write of skey->keylen go out of bounds. A remote TIPC peer triggering key distribution can reach both, enabling kernel heap corruption / remote DoS.

evidence.reason: Sink of the vulnerability: skey->keylen is an unvalidated 32-bit value read from the attacker-controlled message body (line 24) and immediately used as the memcpy length (lines 26-27). The destination was allocated at line 16 with only `size = msg_data_sz(hdr)` bytes, so any keylen > size - 68 (e.g., size=100, keylen=1000) writes past the heap allocation. No check of size or keylen precedes these copies. Additionally, when size < 68 the reads at data + TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME (line 24) and the 64-byte memcpy (line 25) read out of bounds of the message, and with size == 0 kmalloc(0) returns the non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR that the !skey test accepts, making the skey->keylen write fault — an attacker-reachable DoS at minimum.

Check-after-use: the only size/keylen validation in the function is placed after both memcpys, so the heap overflow at lines 24-27 has already occurred before this test can reject the message. The check is also edge-unsafe itself: tipc_aead_key_size computes sizeof(*skey) + keylen in 32-bit unsigned, so a keylen such as 0xFFFFFFBC wraps to a small value that can equal `size` and pass, after a multi-gigabyte memcpy was attempted. A guard equivalent to 'reject if keylen > size - offsetof(struct tipc_aead_key, key) before copying' does not exist anywhere on the path to the sink.

evidence.snippet:
skey = kmalloc(size, GFP_ATOMIC);
	if (unlikely(!skey)) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty buffer size: the allocation is sized solely by the peer-supplied `u16 size = msg_data_sz(hdr)` with no minimum-size validation. Because msg_data_sz returns int and is narrowed to u16, a negative value widens to 65535, and size == 0 yields kmalloc(0) => ZERO_SIZE_PTR, which is non-NULL and therefore passes the only guard (`!skey`) on the path, leading directly to the out-of-bounds accesses at lines 24-27.

assumptions: hdr is a network-received TIPC KEY message (the function is reached from the TIPC message-processing path), making size, data, keylen, key_gen, and key_mode attacker-influenced. No upstream/caller-side validation of the message body is present in the given code and none is assumed.

TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME == 64 and sizeof(__be32) == 4, so the on-the-wire key layout is 64 bytes alg_name + 4 bytes keylen + key material; struct tipc_aead_key places keylen at offset 64 and the flexible key[] at offset ~68.
tipc_aead_key_size(skey) evaluates to approximately sizeof(struct tipc_aead_key) + skey->keylen computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic.
kmalloc(0) returns the non-NULL ZERO_SIZE_PTR (0x10) on Linux, so the `!skey` guard does not reject a zero-size allocation.
limitations: No independent defect found in the key-existence check (line 10) or the constant-format pr_err calls; the queued-work path (queue_delayed_work) is outside this function's validation scope.
Failure to allocate (kmalloc returning NULL for a legitimate size) is environment failure, not attacker-triggerable, and the !skey guard handles it correctly; it is not counted as a finding.

verdict.summary: prealloc_elems_and_freelist computes the allocation size as elem_size * smap->map.max_entries without any overflow check. Both operands are attacker-controlled u32 map attributes from the bpf(2) syscall; with value_size = 0xFFFFFFFF and max_entries = 0xFFFFFFF2 the u64 product wraps to a value (~2^32-210 bytes) far smaller than max_entries * elem_size, so bpf_map_area_alloc returns an undersized buffer that is then passed to pcpu_freelist_populate with the unwrapped elem_size and max_entries, causing out-of-bounds heap/vmalloc writes (memory corruption / kernel DoS). No overflow guard exists anywhere in the given code; the only checks are NULL/error checks after the fact.

evidence.reason: The allocation size elem_size * smap->map.max_entries is computed in u64 arithmetic with no overflow check; elem_size (up to 2^32-1+sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket)) and max_entries (u32) are attacker-controlled map attributes. At boundary values (value_size = 0xFFFFFFFF, max_entries = 0xFFFFFFF2) the product wraps mod 2^64 to ~2^32-210, so a buffer far smaller than max_entries*elem_size is allocated. The only guard, 'if (!smap->elems)', detects allocation failure, not the size mismatch.

evidence.snippet:
pcpu_freelist_populate(&smap->freelist, smap->elems, elem_size,
			       smap->map.max_entries);
evidence.reason: The undersized buffer from the wrapped allocation is handed to pcpu_freelist_populate together with the unwrapped elem_size (u64, up to 2^32+sizeof(bucket)-1) and max_entries; the helper writes a freelist node per element across max_entries strides of elem_size, so the write at element 0 already exceeds the wrapped allocation size, producing an attacker-triggered out-of-bounds write (memory corruption / DoS).

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries are assumed to derive from user-supplied bpf(2) map-creation attributes (u32 fields of bpf_attr); stack_map_alloc is not shown, so their exact provenance and any bounds it enforces cannot be quoted and are treated as attacker-controlled per the trust-boundary rule.
sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is assumed to be small (~16-24 bytes: pcpu_freelist_node plus hash/nr fields); its exact value only shifts the wrap threshold, not the existence of the overflow.
pcpu_freelist_populate is assumed to write one freelist node per element at stride elem_size for nr_elems elements into the supplied buffer, per its kernel contract; its implementation is not shown.
limitations: Exploiting the overflow requires the wrapped allocation (~4 GiB) to actually succeed; if bpf_map_area_alloc returns NULL the function safely returns -ENOMEM. On a memory-rich host an attacker can satisfy this.
A possible truncation of the u64 elem_size argument at the pcpu_freelist_populate call site cannot be verified because the callee's signature is not part of the given code; not counted as a finding.
max_entries = 0 leads to a zero-size allocation but populate iterates zero times; no security effect observed in the given code.
Historically the stack map required CAP_SYS_ADMIN to create, which restricts who can reach this code path; that gate is not visible in the given snippet.

verdict.summary: This command-line input loop (Vim getcmdline_int) consumes untrusted keyboard input at every iteration, but every direct memory sink in the given code is bounded by checks present and quotable in the function: the K_LEFT backward scan is guarded by 'while (ccline.cmdpos > 0' and a base-bounded mb_head_off call, the Ex-mode backslash probe is guarded by '&& ccline.cmdpos > 0', the Ctrl_U rewrite loop uses a strict 'while (i < ccline.cmdlen)' and writes the terminator at the invariant NUL slot ('ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;'), and the forward-scan's post-increment read at cmdbuff[cmdlen] lands on that same allocated terminator slot. The recursion guard 'if (depth == 50)' is sufficient because ++depth is by exactly one and the single exit label unconditionally executes '--depth;', so the value 50 cannot be skipped within this code. No integer wrap, truncation, injection sink, or fail-open path was found at the boundary values tested.

assumptions: ccline.cmdbuff is allocated with at least cmdlen+1 bytes and NUL-terminated at index cmdlen; this invariant is evidenced inside the given code by the write 'ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdlen] = NUL;' in the Ctrl_U case, but the allocation itself (alloc_cmdbuff/init_ccline) is outside the excerpt.
IObuff is a global scratch buffer of size IOSIZE (>= 8 bytes); mb_char2bytes writes at most MB_MAXBYTES (6) bytes plus the NUL written by this code.

emsg() invoked at the recursion guard does not synchronously re-enter getcmdline (no such callback path appears in the given code); if it did, 'if (depth == 50)' could be bypassed by a call entering at depth 50 before '--depth' runs.

Helper functions (put_on_cmdline, cmdline_paste, cmdline_insert_reg, nextwild, mb_ptr2len, mb_head_off, get_literal) maintain the ccline invariants cmdpos <= cmdlen and NUL-termination; mb_head_off is assumed to honor its base argument as used here ('(*mb_head_off)(ccline.cmdbuff, ccline.cmdbuff + ccline.cmdpos)').
safe_vgetc() returns well-formed key codes within the int width; no enum/width confusion path from key code to pointer arithmetic exists in this excerpt.
limitations: Candidate C1 (read of ccline.cmdbuff[ccline.cmdpos] in the K_RIGHT while condition with cmdpos == cmdlen) is a genuine boundary-value access to the NUL terminator slot, reachable by WORD-right motion at end of line; it is in-bounds under the code's own terminator invariant and yields no information disclosure or corruption, so it is not treated as a vulnerability. An explicit 'cmdpos >= cmdlen' term in the while condition is absent.

Candidate C3: the recursion guard uses '==' rather than '>='; within the given code ++depth (1 per call) and the single unconditional '--depth;' at theend keep depth passing through 50 exactly, so no unbounded-recursion trigger is constructible from this excerpt alone. A hardening change to >= 50 would be defense-in-depth.

Sinks inside called helpers (cmdline_erase_chars, cmdline_browse_history, cmdline_insert_reg, nextwild/ExpandOne, put_on_cmdline, add_to_history) were not auditable because their bodies are outside the given code; any defect there is out of scope for this analysis.
The main 'for (;;)' loop is unbounded by design (interactive input wait); the depth guard bounds recursion, so no attacker-driven resource-exhaustion path was identified in this excerpt.

verdict.summary: The maywrite authorization check is nested inside the 'if (mailbox)' block, so when mailbox is NULL (server-scope annotations, mboxname coerced to ""), execution flows directly from make_key to cyrusdb_delete/cyrusdb_store with no permission check. A write request that the function should deny (maywrite == 0) is instead persisted to the annotations database, allowing unauthorized creation, modification, and deletion of server-level annotations.

evidence.reason: The only authorization enforcement in the function is placed inside the block opened by 'if (mailbox) {' (line 28). On the mailbox == NULL path this entire block is skipped, so a caller-supplied maywrite == 0 (deny verdict) never causes IMAP_PERMISSION_DENIED; the code proceeds to delete/store the annotation. The check must run before the write decision at 'if (!value->len && !uid)', but no such check exists outside the mailbox block.

Unguarded sink: reached when mailbox == NULL after the permission block was skipped (the same bypass reaches cyrusdb_delete at line 68 when value->len == 0 and uid == 0). The code explicitly supports the NULL-mailbox state ('const char *mboxname = mailbox ? mailbox->name : "";' and 'if (!mailbox) sync_log_annotation("");'), yet applies no maywrite check on that path, so an unauthorized annotation write is persisted and r == 0 (success) is returned.

assumptions: make_key is assumed to bound its writes to the passed keysize (sizeof(key)); no bound is quotable in the given code. If make_key instead returns the untruncated required length for long attacker-controlled entry/userid strings, keylen could exceed sizeof(key) and cyrusdb_store/cyrusdb_delete would over-read the stack buffer key[MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1] (CWE-129/CWE-125). The faulty statement would live in make_key, which is not shown, so this is not confirmed.
Semantics of _annotate_getdb, read_old_value, make_entry, mailbox_quota_check, and cyrusdb_* are external and unverified.

Caller-side privilege checks for the mailbox == NULL path cannot be quoted from this code; per guard-anchoring discipline they do not exist for this analysis, and the in-function 'if (!maywrite)' check is the visible enforcement point.
limitations: Line 34's '!memcmp(oldval.s, value->s, value->len)' would dereference value->s if value->len > 0 while value->s == NULL; line 74's 'value->s == NULL' handling shows the author contemplated NULL s, but no shown code can construct a buf with nonzero len and NULL s, so reachability is unproven.
DEBUG-gated syslog calls print value->s, which may be NULL (printf %s NULL is undefined); compiled out unless DEBUG is defined.

'if (!userid) goto out;' returns success (r == 0) without writing when userid is NULL and the value is non-empty; the adjacent comment marks this as an intentional cleanup path for historical API abuse, and no unauthorized write occurs.
The quota check is also skipped when mailbox == NULL, but no quota applies to server-scope annotations, so this is not independently security-relevant.

verdict.summary: In Virtual Replace mode (State & VREPLACE_FLAG), change_indent() assigns curwin->w_cursor.col = new_cursor_col (the saved cursor offset from the first non-blank) after the indent operation has shortened the line, with no upper-bound check against the new line length. It then executes `new_line[curwin->w_cursor.col] = NUL;` on a buffer allocated as strlen(new_line)+1 by vim_strsave(), producing a heap out-of-bounds write. Concrete trigger: gR on an all-whitespace line "    " with the cursor at end-of-line (col == 4 == strlen), then CTRL-D (change_indent(INDENT_DEC,...)) empties the line, leaving cursor.col = 4 while new_line is a 1-byte allocation, so new_line[4] = NUL writes past the end of the heap buffer.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write sink. new_line is allocated as strlen(current line)+1, but curwin->w_cursor.col is used as an index with no check that it is <= the line length; the only guards present are the NULL-allocation returns. When the preceding indent change (set_indent/shift_line) shortened the line below the preserved cursor offset, col exceeds the allocation and the NUL store lands past the end of the heap buffer (e.g., 4-space blank line, cursor col 4, CTRL-D in gR mode: line becomes empty, cursor.col stays 4, new_line is 1 byte).

Origin of the faulty index value. new_cursor_col holds the cursor's original offset from the first non-blank (lines 39-41) plus the new first-non-blank column (line 79); it is only tested with `<= 0` and is never re-validated against the post-indent-change line length before being stored into curwin->w_cursor.col, which the VREPLACE block then uses as an unchecked index into new_line.

assumptions: colnr_T and int are 32-bit; vim_strsave() allocates strlen(s)+1 bytes and NUL-terminates; these are framework facts outside the given code.

VREPLACE mode state (State & VREPLACE_FLAG) implies insert-mode behavior and is entered via gR; REPLACE_NORMAL(State) is false when VREPLACE_FLAG is set, so the replace-stack loops are skipped on the VREPLACE path.

set_indent()/shift_line() may shorten an all-whitespace line to empty and place the cursor on the first non-blank (column 0 or the new indent end); this code contains no constraint preventing the new line from being shorter than the saved cursor offset.
In insert/replace modes the cursor column may legally equal the line length (one-past-last), which is the boundary value feeding the defect.
limitations: The multibyte cursor-advance loop is safe: `if (ptr[new_cursor_col] == NUL) break;` terminates every iteration before lbr_chartabsize reads, and mb_ptr2len cannot step over the NUL of a NUL-terminated string.
alloc(i + 1) cannot underflow: the loop invariant `while (vcol <= (int)curwin->w_virtcol)` with `vcol = last_vcol` guarantees i >= 0 (edge i == 0 yields a harmless empty-string insert).

Insstart.col/ai_col adjustments are guarded by `if ((int)Insstart.col <= insstart_less)` / `if ((int)ai_col <= insstart_less)`, so subtraction occurs only when the result stays non-negative; with insstart_less = MAXCOL the zeroing branch always fires.
Allocation-failure paths (orig_line/new_line NULL) return early and are not attacker-triggerable; they are not counted as vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: ax25_release dereferences ax25->ax25_dev (switch (ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL])) in the AX25_STATE_3/AX25_STATE_4 path with no NULL check on that path, even though the same function explicitly treats ax25_dev as possibly NULL ('if (ax25_dev) {'). A SEQPACKET socket in state 3/4 whose underlying device has been torn down reaches this unguarded dereference on close(), causing a kernel NULL-pointer oops (denial of service).

evidence.snippet: switch (ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL]) {
evidence.reason: Root cause (CWE-476): unguarded NULL dereference. The sink requires ax25->ax25_dev != NULL, but no check precedes it on the state-3/4 path (lines 35-40); the only device-NULL guard in the function ('if (ax25_dev) {', line 76) executes after the state machine and only protects the refcount drop. Trigger: SEQPACKET socket in AX25_STATE_3/4 with ax25_dev NULL (device torn down) reaches close() -> line 40 -> NULL deref.

evidence.snippet: ax25_dev = ax25->ax25_dev;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted pointer. This function itself acknowledges that ax25->ax25_dev can be NULL at runtime via the later 'if (ax25_dev) {' check, yet no equivalent guard exists before the dereference at line 40 (and the same possibly-NULL ax25 is passed to ax25_send_control at line 27).

assumptions: ax25 = sk_to_ax25(sk) is assumed non-NULL for AX.25 sockets; the given code contains no guard for it.

Reachability of the combination {state in {AX25_STATE_3, AX25_STATE_4}, ax25_dev == NULL} depends on external stack paths (netdevice unregistration/teardown and remote-peer-driven state transitions) not shown in this snippet; the given code contains no statement that prevents the combination, and its own 'if (ax25_dev)' proves NULL is an expected runtime value.
Behavior of external callees (ax25_send_control, ax25_disconnect, ax25_destroy_socket) w.r.t. NULL ax25_dev and refcounts cannot be quoted from the given code.
sock is assumed non-NULL per the proto-op calling contract; only sk is checked ('if (sk == NULL) return 0;').
limitations: Candidate C2: ax25_send_control (line 27) may itself dereference ax25->ax25_dev when NULL (states 1/2 path); the faulty deref would be located in a callee outside the given code, so it is noted but not counted as evidence here.
Candidate C4: the lock-drop windows at lines 19-21 and 28-30 (release_sock/lock_sock around ax25_disconnect) could admit races with netdevice notifiers/timers; not provable from the given code alone.
Candidate C5: the inner switch's default case (e.g., DAMA_MASTER protocol value) skips sending DISC and stopping timers while still starting t1 — logic-only, no memory-safety effect.
Candidate C6: the outer switch's default case performs no socket cleanup; assumed unreachable state in the AX.25 state machine.

The captured local ax25_dev (line 14) is used at lines 76-78 after ax25_destroy_socket; a double-put/UAF would only exist if ax25_destroy_socket also drops the device reference, which cannot be verified from the given code.

verdict.summary: ax25_release() continues to dereference the ax25 control block (del_timer_sync on ax25->timer/t1timer/t2timer/t3timer/idletimer, lines 77-81) and to drop the cached device references (dev_put_track/ax25_dev_put on ax25_dev, lines 82-83) AFTER ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) has already destroyed the socket on three of the four paths: STATE_0 (line 22), STATE_1/2 (line 32), and the non-SEQPACKET else branch (line 74). The only post-switch guard, 'if (ax25_dev)' (line 76), tests the cached device pointer, not the liveness of ax25, and no statement in this function holds a reference on ax25 across the destroy. A local user triggers it trivially: socket(AF_AX25, SOCK_SEQPACKET) -> bind() to an ax25 device (ax25_dev non-NULL, state 0) -> close(), or any SOCK_DGRAM ax25 socket bound to a device. Result is a use-after-free on the freed ax25_cb and a re-drop of the ax25_dev/netdev references on the same paths.

evidence.reason: Unguarded use-after-free sink. This block dereferences ax25->timer, ax25->t1timer, ax25->t2timer, ax25->t3timer and ax25->idletimer (and re-drops the device references) after control has fallen through from paths that already executed ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) at line 22 (STATE_0), line 32 (STATE_1/2), or line 74 (SOCK_DGRAM). The only guard, 'if (ax25_dev)', checks the wrong variable (the cached ax25_dev pointer, not ax25's liveness) and is satisfiable precisely when the socket was bound to a device, which is attacker-chosen via bind(). No refcount hold on ax25 exists anywhere in this function (only sock_hold/sock_put on sk). Trigger: create an AF_AX25 socket, bind it to an ax25 device, and close it while in state 0/1/2 (or close a bound SOCK_DGRAM ax25 socket); del_timer_sync then reads/modifies the timer structs of the destroyed ax25_cb. Root cause: use-after-free (CWE-416).

Origin of the freed object on the simplest trigger path. For a non-SEQPACKET (SOCK_DGRAM) ax25 socket bound to a device, ax25_destroy_socket(ax25) destroys the ax25 control block here, then control unconditionally falls through to the 'if (ax25_dev)' block at lines 76-83, which dereferences the destroyed ax25 (del_timer_sync(&ax25->timer), lines 77-81) and drops ax25_dev's references a second time (lines 82-83). Equivalent destroy sites exist at line 22 (AX25_STATE_0) and line 32 (AX25_STATE_1/2).

assumptions: The body of ax25_destroy_socket() is outside the given snippet. The analysis assumes it destroys/releases the ax25 control block (its name, its exclusive use at socket teardown, and the fact that upstream callers never touch ax25 afterwards support this). Under either reading — immediate free or final-reference drop — the post-switch uses of ax25 at lines 77-81 and the device-reference drops at lines 82-83 occur after the destroy call and are unguarded in this code.

sk_to_ax25(sk) is assumed to return the ax25_cb for a socket reaching this AF_AX25 release callback; a NULL ax25 from sk_to_ax25 would make line 14 ('ax25_dev = ax25->ax25_dev;') a NULL deref, but that cannot be verified from the snippet.
AX25_STATES, AX25_PROTO_* constants and the referenced helpers (ax25_disconnect, ax25_send_control, ax25_clear_queues, timers) are assumed to have their standard ax25 semantics.
limitations: Line 40, 'switch (ax25->ax25_dev->values[AX25_VALUES_PROTOCOL])', has no NULL guard on ax25->ax25_dev even though line 76 treats ax25_dev as possibly NULL. Not confirmed because reaching STATE_3/4 requires an established link, which the ax25 layer only sets up with a bound device; no reachable runtime state with ax25_dev == NULL and state 3/4 could be constructed from inputs this code receives. Recorded as a defensive gap whose enforcing invariant is outside the snippet.

The release_sock/lock_sock windows (lines 19-21, 28-30) expose the socket to concurrent timer/softirq activity while unlocked, but sk is held ('sock_hold(sk)', line 10) and no concrete memory-safety break was provable from the given code alone; noted as a hardening concern, not a confirmed vulnerability.

The severity reflects a local-user-triggerable kernel UAF (potential slab corruption / denial of service via plain socket/bind/close); exact exploitability depends on allocator state and on the contents of ax25_destroy_socket, which is outside the snippet.

verdict.summary: tc_new_tfilter performs its CAP_NET_ADMIN capability check only on the first iteration; the err == -EAGAIN path jumps back to the replay: label, which is after the check, re-parsing and re-executing the attacker-supplied netlink request without any re-validation. On the replayed iteration the request can take the tcf_proto-create path with rtnl_held forced true, so an unprivileged caller in control of a subordinate user namespace (or racing a concurrent flush to force EAGAIN) gets the operation executed outside the authorization context it was originally validated under — an order-of-check authorization gap.

evidence.snippet:
if (!netlink_ns_capable(skb, net->user_ns, CAP_NET_ADMIN))
		return -EPERM;
evidence.reason: The sole authorization check for this request handler sits before the replay: label, so it executes only on the first iteration; every replayed execution of the attacker-controlled netlink message proceeds without it (root cause: missing authorization on the replay path).

evidence.snippet:
replay:
	tp_created = 0;
evidence.reason: Re-execution entry point: control re-enters here after the EAGAIN branch without passing any capability recheck, re-parsing n with nlmsg_parse_deprecated and re-running the full filter-creation logic on unvalidated credentials.

The trigger: err == -EAGAIN (attacker-raceable via chain->flushing) transfers control back to replay:, bypassing the capability check; no recheck of netlink_ns_capable exists on this path, so the replayed request executes unvalidated.

assumptions: The nlmsghdr *n, skb, and all tca[] attributes are attacker-supplied netlink data; their parsing and bounds enforcement (nlmsg_parse_deprecated, rtm_tca_policy, nla_strcmp, tcf_proto_check_kind) are assumed correct as they are not in the given code.

netlink_ns_capable(skb, net->user_ns, CAP_NET_ADMIN) is a per-netlink-message credential check; net->user_ns is derived from the socket, and a process with CAP_NET_ADMIN in a subordinate user namespace passes it — the message itself remains untrusted trust-boundary input.
chain_index is bounded by 'if (chain_index > TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK)' before tcf_chain_get; tcf_chain_get's internal failure mode is not in the given code.
limitations: Candidate B (NULL dereference of chain->flushing after tcf_chain_get returns NULL) is dismissed: the only path to chain == NULL is allocation failure inside tcf_chain_get, which attacker input cannot induce; the code guards it with 'if (!chain) { ... err = -ENOMEM; goto errout; }'.

The EAGAIN replay path also loops at most as many times as an attacker can force chain->flushing to be concurrently true; each iteration re-parses the message, so a concurrent-flush race could in principle be spun into CPU consumption, but unbounded looping is bounded by the attacker's ability to hold a flush, not by a missing bound in this code.

verdict.summary: do_put() never validates a negative 'count' before using it in size computations. The overflow guards test only the upper bound ('count > INT_MAX / yanklen' and 'count > ((INT_MAX - ...) / (yanklen + spaces))'), so a negative count (a value this function itself accepts at entry, per the 'count == -1' sentinel) passes through, makes totlen = count * yanklen negative, and produces an undersized heap allocation (alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1)); the copy loops are skipped, but the subsequent memmove/STRMOVE of the old line text writes oldlen+1 bytes past the allocation. This yields a deterministic heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled register and buffer content in both the MCHAR single-line path and the MBLOCK path.

evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty value: the multiplication-overflow guard tests only the upper bound. Edge case count = -1 (a legal sentinel elsewhere in this function) passes '-1 > INT_MAX / yanklen' == false, so a negative count reaches 'totlen = count * yanklen', producing a negative totlen. No lower-bound check on count exists on any path.

Sink: with count = -1 and yanklen = 5 on a 100-byte line, alloc(-5 + 100 + 1) = alloc(96) succeeds, the count-controlled copy loop is skipped (0 < -1 false), and STRMOVE(ptr, oldp + col) copies oldlen + 1 = 101 bytes into the 96-byte buffer — a heap buffer overflow write of attacker-controlled line content past the undersized allocation.

Same defect in the block-mode path: the overflow check is upper-bound-only, so a negative count passes, 'totlen = count * (yanklen + spaces) + ...' becomes negative, and alloc(totlen + oldlen + 1) under-allocates; the later mch_memmove of oldlen - textcol - delcount + 1 bytes then writes beyond the buffer.

assumptions: alloc(size) takes a size_t argument and returns NULL for huge sizes, so a wrapped-negative 'totlen + oldlen + 1' in [INT_MIN, -2] fails safely (positive-count boundary case).
ALLOC_MULT(char_u *, y_size) performs its own multiplication-overflow check; not verifiable in the given code.
col = curwin->w_cursor.col is bounded by the current line length by the editor's buffer/cursor invariants (internal trusted state); no in-code violation was constructible.
get_yank_register/get_spec_reg return well-formed y_type/y_size/y_array pairs; y_size == 0 is explicitly rejected by 'if (y_size == 0 || y_array == NULL)'.
limitations: With count >= 0, the guards 'count > INT_MAX / yanklen' and 'count > ((INT_MAX - (bd.startspaces + bd.endspaces)) / (yanklen + spaces))' were edge-tested (count exactly at the limit, one past) and are correct; the subsequent 'totlen + oldlen + 1' wrap always lands in the negative range for in-range inputs, yielding a huge size_t alloc that returns NULL and exits safely.

'curbuf->b_op_end.col = bd.textcol + totlen - 1' with negative totlen wraps the unsigned colnr_T and corrupts the '] mark; downstream consumers are outside this code, so it is recorded as a secondary effect of the confirmed finding.
The multi-line MCHAR/MLINE path ('for (cnt = 1; cnt <= count; ++cnt)') merely skips execution for negative count; no memory-unsafe write occurs there.

verdict.summary: tc_new_tfilter is a netlink handler whose attacker-influenced inputs are gated by quotable, correctly-ordered guards: CAP_NET_ADMIN is enforced at entry, attributes are parsed via a size-bounded policy call (nlmsg_parse_deprecated(n, sizeof(*t), tca, TCA_MAX, ...)), the chain index is bounded (if (chain_index > TC_ACT_EXT_VAL_MASK)), the filter kind length is checked with an error path, kind/template/exclusive-handle mismatches are all rejected before the change sink, and every mutex/rtnl lock is released on all exit paths including the EAGAIN replay. No defect is provable from the given code alone; residual candidates depend on unquoted helper contracts and are recorded as assumptions/limitations.

assumptions: rtm_tca_policy and nlmsg_parse_deprecated validate attribute presence, type, and length for tca[]; not quotable in the given code.
tcf_proto_check_kind bounds the copy into char name[IFNAMSIZ]; the call-site error branch is present but the bound enforcement itself lives in the helper.
__tcf_qdisc_find guarantees q->ops->cl_ops is non-NULL when it returns 0 with *q set; the check is inside the helper and not quotable here (the given code's 'q &&' guard only covers q == NULL).

tcf_chain_get, tcf_chain_tp_find, tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique, tp->ops->get/change and tcf_proto_put follow the documented refcount contracts; in particular that the errout_tp path (insert failure, tp_created == 1) is either unreachable or cleaned up inside tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique.
The netlink core validates nlmsg_len so that nlmsg_data(n) + sizeof(struct tcmsg) is in-bounds.
limitations: If tp->ops->change() returns an error after a successful tp->ops->get() (non-EXCL path), the given code never calls tfilter_put(tp, fh); this is only a leak if classifier change() implementations do not consume the handle reference on failure, which cannot be determined from the given code.

On the goto errout_tp path (tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique returning ERR_PTR) the code skips tcf_chain_tp_delete_empty and skips tcf_chain_put(chain) because tp_created == 1; if the helper can fail without internal cleanup this leaks the chain reference and tp_new, but reachability of that failure is not provable from the given code.

The window between mutex_unlock(&chain->filter_chain_lock) and tcf_proto_create/tcf_chain_tp_insert_unique is closed only by the chain->flushing check plus re-lookup/re-serialization inside the callee; that mitigation is external to the given code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled BMP header fields are validated before use, and every pixel-buffer access uses a scanline stride provably no larger than the allocation stride 'AcquireVirtualMemory(image->rows,MagickMax(bytes_per_line,image->columns+256UL))' computed before any read; colormap writes are bounded by the AcquireImageColormap success check and the byte-count check; edge cases (odd columns, columns<8, RLE4 bit-shift, 16/24/32-bit strides at columns=1 and 2, size_t products bounded by 2^31 inputs) were tested and remain in bounds. No surviving vulnerability.

assumptions: DecodeImage(image,compression,pixels,image->columns*image->rows) honors its length argument and does not write beyond columns*rows bytes; its internals are not in the given code.

IsValidColormapIndex(image,index,&index,exception) always assigns a colormap-safe value to its out-parameter even when returning MagickFalse; its internals are not in the given code, and the callers here discard its return value.
SetImageExtent(image,columns,rows) rejects or fails on extreme dimensions; its behavior is external to the given code (the code does handle its MagickFalse return).

The declared widths of BMPInfo mask fields are not shown in the given code; if they are 32-bit, the mask shift loops bounded by 'if (shift.red > 32U) break;' evaluate 'mask << 32' (potentially undefined) once before breaking.
limitations: The shift-by-32 evaluation in the mask/quantum_bits loops (e.g. 'while (((bmp_info.red_mask << shift.red) & 0x80000000UL) == 0) { shift.red++; if (shift.red > 32U) break; }') is a latent undefined-behavior concern if the mask fields are 32-bit wide, but the field types are not declared in the given code and no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds access results from it.

Ignoring the return value of IsValidColormapIndex with '(void)' relies on that function's out-parameter always being set to a valid index; if that contract were violated upstream, case 4/8 could write invalid colormap indices, but no such defect is visible in the given code.

The '(MagickSizeType) length/8 > GetBlobSize(image)' check divides a byte count by 8, making it weaker than a direct length comparison; it is compensated by the stricter 'count != (ssize_t) length' short-read checks on both read paths.

verdict.summary: In nfcmrvl_nci_unregister_dev, the code calls nci_unregister_device(ndev) first and only then dereferences priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress. nci_unregister_device unregisters and releases the last reference to the NFC device (via nfc_unregister_device/device_unregister), so priv->ndev->nfc_dev can already be freed when line 6 reads it — a use-after-free read whose result additionally gates a call to nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort on stale state. The correct ordering (check/abort before unregister) is absent from the code.

evidence.reason: Use-after-free: nci_unregister_device(ndev) releases the NFC device, after which priv->ndev->nfc_dev->fw_download_in_progress dereferences the freed object; no refcount, NULL/liveness check, or reordering guard exists between the unregister call and the dereference. If the stale flag reads true, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort(priv) additionally operates on freed/stale download state. Trigger: any device teardown reaching this unregister callback; the read occurs on every path.

assumptions: nci_unregister_device internally calls nfc_unregister_device, which unregisters the nfc_dev and drops its last reference (freeing it via the device release callback) — the free happens inside the callee, but the faulty ordering is in the given code.
fw_download_in_progress can be set by user-initiated firmware-download requests, but the UAF read at line 6 occurs regardless of the flag's value.
limitations: gpio_is_valid(priv->config.reset_n_io) at line 11 correctly guards gpio_free at the boundary values (negatives invalid, 0 valid); dismissed.
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit at line 9 executing after ndev's workqueues were destroyed is part of the same teardown-ordering defect and is not counted as a separate finding.

verdict.summary: g_socket_client_connected_callback dereferences data unconditionally after g_socket_connection_connect_finish succeeds, but the code's own comment states 'data is NULL once the task is completed', and the success path of a parallel attempt sets attempt_entry->data = NULL while this attempt's async callback is still pending. A losing attempt whose socket connect completed just before cancellation still receives a successful connect_finish result, skips the short-circuit guard 'if (data && ...)', and crashes on 'data->socket = g_steal_pointer (&attempt->socket)'. An attacker controlling the connection peer (and/or DNS) can steer this race to crash the client (denial of service).

evidence.snippet:
data->socket = g_steal_pointer (&attempt->socket);
  data->connection = g_steal_pointer (&attempt->connection);
evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional dereference of data on the connect-finish success path. No 'if (data)' or cancellation re-check exists between g_socket_connection_connect_finish succeeding and these lines; the only data==NULL guards in the function ('if (data && g_task_return_error_if_cancelled (data->task))' short-circuits to false when data is NULL, and the 'if (data)' branch is on the failure path only) do not protect this path. Trigger: task completed by a parallel attempt (attempt->data set to NULL) while this attempt's connect had already succeeded, so connect_finish returns TRUE and data is NULL → NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476), enabled by the task-completion race (CWE-362).

Origin: the success path of the winning attempt sets each losing attempt's data to NULL while the losing attempt's async connect callback is still pending. The preceding g_cancellable_cancel does not guarantee the in-flight connect_finish fails (the connect may have already completed), so the losing attempt can later execute the success path with data == NULL and crash at the data->socket dereference.

assumptions: The reference-counting contract of connection_attempt_unref / connection_attempt_remove / connection_attempt_new (whether the list and each in-flight callback hold separate references) is not shown in the given code; the apparent double-unref pattern around connection_attempt_unref (attempt) after the loop that already unrefs every list entry could not be verified and was not relied on.

Task-completion paths outside this function (enumerator exhausting addresses, returning the final error) are assumed to cancel remaining attempts; if they do not, the failure-path deref 'set_last_error (data, error)' guarded only by 'if (!g_cancellable_is_cancelled (attempt->cancellable))' would also be reachable with data == NULL.

Whether g_object_unref (data->task) at the top actually frees the task (leaving data->task dangling for the later 'g_task_get_cancellable (data->task)') depends on external task ownership and could not be established from the given code.

Behavior of g_socket_connection_connect_finish when cancellation races with an already-established connect (returning TRUE despite the cancelled cancellable) is a property of the GSocketConnection API, not of this code; the code nevertheless performs no compensating check.
limitations: A NULL 'protocol' from g_proxy_address_get_protocol reaching g_hash_table_contains could crash if app_proxies uses a NULL-intolerant hash, but no path in the given code produces a NULL protocol, so it is speculative.

If the race cannot be won in practice (e.g., the connect task is guaranteed to fail on late cancellation by the GIO implementation), the defect degrades to unreachable dead handling; however, nothing in the given code enforces that guarantee, and the code itself models data == NULL as a live state.

verdict.summary: g_socket_client_connected_callback unreffs the shared per-connection GTask (data->task) whenever the per-attempt cancellable is cancelled, but a successful sibling attempt cancels exactly those sibling cancellables in its cleanup loop (g_cancellable_cancel (attempt_entry->cancellable)). Each cancelled sibling callback then executes g_object_unref (data->task) while the winning attempt is still using the task (g_task_get_cancellable, TLS handshake / proxy negotiation, and the eventual g_task_return_* + unref). With one sibling the task reference is dropped prematurely (dangling data->task); with multiple siblings the unref executes multiple times, causing premature free/double-unref and a use-after-free in a commonly reachable path (any host resolving to multiple addresses).

evidence.reason: The OR condition lets a per-attempt cancellation alone reach g_object_unref (data->task). A sibling attempt cancelled by the winning attempt satisfies g_cancellable_is_cancelled (attempt->cancellable) even when the task is neither completed nor globally cancelled, so the shared GTask is unref'd (prematurely, and once per cancelled sibling) while the winning attempt's path still dereferences data->task afterwards (line 98 g_task_get_cancellable (data->task), line 66 g_socket_client_tls_handshake (data), line 95 g_proxy_connect_async). Use-after-free / double-unref, CWE-416.

Origin of the trigger: after one attempt succeeds, every remaining parallel attempt's cancellable is cancelled here. Each such sibling's connect then fails and re-enters this same callback with g_cancellable_is_cancelled(attempt->cancellable) true, driving the top-branch unref of the still-live shared data->task.

Second manifestation of the same defect: when connect_finish fails and the attempt's cancellable was cancelled by a winning sibling, this branch also unrefs the shared data->task that the winning attempt still owns and will use/unref again, producing an unbalanced extra unref (premature free).

assumptions: connection_attempt_new/ref/unref, task_completed_or_cancelled, connection_attempt_remove, g_socket_client_async_connect_complete and enumerator_next_async are not shown; their exact reference-counting is unknown. The success path unrefs the winning attempt both in the loop (line 52) and at line 56, which is only sound if each pending attempt holds >= 2 references (list + callback); this is assumed from upstream conventions but cannot be quoted here.

data->task is created via g_task_new with a single reference owned by the shared async-connect data (not shown in this excerpt); the unrefs at lines 14 and 38 are therefore assumed to consume that single shared reference rather than a per-attempt one.

Multiple parallel connection attempts (happy-eyeballs style) exist at runtime, inferred from the loop over data->connection_attempts cancelling sibling attempts; the code that appends attempts to that list is not shown.
limitations: Potential NULL-deref if g_proxy_address_get_protocol (data->proxy_addr) can return NULL and it is passed to g_hash_table_contains (data->client->priv->app_proxies, protocol): whether a GProxyAddress can be constructed with a NULL protocol cannot be determined from this code, so this candidate is unproven and not counted.
g_critical on a non-TCP proxied connection and the 'wrong, but backward compatible' blocking flag are correctness/robustness issues, not security vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: This BMP decoder validates every trust-boundary value before use: dimensions, planes, bits-per-pixel, compression/bpp pairing, colormap size (bounded to 2^bits_per_pixel via 'if (bmp_info.bits_per_pixel < 16 && bmp_info.number_colors > (1U << bmp_info.bits_per_pixel))'), full-length blob reads ('count != (ssize_t) length'), seek results ('if (offset < 0)'), allocation failures, and per-row pixel strides that I edge-tested (columns 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 15, 16) and found exactly equal to or within the allocated row stride 'AcquireVirtualMemory(image->rows,MagickMax(bytes_per_line,image->columns+256UL))'. The theoretical 64-bit overflow of bytes_per_line*rows requires dimensions whose pixel-cache allocation (gated by SetImageExtent, whose failure is handled) cannot succeed, so it is unreachable. Remaining weaknesses (fail-open on file_size mismatch, possible false rejection of valid RLE files, stale start_position for BA frames) are functional or fail-closed with no memory-safety or authorization effect.

assumptions: IsValidColormapIndex (helper not shown) is assumed to assign *packet on both success and failure; if it left 'index' unset on failure, SetPixelIndex(indexes,index) would store uninitialized data. The trigger cannot be proven from the given code.

DecodeImage (helper not shown) is assumed to bound its writes to the number_pixels argument passed as image->columns*image->rows; the buffer allocated is rows*max(bytes_per_line,columns+256) which is >= columns*rows for the RLE bit depths.

SetImageExtent (framework) is assumed to fail for dimensions whose pixel-cache allocation cannot succeed; this is what makes the bytes_per_line*rows 64-bit overflow (requires columns*rows >= ~2^62) unreachable.
64-bit size_t/ssize_t assumed; on 32-bit builds width*height arithmetic could overflow earlier, but SetImageExtent feasibility still gates those dimensions.
ThrowReaderException/ThrowMagickException assumed to record errors (and ThrowReaderException to destroy the image list and return), per framework contract.
limitations: The file_size-vs-blob-size mismatch records a CorruptImageError but continues decoding instead of returning; all subsequent pixel consumption is still bounded by ReadBlob count checks ('count != (ssize_t) length', 'count != (ssize_t) (packet_size*image->colors)') and the blob size, so this fail-open has no security effect.

The guard 'if (((MagickSizeType) length/8) > GetBlobSize(image))' compares the DECODED raster size to the blob size and can falsely reject valid RLE-compressed BMPs whose compressed stream is smaller than 1/8 of the raster (functional, fail-closed).

For multi-frame files traversed via a BA record offset, start_position is not refreshed when ba_offset != 0, so later frames may read pixel/colormap data from incorrect file offsets; the count checks bound the reads to the file, so the effect is corrupted pixels or rejection, not memory unsafety.
The trailing 'if (x < (ssize_t) image->columns) break;' in the 4-bit case is dead code (x always equals columns when reached) but harmless.

verdict.summary: do_tag() uses the caller-supplied `count` and the derived `tagstackidx` to index the fixed-size array curwin->w_tagstack without validating the index on every path. A :pop with count (tagstackidx -= count clamps negatives only via an emsg branch that still falls through to tagstack[tagstackidx].fmark reads when tagstackidx + count != 0), a tag jump with a huge count (`tagstackidx += count - 1` signed-overflows and passes the single-sided `>= tagstacklen` check), and the push path after the tagstack-full shift (`--tagstackidx` can leave tagstackidx == -1 when tagstacklen was 0, immediately followed by the unguarded write `tagstack[tagstackidx].tagname = vim_strsave(tag)`) all produce out-of-bounds reads and an out-of-bounds pointer write on the static TAGSTACKSIZE-element array.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds array write (root cause CWE-129). When the tagstack is full, the shift-down loop executes and `--tagstackidx` decrements the index; if tagstackidx was 0 it becomes -1 (and when tagstacklen was 0 the full-branch makes tagstacklen == TAGSTACKSIZE with idx still 0 -> -1). The very next statement writes `tagstack[tagstackidx].tagname = vim_strsave(tag)` with no `tagstackidx >= 0` check anywhere between the decrement and the write, storing a heap pointer before the array. Trigger: entry state tagstacklen == TAGSTACKSIZE (or 0 with idx 0) plus `:tag <name>` reaching this push path.

Out-of-bounds read (CWE-129). The guard `if (tagstackidx + count == 0)` only handles the exact-bottom case; for any other negative result the code prints an error but falls through to `saved_fmark = tagstack[tagstackidx].fmark` — after the shown clamp `tagstackidx = 0` this specific fall-through is safe for the fmark read, but the same unchecked `count` reaches `tagstackidx += count - 1` (candidate B) and `tagstack[tagstackidx]` accesses after `--tagstackidx` paths, where no equivalent `tagstackidx = 0` clamp exists on the `:tag` and next/prev paths.

Signed integer overflow feeding an out-of-bounds read (CWE-190 consequence CWE-125/CWE-129). The guard is single-sided (`>= tagstacklen`) and its own arithmetic is unchecked: with attacker-chosen count (e.g. count == INT_MIN or 2, count == 1 causes `count - 1 == 0` — and count == 2 with tagstackidx == 0 gives `tagstackidx = 1 >= tagstacklen == 1`, clamped to tagstacklen - 1 == 0, safe; but count large enough that `tagstackidx + count - 1` overflows to a negative value passes BOTH the `>=` and, if it lands negative, the `< 0` branch goto's out; the case `tagstackidx + count - 1` overflowing to a small non-negative value, or count negative such that the sum is negative but the `< 0` emsg path is taken, leaves `cur_match = tagstack[tagstackidx].cur_match` reading the array with an index that was never range-checked against [0, tagstacklen)). Trigger: `:tag` with count N where the addition wraps.

assumptions: TAGSTACKSIZE is a small compile-time constant (upstream vim: 20) — not visible in the given snippet; the OOB conclusion does not depend on its exact value.

`count` is the ex-command count (e.g. `5CTRL-T`, `:5tag`), attacker-influenced through scripted input, macros, or any front-end that feeds editor commands; do_tag is an internal entry point invoked from ex_tag with user-controlled count.

FEAT_QUICKFIX / FEAT_EVAL / FEAT_CSCOPE are enabled in the common build; paths through g_do_tagpreview != 0 divert some candidates but the push path (candidate A) and the count arithmetic (candidate B) are feature-independent.
The caller of do_tag does not validate count against tagstacklen; no such validation is quotable in the given code, so per the rules it is treated as absent.
limitations: Candidate A (push-path OOB write) requires the tagstack to be full (tagstacklen == TAGSTACKSIZE, i.e. 20 nested successful tag jumps) or the degenerate empty-stack-but-full-branch state; this is a normal, reachable user state, so the candidate stands, but exploitation needs that setup.

Candidate on `sprintf((char *)IObuff, _("tag %d of %d%s"), ...)` was examined: IObuff is IOSIZE-sized and the format is fixed with three bounded expansions; %d of int values plus a short literal cannot overflow IOSIZE (256). Dismissed — not attacker-controllable format string, no CWE-134.
Candidate on `vim_snprintf(IObuff, IOSIZE, ":ta %s\r", name)` — bounded by IOSIZE via vim_snprintf's size argument. Dismissed.

Candidate on `tagstack[tagstackidx].user_data = vim_strnsave(tagp.user_data, tagp.user_data_end - tagp.user_data)` — pointer difference within a parsed tag line from parse_match(); parse_match is outside the given code, so under GUARD ANCHORING its invariants are unverifiable here; recorded as an assumption, not a confirmed finding.

Use-after-free of the static `matches`/`num_matches` across calls was examined: FreeWild is called before reassignment and at DT_FREE; no double-free path found within this function's own control flow.

Candidate B's practical severity depends on INT wrap: counts are typically clamped by the ex-command parser to small positives upstream, but that clamp is not quotable in this code, so the candidate is kept with reduced confidence rather than dropped.

verdict.summary: cgroup1_parse_param validates every attacker-supplied mount option before use: source/release_agent are single-instance guarded, subsystem names are matched against a compile-time table before the '1 << i' shift, and the 'name' option is bounded by 'param->size > MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN - 1' with a strict [\w.-]+ character loop run before ownership transfer. No unguarded memory, injection, or fail-open sink exists in this code.

assumptions: param->key is NUL-terminated and param->string is at least param->size bytes, as guaranteed by the fs_parameter/fs_parse layer outside this code (cannot be quoted here, but strcmp at the 'source' branch and the name loop depend on it).

for_each_subsys yields i within [0, CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT) with CGROUP_SUBSYS_COUNT <= 31 so 'ctx->subsys_mask |= (1 << i)' stays within the width of subsys_mask; the bound is a property of the compile-time subsystem table, not of this function.
Allocation of fs_context fields (fc->source, ctx->name, ctx->release_agent) is performed by the caller; this code only transfers ownership.
limitations: '1 << i' uses a signed literal and would be undefined at i >= 31; not reachable because subsystem ids are compile-time constants, so this is a hardening note, not a vulnerability in this code.
Opt_none/Opt_all interact with subsys_mask only semantically at mount time; no memory-safety effect in this function.
release_agent path value is unvalidated here (validation of its content occurs elsewhere in cgroup1), but this function performs no dereference, copy, or execution on it.

verdict.summary: In the ACTION_EXPAND completion branch, when the matched word length i equals ins_compl_len(), the code copies i bytes into the fixed-size global IObuff with STRNCPY(IObuff, aux, i) without any in-code bound on i against IOSIZE. i is the length of a word taken from buffer/file line content (trust-boundary data), and the only claimed bound ('IOSIZE > compl_length, so the STRNCPY works') is a comment, not a check. A completion keyword longer than IOSIZE overflows IObuff.

evidence.reason: i is computed as the word length from startp (find_word_end minus find_word_start on line content from ml_get/vim_fgets). When i == ins_compl_len(), i bytes are copied into IObuff (fixed IOSIZE global) with no check that i < IOSIZE anywhere before the copy; the comment asserting the bound is not an executed guard. A user-controlled keyword (buffer content crossing the trust boundary) of length >= IOSIZE causes an out-of-bounds write.

verdict.summary: kvmppc_rtas_hcall is the KVM host-kernel intake point for the guest's RTAS hypercall. A malicious guest supplying a large nargs gets an out-of-bounds/wild-pointer write into host kernel stack memory (guest-to-host memory corruption).

orig_rets = args.rets;
	args.rets = &args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)];
evidence.reason: Sink: guest-supplied nargs (be32, range 0..0xFFFFFFFF, read from guest memory) is used unvalidated as the array index/pointer offset into the fixed-size stack struct 'args'. No bound on nargs is enforced anywhere in this code (the only guards present are the kvm_read_guest error check and the token equality), and the resulting pointer is handed to the RTAS handler at line 35 (d->handler->handler(vcpu, &args)) which stores return values through args.rets, causing an out-of-bounds write for large nargs values (e.g., nargs = 0x40000000 yields a write ~4 GiB beyond the stack object).

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: kvm_read_guest copies guest-controlled memory (token, nargs, nret, rets, args contents) directly into the stack struct 'args'. The subsequent code consumes args.nargs as an index without validating it against the size of the stack object, making this the point where untrusted data crosses the trust boundary into the vulnerable pointer computation.

The definition of struct rtas_args (capacity of the args[] array, sizeof(rtas_arg_t)) is not included in the given code; it is assumed to be a fixed finite array since the struct is instantiated on the stack with sizeof(args) used for the guest copy. Whatever its capacity N is, no comparison of nargs against N (or against any other bound) exists in this code, so the finding holds for any finite N.

The RTAS handler implementations (d->handler->handler) are not shown; per this function's own comment, args.rets is fixed up to point into the local copy so handlers can store return values there, i.e., handlers dereference args.rets.
The rtas token list (vcpu->kvm->arch.rtas_tokens) is populated by host userspace via registration ioctls and is treated as trusted; the guest may only dispatch to tokens the host registered.

args.rets (orig_rets) is restored to the guest's original value before write-back, so the guest's pointer field is preserved and no foreign value leaks into guest memory via that field.

The '& KVM_PAM' mask bounds args_phys to the guest real-address range, so this function itself does not dereference a host-chosen address from r4; reads/writes go through kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest only.

Origin of the tainted data: the macro arguments are tokens read directly from the attacker-controlled table file via getToken and stored into the heap array 'arguments'; these are the values whose full, unchecked length is later appended to tmpFile.line at line 170.

Proof that the bound is required and known: the definition-character loop checks 'tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING' before each single write, establishing that tmpFile.line holds exactly MAXSTRING widechars; the identical check is absent on the argument-substitution branch (lines 166-170), which is the missing-check site. In CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch the return values of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern are ignored (e.g. 'getCharacters(file, &ptn_before);'), so on parse failure the stack locals ptn_before/ptn_after may be used uninitialized (CWE-457); whether the helpers always initialize the CharsStrings on failure is not shown, so this was not counted as confirmed.

verdict.summary: compileRule parses table-file content (attacker-influenced trust-boundary input) and contains three unguarded sinks: (1) macro argument substitution copies arg.chars into the fixed-size tmpFile.line with no bound on tmpFile.linelen — the sibling definition-character loop is guarded by 'tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING' but the substitution loop bypasses it, giving a stack buffer overflow (CWE-787); (2) CTO_SeqAfterExpression copies ruleChars.chars into the fixed-size seqAfterExpression array with no size check (every comparable case checks SEQPATTERNSIZE/LETSIGNSIZE/EMPHMODECHARSSIZE/NOEMPHCHARSSIZE), and writes a terminator at index ruleChars.length, giving a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); (3) in CTO_Match/CTO_BackMatch the return values of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern are ignored, so ptn_before/ptn_after/ruleChars/ruleDots may be used uninitialized (CWE-457). All are triggerable by crafted table text processed at this intake point.

evidence.reason: Stack buffer overflow (CWE-787): macro arguments (attacker-controlled table tokens, length up to a full line) are copied into the fixed-size stack array tmpFile.line without any check of tmpFile.linelen. The only bound, '} else if (tmpFile.linelen >= MAXSTRING) {' at line 157, guards only the definition-character copy at line 164; this branch is reached directly at line 166 with linelen at any value, so linelen + arg.length exceeds the array. Trigger: in a table file, define a macro whose definition places a substitution placeholder near the end of a MAXSTRING-long line and invoke it with a long argument token.

Heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): the CTO_SeqAfterExpression case copies attacker-controlled ruleChars.chars (length taken directly from getRuleCharsText) into the fixed-size array (*table)->seqAfterExpression with no size check anywhere in the function — unlike the sibling cases that quote 'if (((*table)->seqPatternsCount + ruleChars.length + 1) > SEQPATTERNSIZE)', '> LETSIGNSIZE', '> EMPHMODECHARSSIZE'. The terminator at line 983 is additionally written at index ruleChars.length, i.e. one-past when the array is exactly full. Trigger: a table line 'seqafterexpr <more characters than the array capacity>'.

Use of uninitialized values (CWE-457): the return values of getCharacters/getRuleCharsText/getRuleDotsPattern are ignored (every other call in the function is checked, e.g. 'if (!getRuleCharsText(file, &ruleChars)) return 0;'), yet the uninitialized locals ptn_before/ptn_after are immediately read at line 239 ('if (ptn_before.chars[0] == '-' && ptn_before.length == 1)') and their length is passed to _lou_pattern_compile. Trigger: a malformed 'match'/'backmatch' line with missing operands causes the parse to fail and the stack structs to be consumed uninitialized. The same pattern exists in CTO_BackMatch.

assumptions: Exact capacities of tmpFile.line, seqAfterExpression, and the value of MAXSTRING are not visible in the given snippet; the overflow conclusions rest on the code's own asymmetry (all comparable sinks are explicitly size-checked, these are not) and on the terminator write at index ruleChars.length, which is out-of-bounds whenever the array is exactly full.

Behavior of unseen helpers (getToken, getCharacters, getRuleCharsText, getRuleDotsPattern, getOpcode, _lou_pattern_compile, compileMacro, putChar, addRule) is assumed per their conventional contracts; e.g. whether getCharacters initializes its output on failure is unverifiable here, which bounds the confidence of the CWE-457 finding.

Line numbers were counted from line 1 being 'compileRule(FileInfo *file, ...'; whitespace in snippets reproduces the source's tab indentation approximately.
limitations: CTO_MultInd writes 'ruleChars.chars[ruleChars.length++] = (widechar)opcode;' with no explicit bound on ruleChars.length; safety relies on the tokenizer consuming at least one character plus one separator per token, which cannot be quoted from the given code — not confirmed.
