verdict.summary: njs_object_iterate_reverse() consumes the int64_t indices args->from and args->to (entry-point parameters, attacker-influenced via JS-level state such as the generic receiver's length) without validating them against the iterated value's bounds. The fast-array path guards only the upper bound (`from < array->length`, no `from >= 0`), so `to < 0` makes the loop body read `array->start[-1]` out of bounds; the byte-string path computes `p = string_prop.start + from` with no check that `from < string_prop.size` and copies 1 byte from `p` each iteration; the UTF-8 path lets `njs_utf8_prev(p)` walk below `string_prop.start` when `to < 0` or `from` exceeds the character count. Result: attacker-influenced heap out-of-bounds reads whose contents are passed to the iterator handler and become script-observable.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted indices: `from` and `to` are unvalidated int64_t entry-point parameters (declared at line 5) read from `args`; no statement in this function bounds them against the length of `value`, and every later memory access is sized solely by them.

The fast-array sink guard supplies only an upper bound. The body of `while (from-- > to)` executes for every f >= to, so with to = -1 and a non-empty fast array the body runs with from = -1; the signed comparison `-1 < array->length` passes, and `njs_is_valid(&array->start[from])` / `&array->start[from]` read an njs_value_t before the array data. No `from >= 0` check exists anywhere in the function (root cause: improper validation of array index, CWE-129; effect: out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

Byte-string sink: `p` is derived directly from the unvalidated index `from` with no check that `0 <= to <= from < string_prop.size` (the only comparison in the branch, `(size_t) length == string_prop.size`, merely selects the branch). With from == string_prop.size the first `njs_string_new` copies one byte past the buffer; with to == -1 the last iteration (i == -1) reads start[-1]. Heap OOB read whose byte becomes an njs_value_t handed to the handler.

UTF-8 sink: `from` is never checked against the character count, and `to` is never checked to be >= 0. njs_string_offset clamps an oversized `from` to `end`, yet the loop still runs from-to+1 times; once `p` reaches `string_prop.start`, further iterations make `njs_utf8_prev(p)` read bytes before the buffer, an out-of-bounds heap read whose bytes are copied into `character` by `njs_string_new`.

assumptions: In the complete njs source, callers of njs_object_iterate_reverse are expected to pass 0 <= to <= from < length(value) (indices derived from ToLength of the generic receiver). That invariant is NOT enforced by any statement in the given code, so per guard-anchoring it is an assumption, not a fact; this function performs no last-line validation of `from`/`to`.
`array->length` is assumed to be an unsigned zero-based count (njs internal type), making the `from < array->length` comparison purely an upper-bound check with no lower bound.
limitations: `from - to` at njs_fast_object(from - to) can overflow int64 for extreme caller values (UB), but it only selects a branch and is subsumed by the same missing-validation root cause; triggering it with realistic JS-derived lengths is impractical.

NaN from njs_string_to_index would pass the `idx < to || idx > from` filter, but `keys` are canonical index strings produced by njs_array_indices within this code and `idx` is only used for a property lookup, so no memory-safety effect in this function.

For an empty string with from = -1 the OOB pointer `string_prop.start + from` is computed but never dereferenced because the loop does not execute; the defect requires the loop body to actually run at the boundary index.

The concrete reachability of out-of-range from/to depends on callers outside the given code; per the analysis rules, entry-point parameter values a caller may pass are treated as attacker-reachable, which drives the 0.7 confidence rather than a higher value.

verdict.summary: The only type guard in the function is `if (input1->type == kTfLiteUInt8 || input1->type == kTfLiteInt8)`, which validates input1 alone. input2's type is never checked, yet `input2->params.zero_point` (line 5), `input2->params.scale` (line 14), and `GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2)` (lines 28/33) are consumed unconditionally: for a model declaring input1 quantized and input2 non-quantized (e.g., float32), uninitialized quantization parameters are used and input2's raw buffer is reinterpreted with the wrong dtype (type confusion; potential OOB read for narrower-storage element types such as packed 4-bit). Additionally, the guard has no else branch, so any non-quantized input1 type makes the function silently return without writing output, leaving the output tensor uninitialized for downstream consumers (fail-open). Trigger: an untrusted model file (the trust boundary this kernel serves) with mismatched input tensor types.

evidence.reason: The guard checks only input1->type; there is no statement anywhere in the function validating input2->type or output->type. With input1 declared kTfLiteInt8 and input2 declared kTfLiteFloat32 in the model, this branch is taken and `input2->params.zero_point` (and `input2->params.scale` at line 14) are read from a tensor that was never initialized as quantized, and input2's data is later reinterpreted as input_dtype — a type confusion on attacker-controlled model data.

Sink: `GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2)` reinterprets input2's raw buffer as input_dtype with no type check on input2 anywhere in this code, and `GetTensorData<bool>(output)` assumes an unchecked output->type. The same unchecked reinterpretation occurs on the broadcast path (lines 26-29). No check on shapes is performed either before taking this non-broadcast path.

Fail-open: the type guard at line 3 has no else branch, so when input1->type is any non-quantized value (float32, int32, bool, ...), control falls straight through to this return and the output tensor is never written, leaving attacker-shaped output memory uninitialized for downstream consumers.

assumptions: Tensor descriptors (type, params, shape, data buffers) originate from a loaded model file, which is untrusted serialized data; this kernel function is part of the intake path for that data.

For a narrower-storage element type such as packed 4-bit (kTfLiteInt4), GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) with a shape of N elements reads N bytes from a buffer of about N/2 bytes, which would be an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125); this consequence depends on TFLite storage details not present in the given code, but the missing input2->type check that would prevent it is verifiably absent here.
`bool requires_broadcast` and the shape consistency it implies are supplied by the caller; no statement in this code constrains them (guard anchoring: cannot be quoted here).

Behavior of reference_ops::ComparisonWithScaling / BroadcastComparison4DSlowWithScaling (e.g., whether they iterate over MatchingFlatSize of the first shape) is outside the given code and could not be verified.
limitations: Candidate C4 (out-of-bounds read/write on the non-broadcast path when shapes mismatch) was not confirmed as an independent finding because the loop bounds live in reference_ops, which is not part of the given code; the in-code absence of a shape-equality check is noted.

Candidate C5 (uint8 vs int8 value confusion via the `||` in the type guard with a single input_dtype instantiation) affects computed comparison values only; both types are 1 byte wide, so no memory-safety impact was proven.

The missing output->type == kTfLiteBool check does not by itself cause an out-of-bounds access, since sizeof(bool)=1 is not larger than any TfLite element type; it is reported as part of the missing-validation root cause rather than as a separate memory-safety finding.

verdict.summary: LoadAndRemapMatrix::Compute derives min_old_row/max_old_row directly from the attacker-controlled row_remapping tensor and uses them in the slice-building while loop without any magnitude bound or overflow check. With row_remapping containing INT64_MAX (e.g., [INT64_MAX] with num_rows_=1), 'row_start += slice_length' and 'max_old_row - row_start + 1' overflow (signed int64 UB): row_start wraps to INT64_MIN, the slice_length becomes 0 on every subsequent iteration, and the loop pushes zero-length TensorSlice objects into tensor_slices forever, hanging the process and exhausting memory (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Sink: slice-construction loop. max_old_row/row_start come straight from attacker-controlled row_remapping values; 'max_old_row - row_start + 1' (INT64_MAX + 1) and 'row_start += slice_length' (INT64_MAX + 1) overflow signed int64 with no guard anywhere in the function. After the wrap, slice_length computes to 0 (both the ternary and std::min branches yield 0), so row_start never advances and the loop pushes into tensor_slices indefinitely: signed integer overflow (CWE-190) leading to infinite loop / unbounded memory growth (CWE-400), triggerable with row_remapping = [INT64_MAX].

Origin: max_old_row is assigned the raw attacker-controlled int64 row_remapping(i) with no upper bound (not clamped to tensor_shape.dim_size(0) or INT64_MAX-safe range); this unbounded value is what reaches and overflows the arithmetic in the while loop at lines 112-122.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap is not shown; it is assumed to size row_id_present/col_id_present to the input vector length, which the quoted checks row_remapping.size() == num_rows_ and col_remapping.size() == num_cols_ then tie to num_rows_/num_cols_.

TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape and BundleReader::LookupSlice are outside this code; whether they reject out-of-range or negative-length slices (for candidate B: unvalidated old row IDs vs tensor_shape.dim_size(0)) cannot be verified by quoting, so no finding rests on them.

num_rows_, num_cols_, max_rows_in_memory_ are op attributes assumed settable by the graph author; the confirmed defect triggers for any value of max_rows_in_memory_ (both the <=0 and >0 branches yield slice_length 0 after the wrap).
limitations: Candidate B (old row IDs not validated against tensor_shape.dim_size(0) before SliceTensorShape/LookupSlice) is reachable, but any out-of-bounds consequence depends on unshown framework code; it is not counted as a vulnerability of this code by itself.

The min/max and copy loops use 'int' counters against int64 sizes (for (int i = 0; i < row_remapping.size(); ++i)); overflowing these requires an input tensor of >2^31 int64 elements (~17 GB), which is not a practical trigger.

The op by design reads a checkpoint file at an attacker-supplied path (ckpt_path) and tensor name; exposing this op to untrusted clients is a design/exposure concern, not a memory-safety defect in this code.

Guarded sinks verified safe: the output write is protected by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, new_row < num_rows_ && new_col < num_cols_ && new_row >= 0 && new_col >= 0, ...)' and the initializing_values read by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, initializing_values_index < initializing_values.size(), ...)'.

verdict.summary: fiber_switch consumes internally parsed argc (len), a validated fiber object, and VM-internal dispatch flags. The stack sizing at mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) provably covers every subsequent write (stbase[0..len]) for all len >= 0, and the only state-dependent dereferences (cibase->proc, ci[1].stack) depend on invariants established at fiber construction and by the vmexec calling protocol outside this code. No candidate survived the trigger-proof and counterfactual patch tests: no statement in this code produces the faulty states a trigger would require, and the bounds this code does own were edge-tested and hold.

assumptions: fiber_check(mrb, self) validates the Fiber object and returns a non-NULL context; its validation is not present in the given code.
fiber_check_cfunc(mrb, c) rejects cfunc fibers before any context switch; not present in the given code.

len is the argument count parsed by the callers (fiber_resume/fiber_transfer via mrb_get_args '*'), which yields len >= 0; the non-negativity bound is not quotable in the given code. If a negative len could reach this code, c->cibase->n = len would store a negative argc consumed by the VM.

For a fiber in MRB_FIBER_CREATED state, c->cibase->proc and its ENV are installed at fiber construction; the given code checks c->ci->proc but dereferences c->cibase->proc, and the safety of the latter relies on construction code not shown.
When vmexec is TRUE, ci[1] is the fiber's own pushed/suspended callinfo frame with a valid stack pointer; established by the calling protocol, not by statements in this code.
mrb->root_c is non-NULL because the root context is created at interpreter init before any Ruby code runs.
mrb_stack_extend operates on the newly current context c (after fiber_switch_context) and ensures capacity for len+2 slots from the fiber's base.
limitations: Theoretical len+2 signed overflow requires passing roughly MRB_INT_MAX arguments, which the call machinery and memory cannot deliver; not attacker-feasible.
The guard/use mismatch (checks !c->ci->proc but dereferences c->cibase->proc) is a latent code smell, but no path within the given code can create a CREATED fiber with NULL cibase->proc.

Negative len reaching this function would make b + len pointer arithmetic formally UB and store a negative argc in cibase->n, but no caller in the module can pass a negative count; the input is internally parsed, not raw boundary data.
Only this function was analyzed; helper functions (fiber_check, fiber_check_cfunc, fiber_result, fiber_switch_context) and callers were not available for inspection.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is provable from the given code. The fulfilled promise value (the only trust-boundary input) is a tagged, fixed-width njs_value_t that flows only through struct copies into VM-managed scope/retval slots and into reject() — there is no bounds, injection, pointer-scaling, or format sink for it here. The remaining defects (ctx leak and unsettled promise on the memory-error early-return path, and unchecked internal pointers vm->top_frame->function->context / ctx->await / ctx->capability) are gated on allocation failure or on internal invariants maintained by njs machinery outside this function, neither of which trust-boundary data can trigger through any path in this code.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) clamps index 1 to the argument count and returns a pointer to a valid njs_value_t (e.g., njs_value_undefined) when nargs <= 1; this behavior is not present in the given code and cannot be quoted.

njs_vmcode_interpreter, njs_function_call, njs_scope_value, njs_function_closures, and njs_async_context_free are assumed to enforce their own contracts (frame validity, scope-index validity, exactly-once semantics of the free); none of these implementations is visible in the given code.

ctx->capability->resolve is assumed to be the native promise resolve function that returns NJS_OK without suspending (NJS_AGAIN) or synchronously re-entering with the same ctx; if it could return NJS_AGAIN or re-enter, the njs_async_context_free at line 47 would become a use-after-free, but no statement in the given code proves either behavior is reachable.

vm->top_frame, vm->top_frame->function, ctx, ctx->await, async->function, and ctx->capability are assumed non-NULL by invariants of the njs async/promise machinery that invoked this callback; the given code contains no guard for them.

Promise jobs enqueued by resolve() are assumed not to run synchronously inside njs_function_call; if they did, njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) at line 47 could free memory still referenced by a queued job.
limitations: On the interpreter memory-error path, the early return 'if (njs_is_memory_error(vm, &vm->retval)) { return NJS_ERROR; }' skips both njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx) and the reject() call: the async context leaks and the promise never settles. Trigger requires an allocation failure inside njs_vmcode_interpreter (OOM), which trust-boundary input cannot deterministically induce, so this is recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The pointer chain 'vm->top_frame->function->context' and the dereferences of 'ctx->await' and 'async->function' are unguarded; a NULL in any of them would crash the VM. No path in this code lets external data set these to NULL, so the trigger is not attacker-reachable from the given code.

njs_function_call at line 44 passes '&vm->retval' as both the single argument and the retval destination; if the callee writes retval before reading args[0], the resolved value could be corrupted. No statement in the given code demonstrates such ordering, so this remains a latent aliasing hazard only.

verdict.summary: MqttClient_WaitType re-enters its receive/decode/dispatch loop via 'goto wait_again' whenever a decoded packet fails the wait match. The loop's exit depends entirely on attacker-controlled network data (decoded packet_type/packet_id from MqttPacket_Read/MqttClient_DecodePacket), and the only time bound, timeout_ms, is re-armed fresh on every iteration, so a malicious or MitM MQTT peer can keep the calling thread processing packets and blocked in this function indefinitely (unbounded loop / uncontrolled resource consumption, CWE-400). No iteration cap or cumulative deadline exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Unguarded re-wait loop: when the received packet is not the awaited one (waitMatchFound = 0) and rc >= 0, control jumps back to 'wait_again' with no iteration counter and no cumulative deadline. The caller's timeout_ms only bounds each individual MqttPacket_Read (lines 91-92), so a peer that keeps sending valid non-matching packets (e.g., PUBACK with a different packet_id, or PINGRESP while the client waits for SUBACK id 1) makes the loop run forever, repeatedly invoking MqttClient_DecodePacket and MqttClient_HandlePacket. A searched-for fix (elapsed-time or iteration bound before the goto) is absent from the code.

evidence.snippet:
if ((wait_type == MQTT_PACKET_TYPE_ANY ||
                 wait_type == packet_type ||
                 MqttIsPubRespPacket(packet_type) == MqttIsPubRespPacket(wait_type)) &&
               (wait_packet_id == 0 || wait_packet_id == packet_id))
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted loop-control value: packet_type and packet_id are decoded from network data received by MqttPacket_Read (lines 91-92) via MqttClient_DecodePacket (lines 102-103) and are fully attacker-controlled. This match decision is the sole determinant of waitMatchFound, which gates the unbounded 'goto wait_again' loop; the attacker only needs each received packet to fail this test (or satisfy wait_packet_id == 0 as a bypass of the id check) to keep the loop spinning.

assumptions: MqttPacket_Read, MqttClient_DecodePacket, MqttClient_HandlePacket, MqttClient_RespList_Find, and wm_Sem* are external; their internal bounds/lock correctness cannot be quoted here and is assumed, not verified.

MqttIsPubRespPacket's return values are defined outside this code; the observed '==' comparison of two Is-predicate results could accept received packets whose type differs from wait_type whenever both are non-pubresp types and the id test passes (wait_packet_id == 0 accepts any id), dispatching the caller's typed packet_obj to MqttClient_HandlePacket under an unrelated packet_type (fail-open request satisfaction, e.g., PINGRESP accepted for a CONNACK wait). The trigger could not be proven without quoting the predicate's semantics, so it is not counted as a confirmed finding.
The sign/value of MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE is external; the state-preservation logic at 'if (rc != MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE)' implies it reaches the tail path, but its numeric value cannot be anchored here.

All in-tree packet structures are assumed to place MqttMsgStat first, per the comment at line 18; the cast 'mms_stat = (MqttMsgStat*)packet_obj' has no runtime check, so a foreign caller passing a different layout would corrupt state dispatch.
rx_buf sizing versus rx_buf_len is enforced inside MqttPacket_Read, outside this code.
limitations: Multithread/nonblock lock-inconsistency candidate: re-entry at MQTT_MSG_WAIT or MQTT_MSG_AUTH acquires no lockRecv, yet the READ case unconditionally asserts 'readLocked = 1; /* if in this state read is locked */' and the tail 'if (readLocked) wm_SemUnlock(&client->lockRecv);' would then unlock a mutex this thread may not hold. The trigger depends on the unquotable value/sign of MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE and on WOLFMQTT_MULTITHREAD+WOLFMQTT_NONBLOCK builds with a competing thread, so it is recorded rather than confirmed.

On fresh entry at MQTT_MSG_READ (nonblock continuation), the local packet_type resets to MQTT_PACKET_TYPE_RESERVED and flows into the match decision and HandlePacket dispatch; the security effect is determined inside MqttClient_HandlePacket, which is outside the given code.

The confirmed loop finding's worst outcome is indefinite blocking/CPU consumption of one client thread by its MQTT peer; the peer must keep sending valid packets faster than timeout_ms expires. Severity is therefore rated low.
Functions, struct definitions, and macros referenced here are not part of the given code; the analysis judges only the statements present.

verdict.summary: check_passwd is memory-safe and fail-closed for all runtime-reachable inputs: the buffer is sized with the same hash_len used at every sink (calloc(hash_len*2), writes of at most hash_len bytes to each half), both comparison sites use constant-time crypto_memneq, and the no-hash/read-error paths return -EINVAL or jump to err. Remaining concerns are compile-time configuration properties (PBKDF2_SALT_LEN < PBKDF2_LENGTH, nonzero digest length) or OOM-only robustness (digest-handle leak on the -ENOMEM path), none of which runtime attacker input can induce.

assumptions: PBKDF2_SALT_LEN < PBKDF2_LENGTH at build time; the constants are not shown in this code. If PBKDF2_SALT_LEN >= PBKDF2_LENGTH, keylen = PBKDF2_LENGTH - PBKDF2_SALT_LEN would be <= 0 and crypto_memneq(passwd1_sum, key, keylen) would read out of bounds (negative int widened to huge size_t), or with keylen == 0 would compare equal for any password (ret = 1).

digest_length(d) returns a small positive value for the configured PASSWD_SUM digest; a zero-length digest would alias passwd1_sum and passwd2_sum and trivially pass the comparison, and hash_len > INT_MAX/2 would overflow hash_len * 2.

read_env_passwd and read_default_passwd return a negative value on failure and fill exactly hash_len bytes into the destination on success; if a ret == 0 path could return without filling, the comparison would run against calloc-zeroed bytes (initialized, so no uninitialized read, but a weaker comparison).
digest_free(NULL) is safe (PBKDF2 mode leaves d == NULL until the err label).
The caller of check_passwd treats ret == 1 as success and ret <= 0 (including 0 for a wrong password) as failure; this code's own convention supports that but the caller is outside the given snippet.
passwd and length are supplied as a matched buffer/length pair by the caller; no NUL-termination is required by the sinks used.
limitations: The digest handle d is leaked if calloc fails (return -ENOMEM before digest_free); reachable only under allocation failure, no attacker-controlled exhaustion path, no security effect.

If keylen could ever be 0 (build-time constant misconfiguration), !crypto_memneq(a, b, 0) evaluates true and any password would authenticate; this is a configuration-boundary case, not reachable by runtime input in this code.
PBKDF2 iteration count and salt length strength are build-time hardening parameters defined outside this snippet; not evaluated as a code defect here.

verdict.summary: The NE entry-table parser reads from bin->entry_table at an offset that is incremented without any revalidation before each read. The bundle_type read at line 38 executes after `off++` with no bounds check, so off == EntryTableLength reads one byte past the table. In the movable-segment branch, `off += 2` is followed by an unchecked read of segnum (line 57), and the subsequent guard `if (off > bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength)` uses `>` instead of `>=` and is evaluated after the increment, so at off == EntryTableLength the r_read_le16 at line 62 reads two bytes past the table. A crafted NE file reaching this entry-point parser causes heap out-of-bounds reads (crash/DoS, and OOB-derived values flow into returned entry->paddr).

evidence.snippet:
off++;
		ut8 bundle_type = *(ut8 *)(bin->entry_table + off);
evidence.reason: Root cause: after `off++`, `*(ut8 *)(bin->entry_table + off)` reads bundle_type with no check of off against EntryTableLength or tableat+off against r_buf_size on this path. Trigger: enter the while loop with off == EntryTableLength-1 (passes line 29 `off < bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength` and line 30), read a nonzero bundle_length, then off becomes EntryTableLength and line 38 reads one byte past the table — exactly-at-limit off-by-one OOB read (CWE-125).

Root cause: the segnum read at line 57 follows `off += 2` with no bounds check at all (the only prior check, line 42, was against the file-buffer size at a pre-increment offset), and the subsequent guard uses `>` where `>=` is required and is placed after the `off++`. Trigger: bundle_type == 0xff with off == EntryTableLength after line 58; line 59's `off > bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength` is false at exactly the limit, and line 62's r_read_le16 reads bytes at EntryTableLength and EntryTableLength+1 — OOB heap read (CWE-125).

assumptions: The allocated size of bin->entry_table is not established anywhere in this function; the only length the code ever uses to bound reads into it is bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength (lines 29, 59, 67), so off >= EntryTableLength is treated as out-of-bounds for entry_table. If the constructor allocates entry_table with EntryTableLength bytes (the only reading consistent with this code), all three confirmed OOB reads are heap overreads.
bin->segment_entries is assumed to contain SegCount elements as allocated by the object constructor (outside the given code); the index guards at lines 63 and 71 are otherwise sound.
r_list_get_n is assumed to return NULL for out-of-range indices; line 23 handles NULL, so no OOB access occurs there.
limitations: RBinAddr objects allocated at line 45 are leaked on the break paths at lines 43, 60, and 68. The leak is bounded by EntryTableLength (ut16), so there is no attacker-driven unbounded exhaustion path; recorded as a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.
When the segnum/bundle_type guards (lines 63, 71) fail, entry->paddr remains 0 from R_NEW0 and the zeroed entry is still appended; cosmetic/robustness only, not an uninitialized-value defect.
`int off` cannot overflow here because it is bounded by EntryTableLength (<= 65535) plus small constants; not a defect.

verdict.summary: SWTPM_NVRAM_CheckHeader validates the blob length against sizeof(bh) — the size of a pointer (4/8 bytes), not the blobheader struct (>=10 bytes of members) — so an NVRAM state file of 8-9 bytes with totlen matching its length passes both checks and causes out-of-bounds reads at bh->version (offset 8) and bh->min_version (offset 9). Additionally, the attacker-controlled hdrsize field is returned as *dataoffset with no check against the header size or the buffer length, making this header-validation intake point fail open for the body offset it certifies.

evidence.snippet:
blobheader *bh = (blobheader *)data;

    if (length < sizeof(bh)) {
evidence.reason: The minimum-length guard uses sizeof(bh), which is the size of the pointer (4 on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit), not sizeof(*bh) (the blobheader struct, whose members totlen/hdrsize/flags/version/min_version occupy at least 10 bytes). A crafted NVRAM blob of length 8 (or 9) with totlen == htonl(length) passes this guard and the totlen check, after which bh->version at offset 8 and bh->min_version at offset 9 are read out of bounds (CWE-125).

hdrsize is an attacker-controlled 16-bit field from the state file; ntohs(bh->hdrsize) can be 0..65535 and is written to *dataoffset with no check that it is at least the header size or at most length. This function is the validation intake point for the parsed blob header, so the missing bound is a fail-open validation gap (CWE-20): a blob with hdrsize = 0xFFFF and totlen == length is accepted and certifies an offset far beyond the buffer.

assumptions: blobheader's definition is not shown, but the code itself reads totlen (u32, offsets 0-3), hdrsize (u16, 4-5), flags (u16, 6-7), version (u8, 8) and min_version (u8, 9), so the struct is at least 10 bytes — strictly larger than any pointer width, making the sizeof(bh) bound wrong on every ABI.
data points to a buffer of exactly length bytes, and the NVRAM blob originates from a state file whose contents and size are attacker-influenced (swtpm persisted-state context).
BLOB_HEADER_VERSION is a small constant; the min_version comparison (uint8_t > constant) cannot overflow.
limitations: The totlen==length check on line 14 is correct in itself (uint32 vs uint32, no wrap) and properly guards only the totlen field, not the later reads.
The diagnostic on line 18 prints htonl(bh->totlen) (wrong byte order) — a cosmetic error-message defect with no security effect.

The cast blobheader *bh = (blobheader *)data may perform misaligned access on strict-alignment targets, but that depends on the caller's buffer alignment and the target ABI, neither of which is established by this code.
A NULL data pointer with length >= 8 would be dereferenced, but no attacker-controlled input in this code can produce that state; it requires a caller precondition violation.

The out-of-bounds read of 1-2 bytes past a heap buffer typically has limited exploitability (info-influence on the version fields or a crash at a page boundary), hence medium rather than high severity.

verdict.summary: In the VNC SetEncodings handler, the client-controlled encoding count `limit` (read_u16(data,2)) is used to drive an in-place byte-swap loop that reads (read_s32) and writes (memcpy) at data + 4 + i*4 for i in [0, limit), but the code never validates that 4 + limit*4 <= len. The only length handling is `if (len == 4) { ... return 4 + (limit * 4); }`, which is bypassed by the `else` branch, so any handler invocation where fewer than 4 + limit*4 bytes are buffered causes a heap out-of-bounds read and write of up to ~256KB past the message buffer, letting a malicious VNC client corrupt adjacent heap memory or crash the server (DoS).

evidence.reason: Root cause / missing-check site: on the `else` path (any len other than 1 and 4) the attacker-controlled uint16 `limit` is taken from the message and used directly as the loop bound with no comparison of `limit` (or 4 + limit*4) against `len` anywhere. Edge case: limit=0xFFFF with a short buffered message makes read_s32 read and memcpy write (a byte-swapped value) at data[4..262139], far past the buffer — heap out-of-bounds read and write (CWE-129 leading to CWE-787). The minimal fix — reject when 4 + limit*4 > len before the loop — is absent from the code.

evidence.snippet: set_encodings(vs, (int32_t *)(data + 4), limit);
evidence.reason: Consumer of the same unvalidated value: the pointer/length pair (data + 4, limit) is passed to set_encodings without any check that the buffer actually holds limit*4 bytes, so the same attacker-controlled `limit` drives an additional out-of-bounds read of the encoding array when len < 4 + limit*4.

assumptions: The caller/framing layer that invokes protocol_client_msg and the accessors read_u8/read_u16/read_u32/read_s32 are not part of the given code; their exact semantics (especially whether the handler can be invoked with len different from the exact requested message size) cannot be quoted and are therefore assumptions. The code's own partial-state exits (`if (len == 1) return 20;`, `if (len == 4)`, `if (len == 8)`, `if (len == 2)`) show that invocations with incomplete messages are a supported state of this handler, which is why the missing limit-vs-len check is judged as this code's responsibility.
The `data` buffer is valid for at least 1 byte (handler is registered for at least one byte) and `vs`/`vd` are initialized server state.
Whether VNC authentication is enabled is a deployment configuration outside this code; the vulnerability is reachable by any client that reaches the protocol stage.
limitations: Secondary, same-class findings not promoted to primary evidence: (1) CUT_TEXT line 67 `return 8 + dlen;` — `dlen` is uint32_t so values like 0xFFFFFFFC wrap 8+dlen to 4, bypassing the 8+dlen framing and later reaching `client_cut_text(vs, read_u32(data, 4), data + 8)` (line 70) with no check that len >= 8 + dlen (integer wrap CWE-190 plus missing length validation); (2) SET_PIXEL_FORMAT reads offsets up to 16 after only `if (len == 1) return 20;` with no check for len in 2..19; (3) AUDIO SET_FORMAT reads offsets up to 9 (`vs->as.freq = read_u32(data, 6)`) after only `if (len == 4) return 10;`, and the audio default printf reads data[4] when len may be 3. These produce smaller out-of-bounds reads and depend on the same missing framing validation; their sinks are partly external to this code.

The out-of-bounds write in the SetEncodings loop stores byte-swapped copies of whatever heap data it over-reads back to the same out-of-bounds locations, so the write is value-constrained; the reliably attacker-controlled effects are heap metadata/object corruption with swapped values and a denial-of-service crash, with potential for further impact depending on adjacent heap layout.

verdict.summary: In this op-kernel entry point, the attacker-controlled input list `params_nested_splits` is validated only by `DCHECK_GT(params_nested_splits_in.size(), 0);  // Enforced by REGISTER_OP.` — a debug-only assertion that is a no-op in release builds, with the comment deferring enforcement to code outside this file. Nothing in this code prevents an empty list from reaching `params_nested_splits_in[0]`, which performs an out-of-bounds read of the input-list vector and dereferences a wild Tensor pointer (crash, CWE-125). Additionally, `SPLITS_TYPE num_params = params_nested_splits_in[0].dim_size(0) - 1;` has no check that the first splits tensor is rank-1 with first dimension >= 1; a first-dimension size of 0 underflows num_params to -1, and that sentinel is then passed as the validation bound in `ValidateIndices(indices_in, num_params)`. Both triggers are reachable purely from attacker-supplied raw-op inputs (list length N, tensor shapes).

evidence.reason: The sole guard before the element access is a DCHECK, which is compiled out in release builds; no OP_REQUIRES or equivalent runtime check on `size() > 0` exists anywhere in the code, so an attacker supplying an empty `params_nested_splits` list (N=0) at this raw-op entry point reaches `params_nested_splits_in[0]` as an out-of-bounds vector read and wild-pointer dereference. Furthermore, `dim_size(0) - 1` is unchecked: with `params_nested_splits[0]` of shape [0] (or rank 0), `num_params` underflows to -1 and is fed as the index-validation bound. Trigger: call the op with N=0, or with a first splits tensor whose dim 0 has size 0.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, context->input_list("params_nested_splits",
                                                &params_nested_splits_in));
evidence.reason: Trust-boundary origin of the tainted values: the variadic input list whose length and element shapes are fully attacker-controlled is ingested here, and no subsequent statement in this code constrains its size or its first element's rank/dimension before the [0] access and the dim_size(0)-1 subtraction at lines 11-12.

assumptions: The comment '// Enforced by REGISTER_OP.' claims the op registration guarantees params_nested_splits is non-empty; that enforcement is outside the given code and cannot be quoted, so it is treated as an assumption, not a guard. The DCHECK itself is a no-op in production (NDEBUG) builds.
Bodies of ValidateIndices, MakeSplits, WriteSplits, and WriteValues are not shown; any validation they perform is unverifiable here and is not relied upon.
SPLITS_TYPE is assumed to be a signed split type (int32 or int64), consistent with TensorFlow ragged-tensor split types; with a signed type, dim_size(0)==0 makes num_params == -1.
OpKernelContext::input()/input_list() plumbing (input ordering at indices size() and size()+1, behavior on missing inputs) is framework-internal and not shown.
limitations: The concrete impact of num_params == -1 depends on the unshown ValidateIndices body; if it rejects all indices when the bound is -1, that sub-path degrades to an InvalidArgument error, though the missing shape/size validation at lines 11-12 remains a genuine intake-point defect.

Whether MakeSplits/WriteValues bounds-check attacker-supplied split values (e.g., splits containing values exceeding params_dense_values) cannot be determined from this code; a candidate about malformed split values was dismissed only because its trigger lies entirely in unshown code.

The DCHECK does abort in debug builds, and the upstream op registration may reject N=0 at graph-construction time in some TensorFlow versions; the verdict treats this code, per the analysis rules, as the last line of defense for its own inputs.

verdict.summary: At the shared 'beach' error label, load_buffer unconditionally executes 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;'. Two attacker-reachable error paths reach this label with obj NULL: (1) when get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 fails on malformed attacker-controlled Mach-O data, obj is still the NULL initialized at declaration and was never allocated; (2) when r_cf_value_dict_parse fails on malformed attacker-controlled prelink plist data, the handler calls R_FREE (obj) — freeing obj and setting it to NULL — before 'goto beach'. The write through NULL crashes the process (denial of service) whenever a crafted kernelcache file triggers either parse failure. No NULL or liveness check on obj exists on any path to line 67.

evidence.reason: Sink: the error label dereferences obj unconditionally. On the path taken when prelink-range extraction fails on attacker-controlled file data ('if (!prelink_range) { goto beach; }'), obj is still NULL from 'RKernelCacheObj *obj = NULL;', so 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' is a NULL pointer write and a crash. No 'if (obj)' or reassignment exists on any goto path to this label.

Origin of the same defect on a second attacker-reachable path: when the prelink info plist (attacker-controlled file bytes at prelink_range->range.offset with nonzero range.size) fails to parse, R_FREE (obj) frees obj and sets it to NULL, then 'goto beach' falls into 'obj->cache_buf = NULL;' which writes through the NULLed/freed pointer.

assumptions: R_FREE follows radare2 macro semantics: it frees the pointer and sets it to NULL. If R_FREE did not null the pointer, line 67 would instead be a use-after-free write, which is no less severe.

get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0 and r_cf_value_dict_parse can fail on malformed attacker-controlled file content; the code itself contemplates both failures ('if (!prelink_range)' at line 14 and 'if (!prelink_info)' at line 28), so these paths are reachable by design.
load_buffer is the bin-plugin entry point for a file selected by the user/attacker; file bytes cross a trust boundary here, so parse failures are attacker-controllable.

get_prelink_info_range_from_mach0's internals and r_cf_value_dict_parse's internals are outside the given code; their failure behavior is assumed only insofar as the given code explicitly branches on NULL returns from them.
limitations: rebase_info (allocated at line 10) is leaked on every 'goto beach' path; this is a per-load resource leak with no exhaustion path within this function, so it is not promoted to a CWE-400 finding.

The Path B and Path D variants of the NULL deref (R_NEW0 failure at line 19; r_list_new failure at line 37) additionally free/null obj before 'goto beach' but require allocation failure, which attacker input cannot induce; they are not counted as separate vulnerabilities.
On Path D (r_list_new failure), obj is freed via R_FREE and then dereferenced at beach under the same pattern, but the trigger requires OOM.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect exists in this code. The attacker-controlled CAP LS extension list can reach the outgoing 'CAP REQ' string only through g_strlcat calls that are each bounded by sizeof(buffer) (safe truncation, always NUL-terminated) and only after an exact-match whitelist comparison against supported_caps, so no buffer overflow or CRLF/protocol injection is possible. The constant offsets and lengths used (buffer + 9 for the 9-byte literal 'CAP REQ :', and tcp_send_len length 9 for the 9-byte literal 'CAP END\r\n') are correct at the boundary.

assumptions: g_strsplit, g_strlcat, g_strchomp, and g_strcmp0 are assumed to honor their documented GLib contracts (g_strlcat never writes more than dest_size bytes and always NUL-terminates; g_strcmp0 is exact string equality). The bound argument sizeof(buffer) is present verbatim at every append site, so this assumption is about library semantics, not about an unguarded sink in this code.

tags_data is assumed non-NULL at the two dereferences (tags_data->timestamp); no NULL check exists in this code. Callers are the internal IRC message dispatcher (not shown), so no trigger reachable from this code's own entry points could produce a NULL; recorded as a latent robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

extensions_str is assumed non-NULL per g_strsplit's contract; the internal dispatcher is assumed to always pass the CAP LS parameter. If it could be NULL, g_strsplit would emit a GLib critical — not demonstrable from the given code.
supported_caps is assumed to be a compile-time constant table of benign capability names (no CR/LF), matched by g_strcmp0 exact equality; this is the code's own whitelist mechanism quoted at line 35.
limitations: Truncation effect: a very long CAP LS list can cause g_strlcat to truncate the CAP REQ string mid-capability, producing a degraded request (server may reject the split name). This is a protocol-correctness degradation, not a memory-safety or security failure.

Memory allocated by g_strsplit is proportional to the attacker-supplied line length, but the iteration terminates at g_strsplit's NULL terminator and IRC line framing (outside this code) bounds the input; no unbounded consumption defect exists in this function.
NULL dereference of tags_data would crash if any internal caller passed NULL; no such caller is present in or reachable from the given code.

verdict.summary: do_i2c_md parses the display length from argv[3] into a uint (line 48) with no upper-bound check, then narrows it via 'nbytes = length;' (line 65). For any attacker-supplied length >= 0x80000000 (e.g. 'ffffffff'), nbytes and hence linebytes become negative, because the clamp at line 70 only bounds the upper side ('nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes'). The negative linebytes is then passed as the read length into the fixed-size stack buffer linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] via dm_i2c_read/i2c_read (lines 73/75), producing an out-of-bounds stack write once the callee's unsigned/16-bit length field reinterprets the negative value as a huge count. The loop guard 'while (nbytes > 0)' (line 98) executes only after the first read, so it cannot prevent the first negative-length read.

evidence.reason: The sink: linebytes (an int derived from the uint 'length') is used as the read length into the fixed-size stack buffer linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] (declared line 67). The only guard, 'linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;', clamps only the upper bound; when nbytes is negative (length >= 0x80000000, e.g. 'i2c md 0x50 0.2 ffffffff'), linebytes is negative (e.g. -1) and is passed unchecked to dm_i2c_read/i2c_read, causing an out-of-bounds write past linebuf once the callee's length field (typically unsigned/16-bit) reinterprets it as a huge count. No lower-bound or pre-read 'nbytes > 0' check exists before this point; the 'while (nbytes > 0)' exit at line 98 is evaluated only after the first read.

evidence.snippet:
if (argc > 3)
			length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled CLI parameter argv[3] is converted with hextoul into the uint 'length' with no range validation (any value up to 0xFFFFFFFF is accepted). This unbounded uint is later narrowed at 'nbytes = length;' (line 65), so values >= 0x80000000 become negative ints — the integer signedness/overflow root cause that reaches the read sink at lines 73/75.

assumptions: The function is a U-Boot shell command handler (public CLI entry point); argv/flag/argc come from the shell parser and may be supplied by an untrusted console or scripted input.
DISP_LINE_LEN, DEFAULT_ADDR_LEN, and the DM_I2C build flag are compile-time configuration; both the DM and non-DM branches were analyzed.

hextoul performs base-16 conversion of the whole string; get_alen can return -1 on malformed input, as evidenced by this code's own test 'if (!ret && alen != -1)' at line 53 — its full implementation is not shown.

The behavior of i2c_get_cur_bus_chip, dm_i2c_read, i2c_read, and i2c_set_chip_offset_len is external to this code; no bounds they might or might not enforce were assumed for the verdict (per guard-anchoring, the negative-length value is unguarded at this code's sink).
limitations: Secondary gap: 'if (alen > 3)' (line 40) does not reject alen == -1; the DM path merely skips offset-length setting via 'alen != -1' (line 53), and the non-DM path passes alen = -1 raw to i2c_read (line 75). The consequence depends on the unseen i2c_read implementation, so it is recorded but not counted as a confirmed vulnerability.

A very large positive length (up to INT_MAX, e.g. '0x7fffffff') drives up to ~2^27 I2C transactions with no ctrlc()/abort check inside the do-while loop — an attacker-reachable unbounded resource-consumption/DoS path (CWE-400), kept as a secondary low-severity observation.
The do-while structure executes one read even when length == 0 (linebytes = 0); no memory-safety effect observed for that boundary value.
addr (uint) wraps in the display loop; cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: The header length check 'if (length < sizeof(bh))' compares against the size of the pointer (8 bytes on 64-bit) instead of the size of the blobheader struct (12 bytes), so blobs with 8 <= length < sizeof(blobheader) pass validation. The subsequent read 'ntohl(bh->totlen)' dereferences bytes 8..11 of a buffer that may be only 8-9 bytes long, an out-of-bounds heap read whose contents can also be leaked to stderr via the logprintf of htonl(bh->totlen). Additionally, for length 10-11 the function certifies *dataoffset = sizeof(blobheader) = 12 > length with TPM_SUCCESS, handing the caller a validated offset beyond the buffer.

evidence.snippet: if (length < sizeof(bh)) {
evidence.reason: The only bounds guard uses sizeof(bh) — the size of the pointer (8 on 64-bit) — rather than sizeof(*bh)/sizeof(blobheader) (12). At the boundary length=8 the check '8 < 8' is false, so undersized blobs pass; the missing-check site for both the OOB read and the dataoffset>length certification.

evidence.snippet: if (ntohl(bh->totlen) != length) {
evidence.reason: Sink: totlen is a uint32_t member residing at bytes 8..11 of the struct (after two uint8_t and two uint16_t members), so for an attacker-supplied blob of length 8 or 9 that survived the line-8 check this read goes past the end of the buffer; the raw bytes are then printed via logprintf("broken header: bh->totlen %u != %u", htonl(bh->totlen), length), leaking out-of-bounds heap data to stderr.

assumptions: The blobheader struct definition is not shown; its layout (version, min_version uint8_t; hdrsize, flags uint16_t; totlen uint32_t) and minimum size of 10 bytes (12 with alignment) are inferred from the member accesses bh->version, bh->min_version, bh->hdrsize, bh->flags, bh->totlen in the given code.
A 64-bit platform is assumed, where sizeof(bh) = 8; on a 32-bit platform sizeof(bh) = 4 and the out-of-bounds window widens to lengths 4..11, making the finding strictly worse.
dataoffset/hdrflags/hdrversion out-pointers are assumed non-NULL per the caller contract; this code contains no NULL check for them.

The NVRAM blob (data/length) is treated as trust-boundary data (file/saved-state contents), which is the role this validator plays; the caller's use of the certified dataoffset beyond the buffer is a direct consequence of this function's failed validation.
limitations: The misaligned-pointer cast '(blobheader *)data' (line 5) is UB if a caller passes a non-aligned buffer, but no attacker-controlled input value within this code's contract can produce misalignment; not counted as a vulnerability here.
A NULL 'data' with length >= 8 would crash at line 15, but that requires the caller to violate the basic non-NULL argument contract rather than any attacker-controlled data value; not counted.
The out-of-bounds read is bounded to at most 4 bytes (offsets 8..11) and the information leak is confined to the error message on stderr; no write primitive exists in this function.

verdict.summary: In multithreaded non-blocking builds, when MqttPacket_Read (line 91) returns MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE for a partially received, attacker-fragmented packet, MqttClient_WaitType preserves the message state as MQTT_MSG_WAIT (line 216 skips the reset) but unconditionally releases the recv mutex (lines 224-225). On re-entry the switch dispatches directly to case MQTT_MSG_WAIT, which never acquires lockRecv (the only acquisition is in case MQTT_MSG_BEGIN, line 44), so MqttPacket_Read parses network data into the shared client->rx_buf without the lock while another thread holds it; when flow reaches case MQTT_MSG_READ, line 124 sets readLocked = 1 and line 225 unlocks a mutex owned by another thread. This breaks mutual exclusion over the shared receive path, allowing unsynchronized concurrent parsing of attacker-controlled data (CWE-362).

evidence.reason: Faulty site: when rc == MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE (<0, negative because line 174 tests it before the rc >= 0 success branch at line 182) is returned by MqttPacket_Read in case MQTT_MSG_WAIT, control breaks out at line 94, line 216 ('if (rc != MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE)') prevents the state reset so *mms_stat stays MQTT_MSG_WAIT, yet lines 224-225 release lockRecv even though readLocked == 1. The caller re-invokes, the switch enters case MQTT_MSG_WAIT directly, which contains no wm_SemLock(&client->lockRecv), and MqttPacket_Read runs unlocked against shared client state; the subsequent readLocked = 1 at line 124 then unlocks another thread's mutex.

Sink reached without the recv lock on the WAIT-resume path: this MqttPacket_Read call executes with no lockRecv held when the function is re-entered in the preserved MQTT_MSG_WAIT state, allowing a concurrent thread (serialized in normal operation solely by lockRecv) to read/parse the same socket and rx_buf simultaneously; the 'if (rc <= 0) break' at line 94 routes the attacker-triggered CONTINUE code to the unconditional unlock at line 225.

evidence.snippet:
#ifdef WOLFMQTT_MULTITHREAD
            readLocked = 1; /* if in this state read is locked */
        #endif
evidence.reason: Origin of the secondary fault: readLocked is set to 1 as an assumed invariant ('if in this state read is locked') without any lock acquisition on this path; reached from the WAIT-resume flow where line 225 already released lockRecv, this causes wm_SemUnlock(&client->lockRecv) at line 225 to release a mutex currently owned by another waiting thread, collapsing mutual exclusion for all concurrent waiters.

assumptions: MqttPacket_Read returns MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE for a partially received packet in non-blocking builds; its return-code value is not defined in the given code, but the given code itself proves CONTINUE < 0 because line 174 tests rc == MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE before the rc >= 0 success test at line 182 (a non-negative CONTINUE would be consumed as success).
Callers re-invoke MqttClient_WaitType after receiving MQTT_CODE_CONTINUE; this is the only purpose of the state-preservation block at lines 215-221 (non-blocking resume protocol).
MqttPacket_Read respects the client->rx_buf_len length parameter passed at line 91; the upper bound rc <= rx_buf_len cannot be verified in the given code.

MqttClient_RespList_Find/Remove semantics, the stack ownership of pendResp objects, and MqttIsPubRespPacket's type set (PUBACK/PUBREC/PUBREL/PUBCOMP sharing one structure) are external to the given code.
Multiple threads concurrently calling this function on one client is a supported mode; the pendResp machinery at lines 62-86 and 148-167 exists for exactly that usage.
limitations: If wm_SemLock(&client->lockClient) fails at line 189, pendResp->packetDone is never set and the waiting thread can hang; triggering requires a semaphore failure, which attacker input cannot induce.

The non-blocking early return at lines 174-177 leaves pendResp->packetProcessing set without marking the entry done; no quotable path shows HandlePacket returning CONTINUE for a pendResp-matched (ack-type, fully buffered) packet, so this is not confirmed.

The 'goto wait_again' loop at line 238 can keep processing while a peer floods non-matching packets, but each iteration is bounded by the per-read timeout_ms and consuming the ordered packet stream is the protocol's required behavior; treated as at most weak resource consumption, not confirmed.
rc == 0 from MqttPacket_Read is correctly rejected as failure by 'if (rc <= 0)' (line 94); no defect found there.

verdict.summary: njs_await_fulfilled is a native promise-reaction callback. Its only attacker-influenced input is the fulfillment value (args[1], arbitrary JS-controlled tagged value), which is consumed exclusively by type-tag reads and fixed-width njs_value_t copies (*njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) = *value; vm->retval = *value; passing to resolve/reject); njs_arg returns the static undefined for the boundary cases nargs=0 and nargs=1, so no out-of-bounds read or overflow is reachable. The internal async-context lifetime is handled symmetrically: njs_async_context_free is called exactly once on the NJS_OK and NJS_ERROR/failed paths, the NJS_AGAIN path intentionally retains the context for the next await, and the early error-fulfilled goto occurs before any frame/level swap, so saves and restores stay balanced. The residual defects are not attacker-triggerable: the memory-error early return leaks the njs_async_ctx_t, but only when an allocation failure inside njs_vmcode_interpreter produces the internal memory error (environment-gated, pool memory reclaimed at VM teardown), and a NULL or freed ctx on entry would require the external promise machinery to fire the reaction handler twice or expose it to scripts, which nothing in this code permits. No memory-safety, bounds, injection, or authz defect is reachable from the inputs this code consumes.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) returns a pointer to the static undefined value when 1 >= nargs (its implementation is outside this snippet); this bounds the args[1] access for nargs=0 and nargs=1.

The promise reaction machinery invokes this callback exactly once per reaction with a handler function object whose ->context was set to a live njs_async_ctx_t and does not expose that handler object to user scripts; this code never clears the handler's context (it clears function->context/function->await on the async JS function object, a different object).
njs_vmcode_interpreter returns only NJS_OK, NJS_AGAIN, or NJS_ERROR, so the unmodified fallthrough 'return ret;' cannot carry an unhandled code that would skip the free.
njs_value_t is a fixed-size self-contained tagged union, so copying an attacker-chosen fulfillment value cannot corrupt memory.
Memory backing ctx belongs to the VM memory pool and is reclaimed when the VM is destroyed.
limitations: Resource leak (candidate): the branch 'if (njs_is_memory_error(vm, &vm->retval)) { return NJS_ERROR; }' returns without calling njs_async_context_free(vm, ctx), leaking the njs_async_ctx_t and its promise capability. Trigger requires an allocation failure inside njs_vmcode_interpreter to surface as the internal memory error — an environment/allocation-failure condition gated on OOM, with pool-scoped impact; not treated as a security vulnerability per the analysis rules.
Robustness: the '(void) njs_function_call(...)' for the reject path discards the call result; the function still returns NJS_ERROR, so there is no fail-open consequence.

A NULL or already-freed 'vm->top_frame->function->context' on entry would cause a NULL deref or double free, but no path within this code can produce that state; it would require the external promise machinery to re-fire the reaction or leak the internal handler to attacker script (see assumptions).

verdict.summary: The APNG decoder trusts attacker-controlled dimensions and frame-control fields: (1) `imagesize = h * rowbytes` is a 32-bit unsigned multiply guarded only per-dimension (`w > cMaxPNGSize || h > cMaxPNGSize`), so dimensions with w*h*4 >= 2^32 (e.g. w=262144, h=4096) wrap to a tiny allocation while row pointers span the full h*rowbytes range, causing heap out-of-bounds read/write; (2) `delay_den` read from an fcTL via png_get_uint_16 is never checked for zero before `bundle.duration = delay_num * 1000 / delay_den`, giving an attacker-reachable division by zero; (3) fcTL fields are read from chunk.p[12..33] with no check that chunk.size >= 38, a heap over-read on a truncated fcTL.

evidence.reason: CWE-190: rowbytes and imagesize are 32-bit unsigned; the only guard is `if (w > cMaxPNGSize || h > cMaxPNGSize)`, which bounds each dimension but not the product. For w=262144, h=4096 (both within the 1,000,000 upstream limit) h*w*4 == 2^32 wraps imagesize to 0, so `new unsigned char[0]` is allocated while `frameRaw.rows[j] = frameRaw.p + j * rowbytes` spreads row pointers over 4 GiB; the frame-completion loop then reads `frameRaw.rows[y]`/`f[4*x+3]` far out of bounds (and the row callback writes through the same pointers). Trigger: a plain PNG file with IHDR w=262144, h=4096 followed by IDAT and IEND.

Out-of-bounds read sink for the wrapped-imagesize candidate: `f` is a row pointer computed as frameRaw.p + y*rowbytes into an undersized buffer when `imagesize = h * rowbytes` (line 54) wrapped; dereferencing f[4*x+3] accesses unmapped/foreign heap memory with attacker-chosen y and rowbytes.

CWE-369 division by zero: delay_den is the attacker-controlled 16-bit value from `delay_den = png_get_uint_16(chunk.p + 30);` (line 147); the fcTL validation on lines 151-153 checks only w0, h0, x0, y0, x0+w0, y0+h0, dop and bop — never delay_den — and the initial `delay_den = 10;` is overwritten by the first fcTL. Trigger: acTL, IDAT, fcTL with delay_den=0, IDAT, IEND — the next frame completion executes `delay_num * 1000 / 0`, an integer division by zero (SIGFPE).

CWE-125 heap over-read: these reads require the fcTL buffer to hold at least 34 bytes (a valid fcTL is 38), but the only quotable checks on this path are `JXL_ASSERT(chunk.p != nullptr)` (null only) and `chunkIHDR.size == 25` (IHDR only). A truncated fcTL with declared data length 0 yields a 12-byte heap buffer whose bytes 12..33 are read out of bounds; the over-read values then feed the frame-parameter checks, bundle.origin and bundle.duration. Trigger: IHDR, acTL, fcTL chunk of total size 12.

assumptions: cMaxPNGSize is not defined in the given code; the imagesize-overflow trigger requires cMaxPNGSize >= 32768 (the upstream libjxl constant is 1,000,000, which permits it). The per-dimension guard `w > cMaxPNGSize || h > cMaxPNGSize` is the only quotable bound.

read_chunk, processing_start/processing_data/processing_finish and the CHUNK struct are external and not quotable; per the guard-anchoring rule no size guarantee from read_chunk is assumed, so this function is judged as the last line of defense for chunk.size.

sizeof(png_bytep) assumed 8 (64-bit): `new png_bytep[h * sizeof(png_bytep)]` over-allocates the rows array 8x (wasteful, not out-of-bounds); h * sizeof(png_bytep) is computed in size_t and does not wrap.
png_ptr/info_ptr are initialized inside the external processing_start; their uninitialized declaration is not itself a defect in this snippet.
The x0+w0 / y0+h0 guard arithmetic cannot wrap if cMaxPNGSize < 2^31, so h0 <= h and w0 <= w hold and the sub-frame copy loop is in-bounds whenever imagesize did not wrap.
limitations: fdAT path (lines 179-181): for a sub-minimal fdAT (chunk.size < 16) `chunk.size - 16` underflows and a bogus ~4GiB length is written into the buffer, but processing_data is called with `chunk.size - 4` (>= 8 for the minimum 12-byte chunk), which stays exactly within the chunk buffer, so no out-of-bounds access occurs in this code; impact depends on the external progressive-decoder length handling.
Memory leak: the IEND success path breaks (line 139) before the loop-bottom `delete[] chunk.p;` (line 197), leaking the IEND chunk buffer (CWE-401); no exhaustion path is demonstrated.
`io->dec_pixels += w0 * h0;` can wrap in 32-bit unsigned (w0,h0 up to cMaxPNGSize each); statistics counter only, no security effect.

Very large non-wrapping w*h would request multi-gigabyte allocations; treated as robustness since the per-dimension guard bounds each dimension and no attacker-controlled unbounded loop exists in this code.

verdict.summary: testBackingParse is a unit-test callback whose inputs (args, data->rv, data->backing, data->expect) all come from a statically compiled in-file test table, not from an attacker-controlled trust boundary. Every sink in the function is guarded by quotable in-code checks: data->expect is verified non-NULL on every path to STRNEQ via 'if (src && !data->expect) ... return -1;', xml is verified non-NULL via '!(xml = virBufferContentAndReset(&buf))', and src is initialized to NULL at declaration so failure paths are handled. Format strings are literals. No reachable security defect exists in this code.

assumptions: virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute is assumed to return -1 and not set src on failure; this contract is not quotable from the given code, but the in-code initializer 'g_autoptr(virStorageSource) src = NULL;' guarantees src is NULL unless the callee assigns it, so all uses are guarded.

args is assumed to be a valid non-NULL pointer to struct testBackingParseData supplied by the same test file's static table; no NULL check on args exists in this code, but no untrusted caller can reach this unit-test callback.
data->backing and data->expect are assumed to be NUL-terminated static string literals (or NULL sentinels) from the compiled test matrix.
limitations: Line 2 dereferences args without a NULL check (potential NULL deref if the harness passed NULL); not attacker-reachable because the test framework always passes an element of the file's own static data array.

If src == NULL while data->expect != NULL (e.g., contradictory test data with rv = -1 and a non-NULL expected XML), the function returns 0 at 'if (!src) return 0;' without performing the comparison — a vacuous test pass. This is a test-correctness weakness only; the triggering data does not exist in the static table and no attacker can inject it.

Uses fprintf (stderr) with attacker-influenced data in general CWE-676 terms, but all arguments are from the trusted static test table and format strings are literals, so no injection or log-forging exposure exists.

verdict.summary: inbound_cap_ls handles the attacker-controlled CAP LS capability list from the IRC server. It splits the list with g_strsplit (which does not deduplicate tokens) into an unbounded token array, then loops over every token and unconditionally strcat's a fixed literal into the 256-byte stack buffer 'buffer' whenever a token matches a known capability. No check anywhere bounds the accumulated length (the loop guard 'extensions[i]' only tests termination, not bytes written). A server sending e.g. 'multi-prefix' repeated 19 times (9-byte prefix + 19*13 bytes + NUL = 257) or 'znc.in/server-time-iso' repeated 11 times overwrites the stack past buffer[256], yielding a remotely triggered stack buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: Sinks: the loop iterates over every token of the server-supplied capability list and each matching token unconditionally strcat's into the fixed 256-byte stack buffer with no accumulated-length bound; the only guard, 'for (i=0; extensions[i]; i++)', checks token termination, not bytes written. Nineteen duplicate 'multi-prefix' tokens (attacker controls repetition since g_strsplit does not deduplicate) append 19*13=247 bytes to the 9-byte 'CAP REQ :' prefix, writing the NUL and subsequent bytes one past buffer[255] — a remote stack buffer overflow.

evidence.snippet:
extensions = g_strsplit (extensions_str, " ", 0);

	strcpy (buffer, "CAP REQ :");
evidence.reason: Origin of the unbounded data: extensions_str is raw server CAP LS payload (network trust boundary); g_strsplit yields an attacker-sized, non-deduplicated token array consumed by the unbounded strcat loop, while buffer is a fixed 256-byte stack array with only the 9-byte prefix initialized.

assumptions: extensions_str is assumed non-NULL and NUL-terminated by the message dispatcher; this code contains no NULL check before g_strsplit, but whether NULL can reach here is not provable from the given code.
tags_data is dereferenced at tags_data->timestamp (lines 11 and 92) without a NULL check; the caller is assumed to always pass a valid message_tags_data.

The maximum length of a single IRC line (and thus the token count) is assumed to be bounded by the socket reader outside this code; no such bound exists in the given code, so the overflow trigger needs only 19 short tokens, well within any plausible line limit.
prefs.hex_irc_cap_server_time and serv->loginmethod/password/have_cert are treated as trusted user configuration.
limitations: tcp_sendf uses the fixed literal format "%s\r\n" (no format-string injection) and tcp_send_len's hard-coded length 9 exactly matches "CAP END\r\n" — no defect found there.

The 'sasl' branch requires additional client-side preconditions (LOGIN_SASL with non-empty password or SASLEXTERNAL with a cert), so it is not the minimal overflow trigger, though the same unbounded strcat applies to it.
The content appended by each strcat is a fixed literal, not arbitrary attacker bytes; the attacker controls the number and position of appends, which still yields memory corruption past buffer[255].

verdict.summary: protocol_client_msg validates the received length only with exact-equality probes at minimum header sizes (len == 1/2/4/8) and never checks that `len` covers the bytes it actually dereferences. In the SetEncodings path, the attacker-controlled `limit` (up to 65535) is used as the loop bound for read_s32/memcpy at `data + 4 + i*4` with no `4 + limit*4 <= len` check, giving a remote heap out-of-bounds read and write of attacker-chosen extent. In the CutText path, the 1MB cap and length-accumulation logic exist only inside `if (len == 8)`, so any other len bypasses the cap and passes an unvalidated dlen (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) with `data + 8` to client_cut_text. All other cases similarly dereference fixed offsets with no len-coverage check.

evidence.reason: The attacker-controlled 16-bit encoding count `limit` is read from the message and used directly as the loop bound for both read_s32 and memcpy at offsets 4 + i*4. The only length checks on this path are the equality probes `if (len == 1) return 4;` and `if (len == 4) {...}`; there is no statement requiring `len >= 4 + limit * 4` before the loop. Trigger: a client message with len not equal to 1 or 4 (e.g. 5) and limit = 65535 makes the loop read and write up to ~262144 bytes past the received data — heap out-of-bounds read and write (CWE-129 root cause, CWE-787 write).

The 1MB sanity cap on the attacker-controlled cut-text payload length is nested inside `if (len == 8)`, so any invocation where len != 8 bypasses it entirely; the check is a guard that one branch bypasses.

evidence.snippet: client_cut_text(vs, read_u32(data, 4), data + 8);
evidence.reason: The sink re-reads dlen from the message and passes it with `data + 8` with no cap and no `len >= 8 + dlen` check on this path (both the 1MB cap and the `return 8 + dlen` accumulation are confined to the len == 8 branch above). Trigger: len = 9 with dlen = 0xFFFFFFFF delivers an unbounded length and an out-of-bounds pointer/length pair to client_cut_text — the missing check belongs immediately before this line.

assumptions: The external VNC read machinery that invokes this callback (not shown in the given code) may, in the upstream implementation, only call the handler with `len` equal to a size the handler previously returned; if that were quotable here, the len == 1/2/4/8 equality probes would be sufficient. Per the analysis discipline, a framework guarantee absent from the given code is treated as non-existent, and this function is the intake point decoding client messages, so length validation is its responsibility.

read_u8/read_u16/read_u32/read_s32 are assumed to perform unchecked big-endian reads at byte offsets into `data`; their definitions are not in the given code and no bounds checking by them can be relied upon.
client_cut_text, set_encodings, and the audio backend are external; the defect is recorded at this code's sink (the unvalidated length/pointer pair it marshals), not in their implementations.
limitations: Fixed-offset overreads in the other cases (e.g. set_pixel_format reading data[4..16] with only the `len == 1` probe; key/ext-key/audio handlers) are the same root cause with smaller reach and were folded into the primary finding rather than listed separately.

`data[0]` is dereferenced at line 7 with no `len >= 1` guard; triggering it requires the caller to invoke the handler with an empty buffer, a len == 0 boundary of the same missing-length-validation defect.

The invalid audio-format path continues executing after vnc_client_error (nchannels/freq are still read and applied with a stale fmt); this is a minor fail-open logic wart, not the security defect reported here.
printf of attacker-supplied numeric values into constant format strings is not a format-string vulnerability.

verdict.summary: DecodePngV2 carefully validates the attacker-controlled decoded width and height (lines 28-34) but never validates decode.channels, a channel count derived from parsing the untrusted PNG stream via png::CommonInitDecode. Every downstream size is computed in int arithmetic that multiplies this unbounded value: 'new uint16[height * width * decode.channels]' and the row strides 'decode.channels * width * sizeof(uint8/uint16)'. With a channel count outside [1,4] (e.g., channels=32, width=8192, height=4096, which passes every quoted check since 2^26 < 2^29), the int product wraps, producing an undersized or negative-sized heap buffer, after which png::CommonFinishDecode writes channels*width*element_size bytes per row for height rows out of bounds (CWE-190 -> CWE-787), or throws an uncaught bad_alloc aborting the process (DoS).

evidence.snippet:
std::unique_ptr<uint16[]> buffer(
          new uint16[height * width * decode.channels]);
evidence.reason: Sink: the heap buffer element count is computed entirely in signed int arithmetic from the unvalidated attacker-influenced decode.channels. With decode.channels >= 8 and width*height < 2^29 (both quoted checks satisfied), height*width*decode.channels reaches or exceeds 2^31 and wraps, so the allocated buffer does not match what png::CommonFinishDecode then writes (channels*width*2 bytes per row for height rows) — heap out-of-bounds write; a wrapped-negative count yields std::bad_alloc and process abort.

Missing-check site: this is the only validation block in the function, and it bounds only width, height, and width*height. decode.channels — equally attacker-influenced parsed data and equally multiplied into every allocation and stride — appears in no guard anywhere in the code, although the preceding comment concedes dimensions are 'multiplied by channels_ and sizeof(uint16)' with only 'a few bits to spare', which are fully consumed at channels == 4.

Origin of the tainted values: CommonInitDecode parses the untrusted 'input' byte stream (and the channels_ attribute) and populates decode.width, decode.height, and decode.channels; only the boolean success of this call is checked, not the resulting field values. decode.channels crosses the trust boundary here and reaches the allocation/stride sinks unvalidated.

assumptions: The implementation of png::CommonInitDecode and png::CommonFinishDecode is not given; decode.channels is treated as attacker-influenced parsed data because nothing in the given code bounds it. If the external decoder structurally constrains channels to [1,4] (libpng color-type grammar) and CommonFinishDecode independently re-validates rowbytes, the out-of-bounds trigger would be unreachable — no such constraint is quotable in this code, so it is not relied upon.

allocate_output is assumed to produce an output tensor whose element type matches data_type_ (uint8/uint16/float), so flat<T>() and tensor<float,3>() match the allocation; OP_REQUIRES_OK guards only the allocation status, not the dtype.
CommonFinishDecode is assumed to write decode.height rows of decode.channels*width*element_size bytes at the supplied rowbytes; its internals are not given.

channels_ is an op attribute; under the TensorFlow raw-ops threat model an attacker able to construct/invoke the graph may set it arbitrarily, and it is passed directly into CommonInitDecode at line 5.
limitations: Resource amplification (CWE-400 class): the quoted bound deliberately permits width*height up to 2^29-1 pixels, so a ~100-byte header-only PNG claiming 16384x16384 RGBA forces multi-GB allocations (about 2 GB for uint16, about 8.6 GB for the float output) before the decode fails; repeated concurrent calls can exhaust host memory. The bound is an explicit int-overflow-safety policy ('PNG size too large for int'), so this is recorded as a lower-severity resource-consumption observation rather than the primary finding.

A DecodeGif op combined with DT_FLOAT would allocate a 4-D tensor and then call output->tensor<float, 3>(), a dimension-mismatch CHECK failure; this requires an op-registration combination not producible from runtime attacker input in this code, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.

The wrapped-negative variant of the overflow surfaces as an uncaught std::bad_alloc (process abort, denial of service) rather than memory corruption whenever the preceding int64 tensor allocation fails; the OOB-write variant additionally requires that allocation to succeed on a large-memory host.

verdict.summary: This is a libvirt unit-test callback whose entire input space is a statically compiled test table; no attacker-influenced data crosses a trust boundary. All internal sinks are guarded: src is checked with 'if (!src) return 0;' before use, xml is checked with '!(xml = virBufferContentAndReset(&buf))' before STRNEQ, data->expect is guaranteed non-NULL at the comparison by the early return 'if (src && !data->expect) ... return -1;', and test strings are used only as %s arguments, never as format strings. No memory-safety, injection, integer, crypto, or authorization defect is reachable.

assumptions: args is supplied by the libvirt test framework from a statically compiled test table in the same codebase; it is not data crossing an attacker-reachable trust boundary.

data->backing, data->expect, and data->rv are string/int literals from the compiled-in test data, assumed non-NULL and well-formed by construction of the test table; this code is judged as test code with no external input surface.

virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute, virDomainDiskSourceFormat, and virBufferContentAndReset are external library functions whose internal behavior is out of scope; their return values are all checked in this code.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: NULL dereference of args/data (CWE-476) — there is no 'if (!args)' check before 'int erc = data->rv;', but the only caller is the trusted internal test harness, which never passes NULL; not attacker-reachable.

Candidate dismissed: data->backing could theoretically be NULL when passed to virStorageSourceNewFromBackingAbsolute and used as a %s argument, but the compiled-in test table always supplies literal strings; no runtime path can make it NULL.
