verdict.summary: The MKL RequantizePerChannel kernel derives depth solely from input_min_vec.NumElements() and its only size checks are self-referential (dim_size(0) == depth), so nothing binds the per-channel scales vector to the input tensor's channel dimension before reorder_attr.set_output_scales(2, scales), nothing guarantees input_max_vec actually holds depth elements, and the requested min/max scalars are read at index 0 without any size check. Since all these tensors are attacker-controlled public-op inputs, this yields heap out-of-bounds reads and null dereferences (crash/DoS, possible heap-data leak through the scaled quantized output).

evidence.reason: Sink: scales is sized by attacker-controlled depth = input_min_vec.NumElements() and passed with mask 2 (one scale per output channel) to MKL-DNN reorder, whose output descriptor is built from input.shape() (TFShapeToMklDnnDimsInNCHW(input.shape(), FORMAT_NHWC), lines 53-62). No statement in this code compares depth to input.dim_size(3) or input.shape(). Concrete trigger: input shape [1,1,1,64], input_min_vec [8], input_max_vec [8] — all OP_REQUIRES checks pass because the dim_size(0)==depth checks are self-referential — so the reorder consumes 64 per-channel scales from an 8-element heap vector: out-of-bounds heap read reachable from a public op.

Missing-check site: depth is derived only from input_min_vec.NumElements(), and every size check here is tautological or mis-united — 'input_min_vec.dim_size(0) == depth' compares the tensor's own first dimension to its own element count, and 'input_max_vec.dim_size(0) == depth' compares a first-dimension size (not element count) to depth. Nothing references the input tensor's channel dimension, so the per-channel scales length is never bound to the tensor it quantizes.

Sink: 'std::abs(input_max_vec_data[i])' indexes input_max_vec's flat data for i in [0, depth), but the only guard is 'ctx, input_max_vec.dim_size(0) == depth,' which checks the first-dimension size, not the element count. Boundary case: input_max_vec of shape [depth, 0] has dim_size(0) == depth yet NumElements() == 0, so the loop reads depth floats from a zero-element buffer — out-of-bounds read / null dereference. Trigger: input_min_vec [1024], input_max_vec [1024,0], input [1,1,1,1024].

Sink: 'input_requested_min.flat<float>()(0)' (and the identical max read) dereferences element 0 of the requested-min/max tensors with no NumElements()/shape check anywhere in the op; the only related statement, 'if (out_type_ == DT_QINT8) DCHECK(input_requested_min_float < 0.0f);' at line 32, is debug-only and checks a value property, not existence. Feeding an empty [0]-shaped float tensor as requested_min/max makes the unchecked Eigen TensorMap index read past a zero-length/null buffer — attacker-reachable out-of-bounds read / crash.

assumptions: This Compute() implements the MKL-DNN path of the public tf.raw_ops.RequantizePerChannel op; every tensor obtained via ctx->input() is runtime graph input crossing a trust boundary, and no shape/size constraints are enforced by the op definition.
No validation performed inside MKL-DNN/oneDNN (e.g., scales-count-vs-mask checks during primitive-desc creation) is credited; the given code is judged as the last line of defense.
The DCHECK on line 32 is compiled out in release builds and is not treated as a guard.
out_type_ and cpu_engine_ are kernel-construction state not influenced by per-call inputs.
limitations: requested_min_max == 0 (both requested scalars 0.0f) produces Inf/NaN scales through IEEE float division; no crash or memory error is demonstrable from this code, only silent numerical corruption.

The loop counter 'int i' compared against size_t depth can overflow (UB) only if input_min_vec has at least 2^31 elements (~8 GiB), which also requires the runtime to allocate that tensor; recorded as resource-gated, not confirmed.
static_cast<float>(1L << 31) is undefined behavior only on LLP64 platforms where long is 32-bit; Linux LP64 builds are unaffected.
Rank-0 min/max vectors cause dim_size(0) to hit a CHECK (safe abort) rather than memory unsafety.
The catch (mkldnn::error&) handler converts library errors to errors::Aborted without writing outputs, so the error path is not fail-open.

verdict.summary: snd_pcm_oss_sync computes width = snd_pcm_format_physical_width(snd_pcm_oss_format_from(runtime->oss.format)) from the user-selectable OSS sample format and divides by it at two sites without ever checking it for zero. A user who selects a format whose physical width is 0 (e.g., AFMT_MPEG mapping to SNDRV_PCM_FORMAT_MPEG) and then triggers sync with buffer_used > 0 or period_ptr > 0 causes an integer divide error in kernel context, crashing the process and potentially the kernel — an attacker-reachable local denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
format = snd_pcm_oss_format_from(runtime->oss.format);
		width = snd_pcm_format_physical_width(format);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted divisor: runtime->oss.format is the raw user-supplied OSS format code set via SNDCTL_DSP_SETFMT; the derived width (declared unsigned long, assigned from an int return) is never validated for zero or validity anywhere in this function before use as a divisor.

evidence.snippet: size = (8 * (runtime->oss.period_bytes - runtime->oss.buffer_used) + 7) / width;
evidence.reason: Primary sink: division by attacker-influenced width with no zero check on any path; when width == 0 (e.g. format SNDRV_PCM_FORMAT_MPEG selected via AFMT_MPEG) and runtime->oss.buffer_used > 0, this executes a kernel divide-by-zero fault (local DoS). The guard 'if (!width)' is absent from the code.

Second sink on the period_ptr > 0 branch: the same unchecked width is used as divisor ('size * 8 / width'); the preceding branch conditions test buffer_used and period_ptr, not width, so a zero width bypasses to this divide error — the zero-check is missing on this path as well.

assumptions: runtime->oss.format, oss.buffer_used, oss.period_ptr and oss.period_bytes are set by prior user ioctls and write() calls in code not shown here; this function is judged as the last line of defense for those values.

snd_pcm_format_physical_width returns 0 for formats with no fixed physical width (e.g. SNDRV_PCM_FORMAT_MPEG, reachable by selecting AFMT_MPEG via SNDCTL_DSP_SETFMT); the mapping and width table are defined outside the given code.

The invariant runtime->oss.buffer_used <= runtime->oss.period_bytes (and period_ptr <= period_bytes) is maintained by the OSS write/read paths outside this function; it cannot be quoted here, so the size_t subtractions at lines 30 and 41 are unguarded in this code but no trigger for their underflow is constructible from the shown code alone.
snd_pcm_oss_make_ready (line 16) is assumed to fully initialize hardware parameters so that runtime->period_size is non-zero at line 50; that enforcement is not present in the given code.
limitations: Candidate C2 (unsigned underflow of period_bytes - buffer_used / period_bytes - period_ptr leading to an oversized silence fill) was dismissed because the counter invariants live in code not shown and no concrete trigger is reachable from the given statements alone.
Candidate C3 (modulo by zero if runtime->period_size == 0 at line 50) dismissed for the same reason; only indirectly guarded via snd_pcm_oss_make_ready outside this code.

Candidate C4 (rw_ref dropped before the SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_DRAIN at line 57, theoretically permitting concurrent parameter reconfiguration) was examined but no dereference of a reconfigurable buffer exists in this function after line 51, so no use-after-free sink is demonstrable here.
Analysis is static; no runtime verification was performed.

verdict.summary: fastrpc_dma_buf_attach leaks the kzalloc'd struct fastrpc_dma_buf_attachment when dma_get_sgtable() fails: the error path returns -EINVAL at line 16 without freeing 'a' (allocated at line 8) and without adding it to buffer->attachments for later teardown. The attach operation is reachable/repeatable by any process holding a fd for the exported dma-buf, so repeated failing attaches (deterministic for non-page-backed memory, or under induced allocation pressure) exhaust unbounded kernel memory, causing denial of service.

evidence.reason: Memory leak on error path (CWE-401 leading to CWE-400 DoS): 'a' is allocated at line 8, but when dma_get_sgtable() fails, the branch at line 14 returns -EINVAL at line 16 without kfree(a) or any ownership transfer; the only ownership transfer, list_add(&a->node, &buffer->attachments) at line 24, is skipped on this path. No cleanup statement exists between lines 8 and 17, verified by exhaustive search of the function. Trigger: an unprivileged process with a dma-buf fd repeatedly invokes attach on a buffer for which dma_get_sgtable fails (e.g., memory lacking a struct page, a persistent error, or allocation failure under memory pressure); each failed attach leaks a kernel object, enabling unbounded kernel memory exhaustion.

evidence.snippet:
mutex_lock(&buffer->lock);
	list_add(&a->node, &buffer->attachments);
evidence.reason: Origin of ownership: on the success path, 'a' is handed off via list_add so it is freed by the buffer's teardown; the error path bypasses this, which is why the leaked allocation at line 8 has no other release site.

assumptions: The dma-buf attach callback is reachable from userspace through a fd for the fastrpc-exported buffer (standard dma-buf lifetime; the framework calls .attach during import/mapping), and an unprivileged process can hold and repeatedly operate on such a fd. This is the framework contract, not a statement in the given code, but it is the same trust boundary the driver's own .attach export exists to serve.

dma_get_sgtable can fail with a persistent error (e.g., -ENXIO for memory without a valid struct page) or under memory pressure; both are conditions a repeated-attach attacker can realize. The given code treats this branch as reachable (it handles it), so the leak is on an attacker-reachable path.

buffer->size, buffer->virt, buffer->phys and buffer->lock are produced by this driver at buffer-creation/export time and are treated as internally trusted for this analysis; no guard on them is required inside this function.
limitations: Whether dma_get_sgtable itself leaves a partially allocated sg_table on failure is internal to the external DMA-API implementation, not this code; no evidence entry is attached for it.

The leak is strictly a per-failed-attach leak with no memory-corruption consequence; severity is capped at medium (kernel memory exhaustion / DoS) because triggering requires dma_get_sgtable to fail, which is deterministic only for certain memory backings.

No use-after-free, double-free, race, or injection sink exists in this function: kzalloc is NULL-checked at lines 9-10, the list add is mutex-protected (lines 23-25), and dev_err at line 15 uses a fixed literal format string.

verdict.summary: old_tensor_name is fetched and immediately dereferenced via scalar<tstring>()() with no NumElements()==1 validation (unlike ckpt_path), so an empty string tensor causes an out-of-bounds read; additionally, min_old_row/max_old_row are taken unbounded from attacker-controlled row_remapping values, driving a slice-construction loop whose length arithmetic overflows at INT64_MAX and whose iteration/container growth is unbounded, causing a hang and memory exhaustion.

evidence.reason: The old_tensor_name input crosses a trust boundary but is never checked for NumElements()==1 before scalar<tstring>()() dereferences its first element; the analogous guard exists only for ckpt_path ('context, ckpt_path_t->NumElements() == 1'). Trigger: pass an empty (0-element) string tensor as old_tensor_name; element 0 of a zero-element buffer is read out of bounds, crashing or yielding a garbage tstring (CWE-125).

Loop bounds and slice lengths derive solely from attacker-controlled min_old_row/max_old_row with no validation against the checkpoint tensor's row count in this code; with min_old_row=0 and max_old_row=INT64_MAX, 'max_old_row - row_start + 1' overflows int64, the wrapped negative length makes row_start negative and subsequent lengths zero, so the loop never terminates while tensor_slices grows without bound (hang + OOM, CWE-400/CWE-190).

Origin of the tainted bounds: min_old_row and max_old_row are copied verbatim from attacker-supplied row_remapping values (any non-negative int64, including INT64_MAX) with no upper bound, and these unbounded values flow directly into the slice-construction while loop.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap is not part of the given code; its resizing of row_id_present/col_id_present to remapping.size() (== num_rows_/num_cols_, both checked here) and its acceptance of arbitrary non-negative old IDs are assumed, not quotable.
Input tensor dtypes (int64 remappings, string names/paths) are enforced by op registration outside this code.

Tensor::scalar/vec element-count and rank enforcement is DCHECK-only in release builds outside this code; TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape / BundleReader::LookupSlice error-handling for out-of-range slices is framework code not shown.
limitations: The output_matrix write is guarded: 'OP_REQUIRES(context, new_row < num_rows_ && new_col < num_cols_ && new_row >= 0 && new_col >= 0, ...)' lies on every path and rejects boundary values; not a finding.
initializing_values indexing is guarded by 'OP_REQUIRES(context, initializing_values_index < initializing_values.size(), ...)'; not a finding.

col_remapping_t lacks the dims()==1 check that row_remapping_t has; vec<int64_t>() on a non-1-D input may CHECK-fail or mis-size, but the memory-safety consequence depends on unshown framework code — recorded as a hardening note, not confirmed.
LOG(INFO) << ckpt_path permits log forging with arbitrary checkpoint-path content; cosmetic, not elevated to a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The server-side ciphersuite-selection handler scans the attacker-supplied ClientHello ciphersuite vector in a loop that bounds only i < datalen while reading data[i] and data[i+1] per iteration. For an odd datalen (e.g. 1 or 3), the last iteration reads one byte past the end of the handshake buffer. The code does contain a datalen % 2 != 0 validation, but it is executed only at line 78, after the loop (and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites) has already dereferenced the buffer, so the guard is a check-after-use and never protects the first loop. A remote client sending a ClientHello with an odd-length ciphersuite vector triggers a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Sink: the loop bound is `i < datalen` but each iteration reads data[i] and data[i+1]. With attacker-controlled odd datalen (e.g. datalen = 1), the final iteration i = datalen - 1 evaluates data[i + 1] one byte past the ClientHello buffer — an out-of-bounds read of network-controlled-length data (the same defect is repeated at lines 29-30 with data[i+1] in the TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV test). No parity validation precedes this loop in the given code.

The only guard that rejects odd datalen exists here, but it is placed after the SCSV-scanning loop at lines 13-39 and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites(data, datalen, ...) — a check-after-use. This is where the check belongs relative to the sink; moving it above line 13 is the minimal fix, and no equivalent check exists earlier in the given code.

assumptions: `data` and `datalen` are the raw ciphersuite vector and its length from the client's ClientHello, i.e. attacker-controlled network data; this function is the intake/validation point for those values.

`server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites(data, datalen, ...)` is called at lines 42-44, also before the parity check; its internal handling of odd datalen is not shown in the given code, so whether it also over-reads is unverifiable here (same root-cause state, recorded rather than confirmed as a separate finding).
MAX_CIPHERSUITE_SIZE, MAX_ALGOS, and the library-internal helpers are assumed to honor the sizeof(cipher_suites) bound passed at line 50; these are internal/trusted for this analysis.
limitations: The over-read is one byte past a heap buffer; the read value is only compared against fixed SCSV constants (0xff/0x56 and their minors), so the direct impact is a remotely triggerable crash (DoS) or minor control-flow perturbation (spurious safe-renegotiation/fallback handling), not direct data exfiltration by this code.

Candidates dismissed with verified guards: the second and third matching loops' reads of data[j+1] are protected by the parity early-return at line 78 on the only path to them; `retval` is assigned GNUTLS_E_UNKNOWN_CIPHER_SUITE before the loops, so no uninitialized use at the finish label; cipher_suites_size is produced by internal calls bounded by sizeof(cipher_suites).

verdict.summary: The 32-bit `int` loop counters (`auto start_offset = 0`, `auto i = 0`) are compared against 64-bit, attacker-shape-derived bounds (`big_stride`, `flat_segment_id.size()`). When a caller supplies tensors whose dimension products reach 2^31 (e.g. input tstring shape [2, 2^31] with segment_id [2] and num_segments=1), the counter increments past INT_MAX, overflows, and wraps negative while the signed comparison still holds. The outer loop then indexes `output_flat(output_index)` and `flat_input(offset)` with negative values (OOB read/write via tstring append) and can never terminate (no int reaches big_stride, causing an infinite loop / unbounded string growth). The validation loop's counter likewise wraps and reads `flat_segment_id(i)` out of bounds. No statement in the code widens these counters or bounds the tensor element count.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `auto start_offset = 0` deduces 32-bit int while `big_stride` is int64 (declared line 51). Trigger: input shape [2, 2^31], segment_id [2] (values 0), num_segments=1 gives big_stride = 2^31, which passes every OP_REQUIRES shape check in this code. start_offset increments to INT_MAX (still < 2^31), then `start_offset++` overflows and wraps to INT_MIN; `INT_MIN < big_stride` remains true, so `output_index` and `offset` become negative and `output_flat(output_index)`/`flat_input(offset)` access memory out of bounds (tstring read + append = OOB write / OOB read leaked into output). Because no int value can ever satisfy start_offset >= big_stride when big_stride > INT_MAX, the loop is also non-terminating (unbounded appends / OOM). No int64 counter exists in the code (lines 42/57/58 all use `auto ... = 0`).

evidence.snippet:
for (auto i = 0; i < flat_segment_id.size(); i++) {
      OP_REQUIRES(
          context,
          ((flat_segment_id(i) < num_segments) && (flat_segment_id(i) >= 0)),
evidence.reason: Same 32-bit counter defect at the validation sink: `auto i = 0` is int, while `flat_segment_id.size()` is a signed 64-bit element count controlled by the attacker's segment_id shape. With a segment_id tensor of 2^31 int32 elements (input [2^31, 1]), i wraps from INT_MAX to INT_MIN and the signed comparison INT_MIN < size still holds, so `flat_segment_id(i)` reads ~8 GiB below the tensor buffer (OOB read, crash) — and any garbage value that happens to fall in [0, num_segments) is never rejected by this check.

Origin of the overflowing bound: big_stride (int64, line 51) is derived from the attacker-controlled input_shape, and no statement in this code bounds the total element count (the only shape guards are segment_dims != 0, segment_dims <= input_dims, and per-dimension equality), so big_stride can reach or exceed 2^31, which is exactly the value at which the int counter in line 57 overflows.

assumptions: GetStrides, GetFlattenedRelativeOffsets, and GetOutputShape are external to the given code; the analysis assumes big_stride = product of input dims after the segment dims, relative_offset_set.size() == flat_segment_id.size() == segment volume, and output_flat.size() == num_segments * big_stride. If any of these differ, additional out-of-bounds accesses exist that cannot be proven from this code alone.
Standard C++ type deduction is assumed: `auto x = 0` yields int; `flat().size()` returns Eigen's signed 64-bit DenseIndex; `std::vector::size()` returns size_t.
`separator_` is an op-attribute constant set at construction, not per-call attacker data.

No `num_segments >= 0` check exists in this code; the consequence of a negative num_segments (with a zero-sized segment dim making validation vacuous) depends on external TensorShape/allocate_output checks and is unverified here.

`num_segments_tensor.scalar<NUM_SEGMENTS_TYPE>()()` is guarded only by `NumElements() != 0`, not by exactly-one-element or dtype/size checks visible here; release-build behavior relies on external DCHECKs.
limitations: The inner write-loop counter `auto i` (line 58) also overflows for >2^31 relative offsets, but because relative_offset_set.size() is unsigned, the wrapped value fails the comparison and the loop exits (truncated output plus undefined behavior), not an out-of-bounds access.

The segment-id validation itself is correct for all in-range shapes (strict `< num_segments` and `>= 0` cover the full [0, num_segments-1] range); the OOB arises only past the 2^31-element counter boundary.

Triggering the confirmed defects requires tensors with at least 2^31 elements (tens of GB for tstring, ~8 GB for the segment-id variant); on hosts where such allocations fail, the code fails safe at allocation, so practical impact is environment-dependent (DoS/OOM/infinite loop and formal OOB write rather than reliable exploitation).

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found in the given code. All memory-relevant sinks are guarded by present, edge-tested checks: argv access is bounded by 'if (argc < 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' and 'if (argc > 3)', the linebuf stack buffer is protected by 'linebytes = (nbytes > DISP_LINE_LEN) ? DISP_LINE_LEN : nbytes;' (correct at 0, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit and max-uint), the alen value is validated by 'if (alen > 3) return CMD_RET_USAGE;' which also rejects an error return of -1 stored as unsigned 0xFFFFFFFF, and 'dev' is always initialized before dm_i2c_read because 'if (ret) return i2c_report_err(ret, I2C_ERR_READ);' exits on any i2c_get_cur_bus_chip failure. The only unbounded behavior — a user-supplied dump length up to 0xFFFFFFFF driving the do-while loop — is the command's specified function and its only trigger requires the already-privileged U-Boot console operator, so no trust boundary is crossed.

assumptions: DISP_LINE_LEN (defined externally, typically 16) equals the declared size of 'unsigned char linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN];'; the min() against it is the sole bound on linebytes.
get_alen (external helper) returns either a small address length or an error value; an error of -1 stored into 'uint alen' becomes 0xFFFFFFFF and is rejected by 'if (alen > 3)'.

The globals i2c_dp_last_chip/addr/alen/length are initialized and not written by other translation units without equivalent validation; within the given code the only writers are the four assignments at function end, which store previously validated values.
hextoul safely parses the non-NULL argv strings guaranteed by the argc checks, and dm_i2c_read/i2c_read respect their length arguments and do not write beyond linebuf.
The U-Boot shell console is a privileged operator context; argv values are supplied by the operator who already has full platform control.
'alen != -1' in the DM branch is dead code (alen is always 0..3 here) but has no security effect.
limitations: CWE-400 candidate dismissed: 'length = hextoul(argv[3], NULL);' is unbounded and the do-while dump loop has no upper bound or ctrl-c hook, so 'i2c md <chip> <addr> ffffffff' can lock the console for a very long time. Dismissed because the only principal able to supply the CLI argument is the interactive console operator, who already holds full bootloader control (no privilege boundary crossed); dumping a user-specified length is the command's intended function, matching the generic 'md.b' behavior.
Truncation of hextoul's unsigned-long result into 'uint chip/addr/length' (e.g., hex 100000000 truncates to 0): value-correctness only; no memory-safety sink in this code consumes the widened value.
alen == 0 passes 'if (alen > 3)' (e.g., address argument '0.0'), forwarding an unusual chip-offset length to the driver layer; robustness concern only, with no unsafe use in this code.
On read failure mid-loop the function returns without updating i2c_dp_last_* globals, so a later repeat reuses stale parameters; consistency issue only.

verdict.summary: The NE entry-table decoder indexes bin->segment_entries with the attacker-controlled byte segnum guarded only by 'segnum > 0' (no SegCount upper bound, unlike the sibling fixed branch), and its r_buf_size guards lag behind the off increments, so the bundle_type read and the second byte of the movable ut16 read touch one byte past the validated range — attacker-reachable heap out-of-bounds reads on a crafted NE file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing upper-bound validation of the array index. segnum is a ut8 read from the file-controlled entry table (range 0-255), and the only guard on the path to the sink is 'if (segnum > 0)', which bounds only the lower end. The fixed branch validates the equivalent index with 'if (bundle_type < bin->ne_header->SegCount)' (line 64), but the movable branch performs no SegCount comparison, so segnum=0xFF with SegCount=1 indexes segment_entries[254] — heap out-of-bounds read. Trigger: crafted NE file with a small SegCount and a movable bundle entry carrying segnum 0xFF.

Off-by-one out-of-bounds read. The loop guard 'if (tableat + off + 4 >= r_buf_size (bin->buf))' (line 42) validates entries only through tableat+off+4, but this path advances off by 3 more and then reads a ut16 at off+4..off+5; the byte at off+5 is exactly one past the validated range (guard uses '>= r_buf_size', so tableat+off+4 == r_buf_size-1 passes and the second byte read is out of bounds). Trigger: entry-table data at the very end of the file buffer with a movable entry.

evidence.snippet:
off++;
		ut8 bundle_type = *(ut8 *)(bin->entry_table + off);
evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds read. The only guards before this read — 'while (off < bin->ne_header->EntryTableLength)' and 'if (tableat + off >= r_buf_size (bin->buf))' — are evaluated with the pre-increment off; after 'off++' the read at off+1 is unchecked against both limits. Edge trigger: tableat+off == r_buf_size-1 (or off+1 == EntryTableLength) passes the guards, then the read touches exactly one past the limit.

assumptions: bin->entry_table is a buffer populated from file bytes at file offset tableat = header_offset + EntryTableOffset; its exact allocated size is not established in this code, so even taking the r_buf_size guards at face value they under-check the reads by one byte.
bin->segment_entries is allocated with SegCount elements; this is inferred from the code's own guard 'bundle_type < bin->ne_header->SegCount' at line 64, since the allocation is not shown.
r_list_get_n is assumed to return NULL for out-of-range indices (used safely via 's? s->paddr: 0'); its implementation is not shown.
ne_header field widths (ut16 SegCount/EntryTableOffset/EntryTableLength, csEntryPoint) are inferred from the radare2 NE header layout and are not shown in this code.
limitations: The 'segments' list is leaked on the early-return paths at lines 16-19 and 46-49, but these are reachable only on R_NEW0 allocation failure, which attacker input cannot induce — not a vulnerability.

The ut64 arithmetic '(ut64)segment_entries[i].offset * bin->alignment + segoff' at lines 61/65 may wrap, but the result is only reported entry metadata (paddr) and never used as a memory-access size or offset.
Per-bundle work is bounded by bundle_length <= 255 and the tableat/r_buf_size checks, so no unbounded resource consumption beyond the off-by-one reads was found.

verdict.summary: In cvtchar, the '^' escape branch reads the character after '^' with 'c = UChar(*++sp);' and unconditionally returns len = 2, with no check for the string terminator. For an input string ending in a bare '^', the function consumes and counts the NUL terminator, so the caller advances sp one byte past the end of the string buffer; subsequent reads run out of bounds while parsing attacker-supplied terminfo data. The sibling '\' branch proves the intended invariant via 'case '\0': c = '\\'; len = 1;' — the identical check is missing on the '^' path.

evidence.reason: Missing terminator check on the '^' escape path. Trigger: a capability string whose remaining content is exactly "^" (caret immediately before the NUL). '*++sp' reads the NUL, c becomes 0, and len is unconditionally set to 2, so the function reports having consumed the terminating NUL. The caller then advances sp by len, landing one byte past the end of the string buffer, and the next iteration's 'switch (*sp)' reads out of bounds. The '\'-branch handles the identical boundary with 'case '\0': c = '\\'; len = 1;' (lines 17-19), proving the invariant that len must never count the terminator — that check is absent here.

Origin-of-invariant evidence: the '\' branch explicitly detects the terminator after 'switch (*++sp)' and returns len = 1 so the caller stays inside the string. The '^' branch (lines 37-43) lacks this exact check, which is the root cause of the off-by-one return value for a trailing '^'.

assumptions: The caller of cvtchar advances the string pointer by the returned len and continues parsing, as the function's documented purpose ('convert a character to a terminfo push' plus a consumed-length return value) and the terminator-careful len computations elsewhere imply. The caller's source is not part of the given code.
sp points into a NUL-terminated, heap-backed capability string supplied by the terminfo parser; the strings originate from attacker-controlled terminfo data at this trust-boundary intake function.
The global dp and save_string/save_char are assumed to manage output-buffer growth correctly; their implementations are outside the given code.
limitations: The octal loop 'while (isdigit(UChar(*sp))) { c = UChar(8 * c + (*sp++ - '0')); len++; }' accepts an unbounded number of digits; '8 * c + (*sp++ - '0')' promotes c to int (max 8*255+9 = 2049, no int overflow) and wraps on assignment to unsigned char (defined mod-256 behavior). With 4+ digits (e.g. "\\3777") the encoded character value is silently wrong, but this is value corruption only — no memory-safety, availability, or injection effect — so it is not counted as a vulnerability.
isdigit/isgraph are always called with values in 0-255 (via UChar / unsigned char c), so no domain violations occur there.

A trailing '^' that is also the final byte of an unterminated buffer would be an OOB read at line 38 itself, but this requires a non-NUL-terminated buffer, which this code cannot establish; the confirmed defect is the len off-by-one for a NUL-terminated string.

verdict.summary: This is the post-fix fastrpc dma_buf attach path. Every security-relevant sink is guarded by quotable, on-path checks: allocation failure is handled by 'if (!a) return -ENOMEM;', the scatterlist failure path is guarded by 'if (ret < 0)' and frees 'a' before 'attachment->priv' is set or 'a' is listed (no UAF/double-free/leak path), and the shared-list mutation is serialized by 'mutex_lock(&buffer->lock)' / 'mutex_unlock(&buffer->lock)' around 'list_add(&a->node, &buffer->attachments)'. The consumed buffer fields (dev, virt, phys, size) are kernel-internal objects produced by the driver's own allocation path, not attacker bytes at this function's boundary, and they are consumed through a bounds-safe kernel API (dma_get_sgtable). No reachable memory-safety, race, injection, or fail-open defect exists in this code.

assumptions: The dma-buf framework invokes this ops callback only on dmabufs exported by fastrpc itself, so 'dmabuf->priv' is a valid 'struct fastrpc_buf' and 'buffer' is non-NULL; this is not verifiable from the given snippet.

dma_get_sgtable is assumed to return 0 on success or a negative errno only, and to leave 'a->sgt' unallocated on failure (so the error path's kfree(a) without sg_free_table is correct); the API contract lives outside this code.

The detach/release counterpart of the dma_buf ops (not shown) is assumed to take the same 'buffer->lock' before touching 'buffer->attachments', and to free the sgtable and attachment under the same ownership rules this code establishes.
Invariants on buffer->virt/phys/size (non-NULL, page-aligned, sane size) are assumed to be established by the fastrpc buffer-allocation path, which is not part of the given code.

Concurrent attach/detach serialization provided by the dma-buf core (e.g., reservation-object locking) in newer kernels is outside this code and was not relied upon for the verdict; the in-function mutex is the quoted guard.
limitations: Candidate 'race condition on buffer->attachments (CWE-362)' dismissed: the fix (a lock around list_add) is present and quoted — 'mutex_lock(&buffer->lock); ... list_add(&a->node, &buffer->attachments); mutex_unlock(&buffer->lock);'.

Candidate 'use-after-free / double-free of the attachment object' dismissed: the only kfree(a) is inside 'if (ret < 0)' and returns before 'attachment->priv = a;' is executed, so the freed object is unreachable.

Candidate 'unvalidated buffer fields reaching dma_get_sgtable' dismissed: the fields are kernel-internal values produced by code outside this snippet; no trigger with values this code can receive was constructible.
Candidate 'ret > 0 bypassing the ret < 0 check' dismissed: it requires the external DMA API to violate its documented return-value contract; recorded as an assumption, not a reachable defect.
The error path returns -EINVAL instead of propagating the actual 'ret' (line: 'return -EINVAL;'); this is a cosmetic robustness issue (loss of precise errno) with no security effect.
The analysis covers only the attach callback; defects in sibling dma_buf ops (map/unmap/release/detach) or in the buffer-allocation path cannot be assessed from this snippet.

verdict.summary: The S3M order list is copied into the fixed-capacity struct array header->ord with no bound on the write index: the loop is bounded only by the file-controlled 16-bit ordnum (up to 65535) and the 255 marker, so a crafted module whose order entries contain no 0xFF byte makes j grow up to ordnum and writes past the end of header->ord (e.g., ordnum=257 overflows by one, ordnum=65535 by ~65 KB) with attacker-controlled byte values, corrupting the heap-resident module header. No clamp on j or on ordnum exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-129/CWE-787): header->ord[j++] is written with no check that j stays within the capacity of the fixed-size header->ord array. The only guards are the loop bound 'i < header->ordnum' (file-controlled, 0..65535) and 'if (orders[i] == 255) break;'. Trigger: an S3M file with ordnum=257 (or any value above the array capacity, up to 65535) whose order bytes contain no 0xFF value writes header->ord[0..ordnum-1], overflowing the struct member with attacker-chosen bytes 0x00-0xFE. The minimal fix (break when j reaches the array capacity before the store) does not exist anywhere in the function; line 86 'header->ordnum = j;' even stores the unclamped count.

evidence.snippet: header->ordnum = f.readWord(); // number of positions in order list (songlength)
evidence.reason: Taint origin: ordnum is read as a raw 16-bit word from the module file (range 0..65535) and used both as the allocation size for the temporary orders buffer and, unclamped, as the loop bound for the unbounded copy into the fixed-capacity header->ord array at lines 77-84.

assumptions: safeRead(packed, index, size, def) is a helper not present in the given code; based on its name and call pattern (index passed repeatedly, never incremented in the visible loop) it is assumed to bounds-check against size and advance index by reference. If it does not advance index, the 'while (index<size)' pattern loop would be an attacker-triggerable infinite loop (CWE-400); this cannot be verified from the given code.

The capacity of module->instr, module->smp and module->phead is not declared or checkable in this code (they are only checked non-null at line 12, before insnum/patnum are read at lines 30-31). If the caller sized them smaller than the file's insnum/patnum, the indexing at instr[i], smp[s], phead[i] and convertS3MPattern(&phead[i],...) would also be out of bounds; this cannot be proven or refuted from the given code.
module->loadModuleSample is assumed to validate samplen/loopstart/looplen consistency; no such validation exists in the given code.

The capacity of header->ord (a fixed compile-time struct member, 256 in standard ST3-style headers) is not visible in the given code, but no bound check on j exists regardless of the exact constant, and a fixed struct array cannot hold up to 65535 entries.
limitations: Indexing of caller-allocated instr/smp/phead arrays by file-controlled insnum/patnum: potential OOB, but depends entirely on caller allocation sizes outside this code; recorded as assumption rather than a confirmed finding.
Validation of sample loop points (loopstart/looplen vs samplen) is delegated to loadModuleSample, which is not part of the given code.
header->channum can become 0 (if channelSettings[0]==255) or be clamped to 0; any downstream division by channel count occurs outside this function.
strcpy(header->tracker,"Screamtracker 3") writes a fixed 16-byte literal including NUL; safe for any destination of at least 16 bytes (destination size not visible).

verdict.summary: The ClientHello cipher-suite list (data, datalen) is parsed in a loop reading data[i] and data[i+1] before the function verifies datalen is even. An attacker sending a ClientHello with an odd cipher-suite list length (e.g. datalen == 1) causes a one-byte out-of-bounds read of data[i+1] on the final loop iteration. The only parity guard, 'if (datalen % 2 != 0) ... return GNUTLS_E_UNEXPECTED_PACKET_LENGTH;', is placed after this loop (and after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites), so the check is performed after the use.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the loop condition 'i < datalen' with stride 2 permits i == datalen-1 when datalen is odd, and the body then reads data[i + 1] = data[datalen], one byte past the attacker-sized cipher-suite buffer. Trigger: a TLS client sends a ClientHello whose cipher-suite list has odd length (minimal case datalen == 1). The only even-length validation, 'if (datalen % 2 != 0) { gnutls_assert(); return GNUTLS_E_UNEXPECTED_PACKET_LENGTH; }', appears later in the function (after server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites and _gnutls_remove_unwanted_ciphersuites), i.e. after the use, so no guard exists on any path before this sink. The Fallback SCSV branch (data[i+1] == GNUTLS_FALLBACK_SCSV_MINOR) in the same loop repeats the OOB read and feeds the byte into comparison/control flow.

evidence.snippet: unsigned int datalen)
evidence.reason: Taint origin: datalen is the peer-controlled length of the ClientHello cipher-suite list, entering the function with no parity or range validation at entry; its odd values are not rejected until after the parsing loop that over-reads.

assumptions: datalen is bounded by the TLS handshake record size (~2^16), since it is the parsed ClientHello cipher-suite list length; this prevents unsigned wrap of i+1 but is enforced outside this code.

server_find_pk_algos_in_ciphersuites(data, datalen, ...) is called before the parity check with a possibly odd datalen; its body is not in the given code, so its internal bounds handling could not be quoted or verified — the confirmed OOB read is the loop in this function.

_gnutls_cipher_suite_get_name and the other helpers' internal contracts are not part of the given code; the later memcmp/memcpy loops over cipher_suites[] are bounded by _gnutls_supported_ciphersuites(session, cipher_suites, sizeof(cipher_suites)) and by the 'if (ret <= 0)' check.
limitations: Unsigned overflow of 'i += 2' in the first loop was tested (datalen up to 2^32-1) and rejected as a candidate only because datalen cannot exceed the ~2^16 TLS fragment size at this call site; this bound is not enforced inside the given code.

The one-byte over-read's exploitability beyond denial-of-service/heap probing depends on the caller's buffer placement, which is outside the given code; the memory-safety violation itself is fully confirmed.

verdict.summary: ReadMATImage uses the file-supplied 32-bit frame count 'Frames' (read at 'Frames = ReadBlobXXXLong(image2);' in the DimFlag==16 case) as the bound of an allocation loop without any validation: 'if(--Frames>0) { ... goto NEXT_FRAME; }' has no EOF check, no sanity cap, and its only exits are allocation failure or frame-count exhaustion. A short ReadBlob inside the loop merely does 'goto ExitLoop', after which flow still performs RotateImage/AppendImageToList and AcquireNextImage, permanently adding images to the list before jumping back to NEXT_FRAME. Additionally, '--Frames' on 'unsigned Frames' underflows at the boundary value 0 to 4294967295, so a tiny crafted MAT file (DimFlag 16, z=1, Frames=0 or 0xFFFFFFFF, 1x1 matrix, truncated data) drives billions of iterations that each allocate and retain images, quantum info, and scan buffers, causing guaranteed memory and CPU exhaustion (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Missing-check site / sink: the frame loop's only guard is the decrement itself. There is no EOFBlob check, no cap on Frames, and no validation that data remains for the next frame; failed row reads earlier only 'goto ExitLoop', after which RotateImage (AppendImageToList at lines 384-385) and AcquireNextImage (line 406) permanently add images to the list before control returns here. 'unsigned Frames' (line 18) underflows when Frames==0, producing 4294967295 iterations of unbounded allocation, so a truncated crafted MAT file with DimFlag 16 causes memory/CPU exhaustion (CWE-400, amplified by the unsigned wraparound, CWE-190).

Origin of the tainted loop bound: Frames is read directly from the attacker-controlled MAT file (DimFlag==16 path) with no range or sanity validation anywhere in the function; it is only ever assigned here, defaulted to 1 at 'Frames = 1;', and consumed at 'if(--Frames>0)'.

assumptions: The MATHeader struct definition is not in the given code, so the exact width of MATLAB_HDR.SizeX/SizeY cannot be quoted. If SizeX were exactly 32-bit, 'ldblk = (ssize_t)(8 * MATLAB_HDR.SizeX)' (and the 2x/4x variants) would wrap in 32-bit arithmetic and under-size BImgBuff relative to image->columns, enabling a heap overflow in ImportQuantumPixels; with a >=64-bit field the products cannot wrap. Neither the defect nor a guard is provable from the given code, so this is recorded as an assumption rather than a finding.

z2qtype[], CalcMinMax, InsertComplexDoubleRow/InsertComplexFloatRow, DecompressBlock, ReadBlobDoublesXXX/ReadBlobFloatsXXX and the ReadBlob* helpers are not defined in the given code; their internal bounds behavior (e.g., that ReadBlobDoublesXXX(image2, ldblk, ...) writes at most ldblk*8 bytes, exactly the BImgBuff allocation of ldblk*sizeof(double)) is assumed per ImageMagick conventions.
ThrowReaderException is assumed to terminate the reader (return DestroyImageList), and DeleteImageFromList/DestroyImageInfo are assumed to NULL their argument per ImageMagick convention.
limitations: image->colors = one << image->depth is undefined behavior when image->depth == 64 (reachable via miINT64/miUINT64/miDOUBLE), but the resulting colors value has no security-relevant use in this code (only copied to rotated_image->colors), so it is not counted as a vulnerability.

The ping path swaps image->columns/image->rows and 'goto done_reading' skips SetImageExtent (author-flagged '!!!!!! BAD !!!!'), causing misreported dimensions and a per-frame quantum_info leak; the effect is incorrect metadata plus a bounded leak, not memory corruption.
'(void) ReadBlob(image2, 4, (unsigned char *) &size);' partially overwrites the 8-byte size_t 'size' (upper bytes stale), but the value is never used afterward; no security effect.
ThrowReaderException paths after BImgBuff/quantum_info allocation leak those buffers; leak-only, bounded per file, no exhaustion path distinct from the confirmed Frames finding.

Loop counters 'int i' compared against '(ssize_t) MATLAB_HDR.SizeY' would overflow signed int for SizeY > INT_MAX, but reaching that point requires a multi-gigabyte SetImageExtent to succeed first, which fails the resource-limit check at lines 265-267.

verdict.summary: No reachable memory-safety, bounds, injection, or authz defect in the given code. The dynamic packet array growth is correctly guarded on every path by 'if (alloced <= i) { alloced *= 2; all = xrealloc(all, alloced * sizeof(*all)); }' with the exactly-at-limit case caught by '<='; the success path is fail-closed via 'rc = (digp && (p == pend) && expect == 0) ? 0 : -1;' and 'if (xx) break;'. Residual issues: a bounded one-object leak of 'selfsig' on early-break paths, and behaviors whose safety depends on code outside the given snippet (decodePkt length bounds, pgpDigParamsFree returning NULL, xmalloc non-NULL).

assumptions: decodePkt(p, (pend - p), pkt) is assumed to reject packets whose head/body/blen exceed the remaining 'pend - p' bytes; this bound is enforced inside the unseen helper, not in the given code.

pgpDigParamsFree(selfsig) is assumed to return NULL and the result re-assignment is the rpm 'x = Free(x)' idiom; if it returned non-NULL, 'selfsig ? selfsig : digp' on the next iteration would be a UAF.
xmalloc/xrealloc are assumed to abort on failure (rpm convention), so NULL 'all' and allocation-failure paths are not treated as attacker-triggerable.
pgpVerifySelf(digp, selfsig, all, i) is assumed to index only the initialized entries all[0..i]; its bounds are not visible in the given code.
Security effect of a bare (self-unsigned) key blob returning rc=0 depends on caller policy and pkttype usage, which are outside this code.
limitations: Memory leak: 'selfsig' is allocated via 'selfsig = pgpDigParamsNew(pkt->tag);' and freed only after pgpVerifySelf; the 'if (pgpPrtPkt(pkt, selfsig ? selfsig : digp)) break;' and 'if (selfsig->sigtype != PGPSIGTYPE_SUBKEY_BINDING) break;' paths exit without freeing it. Bounded to at most one small object per call with the loop terminating at the break, so there is no attacker-amplifiable exhaustion path; not counted as a vulnerability.

Integer overflow of 'alloced *= 2' requires more than 2^30 successfully decoded packets (gigabytes of input); the same attacker cost bounds practical exploitation to a degradation/abort, so it is not treated as a security vulnerability here.
Pointer advance 'p += (pkt->body - pkt->head) + pkt->blen;' can overshoot or fail to advance only if decodePkt accepts zero-length or oversized packets; unverifiable within the given code.

A primary key whose blob contains no self-signature can still yield rc=0 (verification only occurs in the selfsig path); whether that constitutes missing signature verification (CWE-347) depends on the caller's pkttype and use of the result, which are outside this code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability found. The function is a kernel driver-internal constructor: no statement in the given code parses or consumes external/trust-boundary data. The observable defects (unchecked vzalloc/kstrdup return values, a leak of e->name and e->encoder_buf on the !ctx path where only kfree(e) runs, and cpu_to_be16 truncation of es_pid) all require allocation failure or a caller-supplied out-of-contract argument that this code's in-kernel callers, which pass fixed constants, cannot produce. Allocation-failure-only NULL dereference and a one-shot init-time leak are excluded per the trigger rules.

assumptions: args is supplied by in-kernel vidtv driver code with hardcoded constants (name string, es_pid, src_buf from the internal mux); no line in the given code routes network, file, or user data into args.
vidtv_s302m_encoder_init is not an EXPORT_SYMBOL public API; its callers are sibling init code within the same driver, so its parameters are not treated as untrusted external input.
e->name = kstrdup(args.name, GFP_KERNEL) and e->encoder_buf = vzalloc(...) are dereferenced only in vidtv_s302m_encode/destroy, which are outside the given code.
limitations: Unchecked vzalloc (line 14): e->encoder_buf can be NULL while e->encoder_buf_sz is set to VIDTV_S302M_BUF_SZ; downstream encode would NULL-deref, but only under allocation failure an attacker cannot induce, and the deref site is not in this code.
Unchecked kstrdup (line 12): e->name can be NULL under allocation failure; deref sites are outside this code.

Memory leak (lines 24-28): if kzalloc of ctx fails, kfree(e) frees only the struct, leaking e->name (kstrdup) and e->encoder_buf (vzalloc); trigger is allocation-failure-only, one-shot at init, with no attacker-driven exhaustion path.
cpu_to_be16(args.es_pid) (line 37) silently truncates es_pid values above 0xFFFF; no caller in this code produces such a value.

The args.head walk (while (args.head->next)) has no cycle detection or bound; a cyclic or corrupt caller list would cause an unbounded loop or wild deref, but every node this code creates terminates with e->next = NULL, so its own construction cannot produce the trigger.
src_buf_sz is stored without validation against the actual extent of src_buf; the consuming read sink lies in vidtv_s302m_encode, which is not part of the given code.

verdict.summary: The BootstrapMethods attribute decoder reads a 2-byte count at buffer[6] via R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) without ever checking sz >= 8. sz is attacker-controlled (class-file attribute length), so a truncated attribute with sz <= 7 causes a 1-2 byte out-of-bounds read; the only bounds check in the function (if (offset >= sz) break;) is inside the loop and executes after this read.

evidence.reason: offset is advanced to 6 and R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) dereferences buffer[6..7] unconditionally inside 'if (attr)'. No statement in the function compares sz (or offset) against the 8 bytes this header+count requires before the read; the sole check 'if (offset >= sz) { break; }' appears later inside the for-loop and cannot guard this read. Trigger: a crafted class file whose BootstrapMethods attribute is passed with sz = 0..7 (e.g. sz = 6, a header-only attribute), yielding a 1-2 byte out-of-bounds read (crash/info-leak) at the exact boundary sz = 7 / in-bounds at sz = 8.

assumptions: r_bin_java_default_attr_new(bin, buffer, sz, buf_offset) is assumed to return non-NULL for small sz; nothing in the given code shows it rejects sz < 8, and only 'if (attr)' gates the faulty read.

r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new(buffer + offset, sz - offset, ...) is assumed to validate its size argument and to set bsm->size to bytes consumed <= sz - offset; this is not quotable in the given code, so 'offset += bsm->size' (possible ut64 wrap or offset > sz, and inflated attr->size = offset) is unverified here and not counted as a confirmed defect of this snippet.
Callers of this R_API decoder are assumed to pass sz derived from the attacker-controlled attribute length in the class file, so small sz values are reachable at this trust-boundary intake point.
limitations: If bsm->size can be 0, the loop re-parses the same bytes up to num_bootstrap_methods (max 65535) times, appending up to 65535 objects — bounded, mild resource consumption (CWE-400-like), not an unbounded loop.

The silent 'bsm == NULL' TODO branch skips malformed entries and continues parsing; robustness issue only, with no memory-safety effect since the loop-top guard re-validates offset before the next buffer access.

verdict.summary: The frame index is used to dereference gif->frames[frame] before any range check exists, and the only range check uses '>' instead of '>=', so frame == frame_count_partial (or any large value on the first statement) performs an out-of-bounds/uninitialized read of the frame table at an attacker-chosen index. Separately, the LZW-decoded colour byte (0-255) and background_index are used to index colour_table without any bound against colour_table_size, so entries past the initialized extent of the table (uninitialized memory, or out of bounds if the table is sized to colour_table_size) are written into the output bitmap.

evidence.reason: Improper validation of array index (CWE-129): gif->frames[frame].display is dereferenced at line 19 BEFORE the only range check, which appears at line 24 and is off-by-one — 'frame > gif->frame_count_partial' accepts the exactly-at-limit value frame == frame_count_partial, whose frames[] slot is beyond the initialized frame set. A caller of this decoder entry point passing frame == frame_count_partial (or any value, for the line-19 access) reaches the out-of-bounds/uninitialized frame-struct read; the same unchecked index is reused at lines 35, 274-276, 297 and 315-321.

Use of uninitialized value (CWE-908): colour is an attacker-controlled decoded byte in 0..255, but the colour table's initialized extent is colour_table_size (2..256, set at line 100 and filled only while 'index < colour_table_size' at line 117). There is no 'colour < colour_table_size' check anywhere, so a GIF with a 2-entry local colour table and LZW data emitting e.g. colour=200 reads a never-written table entry and copies it into the output bitmap (information leak of uninitialized memory, or out-of-bounds read if the table is allocated to colour_table_size entries). The same unbounded pattern appears at line 306 with gif->background_index.

Origin of the tainted extent: colour_table_size is derived from attacker-controlled flags (2 to 256) and the fill loop initializes exactly colour_table_size entries, yet nothing constrains the later index 'colour' (0-255) to this extent — this is the missing-check site for the CWE-908 finding anchored at the line-277 sink.

assumptions: gif->frames allocation capacity and initialization are performed by external gif_initialise code not shown; if the frames array is grown to a larger capacity, frame == frame_count_partial yields an uninitialized-struct read rather than a hard out-of-bounds read — either way the check-after-use at line 19 and the off-by-one at line 24 remain defects in this code.

lzw_decode_init/lzw_decode are assumed to keep stack_pos within [stack_base, stack_end]; this invariant is not quotable in the given code, so burst_bytes = (stack_pos - stack_base) at line 266 cannot be verified here.
gif_interlaced_line(height, y) is assumed to return a value < height; not quotable in the given code, so the interlaced decode_y bound relies on it.
The bitmap buffer from bitmap_get_buffer is assumed to hold gif->width * gif->height ints; the offset/width/height guard at lines 92-93 is quoted and verified, but the buffer size itself is external.

colour_table (local_colour_table/global_colour_table) array widths are not declared in the given code; if they are fixed 256-entry arrays the line-277 defect is an uninitialized read, if sized to colour_table_size it is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
limitations: Recursion at line 228 (gif_internal_decode_frame(gif, last_undisposed_frame, false)) has depth linear in the attacker-controlled frame count; a GIF with many GIF_FRAME_RESTORE frames can drive stack exhaustion (CWE-400) — a secondary denial-of-service risk, not counted in the CWE list.
memset with an int fill value at lines 305-307 writes only the low byte of the colour; this is a colour-correctness bug with no memory-safety effect.
The early return at lines 43-44 was verified to occur BEFORE gif->buffer_position is modified (lines 48-49), so it does not corrupt parser state.

verdict.summary: readconf_main() appends node/euid suffixes to a configuration file name with unbounded sprintf calls at the end of the filename string inside the fixed-size global big_buffer. suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename) leaves no guaranteed room: string_nextinlist can fill big_buffer up to exactly big_buffer_size bytes, and the sprintf (".%ld.%.256s" etc.) then writes up to ~282 bytes with no length check anywhere in the loop, producing an out-of-bounds write for any list entry whose length is within ~282 bytes of big_buffer_size.

evidence.snippet: sprintf(CS suffix, ".%ld.%.256s", (long int)original_euid, uts.nodename);
evidence.reason: Unbounded append sink: sprintf writes "." + %ld + "." + up to 256 bytes of the externally obtained uts.nodename at suffix, which points at the end of filename inside the fixed-size big_buffer. No statement in the loop compares Ustrlen(filename) or the suffix length against big_buffer_size, so a filename occupying big_buffer_size - 282 or more bytes (copyable by string_nextinlist, which is bounded only by big_buffer_size) causes an out-of-bounds write past big_buffer. Identical unguarded appends exist at lines 30 and 41.

evidence.snippet: uschar *suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename);
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty pointer: suffix is computed as the end of the untrusted filename string copied into big_buffer by string_nextinlist at line 10; the code never reserves room for the suffix that the subsequent sprintf calls append, so every sprintf target can lie at or past the end of big_buffer.

assumptions: config_main_filelist is a global consumed here whose provenance is not constrained by this code; the code's own comment about files 'specified on the command line' (config_changed) indicates the file list can be supplied/replaced by a caller, which is the mechanism by which an overlong list entry can reach the sprintf.
big_buffer and big_buffer_size are globals declared outside this excerpt; big_buffer is a fixed-size buffer of big_buffer_size bytes.
The overflow sinks are compiled only when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID are defined.
uts.nodename is in practice kernel-limited (typically 64 bytes), but the only bound present in this code is the %.256s format field.
limitations: long int n = Ustrtol(s, &end, 0) uses the result of expand_string(host_number_string) without the NULL check that all sibling expand_string calls perform; an expansion failure would NULL-deref. Dismissed as not attacker-reachable because the config file is guarded here by the quoted fstat owner/mode check (root-owned, not group/world-writable), and the only bypass (config_changed, command-line-specified config) is the path where privileges were already dropped.

The localhost_number validation checks only the upper bound (if (n > LOCALHOST_MAX)) and accepts negative values; same trusted-config reasoning as above, and host_number = n has no memory-safety effect within this code.

The fstat ownership/mode check is intentionally skipped when config_changed (command-line-specified config) because privilege was given away at start; a group-writable file owned by root group is accepted by design per the code's comments.

'filename is uninitialized' and 's+10 out of range' candidates were disproven: the while condition assigns filename before any use, and a 10-byte Ustrncmp match guarantees s+10 is at worst the terminating NUL.

verdict.summary: This Linux set_fflags helper from archive_write_disk contains no attacker-reachable defect within the given code. The potential uninitialized read of oldflags is guarded by the on-path check 'if (ioctl(myfd, ..., &oldflags) < 0) goto fail;' placed before every use; the single close is correctly conditioned on the original 'fd' parameter ('if (fd < 0) close(myfd);'), preventing double-close of caller descriptors; the error message is a fixed literal with kernel-set errno on every reaching path. Remaining observations (unsigned-long-to-int truncation of set/clear at 'newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;', fail-open ARCHIVE_OK after open failure, and the absence of O_NOFOLLOW at 'open(name, O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK | O_BINARY | O_CLOEXEC)') are either unreachable from values this module itself produces or are degradation with no security effect, and none is provably attacker-triggerable from the given code alone.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start() never checks fread() return values. If the attacker-supplied input file ends before an SOS (0xffda) marker, every fread at line 13/17 returns 0 at EOF and leaves data[] unchanged, so tag is recomputed to the same non-0xffda value on every iteration and the do/while at line 40 has no reachable exit. A file consisting of just 'FF D8' (or any file truncated after SOI) drives the decoder into an infinite 100%-CPU loop — an attacker-reachable denial of service (uncontrolled resource consumption).

evidence.reason: Both freads that update data[] inside the loop ignore their return values; when the stream is at EOF they write nothing, so tag (recomputed from stale data[0..1], e.g. 0xffd8 left from the SOI read at line 10) never changes. The only in-loop guard, 'if (tag <= 0xff00) return 0;', passes the stale tag 0xffd8, so the loop state is identical each iteration and the only exit condition, tag == 0xffda, is unreachable. Trigger: a truncated attacker-supplied file, minimally the two bytes FF D8.

No check of any fread return value exists anywhere in the function to break the loop.

verdict.summary: In block_insert(), the visual-block append path for a short line assigns count = spaces (line 51) BEFORE the negativity clamp `if (spaces < 0) spaces = 0;` (lines 60-61). The buffer is undersized by |count| bytes, and the subsequent mch_memmove of the inserted text and STRMOVE of the line tail write up to |count|+1 bytes past the end of the heap allocation.

The alloc() size expression then adds the negative `count` to size_t arithmetic, wrapping the size down by |count| bytes. Boundary trigger: spaces == -1 yields allocation L + s_len while STRMOVE(newp + offset, oldp) subsequently writes the terminating NUL at newp[L + s_len] — a one-byte heap out-of-bounds write; more negative values overflow the buffer by the s-copy itself.

Taint origin: on the is_short append path, spaces is computed from operator/buffer virtual columns and can be negative (the code's own comment at line 60 confirms reachability 'when the cursor was moved'), and `count = spaces;` captures that negative value before any clamp exists — no later statement in the function clamps count.

ml_get(lnum) returns a NUL-terminated line buffer; s is NUL-terminated so STRLEN(s) is the exact copy length.
alloc() takes the size as size_t; the negative int count undergoes unsigned conversion/wrap in the size expression, reducing the requested size.
colnr_T is a signed integer type wide enough that (oap->end_vcol - bdp->end_vcol) + 1 can represent small negative values without wrapping.
limitations: Stale `count` (and `spaces` in the is_MAX case) carried across loop iterations can cause over-allocation only; count is never added to offset when spaces == 0 (`if (spaces > 0) offset += count;`), so it is not a memory-safety defect.
The `if (newp == NULL) continue;` path only degrades the operation (line skipped) under allocation failure, which attacker input cannot induce.

verdict.summary: In the Mach-O kernelcache bin loader, attacker-controlled malformed input reaches two error paths that never release acquired resources: the early return when MACH0_(new_buf) fails returns without releasing the RBuffer reference taken by r_buf_ref, and every beach cleanup path leaks the rebase_info allocated by r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0. Each failed load of an attacker-crafted file permanently pins a file-size-proportional buffer plus the rebase structure, so a process that loads many untrusted files (the normal use of r2 as an analysis library) accumulates memory without bound — memory exhaustion denial of service.

evidence.reason: Missing release of the fbuf reference on an attacker-reachable error path. The reference is acquired at line 2 (RBuffer *fbuf = r_buf_ref (buf);) and the only release sites are the success-path ownership transfer (obj->cache_buf = fbuf;) and the beach label (r_buf_free (fbuf);). This return bypasses beach, so any file whose bytes fail MACH0_(new_buf) parsing leaks a reference to the entire file buffer. The fix (r_buf_free before return) does not exist anywhere in this code.

evidence.snippet: RBuffer *fbuf = r_buf_ref (buf);
evidence.reason: Origin of the leaked reference: buf holds the full attacker-supplied file content crossing the trust boundary, so the unreleased reference pins memory proportional to the attacker's file size.

The beach cleanup frees fbuf and main_mach0 but never frees rebase_info, allocated at line 10 (RRebaseInfo *rebase_info = r_rebase_info_new_from_mach0 (fbuf, main_mach0);). Every goto beach path (lines 15, 21, 31, 41) is reachable with attacker-controlled data (e.g., a file that parses as Mach-O but yields no prelink range) and leaks rebase_info; the only other use is the success-path assignment, so no release exists on any error path.

assumptions: r_buf_ref acquires a reference this function is responsible for releasing, inferred from the beach cleanup (r_buf_free (fbuf);) and the success-path transfer (obj->cache_buf = fbuf;) — both quoted in evidence.

R_FREE frees and sets the pointer to NULL (standard r2 macro); if it did not null the pointer, the beach 'if (obj)' would touch freed memory, but with standard R_FREE semantics obj is provably NULL at beach (every goto site R_FREEs it first).

prelink_range->range.offset and range.size are attacker-controlled values passed to r_cf_value_dict_parse (lines 26–27) with no bounds validation in this code; whether that parser bounds-checks its reads against the RBuffer cannot be verified from the given code, so no out-of-bounds-read finding is claimed here.

pending_bin_files is a static global checked and created without any lock (lines 35–36); a TOCTOU exists if load_buffer is ever invoked concurrently, but no statement in this code demonstrates a concurrent caller.
limitations: The prelink_info subtree leak via R_FREE (plain free() instead of the recursive RCFValueDict destructor) at line 40 is reachable only when r_list_new() fails — an allocation failure the attacker cannot induce; recorded, not counted.
The 'if (obj) { obj->cache_buf = NULL; }' at beach is dead code (obj is always NULL there) with no security effect.

No memory-corruption defect exists within this function: all frees occur exactly once per path, pointer copies (pa2va_exec/pa2va_data) are taken before R_FREE (prelink_range), and no arithmetic is performed on attacker lengths here.

The leaks are per-invocation; unbounded accumulation to exhaustion (CWE-400) requires a host application loading many untrusted files in one process, which is the standard deployment of r2 as an analysis library but is outside this code.

verdict.summary: set_fflags_platform re-resolves the attacker-influenced archive entry pathname by calling open(name, ...) and then applies a read-modify-write of the file's inode flags (FS_IOC_GETFLAGS -> FS_IOC_SETFLAGS) on the resulting fd. The only path guard present, O_NOFOLLOW, protects solely against a symlink in the final path component; nothing in this code validates intermediate components or ties the opened fd to the file the caller just created. A local attacker racing the extraction (or an archive planting a symlinked intermediate component) can redirect the flag set/clear operation onto an arbitrary file accessible to the extractor, so the entry's requested flags (including append/immutable/journal) can be applied to or removed from an attacker-chosen target, and that target's current flags are read into the operation.

evidence.reason: This is the trust-boundary sink: the attacker-influenced entry pathname `name` (line 1) is re-resolved here by open() with only O_NOFOLLOW, which per its semantics rejects a symlink solely at the final component. Intermediate components are followed, and there is no verification that the resolved file is the one the caller just created; the subsequent FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/FS_IOC_SETFLAGS read-modify-write (lines 52-69) is therefore applied to whatever the path points to at open time. Trigger: untrusted archive entry with fflags extracted into a directory an attacker can race (or with a planted intermediate symlink), caller passes fd = -1 (explicitly supported by `if (myfd < 0)`), so `open(name, ...)` resolves to the attacker's chosen file and its flags are read, modified by (oldflags & ~clear) | set, and written back. No component-wise check, fd-identity check, or fd-required check exists anywhere in this code (searched line by line in STEP 5).

evidence.snippet: newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;
evidence.reason: The privileged write value is computed from the flags read off the race-redirected file (oldflags, line 52-58) combined with attacker-influenced set/clear, and this value is passed to FS_IOC_SETFLAGS (lines 63-69) on the fd obtained from the unvalidated pathname open — the use site of the race, completing the attacker-chosen flag set/clear primitive.

assumptions: The helper __archive_ensure_cloexec_flag() is external to this code; its behavior when passed myfd == -1 (possible because it is called at line 40 before the `if (myfd < 0)` check at line 42) cannot be verified here and is assumed to fail harmlessly on EBADF.
The archive_set_error / archive machinery referenced via `a` is assumed to be a valid caller-owned struct; this code only writes an error message through it.
errno is assumed to still hold the failing syscall's value at the `fail:` label; no intervening call in this code resets it.
limitations: Fail-open error handling: when open() fails (line 42-43) the function returns ARCHIVE_OK, silently reporting success while applying no flags; impact is limited to a metadata downgrade of the extracted entry itself, not memory safety or authz.

Width truncation: `newflags = (oldflags & ~clear) | set;` computes in unsigned long and truncates into int newflags, so any set bit at or above bit 32 is silently dropped; the ioctl itself copies exactly sizeof(int) into a genuine int, so this is a correctness defect with no memory-safety consequence.

Candidates disproven by quoted on-path guards: uninitialized `oldflags` (guarded by `if (ioctl(... FS_IOC_GETFLAGS, &oldflags) < 0) goto fail;` before every use) and fd leak/double-close (close guarded by `if (fd < 0)`, which exactly matches the branch that opened myfd).

No attacker-reachable memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, or injection defect exists in this code.

vim_free accepts NULL (standard Vim allocator contract); vim_free(p) with p == NULL after a short-circuited 'p != NULL' check is safe.

regmatch_T *rmp is built by internal Vim callers with a compiled regexp program; this function is an internal helper, not an exported/plugin API entry point, so rmp's validity is caller state, not trust-boundary data.

The compiled pattern inside rmp is supplied by the caller/user command line, not parsed from untrusted data by this function; any regexp resource-exhaustion concern belongs to the pattern's construction site.

Catastrophic backtracking in vim_regexec (CWE-400) is bounded by neither this code nor the pattern's origin; the pattern is compiled elsewhere from user-supplied expressions, so any ReDoS finding would localize to the pattern intake, not here.

The 2-byte header read at offset 6 is protected by 'if (offset + 8 > sz)' (requiring sz >= 14, strictly stronger than the sz >= 8 actually needed), and every loop-iteration call to r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new is preceded by 'if (offset >= sz) { break; }', which prevents both an out-of-bounds pointer 'buffer + offset' and an underflow of 'sz - offset' on every path. r_bin_java_bootstrap_method_new (external, not shown) is assumed to bound bsm->size by the size argument 'sz - offset' it receives; if it returns bsm->size > sz - offset, any over-read and any attr->size > sz consequence originate in that callee, not in the given code.

If the callee fails (bsm == NULL) repeatedly, offset does not advance and the loop can call the callee up to num_bootstrap_methods times with identical arguments; bounded CPU waste only.

verdict.summary: ga_concat_shorten_esc's inner repetition-counting loop advances s by clen (the byte length of the FIRST character at p) while its guard only verifies *s != NUL and codepoint equality at the current position. When a byte sequence at s decodes to the same code point c but is shorter than clen (possible with invalid/truncated multi-byte sequences in the attacker-controlled string), s += clen steps over the NUL terminator, and the loop then dereferences out-of-bounds heap memory; p = s - 1 propagates the overshoot into the outer loop, which keeps reading and escaping adjacent heap bytes into the output garray (information disclosure) or crashes (DoS). Minimal trigger: str = bytes C2 80 80 (c=U+0080, clen=2, lone 0x80 decodes to 0x80, stride 2 skips the NUL).

evidence.reason: The guard '*s != NUL' is evaluated at the pre-advance position only, but the stride is clen — the byte length of the character at p, not the character at s. If the sequence at s decodes to the same code point c in fewer than clen bytes (e.g., str = "\xC2\x80\x80": c=U+0080, clen=2, and the lone trailing byte 0x80 decodes to 0x80 == c), s += clen skips the NUL terminator and the next '*s != NUL' / mb_ptr2char(s) reads out of bounds; p = s - 1 (line 35) then carries the pointer past the end into the outer loop, which escapes OOB heap bytes into the output.

evidence.snippet:
c = mb_cptr2char_adv(&s);
	clen = s - p;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted stride: clen is the byte length of the character at p only. It is reused as a fixed stride for every subsequent match in the inner loop even though the loop's condition compares code points (mb_ptr2char(s) == c), which for invalid byte sequences can match across characters of different byte lengths — the mismatch that causes the pointer to skip the terminator.

assumptions: Behavior of the external Vim mbyte helpers is assumed per the standard implementation: mb_cptr2char_adv yields the code point and safe byte length of the character at p (invalid/truncated lead bytes yield length 1 and their own byte value), and mb_ptr2char of a lone invalid byte (0x80-0xBF) yields that byte's own value. If mb_ptr2char instead validated lengths, the trigger would need a different mismatching pair, but no length check exists in the given code either way.
ga_concat / ga_concat_esc are assumed to grow the garray appropriately for the bytes appended; their bounds management is external to this code.

str is a NUL-terminated byte string whose contents (including invalid multi-byte sequences) are attacker-influenced text from files, registers, or messages; this function is the intake point performing the decoding, so no upstream encoding validation can be assumed.
limitations: Integer overflow of same_len (++same_len, int) would require over 2^31 consecutive equal characters — not reachable within Vim's practical string-size limits; not counted as a vulnerability.
vim_snprintf((char *)buf, NUMBUFLEN, "%d", same_len) is bounded by the explicit NUMBUFLEN size argument (256 bytes vs at most 11 characters); no defect.

The (int)(end-p) cast at line 37 truncates only for buffers larger than 2 GiB, which is not a realistic SDP print buffer; also, if p already exceeded end due to the confirmed fmt-list overflow, this length is negative, but that is a downstream symptom of the primary finding, not a separate defect.

Once p exceeds end in the fmt loop, the CRLF writes at lines 32-33 and subsequent helper calls also operate out of bounds; these are consequences of the single confirmed root cause, not independent findings.

verdict.summary: In the error-cleanup path of _gdContributionsAlloc, the loop index u is declared 'unsigned int' and the loop condition 'while (u >= 0)' is therefore vacuously true. After freeing the last valid row (u == 0), 'u--' wraps to UINT_MAX and the loop continues, reading res->ContribRow[UINT_MAX].Weights far out of bounds and passing that garbage pointer to gdFree (invalid free), then decrementing forever (infinite loop). Any failure of the per-row allocation — attacker-triggerable via dimension-derived parameters such as windows_size = 0x20000000 (detected overflow sets overflow_error at u == 0) or a ~4 GB windows_size * 8 allocation that fails — reaches this path, giving an attacker-reachable out-of-bounds read, invalid free, and hang (DoS).

evidence.reason: u is declared 'unsigned int u = 0;' so 'u >= 0' is always true; when the cleanup loop reaches u == 0, 'u--' wraps to UINT_MAX and the loop reads res->ContribRow[UINT_MAX].Weights out of bounds and calls gdFree on the resulting garbage pointer, never terminating. Triggered whenever line 28's error condition holds on any iteration (e.g., windows_size = 0x20000000 makes overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)) true at u == 0, or a ~4 GB windows_size * 8 gdMalloc fails), i.e., by attacker-influenced dimension-derived parameters with no bound enforceable from this code.

evidence.reason: Origin of the wrapped value: the loop/cleanup index u is an unsigned int, so the cleanup loop's termination test 'u >= 0' can never be false and the pre-decrement 'u--' past zero wraps to UINT_MAX; a signed counter or an explicit sentinel comparison is absent from the code, confirming the CWE-190 wraparound is the root cause.

assumptions: overflow2(a, b) correctly reports whether a*b overflows the width used by the multiplication (implementation not shown in the given code); the guards 'if (overflow2(line_length, sizeof(ContributionType)))' and 'if (overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double)))' are treated as correct and were verified to lie on every path to their respective gdMalloc sizing sinks.

sizeof(double) == 8 and unsigned int is 32 bits, so windows_size = 0x20000000 makes windows_size * sizeof(double) wrap 32 bits and windows_size = 0x1FFFFFFF yields a ~4 GB non-wrapping allocation request.
gdMalloc/gdFree behave like malloc/free (NULL on failure, gdFree frees heap pointers).
line_length and windows_size are caller-supplied and derive from image/caller dimensions (trust-boundary data); no constraint on them is quotable inside this code.
The struct definitions LineContribType/ContributionType are not shown; only the pointer field Weights is relied upon.
limitations: Memory leak (CWE-401, not a listed CWE): on the error path, res->ContribRow (allocated at line 17) and res (allocated at line 7) are not freed before 'return NULL' at line 34. No uninitialized read was found: at line 28, 'overflow_error == 1 ||' short-circuits before reading res->ContribRow[u].Weights, and the pointer is freshly assigned on the non-overflow path (line 26).

The out-of-bounds read's typical result is a segmentation fault or hang (denial of service); exploitation beyond DoS (e.g., turning the invalid free into heap corruption) would depend on heap layout not determinable from this code.

verdict.summary: In FSCTL_CREATE_OR_GET_OBJECT_ID, a 64-byte response buffer is allocated with talloc_array (which does not zero memory) but only 48 bytes (offsets 0-47) are initialized by push_file_id_16/memcpy/push_file_id_16, while *out_len is set to any client-chosen value up to 64.
