verdict.summary: lprn_is_black indexes lprn->ImageBuf using (y0 + y) * bpl + bx * lprn->nBw where y0 = (r + h - bh) % maxY, with no bounds validation anywhere in the function. Because C's % truncates toward zero, any call with r + h < bh yields a negative y0 (e.g. r=0,h=0,bh=8 gives y0=-8), producing an index before ImageBuf; misaligned r/h or BlockLine % nBh != 0 lets y0 + bh exceed maxY, and bx * nBw + nBw is never checked against bpl; signed overflow in r+h-bh and in the index product adds further wraparound. The subsequent p[x] reads are out-of-bounds, giving an attacker-reachable crash and value-influenced 'is black' output. The only conditionals present (y < bh, x < lprn->nBw, p[x] != 0) never bound the index, so the defect is unguarded in this code.

evidence.reason: Unguarded array-index sink: the ImageBuf offset (y0+y)*bpl + bx*nBw is computed from unvalidated inputs and dereferenced via p[x]. y0 can be negative (C remainder of a negative dividend, e.g. r=0,h=0,bh=8,maxY=32 gives y0=-8), y0+bh can exceed maxY when r+h is not aligned to nBh, bx*nBw+nBw is unchecked against bpl, and the int arithmetic can overflow; no statement in the function bounds the index, so p[x] reads out of bounds.

evidence.snippet: lprn_is_black(gx_device_printer * pdev, int r, int h, int bx)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: the signed int parameters r, h and bx enter at this entry point with no validation and flow directly into the ImageBuf index computation at line 13; as the intake point for these values, this function cannot rely on caller-side validation that is not present in the code.

assumptions: The allocation size of lprn->ImageBuf and any constraints (nBh > 0, BlockLine >= nBh, BlockLine % nBh == 0, r+h aligned to nBh, 0 <= bx < bpl/nBw) are enforced, if at all, in code outside this function (e.g., put_params or the caller); per guard-anchoring these are not relied upon because they cannot be quoted here.
gdev_mem_bytes_per_scan_line(pdev) is treated as unvalidated external data; its return-value bounds are not visible in this code.
pdev is assumed non-NULL and to actually point at a gx_device_lprn; this cannot be verified from the given code.
limitations: Division-by-zero crashes are possible at line 9 if nBh == 0 and at line 11 if maxY == 0 (BlockLine < nBh or BlockLine == 0); reachability depends on device-parameter validation outside this code, and CWE-369 is not in the permitted CWE list, so this is recorded as a secondary crash-only observation rather than the primary finding.
Signed-overflow hazards in r + h - bh and in (y0+y)*bpl + bx*nBw are folded into the primary out-of-bounds-read finding rather than reported separately.
The sink is read-only: impact is denial of service plus at most a weak one-bit-per-block disclosure (whether out-of-bounds bytes are nonzero) via the return value; there is no write primitive.
If bpl is 0 (empty scan line), every p[x] access is out of bounds; this boundary case is subsumed by the primary finding.

verdict.summary: esp6_output_head performs three tail-append strategies (in-place, page-frag, COW), and every sink is guarded by an in-code, boundary-correct check: the in-place pskb_put is guarded by 'if (tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb))' (exact-equality edge safe), the page-frag descriptor store by 'skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' (strict <, one-past-limit excluded) plus a checked 'skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, ...)' with allocsize = ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) >= tailen, and the COW path by 'nfrags = skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer); if (nfrags < 0) goto out;'. The stale esp->esph after COW is repaired via the saved esph_offset, and the shared x->xfrag page-frag is protected by spin_lock_bh/spin_unlock_bh on every access. No attacker-controlled value crosses a trust boundary into this function's parameters (esp fields and skb metadata are kernel-internal), and no guard was found to be bypassable at boundary values (0, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit).

assumptions: skb_tailroom(skb) returns 0 for non-linear skbs and skb->end - skb->tail otherwise, so 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' is an exact bound for the subsequent pskb_put/skb_put; this is kernel helper semantics outside the given code.

skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) returning >= 0 guarantees tailen bytes of tailroom in *trailer; this contract is enforced outside the given code but its failure IS checked in-code via 'if (nfrags < 0) goto out;'.

skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC) returning true guarantees allocsize bytes are available at pfrag->offset within the page; the in-code check 'if (unlikely(!skb_page_frag_refill(...))) { ...; goto cow; }' diverts on failure.

esp_output_fill_trailer(tail, tfclen, plen, proto) writes at most tfclen + 2 bytes, and the caller-maintained invariant esp->tailen >= tfclen + 2 holds (esp is kernel-internal state, not trust-boundary data).

esp6_output_encap(x, skb, esp) writes an encapsulation header into headroom and does not modify esp->tailen, so the local 'int tailen = esp->tailen;' read before the encap call is not stale for tail purposes; the helper is outside the given code.

esp->tailen is produced by same-file internal computation from bounded SA/packet parameters and cannot approach INT_MAX, so 'int tailen = esp->tailen;' (unsigned to signed) cannot yield a negative tailen in practice; no in-code statement bounds this, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than a quoted guard.
limitations: C1 (pskb_put overflow via in-place path): trigger requires tailen > skb_tailroom(skb) on that branch; contradicted in-code by 'if (tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb))' including the exactly-at-limit edge — not a vulnerability.
C2 (frags[] OOB via __skb_fill_page_desc): trigger requires nr_frags == MAX_SKB_FRAGS; contradicted in-code by the strict 'nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' check — not a vulnerability.
C4 (use of trailer after failed skb_cow_data): contradicted in-code by 'if (nfrags < 0) goto out;' — not a vulnerability.
C8 (race on x->xfrag): all pfrag->offset and page accesses are enclosed by 'spin_lock_bh(&x->lock)' / 'spin_unlock_bh(&x->lock)' on the only path touching them — not a vulnerability.
C7 (esp6_output_encap writing an encap header into a possibly cloned skb head) is inside a helper not included in the given code and cannot be evaluated here.
Potential use of page_address() on a highmem page in the frag path depends on skb_page_frag_refill allocation flags, which are outside the given code; no trigger constructible from this code alone.

verdict.summary: luaG_runerror is an internal Lua VM error helper. The only memory sink (ci_func(ci)->p->source / getcurrentline(ci) at the source-info step) is guarded by 'if (isLua(ci))' on every path before the use, correctly excluding C frames. The format string passed to luaO_pushvfstring is unvalidated in this code, but this is an internal (luaG_/l_noret) function, not a public/exported API; attacker-influenced values can only reach it as varargs (formatted arguments), never as the format string itself, so the CWE-134 candidate is unreachable. No injection, bounds, lifetime, crypto, or authz sink exists in this snippet.

assumptions: fmt is assumed to be supplied only as string literals by internal VM callers; call sites are not part of the given code and no enforcing statement is quotable here.
luaO_pushvfstring is assumed to be Lua's own internal formatter (no C printf semantics, no %n); its implementation is outside the given snippet.
isLua/ci_func/getcurrentline/luaG_addinfo/luaG_errormsg/luaC_checkGC are assumed to have their documented Lua core semantics, implemented outside this snippet.
L->ci is assumed to always reference a live CallInfo while the VM is running (VM invariant); no input this code receives can make it NULL.
limitations: A format-string surface exists at 'luaO_pushvfstring(L, fmt, argp)': if any internal caller ever passed attacker-influenced text as fmt, or supplied a directive count exceeding the varargs, undefined va_arg reads or message injection would result. Dismissed as unreachable because the function is internal and this code provides no path to bind attacker data to fmt.
luaC_checkGC(L) may run __gc finalizers before the error message is created (re-entrancy during an error path); no security effect is visible within this snippet.
Calling luaG_addinfo with a source produced outside this snippet could truncate to LUA_IDSIZE inside luaG_addinfo; no overflow risk exists in this code itself.

verdict.summary: find_match_text() advances the indices len1 and len2 by MB_CHAR2LEN() of decoded codepoint values and reads rex.line and match_text at those indices without ever validating them against the buffers' NUL terminators or length. When the searched text (or pattern literal) contains an invalid multibyte sequence (e.g. a lone 0x80-0xEF byte, which PTR2CHAR decodes to its own value but which occupies fewer bytes than MB_CHAR2LEN of that value), len2/len1 step past the terminator: PTR2CHAR(rex.line + col + len2) at line 26 (and match_text[len1] at line 12) reads out of bounds past the heap buffer, and the unvalidated col+len2 is exported as the match end (reg_endpos[0].col / reg_endp[0]) for callers to slice the line with. Trigger: search a buffer whose line ends with an invalid byte (arbitrary file content) with a pattern whose literal decodes to the same codepoint, e.g. pattern U+00E0 against a line containing a single 0xE0 byte.

evidence.reason: len2 is advanced by MB_CHAR2LEN(c2) (and initialized at line 11 from MB_CHAR2LEN(regstart)), a length derived from the decoded value, not from the bytes actually present. For an invalid UTF-8 sequence in the searched line (e.g. a lone 0xE0 byte at end of line with pattern U+00E0), the advance overshoots the character's actual byte count and lands past the line's NUL terminator; PTR2CHAR(rex.line + col + len2) then reads out of bounds. No statement in the function bounds col+len2 against the line extent.

Same root cause on the pattern buffer: when match_text contains an invalid multibyte sequence (e.g. a trailing lone 0x80 byte, decoded to 0x80 with MB_CHAR2LEN(0x80) == 2), the loop increment len1 += MB_CHAR2LEN(c1) steps past match_text's NUL terminator, so the very guard match_text[len1] != NUL evaluates an out-of-bounds read past the heap buffer.

The unvalidated col + len2 is exported as the match end. When the multibyte length desync pushes len2 past the line's NUL terminator, reg_endpos[0].col / reg_endp[0] designate a position beyond the buffer, which callers (substitute, search, highlighting) then use to slice or copy the line, propagating the out-of-bounds access.

assumptions: rex.line and match_text are NUL-terminated heap buffers (standard Vim invariant; not enforceable from this code).
PTR2CHAR (utf_ptr2char) does not itself read past a NUL once positioned inside the buffer; the out-of-bounds arises from the index len2/len1 landing past the terminator.
MB_CHAR2LEN(c) for enc_utf8 equals utf_char2len(c), which depends only on the codepoint value, not on the bytes actually present; PTR2CHAR returns the leading byte for invalid sequences.
enc_utf8 is TRUE (default multibyte configuration) and Vim preserves arbitrary/invalid bytes in buffer text and patterns.

skip_to_start(), defined outside the given code, is assumed to keep col within the line; its behavior is not quotable here. The confirmed defects trigger on the very first loop iteration (col == startcol) and do not depend on it.

The caller is assumed to have verified that the decoded char at rex.line+col equals regstart; decoded-value equality does not imply equal byte length, which is exactly why the trigger survives even that check.
limitations: With strictly valid UTF-8 in both the pattern and the searched text, c1 is never NUL inside the loop, so a NUL in rex.line always fails the comparison at line 16, and MB_CHAR2LEN matches the consumed byte count; all reads then stay in bounds. The out-of-bounds condition requires invalid multibyte sequences, which Vim nevertheless permits in buffer contents (opened files) and in patterns.
No direct out-of-bounds write was found in this function; impact is a heap out-of-bounds read (crash / information exposure) plus an out-of-range match-end handed to callers.

A caller-supplied startcol beyond the line length would also cause an immediate out-of-bounds read, but no statement in this code constrains startcol; this was not counted as a separate finding since the confirmed desync trigger works with fully in-range startcol.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled fixed-file index (fd, from the cancel SQE) is bounds-checked against ctx->nr_user_files with a correct 'fd >= ctx->nr_user_files' guard before the io_fixed_file_slot() access; unsigned promotion rejects negative values, '>=' rejects the one-past-limit value, and a NULL slot is rejected with 'if (!cd->file) return -EBADF;'. No unguarded sink exists in this code.

assumptions: ctx->nr_user_files is assumed to be declared unsigned int (kernel io_ring_ctx definition); the rejection of negative fd values relies on the usual arithmetic conversions promoting the int fd to unsigned in the comparison 'fd >= ctx->nr_user_files'. If nr_user_files were signed int, a negative fd would pass the check and be passed to array_index_nospec — but that declaration is not in the given snippet.

The invariant that ctx->file_table.files is allocated with at least nr_user_files entries is established in the io_uring file-registration path, which is outside this snippet; the index bound itself is enforced here by the quoted guard.

array_index_nospec(fd, ctx->nr_user_files) is assumed to clamp its first argument into [0, size); its macro definition is outside the given code, and it is only reached after fd has already been validated in-range.

No concurrent shrink of nr_user_files or mutation of the file table is demonstrable from this snippet (comment notes the uring_lock is dropped); any TOCTOU would require racing kernel-internal registration/unregistration not shown here.
limitations: Candidate 'out-of-bounds fixed-file index' (CWE-129) dismissed: guard 'if (unlikely(fd >= ctx->nr_user_files)) return -EBADF;' is present on the only path to io_fixed_file_slot and rejects fd == nr_user_files (>=) and all negative values (unsigned promotion).
Candidate 'NULL deref of cd->file from sparse/empty registered-file slot' (CWE-476) dismissed: 'if (!cd->file) return -EBADF;' is present before any use.
Candidate 'signedness confusion letting negative fd through' (CWE-194) dismissed: edge tests at fd = -1 and fd = INT_MIN show both fail the unsigned-promoted comparison.
Analysis covers only the given snippet; __io_async_cancel internals were not provided and were not evaluated.

verdict.summary: stl_update_connects_remove_1 validates only the lower bound of facet_num ('facet_num < 0') but never checks it against the size of stl->neighbors_start, so any caller-supplied non-negative index up to INT_MAX is used directly to index the neighbors array, causing an out-of-bounds read and attacker-reachable crash/DoS.

evidence.reason: facet_num, an attacker/caller-controlled 32-bit int, is used as the index into stl->neighbors_start with no upper-bound check anywhere in the function. Passing facet_num >= the number of facets (e.g., exactly one-past-limit or INT_MAX, which both pass the 'facet_num < 0' guard) reads neighbor[] fields past the end of the array — out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by improper validation of the array index (CWE-129).

The only guards on facet_num are 'stl->error' and the lower-bound check 'facet_num < 0'; the required upper-bound check (facet_num < stl->stats.number_of_facets, or the neighbors array capacity) is missing on every path to the indexing sink at lines 10-12. Edge case: facet_num == number_of_facets or INT_MAX passes this guard and reaches the out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: stl->neighbors_start is assumed to be an array sized by the loaded file's facet count; that allocation and its bound are not present in this code, so per the last-line-of-defense rule no upper bound is enforced here.
The stl pointer itself is assumed non-NULL; NULL-stl dereference is out of scope of the given snippet.
If stl->neighbors_start can be NULL while stl->error == 0, the same unguarded line 10 also yields a NULL-based OOB read; this state is not provable from the given code alone.
limitations: The stats decrements (connected_facets_1/2/3_edge) could underflow if the counters are unsigned and the facet was never counted, but this is bookkeeping with no security effect.
The OOB read leaks at most comparison results (neighbor[i] == -1) into counter selection; the primary impact is a crash/DoS via an invalid index, not disclosure.

verdict.summary: This static inline helper performs a single bit-set on the state field of the FUSE inode wrapping the passed VFS inode. It consumes no attacker-influenced data, performs no arithmetic, no copying, no allocation sizing, and no injection-sink operations; the only sink (set_bit on &get_fuse_inode(inode)->state) requires only that callers pass a valid FUSE-owned inode, which this internal helper's kernel callers provide. No trust-boundary validation is missing because no trust boundary is crossed here.

assumptions: get_fuse_inode(inode) is a container_of-style accessor that returns the enclosing struct fuse_inode; its definition is outside the given snippet.
FUSE_I_BAD is a compile-time constant bit index within the state bitmask; its definition is outside the given snippet.

Callers of this static inline helper are internal FUSE kernel code passing VFS inode pointers it obtained from the inode cache; the callers are not visible in the given code and their behavior is treated as outside this snippet's responsibility only because this function is not a trust-boundary intake point (it parses no external data).
limitations: Candidate: NULL dereference of inode (CWE-476) — no NULL check exists in the snippet, but triggering requires an internal caller bug or allocation failure that attacker input cannot induce through this code; dismissed per the allocation-failure rule.

Candidate: type confusion if inode is not a FUSE inode — no runtime type check exists, but nothing in this snippet lets external data select the inode's concrete type; not attacker-reachable through this code.

verdict.summary: io_rw_init_file validates its inputs fail-closed: NULL/mode-incompatible files are rejected via 'if (unlikely(!file || !(file->f_mode & mode))) return -EBADF;', attacker-influenced rw flags are gated by the checked return of kiocb_set_rw_flags ('if (unlikely(ret)) return ret;'), and HIPRI/IOPOLL inconsistencies are rejected with -EINVAL/-EOPNOTSUPP before the completion callback is installed. The only unguarded deref, file->f_op->iopoll, cannot be attacker-driven to NULL because struct file objects always carry a non-NULL f_op from VFS allocation and attacker-controlled fd selection is fully resolved upstream. No memory-safety, injection, or fail-open defect is reachable within this code.

assumptions: req->file is populated upstream by io_uring fd/fixed-file resolution; a failed fd lookup never reaches this function with a stale pointer, and req itself is non-NULL (io_uring core invariant, not enforced in this snippet).
kiocb_set_rw_flags performs the actual whitelist validation of req->rw.flags (SQE-derived); this code enforces only the fail-closed return-value check 'if (unlikely(ret)) return ret;'.
ctx->flags (including IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL) was validated at ring-creation time by io_uring setup code outside this function.
io_file_get_flags, io_file_supports_nowait, iocb_flags, and the completion callbacks behave per their kernel contracts; their internals are outside the given code.
limitations: Candidate C1 (CWE-476, NULL f_op deref at '!file->f_op->iopoll') was dismissed: no f_op NULL check exists in this code, but a struct file with NULL f_op is not constructible by any input channel this code or the io_uring submission path exposes; triggering would require an allocation/VFS state failure that attacker input cannot induce.

req->rw.flags originates from attacker-submitted SQE data, but its parsing and validation occur upstream (io_prep_rw) and in kiocb_set_rw_flags; only the error-propagation check is visible and quoted here. dm_offset = CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->iv_len;
	ret = ccp_set_dm_area(&ctx, dm_offset, aes->iv, 0, aes->iv_len);
evidence.reason: Missing bounds validation of aes->iv_len. The only IV check in the function is `if (!aes->iv)` (line 21), which tests the pointer, not the length. Edge cases: iv_len == CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT * CCP_SB_BYTES gives dm_offset == 0 (exactly at limit, safe); iv_len one past makes dm_offset wrap to 0xFFFFFFFF and ccp_set_dm_area writes iv_len bytes out of bounds of the fixed-size workarea allocated at lines 97-99 (same wrapped offset reused at line 197), an attacker-parameter-driven out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: AES_KEYSIZE_128/192/256 denote 16/24/32-byte keys and CCP_SB_BYTES/CCP_AES_CTX_SB_COUNT are fixed engine constants, so CCP_SB_BYTES - aes->key_len at line 82 stays in range only because of the quoted key_len if-chain at lines 24-27; the key path was verified safe via that quoted guard.

The upstream callers may set aes->iv_len to GCM_AES_IV_SIZE and the generic aead layer may require cryptlen >= authsize, but no such statement exists in the given code; per the analysis rules these are external assumptions and were not relied on when judging this code, which is the consumer of those request fields.
ccp_set_dm_area/ccp_init_data/scatterwalk_ffwd internals are not shown; no internal bounds check can be quoted, so their preconditions are treated as unenforced by this code.
limitations: `final[0] = cpu_to_be64(aes->aad_len * 8);` (line 216) truncates aad_len*8 to 32 bits, but exploiting it requires at least 512 MiB of AAD to pass through ccp_init_data first; not treated as a confirmed finding.
Failures of ccp_init_dm_workarea/ccp_init_data (allocation failures not attacker-induced) merely return an error through the checked `if (ret)` paths and are not vulnerabilities.

The cleanup labels e_dst/e_src/e_aad/e_ctx/e_key were reviewed for double-free/use-after-free; with in_place true only src is freed (`if (ilen > 0 && !in_place)`), and tag/final_wa are each freed once per path, so no lifetime defect was recorded.

verdict.summary: get_complex_object stores the signed 32-bit length from get_st32 into ut32 n1 (and n2) with no validation, then computes malloc(n1 + 1) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. A crafted .pyc with magic > 62061 and a length field of -1 (0xFFFFFFFF) makes n1 + 1 wrap to 0, so malloc(0) succeeds and rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, 0xFFFFFFFF) writes remaining file bytes into a zero-length heap block, overflowing it before the post-use size != n1 check runs. The same defect repeats for n2.

evidence.reason: Sink: n1 is ut32 holding an attacker-controlled st32; when n1 == 0xFFFFFFFF, n1 + 1 wraps to 0 in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic, malloc(0) returns a valid minimal block, and rz_buf_read(buffer, s1, 0xFFFFFFFF) copies remaining file bytes into it, overflowing the heap. The size != n1 check is after the overflowing read, and no sign/range check on n1 precedes the malloc.

Origin of the taint: the attacker controls the file magic, selecting the get_st32 branch, and the signed 32-bit length read from the file is stored into ut32 n1, so any negative value becomes a huge unsigned length with no bounds check before use at lines 22/27 (and identically for n2 at lines 38/42/47).

assumptions: get_st32 returns a signed 32-bit value read from the buffer and signals read failure only via the error out-parameter; its return value is otherwise unconstrained (any st32, including -1).
rz_buf_read(buffer, buf, len) writes up to min(len, remaining buffer bytes) into buf; nothing in this code limits that count to the allocated size.
RZ_NEW0 zero-initializes ret, so ret->type/data are not uninitialized reads on success paths.
malloc(0) returns a non-NULL pointer per C standard, so the if (!s1) guard does not reject the wrapped size.
limitations: The error paths at lines 23-24, 39-41, and 43-44 leak ret and/or s1 (CWE-401); each leak is a single small fixed-size allocation per aborted parse with no attacker-driven amplification loop in this function, so it is not counted as the primary vulnerability.
The ut8 branch (magic <= 62061) is safe: n1/n2 are bounded to 0-255, malloc(n+1) allocates at least 1 byte and the read length matches.
The s1[n1] = '\0' out-of-bounds write at line 33 would additionally require size == n1, i.e. ~4 GiB of trailing file data; the reachable defect is the heap overflow at line 27.

verdict.summary: parse_rtcp_bye correctly bounds the BYE reason copy on every path: the reason length is clamped to the destination buffer size via PJ_MIN(sizeof(sess->stat.peer_sdes_buf_), pkt[8]) and to the actual packet payload via PJ_MIN(reason.slen, size-9), with the read of the length byte guarded by 'if (size > 8)' which, for unsigned pj_size_t, guarantees size >= 9 so size-9 cannot underflow. Boundary cases (size==9 zero-length copy, slen==sizeof(buf) exact full-buffer write, pkt[8]==255 with short packet) all remain in bounds. No memory-safety, integer, or bounds defect survives.

assumptions: pj_size_t is unsigned and pj_ssize_t is signed, as in standard pjlib definitions; the analysis of 'size > 8' implying size >= 9 and of the PJ_MIN signed/unsigned comparisons depends on this.

The 'size' parameter accurately reflects the number of valid bytes readable at 'pkt'; this contract is enforced by the RTCP demux/transport outside the given code. If a caller passed a size larger than the real buffer, the source read could go out of bounds, but no statement in this code can prevent that.
'sess' is non-NULL and sess->stat.peer_sdes_buf_ is the fixed-size array whose sizeof supplies the destination bound.
PJ_MIN is the standard ((a)<(b)?(a):(b)) macro.
limitations: Attacker-controlled reason bytes are logged verbatim via PJ_LOG("...reason: %.*s") with no control-character neutralization; a malicious RTCP peer could forge log lines (CWE-117-style log forging). The length is clamped to sizeof(peer_sdes_buf_) so no memory corruption is possible, output goes to an application-configurable level-5 trace log, and no parsing/control-flow effect exists — judged a low-impact output-neutralization weakness, not a confirmed vulnerability.

When size == 9, pj_memcpy(dst, pkt+9, 0) is called with a source pointer one past the end of the packet; a zero-length memcpy is practically harmless and has no attacker-observable effect beyond what the size > 8 guard already permits.

If the surrounding code ever routes an attacker-controlled 'size' larger than the received datagram into this function, the size-9 clamp would not prevent an over-read of 'pkt'; that contract is outside this function.

verdict.summary: sdb_edit passes the raw EDITOR/VISUAL environment value to system() (only a space check routes it there), enabling OS command injection, and it creates a fully predictable temporary file /tmp/sd<pid> in the shared /tmp directory with fopen(...,"w") and no exclusive-create/symlink check, enabling symlink-based arbitrary file clobber and read-back of attacker-controlled content into the procedure body that the interpreter executes.

evidence.reason: Command injection (CWE-78): editor comes from getenv("EDITOR")/getenv("VISUAL") and reaches system() with no metacharacter validation. The only guard, if (strchr(editor,' ')==NULL), merely routes space-containing values into the shell sink; EDITOR="vi; <cmd>" contains a space and system() executes the injected command.

Origin of the tainted value: the command string executed via system() is read directly from the process environment (EDITOR, falling back to VISUAL), an attacker-influenced trust-boundary input, and is used without any validation.

Insecure temporary file (CWE-377): the path is the fully predictable /tmp/sd<getpid()> in a world-writable directory and is opened with fopen(...,"w") with no O_EXCL/mkstemp/symlink check; a local attacker who pre-creates symlink /tmp/sd<guessed pid> causes arbitrary file truncation/overwrite with the procedure body.

Read-back leg of the CWE-377 race: the file at the predictable /tmp path is re-opened and its contents installed as the procedure body that the interpreter later executes, with no integrity check; additionally len=ftell is unchecked ((int)len truncates while myfread uses the untruncated len, and len==-1 makes body[-1]='\0' a one-byte heap underflow), all reachable via a swapped/symlinked temp file.

assumptions: omStrDup allocates strlen(s)+1 bytes, so the filename buffer is 14 bytes for the 13-character literal "/tmp/sd000000".
myfread is a fread-style wrapper whose size arguments follow the fread convention; its failure is not checked here.
pi->data.s.body is the procedure source later interpreted/executed by the Singular interpreter, making read-back of attacker-swapped file content a code-integrity issue.
limitations: One-byte heap NUL overflow at sprintf(filename+7,"%d",getpid()) (line 4): the 14-byte buffer holds only 7 bytes at offset 7, so a 7-digit PID (Linux pid_max allows up to 4194304) writes the NUL one byte past the buffer. The victim's PID is fixed at process creation and an attacker cannot change it for an already-running process, so this is environmental and not confirmed as a vulnerability in this code.
Memory leak: editor=omStrDup(editor) (line 25) is never freed in the exec/fork paths; bounded, no exhaustion path.
The child returns exit(0) even when execlp fails (lines 52-61), reporting success on editor failure; fail-open status only, no direct security effect.

The ftell-failure (len==-1) and (int)len truncation edges at lines 76/80-82 are recorded as aggravating paths of the temp-file race rather than separate findings, since their realistic reachability runs through the same /tmp symlink swap.

verdict.summary: In FurnaceGUI::patternRow, the effect-column color lookup indexes the fxColors and extFxColors arrays with pat->data[i][index] taken from file-loaded pattern data without a complete range check. Only the exact sentinel -1 (line 194) and an upper ladder terminating at <0xe0 (line 215) are tested, so any negative value other than -1 passes the `pat->data[i][index]<0x10` test into fxColors[negative], and any value above 0xff reaches extFxColors[value-0xe0] with no upper bound (index 32..32543), producing out-of-bounds reads whose result then indexes uiColors. Trigger: open/render a song file containing such an effect cell in a visible, non-collapsed channel — crash or palette/heap information leak. The same function correctly two-side-checks the instrument column (line 120) and clamps the volume color (lines 159-160), which shows the effect ladder is missing its endpoint bounds.

evidence.reason: The final else of the effect-color ladder indexes extFxColors with pat->data[i][index]-0xe0 without any upper bound: the preceding chain ends at `pat->data[i][index]<0xe0`, so a cell value of 0x100..0x7fff (attacker-controllable via a crafted pattern/song file) yields an index of 32..32543 — an out-of-bounds read whose result is then used to index uiColors. Root cause: unvalidated array index (CWE-129); no statement in this code rejects values above 0xff before this sink.

The guard `pat->data[i][index]<0x10` is one-sided: it does not exclude negative values, and the only negative handling is the exact sentinel `==-1` at line 194. A pattern cell of -2..-32768 (crossing the file-data trust boundary) takes this branch and reads fxColors[negative] out of bounds, then uses the garbage result to index uiColors. The instrument column at line 120 (`pat->data[i][2]<0 || pat->data[i][2]>=e->song.insLen`) demonstrates the two-sided check this effect path is missing.

assumptions: Sizes and element types of DivPattern::data, fxColors, extFxColors, uiColors, volColors, patChanX, chanShow, chanCollapse, patCache are not declared in the given snippet; the intended ranges [0,0x10) for fxColors and [0xe0,0x100) for extFxColors are inferred from the guard ladder itself, and no capacity is quotable, so capacity-based candidates are recorded rather than relied upon.
The engine/file loader may constrain pattern effect values to [-1,255] and effectRows to at most 14; no such check is quotable in this code, so it is not relied upon for the confirmed finding.
`chans` is assumed consistent with the sizes of patChanX/chanShow/chanCollapse/patCache/pat[] by the caller; this code contains no check of chans against those capacities.
`e->song.patLen` is assumed not to exceed the physical row capacity of DivPattern::data; the in-code check at line 15 bounds i by patLen, whose relation to the array capacity is not declared here.
noteName(...) is an external function; its handling of arbitrary short note/octave values is not analyzable from this code.
limitations: sprintf into static char id[32] was measured at worst ~24-30 bytes across all eight call sites (8-char hex of negative values, multi-digit i/j/k) and does not overflow for any width this code can plausibly receive; only absurd 10-digit row/channel numbers could exceed 32, and those are gated on the unvalidated patLen/chans invariants noted above.
The ord and i range checks (lines 12 and 15), the instrument range check (line 120), and the volume color clamps (lines 159-160) are present, quoted, and edge-tested; they are not defects.
The early visibility return at line 9 occurs before any style push, and the Push/PopStyleColor counts balance on all paths, so no style-stack imbalance exists.

Candidates C (effectRows vs pattern column capacity, line 186-187), D (patLen vs physical row capacity, line 15), and E (chans vs undeclared array capacities) are not confirmed because the violated capacities are not declared in this snippet; if the engine does not enforce those invariants at load time, they become additional OOB reads.

verdict.summary: The function is a pure hash computation over an attacker-supplied snd_ctl_elem_id. Its only memory access, id->name[i], is strictly bounded by 'i < SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN' with short-circuit evaluation, so no out-of-bounds read is reachable; integer wraparound in h is defined unsigned arithmetic and is masked by 'h &= LONG_MAX'. There are no copy, allocation, injection, authz, or crypto sinks, and potential hash-collision or distribution weaknesses depend on consumers outside this code.

assumptions: struct snd_ctl_elem_id declares name as a fixed array char name[SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ID_NAME_MAXLEN] (44 bytes) rather than a pointer; this definition is outside the given code, so the loop bound matching the array size is an assumption, though the guard is fully contained in the quoted loop condition.
MULTIPLIER is a compile-time constant; its exact value is outside the given code.
The function's callers may pass attacker-influenced data (ALSA control ioctls), but within this function all uses of that data are the bounded read and defined unsigned arithmetic analyzed above.
limitations: Signed char bytes (>= 0x80) sign-extend into the unsigned long hash, which can skew hash distribution; this is a hash-quality issue with no memory-safety or security consequence in this code.

If callers insert many colliding ids into a hash container, collisions could degrade lookup performance (CWE-400-like), but the container and its collision handling are not part of the given code, so no such finding can be substantiated here.

verdict.summary: Both device-controlled length sinks are correctly bounds-checked on every path: 'if (sw.len > sizeof(self->rpc))' guards hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc_call(self, sw.len), and 'if (fw.len > sizeof(self->rpc))' guards the fw.len-sized download into &self->rpc. Edge testing at fw.len == sizeof(self->rpc) shows the round-up dword count (fw.len + 3)/4 equals exactly sizeof/4 (sizeof is a multiple of 4 due to the struct's u32 members), so the at-limit value fits; one-past is rejected by the '>' check, which is the correct operator. The dead-device all-ones pattern (sw.len = 0xFFFF) is rejected by the sw.len guard. No candidate vulnerability survives the counterfactual patch test.

assumptions: External helpers are outside the given code and their behavior is assumed per kernel semantics: readx_poll_timeout_atomic assigns fw.val (via hw_atl_utils_rpc_state_get) before returning 0 or -ETIMEDOUT; hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords writes exactly the given dword count to the destination; aq_hw_read_reg returns the raw MMIO value (all-ones on device fault).
self->rpc_addr is consumed as a download address; its provenance (set outside this function, from a device register read during init) is not visible here and is not relied upon.

sizeof(self->rpc) is a multiple of 4 because the struct hw_atl_utils_fw_rpc contains u32 members (e.g. msg_id), forcing 4-byte alignment; this makes the (fw.len + sizeof(u32) - sizeof(u8)) / sizeof(u32) round-up safe at the fw.len == sizeof boundary.
Concurrent callers of this function are assumed serialized by the driver's own locking; no race is reachable from this code alone.
limitations: Historic pre-fix versions of this exact function lacked both length checks, enabling a device-controlled out-of-bounds write of up to (0xFFFF+3)/4 dwords into self->rpc (CWE-120/CWE-787); both checks are present and quotable in the code under analysis, so that defect is not present here.

If a live, actively malicious or faulty device persistently reports fw.len == 0xFFFF with sw.len <= sizeof(self->rpc), the do-while loop has no total iteration bound and can livelock the calling kernel thread (CWE-400 class). Triggering requires attacker-controlled hardware holding the sentinel across every bounded 100 ms poll; the ordinary dead-device all-ones pattern (sw.len = 0xFFFF) is rejected by the sw.len guard, so no host- or network-reachable trigger exists.

The readx_poll_timeout termination condition compares sw.tid == fw.tid as read from device registers; on mismatch beyond the 100000U us timeout the function exits with -ETIMEDOUT, so the poll itself is bounded.

verdict.summary: The ZRLE decoder validates palette indices only against the declared size of palette[128] (mask '& 127' / bppp-bit mask), never against palSize, the number of entries actually initialized. In both the packed-pixels path and the palette-RLE path an attacker-supplied mode byte and index byte select palette entries at indices >= palSize (up to 127, which is never initialized on any path since palSize <= 127), reading uninitialized stack memory that is then written to buf and published via pb->imageRect — a remotely triggerable information disclosure of uninitialized stack contents.

evidence.reason: Packed-pixels sink: the mask bounds index to the bppp-bit range (e.g. palSize=3 gives bppp=2, index up to 3; palSize>16 gives bppp=8, index up to 127), but only palette[0..palSize-1] was initialized, so any index >= palSize reads uninitialized stack memory which is then emitted to the framebuffer via imageRect. Trigger: mode byte 0x03 plus a packed data byte containing bits '11'.

evidence.snippet:
index &= 127;

            PIXEL_T pix = palette[index];
evidence.reason: Palette-RLE sink: 'index &= 127' permits indices 0..127 while the initialization loop filled only 0..palSize-1 (palSize <= 127), so palette[127] is uninitialized on every possible path and any index >= palSize is uninitialized. Trigger: mode byte 0x83 (palSize=3) followed by index byte 0x7F.

Origin of the faulty values: palSize is attacker-controlled (0..127) and only that many palette entries are initialized, while both consumer paths permit indices up to 127; the missing check is 'reject index >= palSize' before each palette[index] use, and no such comparison exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: rdr::ZlibInStream::setUnderlying/is assumed to bound decompression to the attacker-supplied 32-bit 'length' value; that enforcement is outside the given code.

The Rect r and pixel-format parameters are assumed to be constrained by the surrounding RFB layer; no bounds check on r exists in the given code, but tiles are clamped to 64x64 by __rfbmin, matching buf[64*64].
READ_PIXEL and readU8 are assumed to throw on end-of-stream rather than return arbitrary data.
limitations: Signed accumulation 'len += b' in the RLE run-length loops can overflow int given ~8.4M+ consecutive 0xFF bytes; a wrapped-negative len fails 'len-- > 0' and performs no writes, and a large positive len is rejected by the quoted guard 'if (end - ptr < len) throw', so no concrete memory-corruption trigger was constructed (CWE-190 style UB only).
The run-length overflow guard 'if (end - ptr < len)' correctly handles the exact boundary len == end-ptr; no off-by-one found in the buffer-fill loops (all tiles are fully written before imageRect).

verdict.summary: In the DXF LWPolyline decoder, the group-code 42 branch validates only the upper bound of vertexIndex ('vertexIndex<maxVertices') and omits the lower-bound check present in the groupCode<=30 branch, so a group-42 record following a group-90 record (which sets vertexIndex=-1) writes attacker-controlled data to vertices[-1], an out-of-bounds heap write. Additionally, the allocation 'new double[4*maxVertices]' has no upper bound on maxVertices beyond maxVertices>0, so a group-90 value of 2^30 makes 4*maxVertices overflow to 0, allocating a zero-length array that the initialization loop then overflows.

evidence.snippet:
} else if (groupCode==42 && vertexIndex<maxVertices) {
            vertices[4*vertexIndex + 3] = toReal(groupValue);
evidence.reason: The write sink vertices[4*vertexIndex + 3] is guarded only by vertexIndex<maxVertices; the lower-bound test vertexIndex>=0 exists only in the groupCode<=30 branch (line 30) and is not on this path. Since the group-90 branch always sets vertexIndex=-1 (line 17), a DXF file containing a 90 record followed by a 42 record makes -1<maxVertices true and writes toReal(groupValue) to vertices[4*(-1)+3] = vertices[-1], an attacker-controlled heap buffer underflow write (trigger: group 90 value '1', then group 42 with any value).

evidence.snippet: vertexIndex=-1;
evidence.reason: Origin of the negative index: every group-code 90 record sets vertexIndex=-1 regardless of whether the allocation succeeded, and combined with the missing lower-bound check in the 42 branch this yields the negative-index out-of-bounds write.

maxVertices = toInt(groupValue) (line 4) is bounded only by 'if (maxVertices>0)' (line 5) with no upper bound; for a group-90 value of 1073741824 (2^30), 4*maxVertices overflows int to 0, so new double[0] allocates an empty buffer and the very first loop iteration vertices[0] writes out of bounds, corrupting the heap with zeros across ~2^30 iterations (also a resource-exhaustion path).

assumptions: groupCode and groupValue are parsed DXF file content supplied to this decoder from an untrusted file; this function is the trust-boundary intake point, so no upstream validation is assumed.
toInt and toReal are assumed to parse the attacker-supplied groupValue string into int/double; their implementations are outside the given code.

Initial member values of vertexIndex/maxVertices/vertices (before any group-90 record) are outside the given code; the confirmed triggers do not depend on them because line 17 sets vertexIndex=-1 on every group-90 record within this code.

If vertices is a stale pointer from a previous entity (group 90 value <= 0 does not free it), the vertices[-1] write is a heap underflow on a live allocation; on a fresh object with vertices==NULL it is a near-NULL write — both are memory-safety violations, differing only in exploitability.
limitations: The groupCode<=30 branch (lines 30-32) was verified safe: the guard 'if (vertexIndex>=0 && vertexIndex<maxVertices)' bounds the index, and groupCode/10-1 in {0,1,2} keeps the maximum index at 4*maxVertices-2, within the allocation (edge cases vertexIndex=0 and vertexIndex=maxVertices-1 tested).

The maxVertices-1 arithmetic in the increment guard (line 25) can overflow for maxVertices==INT_MIN, but the resulting vertexIndex=0 fails every subsequent bounds check in this code, so no write occurs via that path.

Values of maxVertices strictly between 2^29 and 2^30 cause 4*maxVertices to wrap negative, producing a huge size_t allocation and std::bad_alloc; whether upstream code catches that exception is outside the given code, so that sub-case is only a potential DoS, whereas the exact 2^30 case is a confirmed heap overflow.

verdict.summary: gpg_ctx_add_recipient accepts an attacker-influenced recipient identifier (keyid) and only ensures an exact-match form when it contains '@' (strchr(keyid, '@')). Any recipient without '@' — including bare UID substrings, empty strings, or values containing '<'/>' — is used verbatim (g_strdup(keyid)) and later passed as the GPG --recipient key selector, for which GPG performs substring matching over user IDs. An attacker who controls a recipient string can make the victim's encrypted mail be encrypted under an attacker-chosen or attacker-controlled key, defeating confidentiality. This is the intake point for trust-boundary data, so missing validation here is the vulnerability.

evidence.reason: The only guard applied to the attacker-influenced recipient string is a substring test for '@'. Every value without '@' is copied verbatim by g_strdup(keyid) with no validation of form, bracket balance, or content, so the string reaches the GPG key-selection argument without being forced into an exact-match form. Trigger: a recipient such as 'Alice' (no '@') selects any keyring UID containing that substring via GPG's inexact matching, e.g., an attacker-controlled 'Alice <attacker@evil.example>', causing the victim's encrypted mail to be encrypted under the attacker's key. Additionally, values that already contain '<'/'>', such as '<a@b>', become malformed ('<<a@b>>'), and the empty string is accepted.

evidence.snippet:
gpg_ctx_add_recipient (struct _GpgCtx *gpg,
                       const gchar *keyid)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: keyid is a parameter of this exported entry point and carries recipient identity data that originates outside the program (parsed message/address data crossing a trust boundary). No precondition on its form is enforced anywhere before its use at lines 16-19 except the NULL check at line 12.

assumptions: keyid is a NUL-terminated C string per the gchar* API contract; strchr would read out of bounds on a non-terminated buffer, but this code cannot enforce termination itself.

The recipients array is later marshalled into a GPG argument vector (argv) outside the shown code; no shell is involved, so classic shell metacharacter injection (CWE-78) is not evaluated as a sink of this snippet — only the key-selection semantics are.
gpg->mode values GPG_CTX_MODE_ENCRYPT/EXPORT are internal state fully controlled by this component.
limitations: g_ptr_array_new() at line 10 could theoretically return NULL on allocation failure, making g_ptr_array_add at line 22 dereference NULL, but allocation failure is not attacker-inducible input, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.
g_strdup_printf at line 17 uses a fixed literal format with keyid only as %s; no format-string vulnerability and no length-related memory corruption exists in this snippet.
The NULL-deref candidate for keyid is dismissed because of the always-executed guard 'g_return_if_fail (keyid != NULL);' at line 12, which lies on every path to the strchr at line 16.
No memory-corruption, use-after-free, race, or unbounded-loop defect is present within the shown lines; the confirmed defect is a semantic input-validation/key-confusion flaw.

verdict.summary: In block_insert(), the blockwise-append/short-line branch assigns count = spaces (line 51) where spaces = (oap->end_vcol - bdp->end_vcol) + 1 (line 50), a value the code itself documents can be negative ('if (spaces < 0) // can happen when the cursor was moved', line 75). The clamp fixes spaces only; count stays negative and is added into the alloc() size (lines 79-81), where it wraps in size_t arithmetic, producing a buffer up to |count| bytes smaller than the STRLEN(oldp) + s_len + 1 bytes actually written by the memmoves and the final STRMOVE (line 116). This yields a heap out-of-bounds write reachable via blockwise append (b_insert == 0) over lines where the block ends before EOL.

evidence.reason: The clamp bounds only spaces, not count, yet count (which was assigned the same possibly-negative value at line 51) is added to the alloc() size. In size_t arithmetic a negative count wraps, so e.g. count = -1 yields alloc(STRLEN(oldp) + s_len) while the copy path below writes STRLEN(oldp) + s_len + 1 bytes. No statement in the function lower-bounds count or the computed size; 'if (newp == NULL) continue;' only handles allocation failure.

Origin of the tainted value: the subtraction (oap->end_vcol - bdp->end_vcol) + 1 can go negative (attested by the adjacent clamp's comment), and count = spaces captures the negative value before the clamp, feeding the undersized allocation.

Sink: when spaces was clamped to 0, count's bytes are never added to offset, so STRMOVE writes the remaining tail including the NUL at newp + offset where offset can be at or past the end of the undersized buffer — an out-of-bounds heap write of |count| bytes.

assumptions: block_prep() and ml_get() bodies are not in the given code; bdp->end_vcol provenance and whether it can exceed oap->end_vcol + 1 cannot be quoted here. The given code's own comment at line 75 ('can happen when the cursor was moved') is taken as in-code evidence that spaces < 0 is a reachable runtime state, and line 51 assigns that same value to count on the same path.

alloc() is assumed to take a size_t argument and STRLEN() to return size_t (vim types), so the size expression at lines 79-81 is evaluated in unsigned size_t arithmetic and a negative int count wraps rather than being rejected.

oap, bdp, and s are treated as attacker-influenced per the vim threat model: they derive from user editing commands applied to buffer contents that may come from untrusted files, macros, or scripted inputs; this function is the intake point for those values.
limitations: A potential out-of-bounds read in mb_head_off(oldp, oldp + offset + spaces) (line 63) was considered: if the block-start char is a TAB near end-of-line, offset + spaces can exceed the line length. It was not confirmed because block_prep (not shown) may constrain textcol/startspaces, short lines are skipped for insert (line 23), and vim memline often stores lines with slack. Dismissed for lack of a provable trigger in the given code.
A stale non-negative count across loop iterations (count not reset per iteration) causes only over-allocation on the insert path, not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: mobi_decode_infl never validates the lower bound of the cursor pos in the delete branch. `if (dir == '<') { pos--; }` can decrement pos from 0 to -1, and both buffer guards `if (l < 0 || d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX)` are algebraically independent of pos (d + l == decoded + *decoded_size, resp. +1), so they detect pos > *decoded_size but never pos < 0. evidence.reason: Missing-check site: `pos--` at pos == 0 yields pos == -1, but the only subsequent guard tests `l < 0` (i.e. pos > *decoded_size) and `d + l > decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX`, where d + l == decoded + *decoded_size is independent of pos. No `pos < 0` test exists on this path; the sole such test (`if (pos < 0 || pos > *decoded_size)`, line 22) is confined to the position-setting branch.

The enforcing checks (prefix < strlen, suffix-length equality) exist nowhere in the given code.

The unconditional write *r = '\0' at dst + dst_prefix_len (line 7) is an out-of-bounds write whenever dst_prefix_len >= dst's allocated size; at the boundary src_prefix_len == strlen(src), p is one-past src's allocation and *p is read out of bounds on the first loop iteration.

A dst buffer one byte shorter than dst_prefix_len + 1 + src's suffix length receives an out-of-bounds NUL write here; if the over-read at *p returns a non-NUL, non-boundary byte, the loop continues advancing p and q past both buffers, writing *p, *q and *r out of bounds and passing truncated garbage to stat/mkdir/chmod.

assumptions: Callers are not shown; the intended contract (src = src_prefix + "/" + suffix, dst = dst_prefix + "/" + identical suffix, buffers allocated strlen+1) would keep the accesses in bounds, but no statement in the given code enforces any part of it, so it cannot be relied upon.

The function mutates the caller's src buffer in place (temporary NUL termination at line 13, restored at line 24); a reentrancy hazard only if src is shared concurrently, which this code itself does not cause.

verdict.summary: tilingPatternFill recomputes surface_width/surface_height from attacker-controlled PDF pattern geometry via unchecked `(int) ceil(fabs(...))` conversions inside the `fabs(kx) < 1 && fabs(ky) < 1` branch, where the only bitmap-size bound (`(unsigned long) surface_width * surface_height > 0x800000L`) does not apply; the subsequent check rejects only the value 0, so huge (e.g. 1.8e9) or negative (INT_MIN from out-of-range double-to-int conversion) dimensions reach `new SplashBitmap(...)` (allocation-size corruption/OOM). The later guard `surface_width == 0 || surface_height == 0` rejects only the boundary value 0, so negative or multi-gigabyte dimensions flow to the allocation.

bitmap = new SplashBitmap(surface_width, surface_height, 1,

evidence.reason: Allocation sink: SplashBitmap is constructed with surface_width/surface_height that, on the fabs(kx)<1 && fabs(ky)<1 path, are unvalidated attacker-derived integers (possibly negative via the UB (int)ceil conversion, or huge). The only preceding checks (`(unsigned long) surface_width * surface_height > 0x800000L` on the other branch and `surface_width == 0 || surface_height == 0` at line 119) are absent or test only the zero boundary, so the size precondition of this sink is not enforced.

repeatX/repeatY are raised to the raw caller values x1-x0 / y1-y0, which come from PDF-controlled pattern step sizes and clip geometry and are unbounded in this code (the only related check, `repeatX * repeatY <= 4`, is a lower bound). With repeatX = 131072 and a 16384-wide tile, `result_width = tBitmap->getWidth() * imgData.repeatX` (line 170) overflows signed int to INT_MIN, and the tile loop `for (y < imgData.repeatY) for (x < imgData.repeatX) splash->blitImage(...)` executes repeatX*repeatY attacker-sized iterations, enabling CPU/memory exhaustion from a crafted PDF.

verdict.summary: The sysfs store callback copies attacker-controlled data into a fixed-size stack buffer, but the length guard `if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) return 0;` precedes the copy on the only path, correctly uses >=, and blocks the unsigned-wrap boundary (SIZE_MAX) before `nbytes + 1` is computed; `strscpy(drc_name, buf, nbytes + 1)` with count >= 1 always NUL-terminates, so `strchr` and `dlpar_remove_slot` receive a bounded, terminated string. All boundary cases (nbytes = 0, MAX-1, MAX, SIZE_MAX) are safe. No confirmed vulnerability in this code.

strscpy is assumed to follow its documented kernel contract: for count > 0 it always NUL-terminates the destination. This is standard library semantics, not validation performed elsewhere on the data.
dlpar_remove_slot's body is not part of the given code; any name-lookup or injection defect inside it cannot be audited or attributed here.
The sysfs buffer buf is assumed to contain at least nbytes readable bytes; this is the calling contract of a .store callback.

verdict.summary: handleLWPolylineData trusts the file-supplied group-code-90 value as maxVertices with only a sign check ('if (maxVertices>0)') and uses it in int arithmetic as the allocation size 'new double[4*maxVertices]'. A DXF file with group code 90 and value 1073741824 yields a zero-length allocation that is immediately overwritten out of bounds at vertices[i*4]; follow-up 10/20/30/42 pairs write attacker-controlled doubles out of bounds. Exploitation (use-after-free on a subsequent group 10/20/30/42) requires a caller that catches the allocation exception and resumes parsing with the same object, which cannot be shown from this code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable defect found. All sinks (pskb_put tail append, skb frag descriptor write, page-frag trailer write, returned nfrags) are guarded by checks present verbatim in the code — 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)', 'skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS', the skb_page_frag_refill failure check, and the skb_cow_data error check — and each guard holds at boundary values (exact tailroom fit, nr_frags at MAX_SKB_FRAGS, zero-length, exactly-at-limit allocsz). Exhaustive path analysis shows nfrags is assigned on every return path, the spinlock is released on every exit, and the page reference is taken before the frag descriptor is published. Remaining safety relies on documented contracts of kernel helpers external to this snippet (noted as assumptions), not on any missing in-code validation.

assumptions: skb_tailroom() returns 0 for nonlinear skbs and end-tail otherwise (kernel helper semantics outside this code); this is what makes the skip_cow path safe for paged/TSO skbs.
skb_cow_data(skb, tailen, &trailer) guarantees tailroom >= tailen in *trailer and preserves header offsets across reallocation; its result is error-checked in the code.
skb_put()/pskb_put() contain an internal over-panic check that rejects tail > end, so an exact tailroom fit (tailen == tailroom) is safe and one-past-limit is a panic, not corruption.
skb_page_frag_refill(allocsize, pfrag, GFP_ATOMIC) guarantees offset+allocsize <= pfrag->size on success.
esp->tailen/tfclen/plen are computed in-kernel (esp6_output) from admin-configured xfrm state and alignment math; tailen >= 2, plen <= 7, so zero/negative tailen is not reachable from attacker data.
ESP_SKB_FRAG_MAXSIZE is a fixed kernel constant bounding the page-frag allocation path; allocsz (>= ALIGN(tailen)) is compared against it before the frag path is taken.
No multi-gigabyte skb (needed to overflow the unsigned allocsz = ALIGN(skb->data_len + tailen, ...)) can be constructed by any reachable producer.
limitations: Candidate C1 (skb_put SKB_LINEAR panic via skip_cow on a nonlinear skb) was considered and dismissed: the guard 'tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb)' is present in the code, and skb_tailroom returns 0 for nonlinear skbs, so the path requires tailen == 0 which in-kernel esp->tailen computation prevents.
Candidate C2 (frags[] out-of-bounds write via __skb_fill_page_desc) dismissed: 'skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS' is checked on the only path to the write and is correct at both boundaries.
Candidate C3 (uninitialized nfrags returned, CWE-457/908) dismissed: all six control-flow paths reaching 'out:' assign nfrags first (nfrags = 1, the frag-path assignments, or skb_cow_data's result).
Candidate C4 (page-frag out-of-bounds trailer write / pfrag->offset overrun) dismissed: refill success is checked and failure releases the lock and jumps to cow.
Candidate C5 (unsigned overflow of allocsz) dismissed as requiring ~4GB skb->data_len, not constructible.
Candidate C6 (lock imbalance or page UAF) dismissed: both spin_unlock_bh calls are present and get_page() precedes the frag descriptor publication.
Candidate C7 (unbounded pskb_put on the cow path) dismissed: delegated to skb_cow_data's documented contract with an explicit error check 'if (nfrags < 0) goto out;'.

The only guards are `if (fw.len)` (nonzero) and the 0xFFFF retry sentinel (`if (fw.len == 0xFFFFU)` / `0xFFFFU == fw.len`), so any firmware-reported length in [1, 0xFFFE] reaches hw_atl_utils_fw_downld_dwords; fw.len = 0xFFFE yields (65534+3)/4 = 16384 dwords (64 KiB) written into a buffer far smaller than that, an out-of-bounds heap write driven by data crossing the hardware/firmware trust boundary. The dword count is never compared against sizeof(self->rpc) anywhere in this function.

verdict.summary: add_slot_store copies exactly nbytes attacker bytes into the stack array drc_name and then runs strchr(drc_name, '\n') BEFORE any NUL terminator is written, so the scan reads uninitialized stack bytes drc_name[nbytes..MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN-1] and, when none of them is 0x00 or 0x0A, continues reading past the end of the array; if it finds '\n' beyond the array, *end = '\0' performs an out-of-bounds stack write. Trigger: a write of 1-63 bytes containing neither a newline nor a NUL (e.g., write(fd, "abc", 3)) to the sysfs attribute.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the line 8 guard ('if (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN)') only bounds the copied length; it does not terminate drc_name. After memcpy copies just nbytes bytes, bytes drc_name[nbytes..MAX-1] are uninitialized, yet strchr at line 13 scans the buffer before any terminator exists (the only terminating write, *end = '\0' on line 16, is placed after the scan and cannot guard it). For an attacker write of nbytes in [1, MAX-1] whose bytes contain neither '\n' nor '\0' (legal for a sysfs store, e.g. write(fd, "abc", 3)), strchr consumes uninitialized stack memory and, absent a 0x00/0x0A byte in the remainder of the array, reads out of bounds past the 64-byte stack array; if the '\n' it then finds lies past the array, line 16 writes '\0' out of bounds (kernel stack corruption). The one-line fix — drc_name[nbytes] = '\0' before the strchr — is absent from the given code, confirmed by exhaustive line search.

assumptions: MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN's numeric value (commonly 64 in the pseries dlpar header) is not shown in the given code; only the property nbytes < MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN is used, which the line-8 guard enforces verbatim.

Permission checks on the sysfs attribute (typically root-only) are enforced outside this code; this affects the attacker population and severity, not the existence of the defect at this trust-boundary entry point.
Whether sysfs NUL-terminates buf is irrelevant and not relied upon: only nbytes bytes are copied, so the scanned bytes at indices >= nbytes are uninitialized regardless of buf's own termination.
limitations: Oversized input (nbytes >= MAX_DRC_NAME_LEN) returns 0, making the write a silent no-op with no memory-safety, authz, or availability impact — cosmetic robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

If strchr finds '\n' in uninitialized bytes still inside the array, the code merely passes a garbage DRC name to dlpar_add_slot (lookup failure); this is a sub-case of the confirmed uninitialized-use finding, not a separate one.

The out-of-bounds traversal past the array depends on stack residue containing neither 0x00 nor 0x0A, which is not fully attacker-controlled; the in-array uninitialized read (CWE-908) occurs deterministically for the stated trigger.
