verdict.summary: The io_uring io_read path shown contains its required trust-boundary validations on every path: user iovec import is validated via io_import_iovec with an error return, the file position/length overflow check rw_verify_area is performed before io_iter_do_read, the -EAGAIN/REQ_F_REISSUE routing and the ret=0 reset prevent negative or oversized values from entering the retry loop's io_size -= ret accounting, and iov_iter_revert's revert amount can only be non-negative because iterator counts can only be consumed (never grown) between import and revert. Edge cases (io_size == 0, ret == io_size exactly, empty consumption) are handled by the quoted branches. Remaining concerns (iovec leak if io_setup_async_rw fails, fast-iov stack/heap contract of io_import_iovec, bytes_done/result consistency in kiocb_done) depend on code not present in the snippet or require allocation failure an attacker cannot induce, so they are recorded as assumptions/limitations rather than confirmed findings.

assumptions: io_import_iovec is assumed to fully validate the user-supplied iovec array and length (it is the intake validator called here) and to leave *iovec pointing at a heap array or NULL only in the manners upstream io_uring depends on; its body is not shown, so the concern that *iovec could remain the stack array inline_vecs at kfree(iovec) cannot be verified from the given code.

io_setup_async_rw is assumed to take ownership of (free or persist) iovec on success, matching the 'iovec = NULL;' reset; on its failure path the given code returns without kfree, and whether io_setup_async_rw frees iovec internally cannot be verified here.

kiocb_done is assumed to combine the passed ret with rw->bytes_done consistently; its body is not shown, so the correctness of exiting the retry loop at 'ret == io_size' with partial sums in rw->bytes_done cannot be verified from this snippet.
io_iter_do_read is assumed to never return more than the remaining iov_iter count, preserving the invariant io_size == remaining iterator count used in the STEP 2 analysis.
Whether the core overwrites req->result with the completion value after an error return (req->result is set to io_size before rw_verify_area) is decided outside the shown code.
limitations: Potential memory leak of iovec when 'ret2 = io_setup_async_rw(...); if (ret2) return ret2;' returns an error, and on the early 'return ret ?: -EAGAIN;' path if io_setup_async_rw fails internally; both require an allocation failure (kzalloc of async data) that attacker input cannot deterministically induce, so they are not treated as vulnerabilities.

The signedness-sensitive expression 'io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)' (ssize_t minus size_t) would wrap if the iterator count ever exceeded io_size; no statement in the shown code can produce that state, but the wrap resistance relies on external iterator semantics rather than an explicit in-function guard.

The exit condition 'while (ret > 0 && ret < io_size)' could mis-account the final full chunk relative to rw->bytes_done if kiocb_done does not add them; this cannot be confirmed or refuted without kiocb_done's source.

verdict.summary: sftp_mkdir() checks every external return value it consumes on every path (ssh_buffer_new, ssh_string_from_char, the buffer_add_*/sftp_packet_write chain, sftp_read_and_dispatch, parse_status_msg, sftp_lstat), frees every resource exactly once on all paths, and uses only literal format strings ('SFTP server: %s', 'Received message %d ...'). Server-controlled values (msg->packet_type, status->status, status->errormsg) reach only comparisons, a switch with default, and %s/%d arguments — no memory indexing, pointer arithmetic, local filesystem, command, or SQL sinks exist in this function. The only in-code deref of the session pointer occurs solely on the allocation-failure branch. No attacker-reachable missing guard could be demonstrated from the given code.

assumptions: The behavior of external functions (ssh_string_from_char, parse_status_msg, sftp_read_and_dispatch, sftp_dequeue, ssh_set_error, sftp_get_new_id) is not defined in the given code; in particular, whether parse_status_msg can return non-NULL with status->errormsg == NULL cannot be determined here. The use at 'ssh_set_error(sftp->session, SSH_REQUEST_DENIED, "SFTP server: %s", status->errormsg);' passes errormsg as a %s argument to a literal format, so no format-string injection exists in this code regardless.

sftp_session sftp is assumed valid by library convention; the only direct dereference in this code ('ssh_set_error_oom(sftp->session);') executes only inside 'if (buffer == NULL)', i.e., only under allocation failure.
ssh_buffer_add_ssh_string is assumed to copy (not take ownership of) the string, consistent with the code freeing both buffer and path afterwards.
limitations: NULL sftp parameter: the sole in-code deref (sftp->session) is reachable only when ssh_buffer_new() fails (allocation failure); all other uses of sftp are passed to external functions whose internal derefs cannot be quoted here, so this is treated as caller misuse / allocation-failure-only, not a confirmed vulnerability.

SAFE_FREE(errno_attr) frees only the struct pointer returned by sftp_lstat; if struct sftp_attributes_struct owns heap sub-objects requiring a dedicated destructor, this would leak them — the struct definition and any such destructor are not present in the given code, so the leak cannot be asserted.

The 'while (msg == NULL)' loop has no timeout: a malicious or unresponsive SFTP server can withhold the response and block the client in the external sftp_read_and_dispatch read. Termination relies on the external read failing; this is inherent to the SFTP request/response design, not a demonstrable unbounded computation in this code.
status->errormsg is server-controlled text embedded into the session error string; any log-injection consequence would occur at a downstream logging site not present in this function.

status->errormsg and any attribute strings whose sizes are attacker-influenced could contribute to resource use, but each call leaks/consumes a bounded amount only when the caller drives repeated calls; no uncontrolled-consumption trigger within this code was demonstrated.

verdict.summary: GmfOpenMesh validates every attacker-influenced value it consumes: the filename length is checked before strcpy ('if(strlen(FilNam) + 7 >= GmfStrSiz) longjmp(msh->err, -4);'), ASCII token reads are width-bounded ('%100s') with EOF handled, and every file-derived value (cod, ver, KwdCod, dim) is range-checked on every path before use. The remaining unguarded dereferences (strlen(FilNam); *PtrVer/*PtrDim) can only be NULL if the trusted embedding application violates the API contract; no attacker-influenced input can set them. No attacker-reachable memory-safety, injection, or validation defect exists in this code.

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is assumed to be at least 101 (in libMeshb it is 1024); its numeric value is not visible in the given code, so the safety of 'fscanf(msh->hdl, "%100s", str)' against 'char str[ GmfStrSiz ]' and of the copy into 'msh->FilNam' rests on that constant matching the guard 'if(strlen(FilNam) + 7 >= GmfStrSiz)'.
WrdSiz is assumed to be 4, matching the int-sized fields (&msh->cod, &msh->ver, &KwdCod, &msh->dim) into which read()/safe_fread()/ScaWrd() write; the struct GmfMshSct definition is not shown.
safe_fread/safe_fscanf are assumed to longjmp via the passed 'msh->err' on short reads and conversion failures, as their signatures and every call site suggest; their bodies are not shown.
scanf '%s' semantics are assumed such that fscanf returns either 1 or EOF (no matching-failure-without-conversion), so 'str' is initialized at every strcmp in the do/while loops.
ScaWrd, GetPos, ScaKwdTab, and GmfSetKwd bodies are not shown; their internal handling of file-controlled values cannot be analyzed here.
limitations: NULL 'FilNam' would crash at 'strlen(FilNam)' (CWE-476) and NULL 'PtrVer'/'PtrDim' at '(*PtrVer) = msh->ver;' — but these arguments are supplied by the trusted embedding application; no attacker-controlled value (file contents) can make them NULL, so they are contract robustness issues, not attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in this code.

'if(!ScaKwdTab(msh)) return(0);' returns without free(msh)/fclose(msh->hdl); if ScaKwdTab can return 0 (no such path is visible; its error paths longjmp to the handler that does free), each failed open leaks one struct and one descriptor — a one-shot leak with no amplification loop in this code.
The longjmp cleanup may call close() on a negative msh->FilDes (fails with EBADF, harmless) because the open guard uses 'msh->FilDes <= 0' while cleanup tests 'msh->FilDes != 0'.

The do/while header-scan loops read the entire file linearly until the keyword or EOF is found — linear time in file size with constant memory, inherent to parsing, not a resource-exhaustion amplification.

'fscanf(..., "%d", &msh->ver, ...)' on an out-of-range literal could yield a matching failure; this is caught by safe_fscanf (assumed to longjmp) and by the calloc-zeroed value failing '(msh->ver < 1) || (msh->ver > 4)'.

verdict.summary: get_lisp_indent accumulates attacker-controlled character display widths into the signed int 'amount' (and colnr_T 'firsttry') with no range check anywhere in the function. For the line containing the matched '(' or '[' it walks up to pos->col attacker-chosen bytes (line 97 'while (*that && col)'), adding up to the 'tabstop' option value (settable via modeline, up to 99999) per tab at line 99; the same unbounded accumulation recurs at lines 161-164 and 169. A buffer line with ~21,500 tabs before the '(' (with ts=99999), or ~268 MB of tabs at default ts=8, makes 'amount' pass INT_MAX between iterations, causing signed integer overflow (undefined behavior) and a wrapped/negative value cast at '(colnr_T)amount' and returned as the indent. No statement in the code bounds amount, col, or the line length, so the defect is unguarded in this code.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: 'amount' (int) accumulates lbr_chartabsize_adv results, each up to the 'tabstop' value (attacker-settable via modeline, up to 99999) for attacker-supplied tab characters, over 'col = pos->col' iterations where col is the attacker-chosen byte column of the matched paren. No bound on the running sum exists; the loop's only guards ('*that && col') limit iteration count, not the accumulated value. Edge case: with amount = INT_MAX - k, the next tab addition wraps signed int (UB) before the '(colnr_T)amount' cast; the wrapped value is returned as the indent. Trigger: buffer line of >= ~21,475 tabs followed by '(' with ts=99999 (or ~268M tabs at default ts=8), then invoking lisp indent on the following line.

Second unbounded accumulation site for the same finding: the token loop adds attacker-sized character widths (up to 'tabstop' per tab) to the same signed int 'amount' with no range check; after the overflow initiated in the col-walk loop (line 99), these additions continue on a wrapped/negative value and it is cast to colnr_T at each step, compounding the CWE-190 defect.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer line and findmatch() returns a valid position with lnum >= 1 and col within the line; these are enforced outside the given code and are treated as assumptions, but the accumulation defect does not depend on them being false.

'tabstop' can be set up to 99999 and is settable via a modeline in the edited file; if it were fixed at a small value, the trigger would require a ~268 MB line at default ts=8, still not prevented by anything in this code.

Downstream consumers of the returned indent (open_line/set_indent) are outside this snippet; any memory-corruption consequence there is unproven here, so severity is limited to signed-overflow UB with a corrupted indent value.
limitations: parencount can underflow (--parencount at line 159) when a scanned line contains more ')' than '('; the negative value is truthy in the loop condition at line 146 '|| quotecount || parencount'. This affects only the computed indent number (logic), with no memory, lifetime, authz, or availability effect, so it is not treated as a vulnerability.

All pointer reads of the line text (lines 41, 47, 51, 58 before 60, 97, 143) were edge-tested against boundary values (backslash as last byte, quote as last byte, unterminated string) and are NUL-guarded on every path; no out-of-bounds read was found.
The amount == -1 sentinel cannot collide with a computed value on non-overflow paths since get_indent() returns >= 0 and all other assignments derive from 0 or 2.

verdict.summary: The attacker-reachable memory sink in gem_transmit — copying a guest-controlled DMA fragment length into the fixed s->tx_packet buffer via address_space_read(..., p, tx_desc_get_length(desc)) — is guarded on every path by the explicit remaining-space check `tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet)` (break), which is correctly oriented, precedes the only copy, and is edge-safe: length==0 breaks earlier, p only advances by guarded positive lengths and resets to base, so p - base ∈ [0, max], the subtraction cannot underflow, and total_bytes (maintained identically to p - base) stays bounded with minimum 1 at every send. All other sinks — descriptor stack reads sized by gem_get_desc_len, the desc_first DMA write-back bounded by sizeof(desc_first), packet sends, and loop bounds that always advance p or break — are constrained by statements inside this code or by helper bounds that cannot be quoted from it. No candidate with a constructible trigger survives the counterfactual patch test, in which the exact minimal fix for the tx_packet overflow was searched for and found present verbatim.

assumptions: gem_get_desc_len(s, false) <= DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS: the descriptor stack reads `address_space_read(... desc, sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false))` must fit `uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]`. No enforcing statement is present in the given code; if the helper could exceed the array a stack overflow would exist, but no such trigger is constructible from the given code.

gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) equals or under-estimates sizeof(s->tx_packet): the size guard permits a fragment that fills the buffer exactly (length == remaining), which is in-bounds only under this assumption; both the helper and the buffer declaration are outside the given code.

s->num_priority_queues is within the bounds of s->tx_desc_addr[] and fits int; the loop `for (q = s->num_priority_queues - 1; q >= 0; q--)` and the index `s->tx_desc_addr[q]` assume a sane property value not validated in the given code.

address_space_read/write clip or fault safely on out-of-range guest addresses (standard QEMU behavior, outside the given code), so bogus descriptor addresses — including the TBQPH-truncated queue pointer — are not host memory-unsafe.
tx_desc_get_length/buffer/used/last/wrap are pure accessors of desc, and desc is not modified between the size check and the gather read, so the checked length equals the copied length.
Device-model execution is single-threaded per call, so the guest cannot clear used bits or rewrite GEM registers while the descriptor loop runs.
limitations: C2 (stack overflow of desc if gem_get_desc_len exceeded DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS) and C7 (tx_desc_addr[q] OOB if num_priority_queues exceeded the array) could be neither confirmed nor refuted: the enforcing bounds live in helpers/state declarations outside the snippet and are recorded as assumptions, not findings.

C8: after a last descriptor with wrap set, `s->tx_desc_addr[q] = gem_get_tx_queue_base_addr(s, q);` omits the GEM_TBQPH high bits that the bottom-of-loop wrap path merges (`packet_desc_addr = s->regs[GEM_TBQPH]; packet_desc_addr <<= 32;`). Functional/semantic defect in 64-bit mode, but the truncated value is only used as a guest DMA address, which address_space_read handles safely — no host memory-safety effect.

C5: a guest can pre-fill large RAM regions with valid chained TX descriptors, making the while-loop walk a very long but finite monotonic chain doing proportional work per step; guest-induced slowness with progress each iteration, treated as degradation rather than a DoS vulnerability.
C9: zero-length packets cannot be sent because `tx_desc_get_length(desc) == 0` breaks before p/total_bytes advance; every send has total_bytes >= 1.
C6: every use of desc/desc_first is preceded on the same path by an address_space_read that fills it; no uninitialized stack value reaches control flow or output.

C1/C3/C4 dismissed because their guards/invariants are quoted in the given code: the size check `if (tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet))` is present verbatim, on the only path to the copy, and rejects all out-of-range boundary values tested.

verdict.summary: The pixel-conversion setup performs (void) memset(&quantum_bits,0,sizeof(shift)); where quantum_bits is a PixelPacket but the size operand is sizeof(shift) of the distinct, larger LongPixelPacket type (4 x unsigned int = 16 bytes). In the default Q8/Q16 builds sizeof(PixelPacket) is 4 or 8 bytes, so every successfully parsed BMP file triggers an out-of-bounds zero-write of up to 12 bytes past the stack object quantum_bits. The write is unconditional for any BMP passing the header validations (e.g., a 1x1 24-bpp BI_RGB file), and the correctly sized memset is nowhere present in the given code.

evidence.snippet:
(void) memset(&shift,0,sizeof(shift));
    (void) memset(&quantum_bits,0,sizeof(shift));
evidence.reason: Stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): memset is given the size of `shift` (LongPixelPacket, 4 x unsigned int = 16 bytes) while the destination is `quantum_bits` (PixelPacket, 4 x Quantum = 8 bytes at Q16, 4 at Q8). The size operand names the wrong object, so the call writes past the end of the stack-resident quantum_bits by up to 8-12 bytes. Trigger: any attacker-supplied BMP whose header passes the preceding checks (size >= 40, planes == 1, bits_per_pixel in {1,4,8,16,24,32}, compression BI_RGB/BI_BITFIELDS/RLE) reaches this statement unconditionally before the bits_per_pixel switch; no check in the code bounds the memset to sizeof(quantum_bits).

assumptions: Type layout is inferred from usage in the given code: LongPixelPacket fields (shift.red/green/blue/opacity) are compared against 0x80000000UL after <<=, implying unsigned int members (16-byte struct); PixelPacket fields are set via ClampToQuantum/ScaleShortToQuantum into Quantum-sized members, implying 4 x Quantum (8 bytes at Q16, 4 at Q8). If a build uses 32-bit Quantum (Q32/HDRI), the two sizes are equal and no overflow occurs in that build.

DecodeImage, IsValidColormapIndex, AcquireVirtualMemory, AcquireQuantumMemory, SetImageExtent, ReadBlob, SeekBlob, ThrowReaderException, and GetBlobSize are external to the given code; their bounds/overflow-checking behavior cannot be quoted here.
ThrowReaderException is assumed to unwind/return (it is used as the guard on every error path in this code), otherwise many checked paths would be meaningless.
limitations: 1-bpp and 4-bpp row decoders: p advances ceil(columns/8) or ceil(columns/2) bytes per row, never exceeding the allocated bytes_per_line = 4*ceil(columns*bpp/32) at any boundary (equality at columns multiple of 32/16); no overrun found.
32-bpp BI_RGB alpha-detection scan reassigns bytes_per_line=4*(image->columns), which is exactly equal to the allocated line size 4*((columns*32+31)/32) for all columns; reads stay in bounds.

24-bpp case with BI_BITFIELDS would use a smaller formula than the allocation, but compression==3 combined with case 24 is reachable and the recomputed bytes_per_line=4*((columns*24+31)/32) is identical to the allocation formula (4*ceil(3c/4)); no mismatch.

Potential size_t overflow in length=bytes_per_line*rows (~2^33 x 2^31) requires an image of roughly 2^31 x 2^31 pixels, which SetImageExtent and AcquireVirtualMemory would reject before any access; even after wrapping, the ReadBlob count==length check keeps reads consistent. Treated as unreachable.

bmp_info.file_size mismatch only records an exception via ThrowMagickException without aborting (fail-open style), but all subsequent reads are still bounded by the explicit count checks (count != length, count != packet_size*colors, count != 2), so no memory-safety effect was demonstrated.
pixel_info and bmp_colormap are leaked on ThrowReaderException error paths; a resource leak with no attacker-driven exhaustion path, not counted as a vulnerability.

The bitfield mask loops can evaluate a shift count of 32 (e.g., red_mask==1) before the sample > 32U break; shift-by-32 on unsigned int is undefined behavior but benign on common targets; not counted.
If the build uses a Quantum width that makes sizeof(PixelPacket) >= sizeof(LongPixelPacket) (e.g., Q32 non-HDRI), the confirmed memset finding becomes a no-op in that build.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled values (optlen, optval contents, sca_keylength, sca_assoc_id) are guarded inside this setsockopt handler: 'if (optlen <= sizeof(struct sctp_authkey)) return -EINVAL;' rejects undersized options, 'if (authkey->sca_keylength > optlen - sizeof(struct sctp_authkey))' bounds the key length to the optlen-byte allocation on the only path to the sink, 'if (!authkey) return -ENOMEM;' handles allocation failure, and copy_from_user copies exactly the allocated size. The only code-level defect found is a signedness wart: optlen (int) compared against sizeof (unsigned long) lets a negative optlen past the first check, but every negative value widens to a size_t >= 2^31, so kmalloc(optlen) fails and the function returns -ENOMEM before any tainted-length memory access; allocation failure is not attacker-exploitable, so this is a benign robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: struct sctp_authkey is the UAPI layout { sctp_assoc_t sca_assoc_id (s32); __u16 sca_keylength; char sca_key[]; }, giving sizeof == 8 and the flexible key member at offset 6; if the layout differed, sizeof is still >= the key offset, keeping the check conservative.

sctp_auth_set_key() (not shown) consumes auth_key->sca_keylength in the same native units as the check here and reads no more than sca_keylength bytes from auth_key->sca_key; a different interpretation (e.g., byte-swapped) cannot be verified from the given code.
sctp_id2assoc() (not shown) returns NULL or an association belonging to this socket, never an ERR_PTR and never another socket's association.

kmalloc() rejects sizes above KMALLOC_MAX_SIZE by returning NULL, so any optlen whose (size_t) widening exceeds allocatable memory (all negative optlen, and optlen > ~4MB) fails cleanly at 'if (!authkey) return -ENOMEM;'.
The setsockopt layer passes user-supplied optlen unmodified (negative values can reach this handler).
limitations: Signed/unsigned conversion at 'if (optlen <= sizeof(struct sctp_authkey))': a negative optlen (e.g., -1) is widened to a huge unsigned long and bypasses this EINVAL check. Trigger: setsockopt(SCTP_AUTH_KEY) with optlen = -1. Outcome is limited to kmalloc((size_t)-1) returning NULL and 'return -ENOMEM'; no memory access with a bad length is reachable because the copy length always equals the allocation size and the allocation cannot succeed. Recorded as a robustness wart (CWE-195-style conversion), not a security vulnerability.

On a TCP-style socket, a bogus nonzero sca_assoc_id yields asoc == NULL and the UDP-style-only check ('!asoc && authkey->sca_assoc_id && sctp_style(sk, UDP)') does not reject; sctp_auth_set_key is then called with the endpoint, updating the socket owner's own endpoint key. This is a semantics quirk with no cross-user trust-boundary effect.
No memory leak exists in this code: every path after kmalloc passes through 'out: kfree(authkey);' (error branches use 'goto out').

Potential misuse of sca_keylength inside the external callee sctp_auth_set_key (e.g., different byte order or units) cannot be confirmed or excluded from the given snippet; if the callee interpreted the field differently, the check here would be insufficient, but that enforcing/using code is outside the analyzed fragment.

verdict.summary: io_read consumes attacker-controlled SQE-derived data (req, async_data iterator, imported iovecs) but, within the given code, the security-relevant guards are present and quoted: rw_verify_area validates the file/pos/count before the first read on both import paths, the retry loop is bounded by 'while (ret > 0 && ret < io_size)' with io_size strictly shrinking, rw->bytes_done only accumulates provably positive ret values, and iovec is kfree'd or consumed on every visible path. No missing-check, overflow, injection, lifetime, or authz gap could be triggered from data crossing the trust boundary using only statements in this function. Behavior of helpers (io_import_iovec, io_iter_do_read, io_setup_async_rw, kiocb_done) is outside the given code and is recorded as an assumption.

assumptions: io_import_iovec validates the user-supplied iovec array (base pointers, lengths, UIO_MAXIOV count) and returns a well-formed iov_iter; this validation is not visible in the given code.

io_setup_async_rw consumes or frees the passed iovec on its failure path; if it does not, the early 'return ret2' would leak iovec, but that path requires io_alloc_async_data allocation failure, which attacker input cannot force.
kiocb_done correctly handles ret == -EAGAIN (io-wq requeue semantics) reached via the 'goto done' inside the -EAGAIN branch.
iov_iter_count/iov_iter_reexpand/iov_iter_revert maintain the invariant truncated <= originally requested count, so 'iter->count + iter->truncated' cannot overflow size_t.
req->async_data (rw->iter) was built by a prior valid io_setup_async_rw call whose validation is not shown here.
limitations: Candidate 'iovec leak on io_setup_async_rw failure' dismissed: requires kernel allocation failure not inducible by attacker data.

Candidate 'missing rw_verify_area on retry-loop reads' refuted by STEP 5: the initial region verification at 'ret = rw_verify_area(READ, req->file, io_kiocb_ppos(kiocb), io_size);' covers the region, and retries only read a shrinking prefix of it.
Candidate 'signed underflow of io_size' refuted: loop condition 'ret > 0 && ret < io_size' guarantees io_size - ret > 0 before each subtraction.

verdict.summary: uncompressEntry is an archive intake point that trusts attacker-controlled zip data when handling symlinks: the decompressed entry content is passed unvalidated to File::createSymbolicLink (line 47) so a malicious archive can plant a symlink to any absolute path, and the only symlink guard (line 36) inspects just the parent-directory chain, runs after targetFile.deleteFile() (line 32), and never tests the final component — so a following entry writes through the planted link via FileOutputStream (line 52), yielding an arbitrary file write outside the target directory (Zip Slip via symlinks). Additionally, the public-API parameter index is used unchecked in entries.getUnchecked (line 3), giving an out-of-bounds read for out-of-range indices.

evidence.reason: Root cause (CWE-22): originalFilePath is fully attacker-controlled decompressed archive content and is passed directly to File::createSymbolicLink with no confinement check. The only containment guard, `if (! targetFile.isAChildOf (targetDirectory))` (line 16), checks the entry *name* only, never this target. Trigger: a zip entry named "l" with the symbolic-link flag and content "/etc/cron.d/pwn" plants targetDir/l -> /etc/cron.d/pwn; the guard at line 36 cannot block it because the parent chain is targetDirectory itself.

Root cause (CWE-22): the file-write sink follows a final-component symlink. The only symlink guard, `if (followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no && hasSymbolicPart (targetDirectory, targetFile.getParentDirectory()))` (line 36), checks only the parent directory, is skipped when FollowSymlinks::yes, and is ordered after `targetFile.deleteFile()` (line 32); no statement verifies that targetFile itself is not a symlink. Trigger: after the entry from the previous evidence plants dangling link targetDir/l -> /etc/cron.d/pwn, a second entry named "l" passes line 16 lexically, `targetFile.exists()` (line 27) is false for the dangling link, line 36 sees a clean parent (targetDirectory), and this FileOutputStream open resolves through the link, writing attacker content to /etc/cron.d/pwn — an arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory. The directory branch `return targetFile.createDirectory();` (line 20) escapes the same way, running before any symlink check.

evidence.snippet: auto* zei = entries.getUnchecked (index);
evidence.reason: Root cause (CWE-129): the signed int parameter index from the public API (line 1) is used as an array index with no bounds check anywhere in this function — getUnchecked performs none, and no `0 <= index < entries.size()` statement exists. Trigger: any caller of this exported function passing index = -1 or index >= entries.size() makes line 3 read an out-of-bounds entries element, which is then dereferenced at `zei->entry.filename` (lines 6/8), causing an out-of-bounds read/crash (attacker-reachable denial of service).

assumptions: Framework semantics are not shown in this snippet and are treated as assumptions, not quoted guards: JUCE File::getChildFile/isAChildOf perform lexical path checks; File::exists() (stat) follows symlinks and returns false for dangling links; FileOutputStream/open does not use O_NOFOLLOW so it follows symlinks; hasSymbolicPart is assumed to inspect only the directory chain between its two arguments.

Zip entry metadata (filename, isSymbolicLink, fileTime) and entry stream content are attacker-controlled archive data; no statement in this snippet validates them at parse time, and this function is the intake point for that data.
No bound on index and no confinement of symlink targets is enforced by any caller or framework statement visible in the given code.
limitations: Line 57 (`out << *in`) performs an unbounded decompressed write with no size cap — a potential CWE-400 zip-bomb disk-exhaustion concern; deprioritized here in favor of the two more direct defects due to the CWE cap.

Destructive deletion through a symlink-to-directory at line 32 depends on JUCE File::deleteFile internals not shown in this code; it is folded into the primary symlink finding rather than reported separately.
Lines 60-62 apply attacker-chosen file timestamps (zei->entry.fileTime); low security impact, not reported separately.
Escapes that require followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::yes are explicit caller opt-in; the confirmed trigger works with FollowSymlinks::no.

verdict.summary: cdf_read_property_info walks the property ID table with index i bounded only by the attacker-controlled sh_properties field (line 42) and reads CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1) at p + 8*i without ever checking that the table fits between p and e or inside the stream. sh_len (which bounds e - p) and sh_properties are two independent unvalidated uint32s; a section with sh_len = 12 and sh_properties large, placed at the end of the stream, makes the loop read past the end of the sst_tab heap allocation (heap out-of-bounds read, remotely triggerable by a crafted document).

evidence.reason: The sink CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1) reads 4 bytes at p + 8*i. The loop bound 'i < sh.sh_properties' is the only constraint on i, and sh.sh_properties is a raw attacker-supplied uint32 limited only by CDF_PROP_LIMIT (line 30), never cross-checked against the section length or the bytes remaining in the stream. No statement in the function bounds p + 8*sh.sh_properties to e or to the stream, so with sh_len small (e.g. 12) and sh_properties large, i = 1 already reads past e; placed at the end of the stream this is a heap out-of-bounds read. Trigger: crafted CDF section header at stream end with sh_len = 12, sh_properties = 1000.

This is the only extent validation applied to p and e: it verifies p < e and that e lies inside the stream. It never validates that the 8 * sh.sh_properties bytes of the property ID table starting at p fit within [p, e) or within the stream, which is the missing check whose absence makes the read at line 45 (and the offset read performed on its behalf by cdf_get_property_info_pos at p[(i<<1)+1]) out of bounds.

assumptions: Helpers cdf_offset, cdf_check_stream_offset, cdf_get_property_info_pos, cdf_grow_info, cdf_copy_info and macros CDF_GETUINT32/CDF_TOLE4 and constants CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT/CDF_PROP_LIMIT are external to the shown code; their conventional semantics (offset arithmetic without extra scaling, in-stream bounds checks, growable allocation) are assumed, not verified.

cdf_get_property_info_pos receives (p, e, i) and bounds only the position it returns; it cannot validate the index i without itself reading p[(i<<1)+1], which is subject to the same missing bound as the pi_id read at line 45.
sst_tab is assumed to be a heap allocation sized to the actual stream length, so reads past the stream end are out-of-bounds heap reads.
cdf_copy_info is handed e (lines 77, 84, 91) and is assumed to reject &q[o4] + size beyond e; the scalar edge case left = 4 with o4 = 4 (src == e) relies on that unshown check.
A 64-bit size_t is assumed for the o4 + l analysis in the string loop (lines 110-131).
limitations: On 32-bit (ILP32) platforms, 'if (o4 + l > left)' (line 115) wraps when l is near UINT32_MAX (e.g. o4 = 8, l = 0xFFFFFFF8), letting an in-bounds s_buf be paired with s_len ≈ 4 GB, a downstream over-read; on 64-bit the guard is sound because both operands stay below 2^32.
left = CAST(size_t, e - q) (line 46) would wrap to a huge value if cdf_get_property_info_pos ever returned q > e; this can only be prevented inside the unshown helper.

The DPRINTF at lines 122-125 prints s_buf with %s; s_buf is not NUL-terminated (bounded only by s_len = l), which in debug builds is an additional over-read; DPRINTF is presumed compiled out in production.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element frees the top stack entry while it is still referenced at stack->elements[0] (stack->top is left at 1), so a subsequent matching end tag reads the freed entry via wddx_stack_top (use-after-free, attacker-shaped heap reuse, possible heap corruption); additionally the NULL guard before Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data) is restricted to ST_FIELD, so any other entry type with NULL data causes a NULL pointer dereference. Both are reachable with a well-formed WDDX packet using nested/sequential value elements, e.g. <data><string></string><string>x</string></data> or <data><string><number>1</number></string></data>.

evidence.reason: When stack->top == 1, the else branch sets stack->done = 1 but never unlinks the entry: stack->top stays 1 and stack->elements[0] still points at ent1, which is then efree'd. The function's only entry guard is 'if (stack->top == 0) { return; }', and stack->done is never checked, so the next matching end tag (e.g. a second <string>x</string> after an empty <string></string>) reaches wddx_stack_top and reads this freed entry (ent2->type / ent2->data), then dereferences the garbage data pointer — use-after-free / heap corruption. The top>1 branch decrements stack->top first; the top==1 branch does not, which is exactly the off-by-one boundary defect.

This is the UAF sink for the freed entry: after 'stack->top--' makes the freed elements[0] the new top, wddx_stack_top loads it into ent2 and 'ent2->type' / 'ent2->data' read freed memory on the next group end tag. No check of stack->done or of entry liveness exists on this path.

The NULL guard is type-restricted to ST_FIELD, but the code itself proves entries of other types can hold NULL data (the 'if (!ent1->data)' branch exists for those elements). With a NULL-data entry of any other type below a data-bearing element (e.g. <string><number>1</number></string>), the guard is bypassed and 'Z_TYPE_P(ent2->data)' dereferences NULL — attacker-triggerable denial of service via crafted WDDX XML.

assumptions: The start-element handler (php_wddx_push_element) pushes st_entry values for the element names handled here with ent.data = NULL until character data materializes it; this is evidenced within the given code by the non-trivial 'if (!ent1->data)' branch, which would otherwise be dead code.

<wddxPacket>, <header> and <data> do not push stack entries, so the root value completes at stack->top == 1; evidenced by the main branch's 'else { stack->done = 1; }' which marks completion without popping.

The XML parser (expat) invokes this end-element callback for every end tag of a well-formed document and enforces only XML well-formedness, not the WDDX schema, so tag nesting/sequence is attacker-controlled; stack->done does not stop parsing.
limitations: The EL_FIELD branch ('wddx_stack_top(stack, (void **)&ent); efree(ent); stack->top--;') frees the top entry unconditionally, regardless of its type, and without releasing ent->data/ent->varname, leaking the zval; the same leak occurs when ent2->data is a scalar (ent1->data is dropped without zval_ptr_dtor). Both leaks are bounded 1:1 by input size, so no resource-exhaustion amplification was proven.
'Z_STRLEN_P(ent1->data)+1' in the zend_hash_find call overflows only for a ~2GB class-name string; memory exhaustion would precede it, so it is not treated as reachable.

The free of the dangling elements[0] entry by a later wddx_stack_destroy would be a double free, but that destructor is outside the given code; the UAF reported here occurs entirely within this function.
The __wakeup invocation via call_user_function_ex on the reconstructed object is standard PHP unserialize semantics and was not counted as a defect in this function.

verdict.summary: In do_arg_all's second loop, AARGLIST(alist)[i] is indexed with i bounded only by count <= opened_len (a snapshot of ARGCOUNT taken before the loop), never against the live alist->al_ga.ga_len. The code itself states the arglist size may change under autocommands ('ARGCOUNT may change while doing this, because of autocommands'; 'We still have to watch out for its size to be changed'), and the first loop guards the same access with 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len', but the second loop's do_ecmd(alist_name(&AARGLIST(alist)[i]), ...) has no such guard. An autocommand fired by win_split/do_ecmd that shrinks the arglist (ga_len < opened_len) makes the loop read an aentry_T past the live list and dereference stale/freed ae_fname via alist_name(): heap out-of-bounds read / UAF read, attacker-reachable through :all / :tab drop with an arglist and autocommands under external influence.

evidence.snippet:
(void)do_ecmd(0, alist_name(&AARGLIST(alist)[i]), NULL, NULL,
	      ECMD_ONE,
	      ((buf_hide(curwin->w_buffer)
		   || bufIsChanged(curwin->w_buffer)) ? ECMD_HIDE : 0)
					       + ECMD_OLDBUF, curwin);
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: AARGLIST(alist)[i] is indexed with i < count <= opened_len (snapshot of ARGCOUNT), with no check that i < alist->al_ga.ga_len on any path in this loop. The first loop protects the identical access with 'if (i < alist->al_ga.ga_len && (AARGLIST(alist)[i]...'; here that check is absent. If an autocommand triggered by win_split/do_ecmd shrinks the arglist so ga_len <= i < opened_len, this reads an aentry_T out of bounds and alist_name() dereferences the stale/freed ae_fname. Trigger: args a b c, :all, with a BufEnter/FileType autocommand on the first opened file that removes arglist entries.

Origin of the faulty bound: count is clamped to opened_len, the snapshot of ARGCOUNT taken at function entry, while the code's own comment admits ARGCOUNT (the live arglist length) may change during the loop because of autocommands. The subsequent loop bound 'for (i = 0; i < count && !got_int; ++i)' therefore validates the index against a stale length instead of alist->al_ga.ga_len, which is the root-cause improper index validation (CWE-129).

assumptions: AARGLIST(alist) expands to the aentry_T array stored in alist->al_ga.ga_data and ARGCOUNT expands to the current arglist length (curwin->w_alist->al_ga.ga_len); macro definitions live outside the given code.
alist_name() dereferences the aentry_T fields (returning ae_fname or resolving ae_fnum), so the out-of-bounds entry is actually dereferenced, not merely read.

arglist_locked = TRUE is set in this code, but whatever modification commands it blocks is enforced outside the given code; per the code's own comments ('We still have to watch out for its size to be changed', 'ARGCOUNT may change while doing this, because of autocommands') and the presence of the live-length guard 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' in the first loop, arglist size changes during execution are a state this code itself anticipates and must handle.

Shrinking ga_len (e.g., via :argdel from an autocommand) frees removed entries' name strings and decrements ga_len while leaving the array allocation in place, so indices in [ga_len, opened_len) read stale/freed data.
limitations: opened[i] accesses (lines 102, 202) were edge-tested and are in bounds: 'if (ARGCOUNT <= 0) { ... return; }' guarantees opened_len >= 1, 'alloc_clear' zero-initializes, and 'if (count > opened_len || count <= 0) count = opened_len;' bounds the second loop's i to opened_len-1 on every path.
The first loop's AARGLIST(alist)[i] access is correctly guarded by the quoted 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' short-circuit check on the only path to it; dismissed as not vulnerable.
count edge values (0, negative, equal to opened_len, greater than opened_len) are all handled by the clamp at lines 180-181; no off-by-one found.

win_enter(lastwin, FALSE) without a validity check is safe here because the closing loop cannot close the last window ('if (ONE_WINDOW && (first_tabpage->tp_next == NULL || !had_tab)) use_firstwin = TRUE;' leaves it open), and all later window/tab uses are guarded by quoted win_valid/valid_tabpage checks.
No double free, format string, injection, or resource-exhaustion sink was found in this code; autocmd_no_enter/autocmd_no_leave counters are balanced on all exits.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_block_allocate, the bitmap scan loop advances the u32 block offset by PAGE_CACHE_BITS (32768) each iteration, guarded only by `if (offset >= size) break;`. `size` is an unvalidated u32 derived from on-disk HFS+ metadata (total block count), and `offset` likewise comes from on-disk fork/allocation state; this function checks neither. When the scan reaches offset == 0xFFFF8000, `offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS` wraps modulo 2^32 to 0; the break test then evaluates 0 >= size, which is false for any size >= 1, so the scan restarts at bitmap page 0 and repeats forever while holding alloc_file->i_mutex. Concrete trigger: crafted HFS+ image with total blocks size in [0xFFFF8001, 0xFFFFFFFF] and a fully-allocated (all-ones) allocation bitmap whose pages are readable; any allocation request with *max >= 1 then spins the kernel indefinitely (soft lockup / hung task under a mutex) — an attacker-triggerable denial of service. A second, even cheaper trigger is a caller-supplied offset >= 0xFFFF8000, which wraps on the first page advance. Contributing to the same root cause, `((size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)) / 32` wraps for size >= 0xFFFFFFE0, corrupting the last-page `end` bound. All bitmap writes are otherwise correctly bounded by `if (start >= size)` and `len = min(size - start, len);`, so the defect is the integer wraparound / unbounded scan, not an out-of-bounds access.

evidence.reason: Faulty sink: `offset` (u32) is advanced by PAGE_CACHE_BITS each bitmap-page scan. At offset == 0xFFFF8000 the increment wraps to 0 (2^32 boundary), and the sole termination guard `if (offset >= size)` then evaluates 0 >= size, false for any size >= 1, so the `while (1)` scan restarts at page 0 and never exits while holding alloc_file->i_mutex. Trigger: crafted image with on-disk total block count size in [0xFFFF8001, 0xFFFFFFFF] and a fully-allocated (all-ones) readable bitmap (~512MB of pages), or any caller-passed offset >= 0xFFFF8000; any allocation request (*max != 0) then loops forever. No wrap check and no entry validation of size/offset exists anywhere in this function (searched lines 1-29 and 44-72), so the fix ('break/bail when the incremented offset is smaller than before, or reject size > 0xFFFF8000 at entry') is genuinely absent.

Origin of the size-derived faulty arithmetic for the same finding: `size` is an unvalidated u32 entering at line 1 from on-disk volume metadata. `size + 31` wraps for size >= 0xFFFFFFE0, so the masked `end` understates the final page's scan bound; in the trigger range (size >= 0xFFFF8001) the page at offset 0xFFFF8000 is scanned with a truncated end (e.g. size = 0xFFFF8001 gives end = pptr + 1), after which `offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS` wraps at line 58 and the guard at line 59 fails. Root cause: 32-bit wraparound of size/offset-derived values with no bound check at entry.

assumptions: PAGE_CACHE_BITS is assumed to be PAGE_CACHE_SIZE * 8 = 32768 with a power-of-two page size (4096); the constant is not defined in the given code.

`size`, `offset`, and `*max` originate from HFS+ on-disk metadata (volume header total blocks, fork/extent start, requested run length) produced outside this function; no statement in this code validates their ranges, so they are treated as attacker-influenced at this function's entry point.

The alloc_file pages read via read_mapping_page contain attacker-controlled on-disk bitmap data; the infinite-loop trigger requires those pages (up to ~512MB of bitmap) to be present/readable and fully set to 1.
HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks consistency with the bitmap is maintained by code outside this function and cannot be verified here.
limitations: The write-phase error path (read_mapping_page failure at lines 112-117) exits with previously dirtied pages already marked allocated while *max/free_blocks are not updated, corrupting allocation accounting; treated as metadata-integrity robustness, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

`HFSPLUS_SB(sb).free_blocks -= *max` (line 136) can underflow if the on-disk free-block count is inconsistent with the bitmap; that state is not producible from values this function itself receives and constrains, so it is not confirmed here.

Reads of bitmap bits at indices >= size within a mapped page stay in-page, and every bitmap write is bounded by `if (start >= size)` (line 79) and `len = min(size - start, len);` (line 84), so no out-of-bounds write was confirmed.

The write-phase page advance at line 111 has no `offset >= size` check, but it is driven by the clamped len and exits via `if (len < 32) goto last;`; reaching the wrap there requires the same extreme size values and at worst mis-states accounting (same CWE-190 root cause already reported).

verdict.summary: No attacker-triggerable vulnerability found in this code. All bounds/NULL guards on attacker-influenced request fields (additional_tickets index, etype loop, enc_part.kvno derefs, capath index, S4U2Self checksum verification, realm/krbtgt consistency) are present, quotable, and fail closed. Remaining defects (unchecked krb5_make_principal return in the capath branch leading to a possible NULL sp in krb5_unparse_name; unchecked strdup of realms[0]; several bounded memory leaks on error/referral paths) require allocation failure to trigger or have no security effect, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The caller (_kdc_tgs_rep) has already decrypted and validated the presented TGT (ticket/krbtgt match, verify_flags, transited policy) before invoking tgs_build_reply; this function receives tgt already authenticated.

ASN.1 decoders (KDC-REQ-BODY, decode_PA_S4U2Self) enforce field bounds and consistency (b->realm non-NULL, etype.len==0 implies etype.val==NULL, additional_tickets len/val consistency); none of this is enforced in the given code.

_kdc_db_fetch populates *server when returning HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM (the WRONG_REALM branch dereferences server->entry.principal->realm immediately without a NULL check); if it did not, this branch would be a NULL deref, but the contract is external.

External authorization/validation helpers (check_PAC, check_KRB5SignedPath, check_s4u2self, check_constrained_delegation, kdc_check_flags, verify_flags, _kdc_find_etype, _krb5_s4u2self_to_checksumdata, need_referral, hdb_enctype2key/hdb_kvno2keys) correctly enforce PAC/signature/delegation policy; their internals are not in the given code.
krb5_data_free zero-initializes the krb5_data so repeated free on error paths (e.g., krb5_data_free(&rspac) followed by goto out) is a no-op; Heimdal semantics assumed.
config->check_ticket_addresses default and HDB referral-loop behavior (termination of the goto server_lookup loop) are external to this code.
tgs_make_reply takes ownership of spp; auth_data is a non-NULL pointer supplied by the internal caller.
limitations: Unchecked return of krb5_make_principal in the capath referral branch: 'krb5_make_principal(context, &sp, r, KRB5_TGS_NAME, ref_realm, NULL);' is immediately followed by krb5_unparse_name(context, sp, ...) — on failure sp would be NULL. Reachable only via allocation failure (arguments are proven valid earlier: sp was already built and unparsed from the same realm r, and ref_realm is NULL-checked), so it is a crash-only defect not triggerable by attacker input.

'ref_realm = strdup(realms[0]);' in the need_referral branch does not check for NULL (unlike the other two referral branches); failure is allocation-only and a NULL ref_realm merely skips the referral METHOD-DATA block.

Memory leaks with no demonstrated exhaustion path: the server hdb entry is not freed before each 'goto server_lookup' iteration; tpn/tp are overwritten without free if S4U2Self and constrained delegation both execute; spp and the decoded PA_S4U2Self leak on some early-out paths.

A client DB fetch failure for a cross-realm client falls through with client == NULL and continues (logged); this is intentional cross-realm semantics, and downstream PAC/SignedPath checks fail closed.

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans computes the Boyer-Moore skip-loop bound with unchecked signed int products '12 * len' and '11 * len' (lines 26-28). For a valid kwset whose mind (len) is roughly 358-390 million - a single keyword of that size, which no statement in this code rejects - 12*len wraps as int32 to a small positive value that passes 'if (size > 12 * len)', while 11*len wraps negative, so 'ep = text + size - 11 * len' evaluates to text + size + ~115MB. The loop condition 'tp <= ep' then lets the loop body read d1[U(tp[-1])] far past the end of the size-byte text buffer, an out-of-bounds heap read (crash, and matches found in adjacent memory are returned as offsets). No overflow/width guard on len or the products exists on any path.

evidence.reason: Unguarded signed integer overflow (CWE-190) in the guard's own arithmetic: '12 * len' and '11 * len' are int products with no range check on len. Trigger: len = kwset->mind = 380,000,000 and size >= 380,000,000; 12*len wraps to +265,032,704 so 'size > 12 * len' is true, 11*len wraps to -114,967,296 so ep = text + size + 114,967,296 points ~115MB past the buffer, and the loop body reads d1[U(tp[-1])] out of bounds up to ep. A minimal fix (widening the products, e.g. '(size_t) 12 * len', or bounding len) is absent from every path in this code.

evidence.snippet: int len = kwset->mind;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: kwset->mind is derived from the caller-supplied keyword (of arbitrary length; no cap is quotable in this code) and is truncated into the int 'len' with no magnitude check, enabling the int-overflow of '12 * len' / '11 * len' at lines 26-28 that yields the out-of-bounds skip-loop bound.

assumptions: memchr_kwset, bm_delta2_search, and the U() macro are external to the given code; their contracts (memchr_kwset honoring its length argument; bm_delta2_search never leaving tp beyond text+size and always advancing tp on mismatch) cannot be quoted here and are assumed to hold.

The delta table values d1[...] are assumed to lie in [0, len]; this builder invariant is not quotable in the given code. Under it, the skip-loop arithmetic is in-bounds for all len <= INT_MAX/12; if it were violated (e.g. values up to 255 with len < ~209), additional OOB reads in the skip loop would be reachable, but no such violation is demonstrable from this code.
kwset->target is assumed to have at least len readable bytes (mind <= keyword length).
text is assumed non-NULL whenever size >= len >= 2 (guaranteed by the early returns only if the caller passes a consistent buffer).
limitations: The confirmed CWE-190 trigger requires an extreme input: a single fixed keyword of roughly 358-390 MB and a text buffer at least as large; it is reachable through the kwset API / 'grep -F -f patternfile' but impractical in most deployments, hence severity low.
The tail loop's termination on the d == 0 path depends on bm_delta2_search advancing tp on mismatch; if it did not, an infinite loop would result - this cannot be verified from the given code.

Under the stated assumptions, all other sinks (lines 31-46, 53-57, 69-72) were edge-tested (size == len, size == 12*len+1, d == 0, d == ep-tp exactly, one-past-end tp) and found in-bounds; their guards ('while (d <= ep - tp)', 'if (! tp) return -1', 'text + size - tp') are quoted in the analysis.

verdict.summary: get_lisp_indent accumulates display widths into the 32-bit signed int `amount` (and casts it to unsigned colnr_T) while scanning an attacker-authored buffer line, with no overflow bound; a crafted long line (with tab expansion, tab width attacker-settable via modeline) drives `amount` past INT_MAX, causing signed overflow/UB and a bogus (possibly negative) indent returned to callers. All pointer reads past `that` are properly NUL-guarded, so the defect class is integer overflow, not out-of-bounds access.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `amount` is declared `int` (32-bit signed) and accumulates `lbr_chartabsize_adv` widths (up to tabstop-1 per tab) once per iteration of a loop bounded only by `col = pos->col`, the byte offset of a match inside an attacker-controlled line. No statement anywhere bounds `amount` against INT_MAX, and the value is simultaneously cast to unsigned colnr_T. Trigger: crafted file whose matching '('/'[' line is long enough (e.g. ~2.2 MB of tabs with 'tabstop'=999, or ~268 MB at default ts=8) that the accumulated width exceeds INT_MAX, wrapping `amount` negative (UB) and returning a bogus indent; the same unbounded accumulation repeats at the later `amount += lbr_chartabsize...` sites.

Second unbounded accumulation sink for the same CWE-190 finding: inside the keyword-scan loop driven entirely by attacker line text, `amount` (int) gains up to two chartab widths per character with no overflow check, and the already-possibly-negative value is widened via `(colnr_T)amount`; a sufficiently long attacker line overflows the signed accumulator here exactly as in the primary sink.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated buffer for the current line (Vim invariant relied on for every *that / *(that+1) guard).
findmatch() returns positions within the buffer, so pos->lnum >= 1 and pos->col <= line byte length.

'tabstop' (and 'cpoptions', read at vi_lisp) can be attacker-set via a modeline in the opened file; modeline processing is enabled by default in Vim for non-setuid invocations. If 'tabstop' is fixed at 8 by the environment, the trigger instead needs a roughly 268 MB single line — still attacker-constructible but impractical for most threat models, which lowers severity.
lbr_chartabsize/adv return the display width of one character, bounded by the 'tabstop' setting.
limitations: parencount/quotecount (int) can likewise overflow on lines containing more than 2^31 parentheses (~2 GB+ line); recorded as a variant of the same CWE-190 root cause, not a separate finding.

All candidate out-of-bounds reads past the line terminator were dismissed after verifying the quoted short-circuit guards: line 51 `if (*that == '"' && *(that + 1) != NUL)`, line 58 `if (*++that == NUL) break;` before the line-60 `that[1]` read, line 67 `if (*that == NUL) break;` before the for-increment, line 107 `(*that == '(' || *that == '[')` before `lisp_match(that + 1)`, and line 155 `if (*that == '\\' && *(that+1) != NUL)`.

The effect of the overflow within this function alone is undefined behavior and a wrong (possibly negative) return value; whether callers (open_line/set_indent) turn a negative indent into memory corruption cannot be verified from the given code.

Uninitialized `firsttry`, stale-pointer use of findmatch's static result, and lnum underflow were checked and dismissed: `firsttry = amount;` (line 114) precedes all uses, `paren = *pos;` (line 21) copies before the second findmatch, and `while (--curwin->w_cursor.lnum >= pos->lnum)` cannot reach 0.

verdict.summary: do_cmdline() consumes attacker-influenced command/script lines, but every memory sink in this excerpt is guarded by quotable checks: lines_ga indexing is guarded by 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0 && current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' (edge-safe at ga_len==0 and current_line==ga_len); the endwhile/endfor jump validates 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] >= 0' plus WHILE/FOR/ACTIVE flags before reassignment; recursion is capped by 'call_depth >= 200 && call_depth >= p_mfd' with the early return placed before '++call_depth', so no counter imbalance; the cmdline_copy/next_cmdline aliasing after 'VIM_CLEAR(cmdline_copy)' is safe because branch 1 either breaks the loop or reassigns next_cmdline from lines_ga before any dereference. Candidates involving an unbounded current_line at the breakpoint read or cs_idx overflow depend on invariants enforced in do_one_cmd, which is outside the given code and recorded as an assumption rather than a finding.

assumptions: The upper bound on cstack.cs_idx against the fixed-size cs_flags[]/cs_line[]/cs_pending[] arrays (CSTACK_LEN) is enforced inside do_one_cmd(), which is not part of the given code; this excerpt only reads those arrays after 'cstack.cs_idx >= 0' checks.

'maxfuncdepth' (p_mfd) option range and minimum are enforced by option-setting code outside this excerpt; the recursion check here is taken at face value as 'call_depth >= 200 && call_depth >= p_mfd'.

store_loop_line() growing lines_ga.ga_len and get_loop_line()/do_one_cmd() maintaining cmd_loop_cookie.current_line within ga_len are external to this code; within this excerpt no path shrinks ga_len while 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0' ('if (cstack.cs_looplevel == 0)' gates free_cmdlines).
do_one_cmd() returning a next_cmdline pointer strictly inside the cmdline_copy allocation (so the tail STRMOVE fits) is an external contract.
vim_strsave, VIM_CLEAR, ga_init2/ga_clear, and the various getline_equal/func_* helpers behave per Vim semantics (NULL-tolerant frees, strlen-based allocation).
limitations: The breakpoint recompute '... verdict.summary: AutoParallel::Initialize consumes an attacker-supplied parsed GraphDef without validating it. (1) `dequeue_node` is declared uninitialized (`const NodeDef* dequeue_node;`) and is only assigned if the attacker's graph contains a dequeue op in the fetch fan-in; when it does not, `if (dequeue_node)` reads an uninitialized stack value and, if garbage is non-null, `dequeue_node->name()` dereferences a wild pointer (CWE-457). (2) For any node whose attacker-chosen op string matches an entry of apply_gradients_ops, the code indexes the node's input list at a fixed position (2..9) via `input(gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op])` and `mutable_input(...)` without ever checking `input_size()`, so a crafted node (e.g., op "ApplyAdam" with 1 input) causes out-of-bounds repeated-field access and an out-of-bounds string write (CWE-129).

evidence.snippet: const NodeDef* dequeue_node;
evidence.reason: Origin: the pointer is declared with no initializer; the only assignment (line 82) is conditional on IsDequeueOp(*train_node). Trigger: attacker supplies a graph whose training fan-in has no dequeue op, leaving this pointer uninitialized for the subsequent use.

Sink: when no dequeue node was found (attacker-controlled graph contents), `if (dequeue_node)` reads an uninitialized stack value (undefined behavior, attacker-influenced control flow), and if the garbage value is non-null, `dequeue_node->name()` dereferences an invalid pointer. No `= nullptr` initialization or found-flag exists anywhere in the function, so the required precondition (initialized pointer) is unguarded.

Sink: the index gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] is a fixed constant up to 9, but the node's input count is attacker-controlled; no input_size() check exists anywhere in the function. Trigger: a crafted node with op "ApplyAdam" and fewer than 10 inputs (e.g., 0 or exactly 9 for the one-past-limit case) reaches input(9)/mutable_input(9) out of bounds, including an out-of-bounds string assignment through mutable_input at line 70.

assumptions: item (GrapplerItem) is treated as attacker-influenced: this optimizer runs on a parsed/serialized GraphDef supplied by a model author, which is the trust boundary this function is the intake point for.

gradient_pos[apply_gradients_op] (line 67) is verified safe: its keys (lines 50-60) enumerate exactly the same 11 op strings as apply_gradients_ops (lines 27-37), and names enter apply_gradients_nodes_ only under the check `apply_gradients_ops.find(graph_.node(i).op()) != apply_gradients_ops.end()` (lines 41-42).
all_nodes_[apply_gradient_node_name] (lines 62-63) is safe because every such name was inserted at lines 39-40.

For the CWE-129 finding, the concrete memory-safety consequence at lines 67/70 depends on the protobuf repeated-field accessor's release-build behavior (DCHECK bounds compiled out); the missing size validation in this code is independently provable, and at minimum the trigger causes a crash (DoS).
Bodies of AddNodeDivConst, AddNodeDiv, ComputeTransitiveFanin, IsDequeueOp, and GetNumAvailableGPUs are not in the given code; their behavior is assumed, not verified.
limitations: Duplicate node names make all_nodes_.insert silently keep the first entry (std::map key collision, line 39-40); observed but dismissed as logic-only with no memory-safety effect in this function.

The dereference of dequeue_node at line 106 is safe by construction: input_nodes is only populated inside the branch taken after a real assignment, so that path cannot run with an uninitialized dequeue_node.

verdict.summary: In the USB_DT_OTG branch of composite_setup, the handler computes a copy length (otg_desc_len, 5 or 8 bytes) from gadget->otg_caps->otg_rev — a source decoupled from the actual descriptor — and executes memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value) with no check that cdev->configs is non-empty, that config->descriptors/descriptors[0] are non-NULL, or that the descriptor buffer holds otg_desc_len bytes. A USB host sending a standard GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) control request (bRequestType=0x80, wValue=0x0900, wLength=8) on an OTG-capable gadget triggers a NULL dereference or an out-of-bounds heap read whose contents are then queued back to the host (heap info leak / host-triggered kernel DoS).

evidence.snippet:
value = min_t(int, w_length, otg_desc_len);
				memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value);
evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy of otg_desc_len (5 or 8, derived from gadget->otg_caps->otg_rev at lines 118-124, not from the descriptor itself) bytes from config->descriptors[0]. No check anywhere in this code that config->descriptors or config->descriptors[0] is non-NULL or that the pointed-to descriptor is at least otg_desc_len bytes long. A host-sent GET_DESCRIPTOR(OTG) request (wValue=0x0900, wLength=8) causes a NULL dereference when descriptors is NULL, or a 3-byte heap overread when descriptors[0] is a 5-byte usb_otg_descriptor while otg_rev >= 0x0200; the copied data is then returned to the host, leaking heap contents.

Ineffective guard: when cdev->config is NULL (a state the host can force via SET_CONFIGURATION(0)), config is obtained via list_first_entry on cdev->configs; for an empty list list_first_entry returns the list-head container, which is never NULL, so 'if (!config)' cannot reject the empty-list case and memcpy at line 127 proceeds through a bogus config pointer. No list_empty() check exists anywhere in this code.

assumptions: req->buf and os_desc_req->buf are allocated with at least USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ / USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ bytes respectively by framework code not shown here.
sizeof(struct usb_otg_descriptor) = 5 and sizeof(struct usb_otg20_descriptor) = 8 per the USB OTG specification.
gadget_is_otg(gadget) is true when gadget->otg_caps is set; some real UDCs (OTG controllers) set it, making the path reachable.
Helper bodies (config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, device_qual, fill_ext_prop, count_ext_prop, set_config) are not included in the given code and were not audited internally.
Definitions of list_first_entry/test_bit/MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES are kernel-standard and not shown in the given code.
limitations: buf[8] = count truncates the int result of count_ext_compat to u8; cosmetic only, no memory-safety effect.
put_unaligned_le32/le16 and buf[5]/buf[6]/buf[8] writes into the fixed-size os_desc_req->buf are in-bounds even when w_length is small, since the buffer size does not depend on w_length.
test_bit(endp, f->endpoints) with endp in [0,31] stays within the first >=32-bit word of the endpoints array.
Fill paths that depend on helper functions (config_desc, get_string, bos_desc, fill_ext_prop) could not be verified beyond the guards visible here.

verdict.summary: In em28xx_usb_probe, when the dual-tuner second device initialization fails (em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) != 0), control jumps to err_free, which frees only dev and dev->alt_max_pkt_size_isoc and clears only nr in em28xx_devused. dev->dev_next, created by em28xx_duplicate_dev and initialized with kref_init/mutex_init, is never freed, and its devused bit is never cleared. A crafted dual-TS USB device (attacker-controlled descriptors and device responses) can trigger this path repeatedly, leaking kernel memory and permanently consuming em28xx board slots (driver becomes unusable after EM28XX_MAXBOARDS attempts). Root cause: missing cleanup of the duplicated device on the error path (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: Failure of the second-tuner init branches to err_free while dev->dev_next (allocated by em28xx_duplicate_dev, kref_init'd at line 215, mutex_init'd at line 225) is still alive; nothing on this path frees it or clears its em28xx_devused bit. Attacker reaches this branch by presenting a has_dual_ts board's USB IDs and failing the second init.

The cleanup labels free only the primary dev and its alt_max_pkt_size_isoc array and clear only the primary slot nr; there is no statement anywhere in the error paths that frees dev->dev_next, its alt_max_pkt_size_isoc, or clears the devused bit taken for dev->dev_next->devno, so the duplicated device and its driver slot are leaked on every failed dual-TS probe.

assumptions: The USB core validates and allocates intf->altsetting[], per-altsetting endpoint arrays, and udev->config->interface[] with bNumInterfaces entries; these invariants are not enforceable from the given code (no quotable guard) but are produced by the same subsystem that feeds this probe function, so the loop at lines 133-134 is not counted as a vulnerability.

em28xx_check_usb_descriptor, em28xx_init_dev, and em28xx_duplicate_dev are external to the given code; it is assumed em28xx_duplicate_dev allocates dev->dev_next, its alt_max_pkt_size_isoc, and takes a devused bit for dev->dev_next->devno.
card[] is assumed to be the statically sized EM28XX_MAXBOARDS module-parameter array, matching the nr bound quoted at lines 16-23.

usb_set_intfdata(intf, dev) at line 162 is never undone on the post-162 error paths; whether the USB core dereferences interface data after a failed probe (UAF potential) could not be established from the given code, so it is recorded as an assumption rather than a confirmed finding.
It is assumed that a failed em28xx_init_dev(dev->dev_next, ...) does not itself free dev->dev_next; no statement in the given code suggests otherwise.
limitations: The media_device_register() return value (line 281) is ignored and the function returns 0 regardless; robustness/cosmetic issue with no security effect in the given code.

The leak of dev->dev_next is bounded by the number of em28xx_devused slots (EM28XX_MAXBOARDS) if em28xx_duplicate_dev takes a slot bit; impact is primarily denial of service (driver slot exhaustion and memory leak), requiring a physically proximate attacker with a device claiming a dual-TS board's USB IDs.
try_bulk is assigned on all paths before use (lines 170-177 and 234-241); no uninitialized-value defect.
